<meta>This page serves as the frontispiece—the decorative title page—for Athanasius Kircher’s monumental 1650 encyclopedia of music, Musurgia Universalis. It establishes the book’s theme: that music is a divine, mathematical, and universal force connecting the heavens to the earth.</meta>

<insert>From the library of Saint Catherine of Paris</insert> <note>original: "Ex libris Sanctae catharinae parisiensis"</note>

<image-desc>
A highly detailed allegorical copperplate engraving serving as the frontispiece. 
- At the top center, the Eye of Providence is depicted within a triangle, emitting rays of light and surrounded by numerous cherubim heads in the clouds.
- Below this, two large angels fly toward each other, holding a long, unfurled musical scroll featuring a 36-voice canon.
- In the center of the composition, a female personification of Music (or a Muse) sits enthroned upon a celestial globe. She holds a lyre in her left hand and a panpipe (syrinx) in her right. 
- The globe is decorated with zodiac constellations (including Leo, Cancer, Gemini, Taurus, and Aries) and a biblical inscription. 
- A large, ornate banner wraps around the globe, bearing the title of the work and its dedication to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm.
- In the lower-left foreground, a bearded philosopher (traditionally identified as Pythagoras) sits on a stone block inscribed with a grid of numbers representing harmonic proportions. He points a rod toward a cave in the center.
- Inside the cave, three blacksmiths (the Cyclopes) work at an anvil, symbolizing the discovery of musical intervals through the sound of hammers.
- In the lower-right foreground, another female figure sits amidst an array of musical instruments, including a lute, a viol, an organ, and various wind instruments.
- The background depicts a mountainous landscape with a small group of figures dancing in a circle on a plain.
- Signatures of the artists and a handwritten date are present at the bottom edge.
</image-desc>

<summary>This is the title page of Athanasius Kircher's "Musurgia Universalis" (1650), a definitive 17th-century encyclopedia of music theory, acoustics, and the harmony of the universe. It establishes the work's scope as spanning across all major scientific and theological disciplines.</summary>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>The previous page provided the grand title of the work, "Musurgia Universalis," and introduced Athanasius Kircher as the author. This page serves as a detailed "Synopsis" or table of contents, outlining the encyclopedic scope of the ten books that comprise the two volumes of this work.</meta>

# SYNOPSIS
# OF THE UNIVERSAL MUSURGY
# ARRANGED IN TEN BOOKS.
### Of which the first seven are contained in Volume 1, and the remaining three in Volume 2. ###

Book I. *Physiological*, demonstrates the origin, nature, properties, and effects of natural sound.
<note>original: "Physiologicus." In the 17th century, "physiology" referred to the general study of natural phenomena and physics, not just the human body.</note>

Book II. *Philological*, investigates the first institution and propagation of artificial sound, or Music.
<note>original: "Philologicus." This book covers the history and cultural origins of music among ancient peoples.</note>

Book III. *Arithmetical*, teaches the science of harmonic motions through numbers, and a new "Algebraic Music."
<note>Kircher was a pioneer in trying to use mathematical combinations and "algorithms" to explain and even automate musical composition.</note>

Book IV. *Geometrical*, shows through a manifold variety the origin of consonant and dissonant intervals by means of the geometrical, algebraic, and mechanical division of the monochord.
<note>The monochord is an ancient scientific instrument consisting of a single string over a sounding board, used to measure the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note>

Book V. *Organical*, reveals the structure of musical instruments of every kind through new experiments.
<note>original: "Organicus." From the Greek "organon" meaning tool or instrument; it refers here to the physical construction of instruments like organs, lutes, and harps.</note>

Book VI. *Melothetic*, produces a new and demonstrative method for composing songs of every kind; and it contains whatever curious, rare, and secret thing can be desired concerning this business.
<note>original: "Melotheticus." A term Kircher coined from the Greek words for "melody" and "placing/arranging," essentially meaning "The Art of Composition."</note>

Book VII. *Diacritic*, establishes a comparison of ancient music with modern, detects abuses, commends the dignity of Church song, and reveals the method by which the perfection of "pathetic" music may finally be reached.
<note>original: "Diacriticus" (meaning "judging" or "distinguishing") and "patheticæ" (from "pathos," referring to music designed to move the listener's specific emotions or passions).</note>

Book VIII. *Wondrous*, exhibits the new "Musarithmetic" art, by which anyone, even one unskilled in music, can reach a perfect knowledge of composing in a short time; it contains Combinatoric, Poetic, and Rhetorical Music. It adapts "Musarithmetic Polyglossy" to all languages by a new artifice.
<note>"Musarithmetica" was Kircher's invention: a set of tables and sliders (a "composing machine") that allowed non-musicians to write music by following mathematical rules.</note>

Book IX. *Magical*, produces the more hidden secrets of all music; it contains the "physiology" of consonance and dissonance. Furthermore, it teaches the curious and through new experiments: Musico-medical Magic; "Phonocamptics" (or the perfect doctrine of the Echo, how it is measured and how it is constructed); the new manufacture of "Otic" or ear tubes; likewise the structure of Automata (statues and other musical instruments that sound by themselves), as well as "Sympathetic" structures. To these is joined "Musical Cryptology," by which the hidden concepts of the mind are manifested at a distance through sounds.
<note>Kircher uses "Magic" here to mean "Natural Magic"—the use of hidden physical laws to create wonders like echoes, hearing aids, and mechanical robots.</note>

Book X. *Analogical*, exhibits the "ten-stringed harp" of nature, by which it is demonstrated through 10 steps—as if through 10 "Registers" of Nature—that God, in the construction of the three worlds (the Elemental, the Celestial, and the Archetypal), had regard for musical proportions.
<note>original: "Analogicus." This concluding book argues that the entire universe is built like a musical instrument.</note>

Register 1. The symphonies of the Elements, or Elemental Music.
Register 2. The wondrous symphony of the Heavens in their motions, influences, and effects.
Register 3. Of Stones, Plants, and Animals, in the business of Physics, Medicine, and Chemistry.
Register 4. The music of the Microcosm with the Macrocosm—that is, of the lesser world [man] with the greater world [the universe].
Register 5. Exhibits "Sphigmic" music, or the music of the pulse manifesting itself in the veins and arteries.
<note>original: "Sphigmicam," from the Greek "sphygmos," meaning pulse.</note>
Register 6. The Ethical music shining forth in the sensitive and rational appetite.
Register 7. Political, Monarchical, Aristocratic, Democratic, and Economic music.
Register 8. Metaphysical music, or the music of the internal powers compared to the Angels and God.
Register 9. Hierarchical music, or that of the Angels distributed into 9 choirs.
Register 10. Archetypal music, or the harmony of God with all of nature.

*I will sing praise to You upon a ten-stringed harp.*
<note>A reference to Psalm 144:9 (Vulgate Psalm 143:9): "In decachordo Psalterio Psallam tibi."</note>

<summary>This page provides a comprehensive outline of the ten books of Kircher's Musurgia Universalis, moving from the physics of sound to mechanical composition, acoustics, and finally a grand mystical vision of a musical universe.</summary>
<keywords>synopsis, acoustics, musical instruments, composition, musarithmetic, automata, echoes, microcosm, macrocosm, celestial harmony, Athanasius Kircher</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication of the work to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, following his portrait on the previous page. Athanasius Kircher, the author, begins his rhetorical praise by linking musical harmony to political and divine order.</meta>

[Decorative header composed of repeating floral and geometric patterns]

TO THE MOST SERENE PRINCE
**LEOPOLD WILHELM**
**ARCHDUKE OF AUSTRIA**,
Grand Master of the Teutonic Order <note>A Catholic military order founded in the 12th century; by Kircher’s time, it was a prestigious religious and knightly institution.</note>, Governor of the Low Countries
and Burgundy, etc.
My Most Gracious Lord.
**ATHANASIUS KIRCHER**
of the Society of Jesus <note>The Jesuit Order.</note>
prays for your life and happiness.

[Large decorative initial S] The **GREAT ART OF CONSONANCE AND DISSONANCE** <note>original: *Ars Magna Consoni, et Dissoni*. This is the title of the book, which we now commonly call "Musurgia Universalis."</note> presents itself to the most radiant sight of YOUR Serenity, at the very time when your Germany—the parent of the Roman Empire and of great princes—calls back the excessively dissonant customs of the Christian Republic <note>A term used for the collective body of European Christian states, then fractured by the Thirty Years' War.</note> to a tranquil harmony of peace. GOD, NATURE, and POLITICS teach that the consonant cannot exist without the dissonant, nor the dissonant without the consonant. ALMIGHTY GOD, in His most wise moderation of the world, while He distinguishes all things by number, solidifies them by weight, and defines them by measure <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom 11:21: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note>—what else does He fulfill but the office of a Harmonizer <note>original: *Harmostæ*; a term from Greek for a governor or regulator who brings disparate parts into agreement.</note> perfect in every way? Relying on the aid of this [art], the hand of NATURE acting as a midwife, in the hidden fibers of the things entrusted to her, what does she not

<summary>This page contains the formal dedication of the "Ars Magna Consoni et Dissoni" to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm of Austria. Kircher argues that harmony (consonance) and discord (dissonance) are essential, inseparable elements of the divine, natural, and political orders.</summary>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page concludes the formal dedication to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm. It transitions from the theological role of harmony in God's creation to its practical application in politics and the Archduke's personal virtues, ending with a personal tribute from Kircher.</meta>

...does He not accomplish? Finally, in **POLITICS**, in tempering Empires and directing peoples toward the goals of happiness, he employs this [harmony] as his sole mistress and directress; and no wonder: for this alone is the discipline of order, the rule for things, the basis of human actions, and the support of worldly preservation.

YOU, **MOST SERENE PRINCE**, represent these three things through your outstanding deeds and virtues; while we contemplate justice agreeing with clemency, piety with fortitude, and modesty with magnanimity within your breast; for indeed you are entirely harmonious, and an admirable Harmonizer <note>original: *Harmosta*; a Greek-derived term for one who brings disparate parts into agreement or a regulator of order.</note>, who seizes not only the hearts of subjects, but even those of enemies in such a way that those who often dissonate in customs and religion nevertheless resonate with you in affection and will. For you Princes participate in that divine power "to harmonize" <note>original: $\dot{\alpha}\rho\mu\acute{o}\zeta\epsilon\nu$ (*harmozein*)</note> and in the creative force of universal harmony, so that just as God through it brings celestial and earthly things into accord, in no different way do you couple Peoples with Kings, and kingdoms with kingdoms in an admirable treaty, being in a sense the Rivals and Vicars of divinity. 

But if the Socratic Sirens <note>A reference to Plato’s *Republic*, where Sirens sit upon the celestial spheres, their voices creating the "Music of the Spheres."</note> used to chant praises to the supreme Architect with the sound of the celestial orbs, it would be fitting that the mouths of the entire human race should also be opened in praise of good Princes; but, as that man said, it is a kind of the most exquisite music *to sing within*: which excellent Harmonizers do by art, we do by necessity, while we—unequal to the task of commenting upon the most singular merits of YOUR Serenity—celebrate them with a devoted silence. 

I indeed, who like the Egyptian Memnon <note>The "Colossi of Memnon" in Egypt were famous in the ancient world for producing a musical sound when struck by the rays of the rising sun.</note>, have been excited to song more than once by the rays of YOUR munificent Serenity; surely I would be harder than the stone of Memnon itself, if I did not somehow resonate with the perpetual faith of a grateful soul toward YOUR truly royal beneficence. 

Farewell, ornament of the Imperial House, Pillar of Germany, delight of Belgium, Exemplar of Princes, the unique Type of the **Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance**. 

Rome, December 8, 1649.

->A L<-

<summary>Kircher concludes his dedication by praising Archduke Leopold Wilhelm as a living embodiment of harmony, comparing his political leadership to divine order and himself to the singing statue of Memnon awakened by the Archduke's favor.</summary>
<keywords>Leopold Wilhelm, political harmony, Music of the Spheres, Memnon, Jesuit rhetoric, Musurgia Universalis, divine right of kings</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the prose dedication to a poetic tribute by Pompeo Colonna, Prince of Gallicano. It reinforces the themes of the previous page regarding the Archduke's character—specifically how he balances the "warring" duties of state with the "harmony" of the arts. This marks the beginning of the introductory laudatory verses often found in 17th-century treatises.</meta>

->TO THE MOST SERENE<-
->**L E O P O L D**<-
->ARCHDUKE OF AUSTRIA<-
->On the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance<-
<note>original: *l'Arte grande del Consono, e Dissono*. This refers to Kircher’s monumental work, the *Musurgia Universalis*, which explores the science of sound and universal harmony.</note>
->BY FATHER ATHANASIUS KIRCHER<-
->**C A N Z O N E**<-
<note>A *Canzone* is a traditional Italian lyric poem, often used for serious or celebratory subjects.</note>
->BY THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND EXCELLENT LORD<-
->**P O M P E O  C O L O N N A**<-
->PRINCE OF GALLICANO.<-

**S**IGNOR, you who amid the instruments of war,
To make the cares of your scepter feel less heavy,
Turn yourself to listen to sweet voices,
And fill your heart with musical harmonies.

And showing yourself both strong and mild at once,
Your noble breast finding such delights,
You make your subjects recognize in you
A joyful yoke, made of love and fear combined.

It is only right that if, of the musical art,
**ATHANASIUS** now explains the full breadth
To your name, which the world so highly prizes,
He should consecrate the pages of his deep knowledge.

It is not only music that we hear,
But all that is smelled, and all that is touched,
And everything that the mouth ever tastes,
Which we call flavor; and everything we see.

One looks upon a man, a building, a face,
And to some it brings delight, and to others displeasure.
Know, My Lord, that it is a **silent music**,
Which charms one person, and turns another toward hate;

<margin>152</margin>
<margin>S'ac- <note>This is a catchword, indicating the first syllable of the next page.</note></margin>

<summary>This page features a celebratory poem by Prince Pompeo Colonna dedicated to Archduke Leopold, praising him for finding harmony in governance and endorsing Kircher's work. The poem introduces the central Kircherian philosophy that "music" extends beyond sound to encompass all sensory perceptions and the proportions of the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>Archduke Leopold, Athanasius Kircher, Pompeo Colonna, Musurgia Universalis, universal harmony, aesthetics, sensory perception, silent music</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the poem by Pompeo Colonna, Prince of Gallicano. It moves from the general concept of "silent music" mentioned on the previous page to a specific exploration of the theory of the four humors and how individual temperament dictates personal taste in colors, scents, and flavors. This reflects 17th-century medical and philosophical beliefs where harmony was not just an auditory experience, but a biological and cosmic one.</meta>

Whatever provides delight and creates harmony
Accords with the **humors** <note>In the 17th century, health and personality were believed to be governed by four "humors" or bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. A person's "complexion" or temperament depended on the balance of these fluids.</note> of the one who observes it.
But to another it must then cause annoyance,
If it disagrees with their own, and turns them to anger.

From this the common proverb was born,
That only that which seems so to another is beautiful,
And natural beauty is worth little,
If it is not esteemed as such by the eye.

Regarding colors then: one is fond of **Azure**,
And another abhors it, and invites the eye toward **green**;
There is another to whom **purple** is pleasing,
Another disdains it, and is satisfied with **yellow**.

Nature, My Lord, first wove in her womb
Certain principal colors,
In whose likeness she grafted the **four humors**
Into the human creature.

Now, just as these humors, mixed in various ways,
Create infinite forms of different temperaments,
So too those colored forms,
Through new mixtures, acquire new qualities.

And if, among those mixtures that create
A **harmonic proportion**,
The human eye agrees with those colors, it finds harmony;
But if it is not found there, they are held in hatred.

Understand the same regarding smells and flavors;
And in how a scent that brings delight to one
Brings annoyance to another, it leads you to contemplate,
And there you understand a **hidden music**. <note>Kircher's theory suggests that all senses operate on the same mathematical laws of harmony as music. Therefore, a "bad" smell is literally a "dissonant" chord to the nose.</note>

I know a man who, if by chance
He happens to smell a crimson rose,
Runs a near-mortal danger to his life,
Such a **dissonance** is hidden within him there.

If the follower of **Hippocrates** and **Galen**, <note>Hippocrates and Galen were the foundational ancient Greek and Roman physicians whose theories of the "four humors" dominated medical thought until the 19th century.</note>
In their curing understood music:
And through their studies knew how to investigate
The various notes of Nature in full:

They would realize, with less harm to us,
That ills are not removed by opposites,
But they would see over the years those **natural consonances**
That the remedy has with the sickness: <note>The author is advocating for the principle of "sympathy" (like cures like), a theory popular in 17th-century hermetic medicine, which suggests that a medicine should share qualities with the disease to "harmonize" and remove it.</note>

Because it possesses a similar quality,
And thus restores the sick to health.

A body in which poisonous **leprosy** creeps,
Wretched, if it is deprived of all human help;
When a medical hand cannot assist,
Becoming compassionate then, a **serpent** cures it. <note>This refers to the use of "theriac" or viper-based preparations. In folklore and early medicine, it was believed that the flesh of venomous animals could cure the very poisons or "creeping" diseases they represented.</note>

The venom of a **Viper** levels the Viper.
And the **Scorpion** is a remedy for the Scorpion.
And if ever a pestilential season arrives,
A pestilential **Toad** heals the plague.

It is all because that **concordant harmony**,
Which exists between the remedy and the ill, unites them.
From this then, the effect is born
Of drawing away that which is discordant with man.

For what else is health, but **consonance**,
Born from the mixture of one humor with another?
And what else is it that brings distress to the heart,
But discordant and dissolute qualities?

Now you will have seen through all five senses,
If you add **touch** to those already narrated:
That whatever was ever made sensible
Pertains to the **consonant** and the **dissonant**.

<meta>This page transitions from the celebratory musical canons and logogriphs of the previous section to the formal introduction of the treatise. It marks the beginning of the Preface, where Athanasius Kircher explains the intellectual motivation behind the "Musurgia Universalis" as a sequel to his earlier work on optics.</meta>

1

->P R E F A C E I.<-
->TO THE READER.<-

**S**urely if ever, in this undertaking of ours, I have recognized that saying of Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher.</note> to be true:

*Just as wave is pushed by wave,*
*So do various endeavors toss restless minds.*
<note>original: "Velut undâ truditur unda / Sic varia exagitant tumidas molimina mentes." While attributed here to Lucretius, the first line is more famously associated with Ovid.</note>

A <term>lustrum</term><note>A period of five years.</note> is now slipping away, benevolent Reader, since we exhibited to the public light—according to the small measure of our talent—the Work titled **THE GREAT ART of Light and Shadow** <note>Kircher's *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*, published in 1646, dealing with optics and perspective.</note>. In that work, we gathered an innumerable variety of things, encompassing everything that could be related in any way to the Science of Vision: the properties of visible things, and the theory and practical use of shadows. 

When I understood that this Work was received by the Republic of Letters <note>The international community of intellectuals and scholars.</note> with no unfavorable eye, a desire for always preparing new things immediately entered my mind, which was already pregnant with foreign ideas. That is, a most ardent desire invaded me to treat the **Acoustics** <note>original: *Acusticon*. This refers to the science of sound and hearing.</note>—the companion of vision, or the workshop of hearing—with a similar argument and a similar richness and abundance of subject matter. For indeed, once a certain parallel comparison was established, I perceived a remarkable affinity between Light and Shadow and **Harmony** <note>original: *Consonum*, referring to musical consonance or concord.</note> and **Discord** <note>original: *dissonum*, or dissonance.</note>; so much so, that light is nothing other than Harmo... <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "Conson[antia]".</note>

<summary>Athanasius Kircher introduces his new work on music and sound as a companion to his previous book on light, arguing that the principles of optics and acoustics are fundamentally linked.</summary>
<keywords>Athanasius Kircher, Preface, Lucretius, Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae, Acoustics, Optics, Harmony, Dissonance, Republic of Letters</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the first preface of Athanasius Kircher’s "Musurgia Universalis." After establishing his motivation for the work in the previous page, Kircher here provides a roadmap of the first seven books of his massive encyclopedia of music, detailing his systematic approach from anatomy and history to mathematics and composition.</meta>

->PREFACE I.<-

...of the diversity of sounds and the qualities of voices, both in the collision of solid bodies and in the vocal organs of animals, wise nature has brought forth. I sought to understand these as if from an anatomical source. The **First Book** <margin>Book I.</margin> treats all these matters at length, in which we have first explained the exact anatomy of the voices of both humans and animals as ordained by nature.

Since human industry has, over time, refined these kinds of unorganized <note>original: "ἀτάκτους" (ataktous), meaning disordered or out of rank.</note> and disordered sounds, bringing them into order and—according to their composition <note>original: "κατά τὴν σύνθεσιν" (kata tēn synthesin)</note>—distinguishing them into syllables, words, and sentences, the origin of languages and idioms in human society has flowed from this source. Just so, from the qualities of resonant bodies, the intervals of high and low sound and the whole of harmony arose. The **Second Book** <margin>Book II.</margin> pursues all these things in detail; in it, we treat the first origin of artificial Music and poetry, the construction of ancient instruments used by the first men of the world, as well as by the Hebrews and Greeks.

Since I recognized that sounds of this kind could by no means be understood without numbers and proportions, I searched the more hidden recesses of the science of numbers. I have left nothing undone to place before the eyes of the Curious Reader the sources and origins of each, detected and fortified by the irrefutable arguments of demonstrations. This the **Third Book** <margin>Book III.</margin> aptly provides, in which we have treated the various forms of harmonic numbers with the greatest possible diligence.

Furthermore, noting that the science of sound claims for itself a large part of the science of Geometry, and supported by its aid, I have examined the various qualities of resonant bodies in the cutting of strings and chords. I have attempted to assign a reason for each in theoretical Music through various divisions of the monochord. The **Fourth Book** <margin>Book IV.</margin> (which we therefore call the *Monochord*, or *Musical Geometry*) provides this with the greatest variety.

It remained for those things which I had contemplated in various ways according to theory <note>original: "κατά τὴν θεωρίαν" (kata tēn theōrian)</note> in the preceding book to finally be reduced to practice. Thus came forth the **Fifth Book** <margin>Book V.</margin> which exhibits the foundations of the whole of <term>symphoniurgy</term> <note>From the Greek, meaning the "creation of harmony" or polyphonic composition.</note> or <term>melothesia</term> <note>The art of "setting" or composing a melody.</note>, as well as the reasons and methods for arranging intervals, with an innumerable variety of things. In this book, you will find whatever is rare, unusual, hidden, new, or ingenious in the <term>melothetic</term> <note>The practical art of melody construction.</note> art, treated through a manifold abundance of exquisite examples.

As I realized that nothing in the preceding sections was so hidden or abstract that it could not be adapted to instruments, I began the study of **Organic Music**—that is, the construction of instruments. I have exhibited the qualities hidden beneath each proportion, the method for rightly dividing and arranging them, and countless other things, entirely curious, which until now no one (except perhaps for Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath and author of "Harmonie universelle," whose work Kircher both admired and sought to surpass.</note>) has attempted by mechanical means. All these things are shown in the **Sixth Book**. <margin>Book VI.</margin>

Since I saw a great controversy being stirred among musicians regarding the primacy of Ancient versus Modern Music, I established the **Seventh Book**. <margin>Lib. VII.</margin> In it, by a certain parallel comparison, we explain the nature and qualities of both ancient and modern music. We restore **Affective Music** <note>original: "Patheticam Musicam." This refers to music intended to move the "passions" or emotions of the listener, a major goal of Baroque composition.</note> and teach a new method for Chromatic and Enharmonic compositions, previously unseen and unheard of. In a word, we exhibit in this entire book whatever is unusual, rare, and recondite in the whole scope of music—not for beginners, but for the Masters of the art, and those who are most supreme and skilled. Therefore, I trust that all who drink deeply of the rules prescribed in this book will arrive in a short time not only at a perfect knowledge of composing, but also at that more hidden part of Music which, by a certain admirable virtue and nearly divine energy, seizes and moves men into whatever emotions it desires.

TO THE READER. 9

->**TO THE READER.**<-

But truly, lest we should seem to have composed this work only for the sake of musicians; but rather so that we might extend our method—prescribed in the previous three books as a most profound and **Universal Method**—as far as the limits of human genius would permit; hence we have discovered a **Miraculous Musurgy** <note>original: "Musurgiam mirificam"; Kircher's term for a system of automated or mechanical music composition.</note>, which the **Eighth Book** teaches: <margin>Book VIII.</margin> By the aid of the **Art of Combinations**, through the use of <term>musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for mathematical formulas or "algorithms" used to generate musical melodies and harmonies.</note> for dance-movements, we present to the world a new art, and one attempted by no one before me, so far as I know. It is established with such hidden mechanical artistry that anyone, in a very short space of time—no matter how unskilled in music—can arrive at a perfect knowledge of composing. A specimen of this was first demonstrated here in Rome, to the great admiration of all, by **Bernardino Rocci**, the nephew of Cardinal Ciriaco Rocci and a most worthy Prelate endowed with every natural talent; I urge the reader to contemplate his work, which is placed in its proper location in this book. Indeed, so that we might more fruitfully demonstrate the wide-ranging scope of this invention, we have adapted the art to the principal languages of the whole world—namely **Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Arabic, Samaritan, Ethiopian, Armenian, German, Italian, French, Spanish, and Illyrian** <note>A term then used for South Slavic languages like Croatian or Serbian.</note>—using such a method that no nation, no matter how foreign, exists that could not, by relying on the help of this art, produce learned and elegant compositions set in its own idiom.

Lest, however, this invention become "known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers" <note>original: "Lippis et Tonsoribus"; a Latin idiom meaning something has become common, trivial, or low-brow gossip.</note> and lose its value through public use, we have deliberately omitted that more hidden and <note>original: "καθολικωτέραν" (katholikōteran)</note> **more universal** method, which is reserved only for Princes, great men, and friends. Furthermore, there lie hidden beneath these **Musarithms** of ours certain secrets belonging not only to musicians, but also certain concealed and hitherto inaccessible nurseries of the sciences and arts of **Chemistry** <note>In this context, Kircher likely refers to Alchemy or the "spagyric" arts.</note> and more recondite **Medicine**; I have no doubt these will flourish into most abundant fruit in their own time and place. Moreover, on the occasion of this invention, we stumbled upon another much more excellent discovery, by which one may, with equal daring, write letters in any character and language under the Sun, and understand letters written by the same method; but since we reserve these for a particular work, God willing, it suffices to have merely hinted at them here.

Furthermore, as if carried in a chariot far more sublime than that which they say bore **Triptolemus** <note>A figure in Greek myth who traveled the world in a winged chariot to teach the craft of agriculture.</note>, I have been brought through every order and class of natural things; <margin>Book IX.</margin> as I considered more attentively that admirable **marriage of the starry world with the terrestrial**, I found nothing in the innermost recesses of the world’s mass that did not have the principles and elements of its composition from **Consonance and Dissonance**. I have therefore constructed a new **Magic of Consonance and Dissonance**, which the **Ninth Book** presents. In this book, after an investigation into the causes of Consonance and Dissonance, it is shown what efficacy Music has in the work of the physician and in exciting the affections of the soul. The explanations for **prodigious sounds** collected from the histories of all ages are unraveled. <term>Phonocamptics</term> <note>The science of "bent" or reflected sound; the study of echoes.</note>, or the science of the reflected voice—that is, the **Echo**—is drawn out from its deepest foundations in an entire book. The new construction of **Otica tubes** <note>Hearing trumpets or acoustic listening devices.</note> or ear-pieces is indicated; **Echo-architecture** to be practiced in the palaces of Princes is taught; and many other miracles, whether of nature or of art, to be performed through sound are revealed. The construction of **Automatic instruments**, **hydraulic Organs**, and other machines that sound perpetually by themselves are presented, together with **Cryptology**, by which the secret designs of the mind are indicated to those who are absent through sounds in a manifold way. All these things, as I said, the Ninth Book shows, and for that reason we have not inappropriately named it the **Magic of Consonance and Dissonance**.

Since, finally, Music is nothing other than—according to the testimony of **Plato**—<note>original: "τάξιν τῆς φωνῆς εἶναι" (taxin tēs phōnēs einai)</note> "**the order of the voice**"...

<meta>This page continues the Preface of Kircher’s Musurgia Universalis. The previous page introduced his "Miraculous Musurgy" and the application of his combinatorial art to various world languages. This page concludes the preface by detailing the contents of Book Ten—the culmination of his "Universal Harmony"—and acknowledging his royal and noble patrons.</meta>

->PREFACE<-

...that is, to know the sequence and order of all things; furthermore, I contemplated this sensible world as nothing other than a certain brilliant and mystical **ten-stringed instrument** <term>decachordon</term> <note>original: "decachordon"; a reference to a ten-stringed lute or harp, which Kircher uses as a metaphor for the ten categories of being in his philosophical system.</note> across ten categories of being. By this instrument, the most Wise Creator, using a mixture of the **consonant and the dissonant**—that is, through harmonic proportion—produced that wondrous harmony and concord of all things, which all philosophers until now have not been able to admire enough. <margin>Book X.</margin> We have composed the **Tenth Book**, in which, through ten **Symphonisms** <note>Harmonious correspondences or "symphonies" between different levels of reality.</note> of Nature, acting like the **registers** <note>original: "Registra"; Kircher compares the universe to a pipe organ, where "registers" or "stops" control different sets of sounds.</note> of this great world-organ, we have demonstrated the harmonic unity of all things. For you see here, in the mixture of the elements, a certain exact symphony of things forged from the consonant and the dissonant; in the wondrous consensus of the Heavens, a most absolute system of harmonic proportions; in the fabric of the human body, in the political world, the Angelic world, and the Divine, a marvelous order of harmonic proportions, and countless other things which, as I said, the Tenth Book shows most extensively. Not content with this, I have introduced the methods and reasons by which a sagacious philosopher can reach into the inner sanctuaries of the secret arts—Physics, Medicine, Chemistry, Logic, Mathematics, Metaphysics, and Theology—with the aid of harmonic proportions. And this is the **Universal Summa** of our *Musurgia*.

So that this work might reach its desired port with favorable winds, distinguished promoters were not lacking. First and foremost, the most August and Wise Emperor **FERDINAND III**, our most merciful Lord, who, out of the great genius with which he is gifted—a quality truly rare and unusual in such a great Prince—has remarkably promoted this work through both counsel and aid. To him is added the most Serene **Leopold, Archduke of Austria**, who, equally devoted to both **Mars** <note>The god of war.</note> and **Minerva** <note>The goddess of wisdom and the arts.</note>, deservedly put the finishing touches on this work with his generous munificence; we confess ourselves eternally bound to him for the benefit he has bestowed upon all posterity. Among other Princes of the City of Rome, the most excellent Lord **Pompeo Colonna**, Prince of Gabi (commonly called Gallicano), also assisted; he is refined in every kind of literature, and since he believes the nobility of his blood is best adorned by the inheritance of knowledge, he draws everyone into admiration and love of himself for the supreme zeal with which he burns for the promotion of the sciences at all times. How great the variety of knowledge with which his gifted mind is equipped is clearly demonstrated by that learned four-line Ode composed in the Italian language, which we have prefixed to the work. To these efforts of ours were added various aids from the excellent musicians of the City of Rome, by which this work is adorned and will, unless I am mistaken, sufficiently protect its reputation among posterity.

But if, indeed, any **mocking critics** <note>original: "Momi"; references to Momus, the Greek god of satire and mockery.</note> of a more spiteful character should rise up against it, it must be endured with the same spirit with which all those are forced to endure, who, stimulated by a similar effort, keep a generous mind continually raised and intent upon whatever is high and sublime. Therefore, I have always considered it the mark of a base and dejected soul to care greatly about such "nibbles" and petty bites. It is enough for me to have fulfilled, to the best of my modest talent, the commands of the Emperor, the Archduke, and other supreme Princes; as they incited me to this task, so also we trust that under their patronage, we shall remain safe and secure from all the spite of the critics. Finally, if anything worthy of praise should be found in this work, I would wish it to be ascribed solely to Him from whom all things flow: **God, the Giver of All** <note>original Greek: πανταδότη (pantadotē).</note>. Farewell.

# PREFACE II.

### To the Learned Professors of Music.

[C] **Since I have long been** engaged in the constant work of music, and have weighed the vast and far-reaching scope of all music with exact scrutiny, I have wondered greatly that in such an illustrious age no one has emerged who has undertaken to cultivate this most universal faculty from its very foundations, as its dignity deserves. I was even more astonished when, during frequent gatherings among musical friends, I understood that no art is considered more refined at this time, so much so that it seems scarcely anything can be added to it or taken away. 

In order to investigate the truth of such a boastful claim more deeply, I brought the works—not only of common authors but also of the most excellent ones who have earned no small fame for their mastery of musical doctrine—back to the anvil <note>original: "ad incudem reuocans"; a Latin idiom for revising or reworking a piece of writing or art until it is perfect.</note> for re-examination. I took the trouble to evaluate their transposed **melodies** <term>melothesias</term> <note>From the Greek 'melothesia,' referring to the art of musical composition and the setting of text to music.</note> with the greatest zeal. 

Truly, as I investigated each detail more precisely, many things appeared that were mutilated, defective, and clumsy, bound by no consistent rule. These reveal a no small ignorance of their own profession among the said authors (who are, surprisingly, already famous through the publication of their books). Witnesses to this are many printed volumes; if you were to transpose their compositions, you would find nothing applied according to the exact rule <note>original: "amussim"; literally a mason’s level or plumb-line, meaning here a strict standard of correctness.</note> of musical precepts—a fact which several more distinguished musicians have also marveled at. 

Nor is it enough that these works, when performed, delicately tickle the ears of the ignorant with a sweet murmur; for the hidden flaws of the compositions can easily be covered by the industry of skilled **vocal masters** <term>Phonascorum</term> <note>Teachers of singing or conductors who could mask a composer’s errors through clever performance.</note>, and so concealed that the **composers** <term>Symphonetæ</term> <note>Those who compose polyphonic or "symphonic" music.</note> seem to have achieved something great. But whoever partitions these works correctly into a score will find intolerable errors in the harmonic progressions, in the full harmony, in the commonly known rules themselves, in the obligations of fugues, and in the positioning of accidental signs. When I had scented these out, I was nearly ready to abandon the high opinion I had previously held of these otherwise distinguished men. 

Therefore, so that Music might finally attain its perfection, I sought out with most persistent study all modes and methods which seemed in any way to contribute to our great undertaking. I have gathered all of these in **Books V, VI, and VII**, adapting them to theoretical foundations so that I trust curious musicians will find no small help in perfecting themselves in such a noble faculty.

Since, however, this business seemed too heavy to be completed by me alone, distracted as I am by countless other literary subjects, I decided to consult the greatest masters of this time—both those present and those elsewhere—by letter. I did this so that, aided and supported by their work and advice, I might execute the conceived plan with a more secure design. Truly, when I saw the diverse nature of musical styles, and knowing that not everyone is equally eminent and consummate in all areas, I chose those assistants who, having attained distinguished knowledge in this or 그 style, had established a certain fame for themselves. In this way, in the **Ecclesiastical** style—

Marin Mersenne <note>A French polymath and friar (1588–1648) known as the "father of acoustics." Through this gate, those who are admitted may find treasures hitherto unknown, and thus at last be led by the hand to a perfect knowledge of music. But if perhaps a headlong impulse of **self-love** <note>original: "φιλαυτίας" (philautias); Kircher warns against the trap of vanity or narcissism in one's own work.</note> has deceived me, I see nothing else remaining but to find my reward in the attempt itself; and to console myself with that single desire of helping the **Republic of Letters** <note>The international community of intellectuals and scholars in the 17th century.</note> in any way possible. What is imperfect in this work I leave, like scattered seeds, to be cultivated by others of **greater wisdom** <note>original: "vlteriori Minerua," invoking Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note>. If, however, anything perfect and worthy of praise should be found, let them credit it to God, whose honor alone I strive to serve. 

Farewell, and look with favor upon these undertakings.

->Priest of the same Society <note>The Society of Jesus, or the Jesuits.</note><-

->Greetings to the Kind Reader.<-

[Decorative initial M] **I** also considered it part of my duty to briefly meet with you here, Kind Reader, concerning this work of the *Universal Musurgy* <note>original: "Musurgiæ Vniuersalis"</note>, as one who was continually present at the Author’s side from start to finish <note>original: "à capite ad calcem," literally "from head to heel."</note> during its publication. To that end, I was permitted to draw for myself no small amount of understanding and knowledge of the work. I foresee, therefore, that two things will occur to you in this work: some things which you will praise, wonder at, and admire—as they are excellent, rare, curious, new, and hidden—especially regarding the business of Music. You should know that the Author has been exceedingly well-practiced in this field since his earliest youth. Consequently, he began meditating on this work long ago to consult the science of Music (which he noticed was neglected and lying idle in comparison to other disciplines). Finally, under happy auspices, he has made it public—though only after innumerable consultations with various highly skilled masters of the musical art (as I, an eyewitness, can confirm). In this work, moreover, he has revealed to posterity no few singular secrets of Music (which perhaps someone else might have preferred to keep hidden as private secrets), so that he might add spirit and a spur to other musicians to attempt similar things with laudable effort. For this reason, you will also find in this same work some things that are touched upon only briefly or in passing, both so that an opportunity might be granted to others to perfect these matters, and so that the work would not grow to an excessive size. As there is no doubt that all these things will henceforth be of great benefit to the public good, so no one will deny that they are most worthy of praise and commendation.

As for the second point: I suspect there will perhaps be some *Zoili* <note>A "Zoilus" is a traditional term for a harsh, pedantic, or malicious critic, named after the ancient Greek grammarian who criticized Homer.</note> who will attempt to seize upon certain things in this work with a biting tooth. But you, Kind Reader, will easily condemn their cavils and malice, or certainly despise them, if you consider more attentively and weigh in a fair balance the laborious mass of two volumes completed within the space of a single year; the labors and difficulties of the innumerable figures, both in copper <note>Copperplate engravings.</note> and in wood <note>Woodcut illustrations.</note>; the abundance and explanation of most intricate matters; the recesses of deeper Music—known to very few—which were penetrated not without great industry (such as, among other things, those matters regarding the **Chromatic** and **Enharmonic** <term>genera</term> <note>The three "genera" of ancient Greek music were the Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic, involving different tunings and intervals that were a major subject of Renaissance and Baroque theoretical debate.</note> which are handed down with an ingenious and new method); the incredible weariness and troubles of setting musical type; the carelessness of the printers; and finally, the constraints of time. If you weigh these, you will not only temper a more severe judgment, but rather you will strive to easily excuse, protect, and defend through a kind and friendly interpretation whatever might happen to occur that is less polished, erroneous, mutilated, or in any way defective. Indeed, perhaps you will marvel not a little by what means it was possible for such a massive work to rise to such perfection in so little time. And these are the things, Friend Reader, of which I wished you to be briefly advised here. Farewell.

THE great power of Harmony and Discord <note>original: "Consoni, & Dissoni"</note> (that is, that universal Consonance without which the Universe would not hold together) has been reduced to a perfect Art with such industrious genius, such subtlety of doctrine (as is his custom), and such a multiplicity of learning by the Reverend Father Athanasius Kircher of the Society of Jesus, that the Harmony <note>original: "concentum"</note> which mortal intelligence had until now barely perceived through reasoning, the sense of hearing may now plainly perceive; and it is made manifest in the very ears of men. *There are no languages nor speeches where their voices are not heard.* <note>A reference to Psalm 19:3, suggesting that music is a universal language of divine praise.</note> I judge that the world should no longer be deprived of such great delight and utility, so that it may more clearly know those things which tell of the glory of God; and I bear this testimony regarding the release of this Volume to the press (after I diligently examined it according to the charge given to me by the Most Reverend Father Master of the Sacred Palace).
John Baptist Rinalducci, Doctor of Civil and Canon Law <term>I.V.D.: Juris Utriusque Doctor, a degree in both Roman and Church law</term>, of Pesaro.

All things are drawn from the fountain and the innermost recesses of musical science, founded upon the irrefutable reasoning of demonstrations. I can testify that I have neither read anything similar to it, nor found these subjects treated by anyone with a similar order and method in any musical works published until now. Since these things prove the highest skill not only in <term>Theory</term> <note>The mathematical and philosophical study of music.</note> but also in <term>Practice</term> <note>The actual composition and performance of music.</note> in the Author, I judge the Work to be altogether most worthy, indeed necessary, to be brought into public light for the benefit of the Musical World because of its singular and new inventions. Here our Musicians will find much to wonder at and to imitate; and they will finally behold, with admiration, a door opened for themselves to survey the vast treasures of Music.

# UNIVERSAL <term>MUSURGIA</term> <note>original: "Musurgia" - a term coined by Kircher from the Greek for "music-making" or "work of the Muses."</note>

## GREAT ART

### FIRST BOOK: ANATOMICAL
### ON THE NATURE OF SOUND AND VOICE.

[Small decorative ornament]

#### PREFACE.
#### On the excellence and nobility of hearing.

**CONSTITUTING** the universal Idea of the **Art of Consonance and Dissonance** as it shines forth in every individual part of this **worldly fabric** <note>original: "mundanę fabricæ" — a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, divine construction or machine.</note>, it is fitting that I begin its vast dealings there, where its first cradle is set. If, therefore, there were no motion in this visible machine of the world, there would also be no impulse of bodies; and if this impulse ceased, there would be no agitation of the air. If there were no agitation of the air, all things would be immobile and silent, condemned to a perpetual silence utterly repugnant to nature. Therefore, from the motion of bodies comes impulse and the agitation of the air; from the agitation of the air comes the collision of bodies; and finally, from the collision of bodies, various sounds are born according to the condition of the colliding bodies. 

<margin>How sound is made.</margin>

Sound is the unique object of the **acoustic faculty** <note>original: "acusticæ facultatis" — Kircher is one of the early scholars to use "acoustics" in a sense approaching its modern scientific meaning.</note>, or the auditory organ. It has seemed fitting now to speak beforehand of its nobility, excellence, and wonderful uses, so that, having perceived the beauty of these most worthy things, the curious Reader may apply his mind to attaining the knowledge and science of these same things, now to be more fully explained. Meanwhile, you [of the senses]...

A **all**

<meta>This page continues the introductory front matter of Kircher's "Musurgia Universalis." # 2 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

O GOD, giver of all things and of the mind, just as you have granted me hearing, so also graciously grant me the sharpness of mind, so that when the wondrous works of your hands are set before the world, all people may be inflamed with love for your name.

<margin>Nature works sparingly in matters that are not very necessary.</margin>
Nature, which is the Art of God <note>original: "Natura Ars Dei" — a common Renaissance concept viewing the natural world as a divine masterpiece of engineering.</note> and the secondary parent of all things, just as she spends little time and applies little craftsmanship to things intended for less necessary uses, so too she spends a great deal of time and labor on things arranged for the greatest and most numerous uses in this worldly economy. In these, she employs a craftsmanship that is utterly wondrous and most worthy of consideration. Hence, in the proper shaping of man—who is the epitome <note>meaning a "microcosm" or summary of the entire universe</note> of all things—she spends many months of labor and industry. In forming each individual member of the human body, she exhibits such skill as we contemplate with the highest admiration, especially in the construction of the eyes and ears. Therefore, since nature undergoes so much more labor than usual in forming the workshop of hearing—establishing those various windings, tunnels, caverns, cochleae <note>the snail-shaped parts of the inner ear</note>, caves, and hiding places like certain dens and labyrinths—and applies such diligence, it is clearly evident that hearing is most excellent, most useful, and supremely necessary for living well, happily, gloriously, pleasantly, conveniently, and tranquilly. For it provides us with such benefits—to say nothing of other living creatures for the moment—it so adorns and perfects life, so graces us with all disciplines and virtues, and finally confers such a splendid, blessed, pleasant, safe, and convenient way of living, that the entire science of sounds, and whatever is produced in the nature of things by sound and voice, was created for this purpose. 

And as for a splendid life, is not the greatest power for living gloriously placed in the sense of the ears? By this, we are instructed in all knowledge; by this, we are made fit for both giving and receiving counsel; by this, we are properly human. By this alone, we do not merely excite in ourselves all the passions of the mind—gentleness, love, anger, fear, mercy, emulation, joy, shame, sorrow, imprudence, contempt, confidence, indignation, envy, desperation, desire, and almost infinite other emotions represented by the sound of the voice—but we also restrain and moderate them, according to that saying:
*No one is so savage that they cannot become mild,*
*If only they lend a patient ear to cultivation.* <note>original: "Nemo adeò ferus est..." — quoted from the Roman poet Horace, Epistles 1.1.39.</note>

<margin>The wondrous structure of the ears. The excellence of hearing.</margin>

<margin>The will of God is made known to us through hearing.</margin>
Certainly, the will of God can become known to us through no other sense than this, according to the words of Saint Paul: *faith comes from hearing* <note>Romans 10:17</note>. These things are so clear that the Philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> judged that this sense should be titled by no better name than the "sense of discipline" <note>or learning</note>. If we move from these things to the matter of delight, what can be more pleasant or sweeter than this? By this, we relax the mind when it is weary and exhausted by sadness, grief, study, and care, using the sweetest harmony and concord of music. We restore it to wholeness through charming and familiar conversation; by this, we foster the mutual commerce of mortals. With its help, justice thrives, the wicked are corrected, and the good are rewarded. Hence, it was called the "sense of justice" by Stilicho <note>Flavius Stilicho, a high-ranking Roman general</note>, who required "ass's ears" <note>likely an allusion to the need for large, attentive ears or the legend of King Midas, used here to emphasize the need for a judge to hear all sides</note> in a judge for the proper administration of justice. In a word, this sense, joined to its brother, sight, acts upon, perfects, explores, manifests, affects, obstructs, infects, orders, directs, composes, and resolves everything in the nature of things. It governs all (as will be seen in the context of this book). Since this is so, nothing remains but for us to turn our pen to describing the nature of such a noble power with all diligence. This will be done after we first lay down certain things concerning the nature of sound and its object.

<margin>The sense of justice.</margin>

# CHAPTER I.
## On the definition of sound.

**SINCE** every audible thing is the object of hearing, we shall take the beginning of our discussion from it, so that by proceeding in the order of nature, we may more beautifully execute the matter proposed to us. ### Book 1. Anatomical Discourse on the Nature of Sound and Voice: 3

[Aristotle] defines sound to be the motion of that which can be moved by that motion with which those things that rebound from bodies struck against one another are moved. <margin>Sound is defined by Aristotle.</margin> Some define it as: a sensible quality, and the proper object of the sense of hearing, striking the sense. Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a Roman philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the fundamental music theory text of the Middle Ages.</note> says that sound is nothing other than an unbroken percussion of the air reaching all the way to the ears; others define it in other ways.

We define sound <margin>The Author’s Definition.</margin> as being a successive passive quality <note>original: "qualitatem passibilem" — in Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to a property that acts upon the senses and is produced by some change or impact.</note> produced from the trapping and squeezing out <note>original: "elisioneque" — a forceful expulsion or striking out of a substance.</note> of air or water following the collision of sounding bodies, which is fit to move the sense of hearing.

In this matter, it must be noted that three things can be considered in all **accidents** <note>In historical philosophy, an "accident" is a characteristic or quality (like color or sound) that exists within a subject but is not part of its essential essence.</note>, from the knowledge of which their nature is revealed. These are, namely: their **subject**, **genus**, and **cause**. Through these—depending on the different intention and goal of the person defining the term—accidents are defined either by expressing all three, or by the **subject** and **genus** alone (while omitting the cause), or by accepting the **cause** alone without expressing the others. In the first way, knowledge is perfect and absolute; in the two latter ways, it is imperfect and incomplete...

Book I. Anatomical Discourse on the Nature of Sound & Voice. 5

...as we were saying, sound resides not in the object, but in the subject—or, what is the same thing, not in the resonant bodies themselves, but in the <term>intermediate medium</term> <note>original: "intermedio"; the substance, such as air or water, that sits between the source of a sound and the ear.</note>. For this medium, as was said in the preceding sections, contributes to the <term>creation</term> <note>original: "genesim"; literally the "genesis" or birth of the sound.</note> of sound as its material cause. If sound were contained only within the resonant bodies, the sound flowing from them would be in no way hindered by the wind—yet experience teaches us that this is false <note>The author argues that because wind (moving air) can blow sound away or muffle it, the sound must be "living" in the air, not inside the object making the noise.</note>. Again, if sound resided in the sounding bodies, one would either have to deny that sound results from the "shattering" and compression of the intermediate medium, or one would have to claim that this shattered and crushed medium reacts back upon the sounding objects and produces the sound within them. Neither of these would be admitted by any philosopher of sound mind. 

To respond to the arguments proposed at the beginning of this chapter, we say that it is a unique property of sound that it does not cling to a "subject" (a physical home) like other <term>sensible qualities</term> <note>The "five senses" of Aristotelian philosophy: sight, smell, taste, touch, and hearing.</note> such as smell, taste, and color. Those qualities have a fixed and stable existence; they flow from the very makeup of their natural objects and are the means by which we recognize and distinguish them. Sound, however, does not exist except while it is being made, and it does not stay with the substance of the sounding bodies. Therefore, where it is birthed—that is, in the intermediate medium—there it is received as if in a subject. (Even though it reveals its objects—the sounding bodies we say we "hear"—no differently than other sensible qualities do.) This does not apply to other qualities; for example, they only bring the appearance of the things they inhabit into our senses. For instance: if color existed in the medium of sight <note>The air or light through which we see.</note>, we would perceive the appearance of the air, not the object itself. To this we might add that when the sense of taste is corrupted or infected by some other quality hostile to its nature, flavorful things are judged poorly. 

As for the objection raised above—that the same thing cannot be both the medium and the subject—this must only be understood regarding the same parts of a thing. In respect to different parts, it is not at all absurd for the same thing to be both medium and subject. Finally, regarding the third objection—that sound must reside in the sounding bodies because they are called "resonant"—this is to be understood not <term>subjectively</term> but <term>effectively</term> <note>A distinction in logic: a bell is "sounding" because it *effects* (makes) the sound, not because the sound is a permanent physical property *inside* the metal.</note>. That is, bodies that emit sound are called "sounding" not because they are filled with sound, but because they are the things that produce it. For as was already stated, that intermediate thing which we establish as the passive "subject" of sound is nothing other than the air, which contributes to the creation of sound not as an efficient cause, but as a material cause. Thus, our proposition is proven.

### CHAPTER IV.

### Regarding the requirements of the bodies that concur both effectively and subjectively in the creation of sound.

In order that what was said previously may be better clarified here, let us now see what is required in bodies for the perfection and creation of sound. To proceed in an orderly fashion, we say first that the motion of sounding things—by which sound is birthed through the stroke of bodies striking one another—demands above all else, as if by its own right, that these bodies be endowed with the power to "shatter" the intermediate medium very quickly. Only bodies capable of attacking each other with great force possess this faculty; for these alone can tightly compress the medium, and once compressed, drive it forward strongly and rapidly, and aptly break the impulse. 

First, then, bodies of this type are required: those that possess the power to resist each other and to collide with one another at high speed. By reason of strong resistance, one receives the blow of the other forcefully—forcefully, I say, if the percussion itself is joined with physical strength. If you take away this resistance from bodies, they are not suited for the creation of sound, but rather acquire a certain impotence in its production. For example, if two bodies otherwise suited for violent collision are struck together softly and gently or weakly—as when you strike a table with your hand, or clap your hands together without any force, using a mere sliding motion or a gentle touch—no "shattering" occurs in the intermediate medium, and consequently, no sound will be caused.

Second—

6 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Secondly, to produce sound, the speed of the impact must necessarily be joined with the resistance of the bodies. Since this swift motion causes a certain <term>tremor</term> <note>original: "tremorem"; what we would today describe as vibration.</note> in the bodies, as will be explained later, it is rightly the sole foundation of the entire diversity of sounds. Indeed, because of the increase and decrease of this speed, bodies sound sometimes higher and sometimes lower, as will be shown more extensively a little later. This speed depends on the force and velocity of the colliding body. Just as hardness grants bodies the power of resistance, and flatness adapts bodies for percussion, so does swift motion make the resistance more violent. Hence all <term>soft bodies</term> <note>original: "mollia corpora"</note>, such as sponges, wool, needles, and the like, produce an imperceptible sound. Furthermore, just as hard, flat, and swiftly and forcefully moving objects are required for sound in a simple sense; so, not absolutely, but for a better quality of sound, the objects about to produce sound ought to be **smooth, concave, porous, etc.** and situated in a fitting and convenient way. Smooth objects, because of their even surface (by which they are fit to intercept and strike the whole air as one continuous whole), contribute to the intensity, smoothness, and clarity of the sound. Uneven and rough objects, however, because of their peaks and depressions—on account of which they do not crush the air as a whole or as a continuous unit, but break it into small pieces—produce an imperfect, harsh, and diminished sound.

<margin>The cause of harsh and smooth sound</margin> Just as sound is created by the breaking of the <term>intermediate medium</term> <note>Usually the air between the object and the ear.</note>, so a harsh sound arises where the medium is not one, continuous, and equal, but is extended and diminished in parts and fragments, or through frequent inequalities. But where the whole medium is one, continuous, and gathered in a heap, and does not bounce back from them in fragments, a forceful, smooth, and clear sound arises. This is no different than what happens with light: the smoother the surface it falls upon, the greater the illumination it will produce. All of these points are confirmed by various experiences. For there is no other reason why the voice of a choir is heard less clearly when straw is scattered in the <term>orchestra</term> <note>original: "orchestram"; referring here to the floor or performance area of a hall.</note>, except for the inequality of the pavement. The same must be said of a hall decorated with various tapestries; since the sound is, as it were, suffocated in them, it is no wonder that the sound is much duller than if the hall were stripped of them. For the same reason, music in a church filled with people is perceived less clearly and distinctly than in an empty church.

<margin>Concave spaces intensify sound</margin> Furthermore, concave objects, by means of their cavity, produce many strikes through reflection after the first impact. Because the medium enclosed inside, when it is shaken out, is struck back against the concave sides, it contributes greatly to the extension and prolongation of the sound. Also, "air"—that is, bodies participating in much air—have the greatest power for clear, loud, and perfect sound, since they concur not only as the efficient cause, but also as the "matter" for producing sound. This is why bronze and silver are more resonant than lead, not by reason of their solidity or softness, as some think, but for reasons to be revealed in the following sections. Therefore, for sound, strong resistance, push-back, and speed of strikes are required, as well as the hardness, smoothness, concavity, and continuity of the parts of the body; which was the point to be proven, etc.

### CHAPTER V
### On the Various Species of Sound.

<margin>The division of sounds</margin> Having explained the required conditions for sounds, various differences among sounds also follow, which the order of our study requires us to examine. Since sound can be produced in various ways, various species necessarily flow from the various combinations of these ways. There is sound that is long or short; there is high and low; another is direct, and another reflected. One type of sound exists in **act** <note>Aristotelian terms: "in act" means currently happening; "in potential" means having the capacity to happen.</note>, and another in **potential**. The formal and inherent subject of the former is air, water, or fire; of the latter, it is iron, bronze, silver, gold, stones, wood, and other hard and smooth bodies. Furthermore, if we consider the manner in which sounds proceed, one sound arises from the breaking of the air caused by the collision of solid bodies. Another arises from <term>allision</term> <note>Striking against something.</note>, as when air moved by a violent wind is dashed against a solid body; in this way, the lung dashes air against the hard parts of the <term>trachea</term> <note>The windpipe.</note> while breathing. Another is born from "coition" <note>A coming together or closing up.</note>, as happens in the tearing of cloth or paper; for lest a vacuum be created, parts of the air rush together very quickly at the sides of the cloth, and there the first parts, pushed by those behind them, are broken, and thus [sound is made]...

We call those "natural" which are formed by bodies colliding by an innate principle, and these are again of two kinds: some belong to animate bodies, others to inanimate. Just as among humans the variety of faces, gaits, and inclinations is almost infinite, so too the diversity of voices arising from the condition of bodies and the constitution of organs is utterly infinite. Truly, these matters will be treated at length throughout this entire work; therefore, let us move on to other things.

### CHAPTER VI.
### On the proximate and principal cause of sound.

Since sound arises from no other source than the <term>tremor</term> <note>original: "tremore"; what we now call vibration.</note> of colliding bodies, as has been said, it is necessary that countless differences of sounds also be born according to the varying condition of those tremors.

In this chapter, therefore, we shall open the door to the hidden power of sounds and to understanding their utterly paradoxical operations without difficulty; wherefore I advise you to apply yourself with the greatest zeal to understanding it. But to the matter at hand.

Therefore, just as we said in *The Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae"; Kircher's 1646 work on optics and light.</note>, the air is filled with infinite images of things radiating from objects through a medium, so too is it filled with infinite <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciebus"; in early modern physics, "species" were the formal qualities or patterns emitted by an object that allow it to be perceived.</note> of sounds. However, only those present themselves to the hearing which are carried by a sensible motion in a manner proportional to the auditory power. <margin>Sounding species emulate visible species.</margin> Furthermore, just as the nature of things is engaged in perpetual motion, so all things are agitated by perpetual motion. From this perpetual agitation of things, the collision of bodies is born; finally, from that collision, depending on the condition of the sounding bodies, infinite varieties of sounds emerge. I do not speak here only of sounds that always fall within the senses, but of those that would be perceived if hearing were strengthened either by a divine power or by the aid of an acoustic instrument (the construction of which is treated at length in our *Magic of Consonance and Dissonance*).

I say, therefore: first, that the condition of bodies sounding from collision is such that while they sound upon impact, they tremble. I assert that from this tremor comes the breaking of the air, and from this, finally, sound is born. Without this tremor (which is itself a certain kind of impulse), it is impossible for sound to be made. Let no one persuade themselves, however, that this tremor is always sensible <note>Meaning "perceivable by the senses."</note>, as I have said; for since it consists of infinite <term>diadromes</term> <note>original: "diadromis"; an early term for the back-and-forth oscillations or frequency of a vibration.</note>, it deservedly far surpasses all the keenness of the senses. Only experience in certain bodies, in which this tremor falls under the senses, has led us to this knowledge.

Moreover, this tremor is a certain kind of local motion, whether an impulse (as I said) or an impetus, by which <margin>Sound is nothing other than tremor.</margin> a collided body trembles entirely within itself and is shaken by certain minute waves and successions. Every body is capable of this tremor, whether it be solid or liquid, homogeneous or heterogeneous, hard or soft, rough or smooth. Indeed, not only does the body itself tremble, but it similarly causes the air (or the intervening medium) to tremble, so that the air also trembles according to the undulations, successions, or tremors of the collided body. Hence, the more fit bodies are for trembling, the more fit they are for producing sound, and the more resonant they are. The more difficulty they have in trembling, the more muffled the sound they produce will be. All of this is taught to us by visual and sensory experience; for if someone even lightly touches a stretched string, they will immediately see it tremble, animated into sound. Thus, the tremor that the eyes perceive, the hand also feels. In the same way, a bell struck even very lightly with a needle trembles all over, striking the neighboring air with continuous undulations; hence the ringing lasts so long...

### FIRST COROLLARY.
### Concerning the wonderful Deaf Stone in Scotland.

Hector Boethius <note>A 16th-century Scottish historian and philosopher known for his work *Historia Gentis Scotorum*.</note> reports that in Scotland, in a province named Pifa <note>Likely referring to Perth or a specific site described in Boethius's chronicles; the author may be phoneticizing the name.</note>, there is a certain rock called the "Deaf Stone" by the natives, because no matter how great a sound is produced nearby (even if a cannon is fired), those hiding beneath it perceive nothing except a violent agitation of the air. The reason for this can be nothing other than the excessive solidity of that rock, so constituted by nature that it blocks every entrance to the external air—which is necessarily required to produce sound—due to the perfect bonding of its individual parts.

For the same thing happens in sound as in vision through a transparent medium: the purer, clearer, and more refined it is, the further it carries visible forms. But the more vaporous it is, the less suited it will be for seeing. Let us demonstrate the matter by experiment.

### An experiment beautifully demonstrating the difficulty of the matter.

First, if someone takes a sheet of <term>Selenite</term> <note>A transparent variety of the mineral gypsum, often used in early scientific experiments for its glass-like clarity.</note>—commonly called Talc—as thin as possible, and looks through it, he will see everything as clearly as if nothing were placed between the eye and the object. Now double the sheet, and you will see everything clearly, but not as before. Then triple the sheet, and now objects will appear a little more obscure; and so the objects will always be represented more obscurely the more you multiply the sheets, until at last they turn into a body that is entirely opaque, non-transparent, and impenetrable to sight. For vision is obstructed by the multiplication of sheets now degenerating into an opaque body, so that it can no longer reach the object; and yet it is certain that within that whole opaque body, plenty of air lies hidden for carrying visible forms.

By a not dissimilar reasoning, if a board were made of wood, bronze, or any material most suited for producing sound, and inserted into a wall, it is certain that from the opposite side, the sound would be perceived as easily as if nothing were in the way. Now multiply the said board, applied precisely <margin>Observation.</margin> to the first; it is certain that the sound will not emerge as clearly from the opposite side. Triple the board and now you will hear somewhat more dully, and thus, due to the plurality of boards applied precisely to the same spot, you will hear more and more faintly, until the boards reach such a thickness that you can perceive nothing at all, just as was said regarding vision. For although air is more abundant between the boards, because it is incapable of receiving the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the sensory information or "images" of sound.</note> due to the multiple interruptions, nor can it vibrate; hence, as if absorbed and dissipated in the middle, failing entirely in the transport of sound, it can in no way present itself to the power of hearing from the opposite side.

Furthermore, this happens in all thicker masses; for although these have internal air, lying hidden in every tiny and entirely insensible cavity of the whole substance to prevent a vacuum; nevertheless, because it is violently blunted by the encounter with multiple surfaces, it follows that the continuous vibration of the parts is gradually dissipated in the thick medium. Being absorbed, it can by no means be communicated to the deeper parts of the mass. But having been weakened in the medium, it expires, as it were; just as the ripples caused in ponds by throwing a stone: the further they are from the center of motion, the more insensible they always

B become,

...they vanish until they come to nothing. These similarities, expressed through a twofold experiment, demonstrate—as clearly as anything else—the process of sound through solid bodies. For the same reason, a voice carried through the medium of the air eventually perishes in a "uniformly-varying" <note>original: "vniformiter difformiter"; a scholastic term used to describe a constant rate of change or deceleration.</note> manner, not so much from its own nature, but because of the many obstacles and barriers of the intervening air that resist the sounding motion. By these, the sound is gradually and perceptibly weakened until it finally fails altogether. This is no different from what we said regarding the medium of sight: thus, objects far away appear blue, which is a color very close to black. There is no other reason for this than the aforementioned "thickening" of the atmospheric surfaces; since visual forms cannot penetrate them, they degenerate into a shadowy color similar to black. For what white and black are to colors, a sharp, piercing sound and a dull or deep sound are to the final degree of audio.
