### SECOND COROLLARY.
### Experimental.

And from this discourse—which was perhaps longer than it should have been—it is clear enough how sound can both originate within water and be perceived inside when it originates outside. Since water is, as it were, a certain thick air (indeed, it is "potential air," as we taught in Book 3 of *The Magnetic Art* concerning the magnetism of the elements), when two bodies collide violently within it, the sound is carried through the trembling medium just as sight is carried through foggy air, and in this way presents itself to the ears. For immediately after the collision is performed, a <term>waviness</term> <note>original: "vndulatio"; the author is describing sound waves as physical ripples in the water.</note> is perceived in the nearby water; after this, another and then another is noted; and thus the ripples or tremors of the water are carried through the air to the ears.

Multiple experiences have taught me that this is the case, especially among the <margin>An experiment on the ripples of sound in a liquid.</margin> **Maltese Divers.** <note>original: "Vrinatoribus Melitensibus." In the 17th century, "urinatores" were professional divers capable of staying underwater for long periods.</note> These men would submerge themselves to search for "dactyls" <note>The "date mussel" (*Lithophaga lithophaga*), a mollusk that bores into limestone rocks.</note> (this is a type of shellfish that hides deep inside rocks and cannot be obtained unless the stones are split). Being a curious spectator on the scene, I observed that as soon as they struck an underwater rock, look!—immediately at every stroke, the water on the surface would perfectly "ripple," <note>original: "crisparetur"; the term describes fine, hair-like curls or ripples on the surface.</note> just as if it were moved by a light wind. After the agitation of the water, a dull sound would be perceived, and this happened after every strike. This is a most manifest sign that the ripples born from the strikes are continued through the medium of the water all the way to the surface.

I also arranged for them to try similar strikes in the deepest parts, but I could note no ripples on the surface of the water. Therefore, I decided the matter should be investigated more carefully. I ordered that they produce a sound always with equal force: first in the deep, then in the middle, and finally in the space just below the surface. And behold, what I had imagined I finally found to be true: in the deep I observed almost none, in the middle a very notable ripple, and near the surface the greatest ripple of all. From this experience, I finally concluded that ripples in water behave exactly the same way as sounds carried through any thick mass; the collision must be violent for the sound to be perceived outside of it.

From this it is clear why the movement of fish in water (which undoubtedly produces some sound) is not perceived; <margin>Why the movement of fish in water is not perceived.</margin> namely, because a weaker collision causes weak ripples which expire before they emerge to the surface. From this experiment, I also recognized the causes of why the <margin>Why the Strait of Sicily is perpetually rippled.</margin> **Strait of Sicily** <note>The Strait of Messina, known for its powerful currents, famously associated with the myths of Scylla and Charybdis.</note>—even in the most serene and tranquil weather—is nevertheless perpetually rippled and agitated as if by constant winds. For it suffers violent tides and has totally contrary currents, which are carried with such force that they move even the bottom of the sea. I can be an "ear-witness" to this: for while I was exploring the said Strait in the year 1638, I more than once distinctly perceived the crashing of flint stones driven by the tide on the bottom. From their violent collision, it is necessary that ripples also arise; when these reach all the way to the surface, it is no wonder that it is subject to so many ripples, which are greatly increased by the violent collisions and struggles of the opposing waves. It is therefore clear from what has been said...

Book 1. Anatomy of the Nature of Sound & Voice. 11

...having said how sound can be excited within water and be perceptible outside it, and vice-versa; namely, through the tremors or undulations of the water carrying the sound. Since the whole nature of sound consists in undulations of this kind, produced from the interception and striking of air or water (as we stated in the definition) following the crash of colliding bodies. But since these things are discussed throughout this work, I do not wish to dwell on them any longer.

-> D I G R E S S I O N. <-
-> Whether sound can be produced in a vacuum. <-

<margin>Experiment on the vacuum.</margin>
Before this difficulty is decided, it must first be determined whether a vacuum, truly and properly so-called, can be assigned in the nature of things. Certainly, there have not been lacking in these times those who, relying on I know not what experiments, have not only asserted that it must be altogether admitted, but have also busied themselves with drawing and compelling others, even against their will, to their opinion. I present an experiment, whose invention—although I am not unaware that others claim it for themselves more ambitiously—is certainly clear to me to have been first detected by Torricelli <note>Evangelista Torricelli (1608–1647), a student of Galileo who invented the barometer.</note>, the noble mathematician of the Grand Duke of Tuscany. Later, four years ago, the Most Serene Cardinal Giovanni Carlo de' Medici deigned to show it to me first of all here in Rome, out of his singular benevolence toward me.

A glass tube HN, closed at one end H, is filled with <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury; called "quicksilver" or "liquid silver" (argentum vivum) in the original Latin.</note> through the open orifice N, and being held upright is immersed in a basin or some vessel OP also filled with some quicksilver, with water additionally poured over it; then the orifice N is closed with a finger, lest the mercury slip out when the tube is inverted. Thus, with the tube immersed within the mercury contained in the vessel, as soon as you remove your finger from the opening of the tube, behold! the mercury contained in the tube immediately descends with the reins loosened, then ascends a little, then again descends and ascends a little, but always less, until by repeated oscillations of this kind, it finally comes to rest in the lower part of the tube, leaving the upper part of the tube without a succeeding body, as they would have it. From this they argue that the space RH in the upper part of the tube is truly and properly a vacuum, since it is impossible for another body to have been substituted in the place of the departing mercury in the meantime. 

<margin>Opinion on the vacuum is dangerous to the faith.</margin>
From this, like insolent and troublesome boasters singing a triumph before the victory, they have babbled many things indeed, not only repugnant to the principles of natural things, but even dangerous to the orthodox faith; as they imprudently boast that they can demonstrate by this most subtle experiment that a "placed thing" can exist without a "place," and <term>accidents</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are qualities like color or weight that cannot exist without a "subject" or physical substance to hold them. This was a sensitive topic because it related to the theology of the Eucharist.</note> can naturally subsist without a subject. 

<margin>Various opinions on the vacuum.</margin>
Other philosophers of better repute, who laugh at this kind of fantastic vacuum, explain that vacuum remaining in the tube in various ways. Some assert that it is not indeed a vacuum, but nonetheless neither does air stay there; but a certain most subtle body, very nearly resembling light, which they call <term>aether</term>, which, since it is diffused through all the bodies of the world, penetrates the innermost pores of everything, and therefore intimately coexists with the mercury enclosed in the tube, so that it is no wonder if, as the mercury recedes, the aether remains in place of the air, etc. Some think that the air from outside...

The mercury level has dropped to R, creating a space (RH) at the top of the tube. Letters C, D, E, F, G, I, K, L, M mark various points of the apparatus.]

...itself, in order to supply the necessities of struggling nature, or even penetrate the very pores of the glass. There are those who think that air does not enter through the pores, but rather between the sides of the tube and the <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "mercurij"</note> through the outermost surface; they say that the mercury does not grip the sides of the tube so tightly that some air cannot always substitute itself into the place of the departing mercury, entering from the outside around the cylindrical boundaries of the tube and the mercury, especially in a time when nature is struggling. Certain others, philosophizing more freely, think that the mercury is held within the tube at a certain space by some external balancing force I know not what. Finally, some think that the parts of the tube abandoned by the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento viuo," literally 'living silver'</note> are refilled by a thin substance or spirit exhaling from the mercury itself; they believe that while the weight of the adhering mercury cannot bear further distension, and while no other body can succeed it, the mercury is violently sustained under such and such a measure and proportion, and consequently at such and such an elevation within the tube. And these are the opinions explaining the reason for that space which certain Moderns <note>original: "Neoterici," referring to contemporary 17th-century scientists like Torricelli and Pascal.</note> asserted to be a pure vacuum; of these opinions, the last one deservedly holds the first place among those that are probable. 

<margin>A beautiful experiment against the existence of a vacuum.</margin>
For it is certain that a vacuum can by no means exist there, since a most manifest sound is perceived within it: something which many years ago I tested here in Rome together with Gaspare Berti <note>Gaspare Berti (c. 1600–1643) was an Italian mathematician who performed this famous water-barometer experiment around 1640, which preceded Torricelli's work with mercury.</note>, a most ingenious mathematician. He ordered a lead pipe one hundred feet long and the thickness of a finger to be prepared, upon the upper end of which he placed a glass phial of remarkable thickness, specifically blown for this purpose and joined to the neck of the tube with such industry and fortified with such skill that every entrance for air was closed off. Inside the phial, at my suggestion, he inserted a small bell together with a little hammer with such dexterity that the iron hammer, attracted and raised by a magnet from the outside, would soon be freed from the magnet and produce the sound of that bell by its own weight.

When everything required for the experiment was thus prepared, he filled the entire tube of the phial with water and, having closed the orifice at the other end with a <term>stopcock</term> <note>original: "epistomio"</note>, immersed it in a tub full of water. This being done, once the stopcock was opened, the water descending within the lead tube did not discharge itself entirely, but stopped at about ten feet <note>The maximum height a column of water can be supported by atmospheric pressure is roughly 34 feet (10.3 meters); Kircher's "ten feet" likely refers to the "ten paces" or "ten cubits" often cited in early hydraulics, or perhaps a measurement quirk of this specific setup.</note> within the tube, not unlike what was said a little while ago regarding the quicksilver enclosed within a glass tube. Whereupon most of the spectators of this so wonderful experiment attempted to infer that the space abandoned by the water was necessarily a vacuum, since no other body could have been substituted there. But we, in order to demonstrate the falsehood of their opinion by the very experience of the ear, applied a magnet we had grabbed to the outside of the glass phial directly opposite the iron hammer; it soon raised the attracted hammer, and when the magnet was pulled away, the hammer produced a very clear sound from that bell by its own weight. From this, certain people of more stubborn brain who were present immediately inferred that sound could be made in a vacuum; but most of the more sensible ones learned from this so manifest experiment that a vacuum can by no means exist where such manifest signs of air are exhibited in sound. And by this single experiment, all were convinced and abjured the opinion of the vacuum for the future. We wished to include a figure here for the better information of the curious reader. The lead tube was **D E F G**; the glass phial joined to the tube **D E**; inside which was the bell **C** attached by an iron wire, and the hammer **O**; the stopcock **G**; the tub full of water **M I K L**; the magnet applied from the outside **A**. The rest was done as described a little before.

<margin>How air enters an inaccessible place.</margin>
The nullity of the vacuum is thus very clearly evident from what has been said. But by what means, or through what hidden ways, the air substitutes itself into the place of the departing water—if anyone should ask me, I will satisfy him only if he first explains to me by what means a magnet penetrates glass and other very hard bodies, or how light penetrates the most solid crystal. For the paths of struggling nature are so secret, so hidden, that they can by no means be grasped by human wit. 

<margin>Nature is ingenious in necessity.</margin>
Nature is so ingenious in a time of necessity that she seems to elude every scrutiny of the human intellect; yet experience makes it certain that air entered there, though how and from where remains hidden. Thus, they philosophize foolishly who, while they conceive of a thing not at all, pronounce more thoughtlessly upon the nature of things.

<margin>Sound can by no means be made in a vacuum.</margin>
We conclude, therefore, that even if a vacuum were possible in the nature of things, sound could nonetheless by no means occur in it. For since sound is an affection of the air—indeed, air is the material cause of sound—when air is lacking, sound must also necessarily be lacking; and on the contrary...

### Designations of the individual parts of the external ear.

<margin>See figures 1 and 2 in Diagram 1.</margin>

**A A A.** The wings or feathers <note>original: "Alæ seu pinnæ"</note> which the Greeks call *pterygoma*; the expanded, broad part reflected from the shell <note>concha</note> toward the temples is called the *pterygion* by others, or the "little feather."

**BBB.** The entire circuit or exterior circumference of the ear, called the *helix* by the Greeks and Latins. It is also called the "tendril" <note>original: "capreolus"</note> by others.

**CCC.** The interior circumference surrounding the shell is called the *antihelix*, as if it were a Helix placed opposite.

**DDD.** The surface extended from the front to the back is called *kyrtoides*, that is, gibbous or bulging.

**E.** Called the *antibole*; it is the boundary or extremity of the helix.

**F.** The *scaphos*, meaning a "skiff" or "boat" <note>original: "Linter siue scapha"</note>, is the small hollow of the little feather.

**GGG.** The cavity opening in the middle of the auricle is called the *concha* (shell); it is also called the *akanos* by Pollux.

**H.** The superior part of the Shell.

**I.** The *prostan* or the floor of the Shell.

**K.** The fold before or next to the opening, where the auricle sits and which is arranged for the drainage of fluids and wax; it is called the *ekchytiskos*.

**L.** The opening itself is the *acoustic pore* or auditory passage <note>original: "meatus auditorius"</note>; it is also called the *kypsela* or the beehive.

**M.** The part that rises from the edge of the temple above the auditory opening is called the *tragus* or the "he-goat" <note>original: "hircus." Named so because of the hair that often grows there, resembling a goat's beard.</note>.

**N.** However, that which is opposite the tragus is called the *antitragus*, which is the end of the antihelix.

**O.** The semi-circle formed by the tragus and antitragus is called the *xysterion*.

**P.** The lower part of the lobe, hanging free from the jaw, is called the *prolobion*, that is, the anterior lobe.

### The structure of the internal ear and the arrangement of its parts.

<margin>Parts of the internal ear. 1. The 4 passages of the ears.</margin>

I shall not speak in this place of all the parts constituting the internal ear, but only of those which nature has placed there for the purpose of forming sound. These are, first, the ducts or passages or paths; second, the Eardrum <note>original: "Tympanum"</note> with its bony circle, three caverns, and three tiny bones.

There are four passages or ducts of the ears. The first is like the "royal road" and principal path, which we just called the auditory passage; in children this is entirely cartilaginous, in adults it is bony-cartilaginous, and finally in the elderly it is entirely bony. The second occurs in the internal space of the skull on the back side of the <term>petrous process</term> <note>The "stony" part of the temporal bone which protects the inner ear.</note>, in which it is carved. From there it proceeds obliquely outward for some distance to the middle seat of this process, where it is separated from the two interior cavities of the true ear only by a thin scale. The third, very similar to a round canal and like the beginning of a thin reed <note>original: "tenuioris calami"</note>, is led from the exterior shell of the stony process's cavity; from where, proceeding obliquely in the middle of four...

The <term>acoustic drum</term> <note>original: "Tympanum acusticũ"</note> is called the auditory membrane, either because this membrane is stretched over the shell in the manner of a war drum, or because—just as the membrane of a wooden military or war drum is struck—this is struck and beaten by the air and sound. It is called by others the <term>Myrinx</term> <note>original: "Myrinx," a Greek term for a membrane</note>, because it separates the inner air from the outer: See Diagram 1. This membrane is the most delicate and thinnest of all membranes, indeed very much like a spider's web, yet endowed with a moderate density; it is clear and transparent, like a kind of mirror, possessing no roughness, but smoothed everywhere inside and out, though not equal or flat. For on the inside, the process of the small bone resembling a hammer—marked as A, as shown in Figure 3—stretches across like a reflected tail at C, from the circumference itself from the top downwards to its very middle and center at C, just as a string is stretched across a military drum; it is connected and born unto a bony circle, to which it is bound and stretched by tendons and muscles, not unlike how the skins of drums are usually stretched tightly with cords. <margin>The eardrum.</margin> <margin>The little hammer bone.</margin>

Furthermore, the <term>petrous bone</term> <note>original: "os petrosum," the exceptionally hard, "stony" part of the temporal bone</note> consists of three small caverns or dens. The first is that little cavern which <term>Vesalius</term> <note>Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), a foundational figure in modern human anatomy</note> calls the <term>pelvis</term> <note>original: "peluim," referring to a basin</note>, because it is hollowed out in the manner of a basin; others call it the <term>cochlea</term> <note>original: "cochleam," meaning snail-shell</note> or the den. It is compared to a hollow drum because, just as the common air struck in a drum produces its own sound, so they think the implanted air, struck by the eardrum and the small bones, expresses the differences of sounds within it, which are then carried to the auditory nerve. <margin>The petrous bone consists of 3 caverns.</margin> <margin>The cavern called the Pelvis.</margin> The second cavern, because of the tunnels of which it consists, is called the <term>labyrinth</term> or the mine. <margin>The cavern called the labyrinth.</margin> The third is named after a <term>buccina</term> <note>a curved Roman horn</note>, the curved and twisted horn with which shepherds are accustomed to call their flock, or after the appearance of a conch shell; hence Vesalius calls that the <term>buccinous den</term> <note>original: "antrum bucinosum," or trumpet-like cavern</note>. <margin>The buccinous den.</margin> But since it is difficult to represent these anatomically, as they have established their seat hidden in the innermost reaches of the organ, I have therefore intentionally decided to omit the figure.

Furthermore, as was said at the beginning, the internal ear consists of three small bones, smallest indeed in quantity, but greatest in shape and use; the composition and operation of these is so ingenious and elegant that it can hardly be explained in words. They are hard and solid both in newborn infants, as <term>Casserius</term> <note>Giulio Casserio (1552–1616), an Italian anatomist noted for his work on the sense organs</note> observed, and in adults, even though all other things vary continually according to the stage of age. However, in children they are much more flaccid than in adults due to a moist stickiness, which is why infants hear more dully than adults. The small bones are mobile and arranged with such natural ingenuity that when one is pulled, the other two are moved consequently. They are not continuous but distinct, as will appear shortly in the anatomy, situated in the outer region of the shell. The names of the three small bones are the <term>Hammer</term>, the <term>Anvil</term>, and the <term>Stirrup</term> <note>original: "Malleus, Incus, & Stapes"</note>, which found their names from their shape rather than their use. <margin>Three small bones.</margin> <margin>The Hammer, Anvil, and Stirrup.</margin> The Hammer is so called because, like a hammer, it lies and rests upon the anvil; just as it is called the Anvil because it receives the hammer like an anvil; the Stirrup is so called from the shape of a stirrup. These small bones are not found in all animals; for in some only the hammer and anvil are found, in some only the anvil and stirrup, and in some, such as monkeys, none at all. But the following anatomy will declare these things better than many windings of words.

But having seen the anatomy of the individual parts of the acoustic organ, nothing remains but for us to now explain the functions of each.

# CHAPTER VIII.
## On the functions of the individual parts of the acoustic organ.

<margin>The wonderful construction of the ears.</margin>

[Large initial V] Just as that admirable majesty of nature is evident in all things, so too in the construction of the ears it is most worthy of admiration; so that the curious reader may understand it, we shall take the beginning of our dissertation from its functions and uses. It is established, therefore, that the ear is not constituted from one simple and uniform part, nor from many parts mixed or confused together; rather, it is an aggregate of many parts existing separately and distinctly, so that it might be most fit for performing its function. For since the perception of sound had to be entrusted to a nerve, its substance did not permit it to be extended outside the head, on account of the many dangers into which the organ could fall. <margin>The utility and purpose of the individual parts of the organ of hearing.</margin> Therefore, it was necessary to interpose something between the nerve and the internal air, through which sound could be conveyed to the nerve. Furthermore, lest the air—sometimes cold, sometimes hot, or sometimes affected by some other harmful quality—should enter and bring harm to the internal medium and the nerve, it was necessary for the ear to have cavities; these are indeed closed to the external air, yet open to the <term>species of sound</term> <note>In 17th-century science, "species" referred to the sensible form or likeness of an object (like a sound wave) traveling through a medium</note>. For the sake of this, the small bones, muscles, and ligaments had to be created. 

Furthermore, if we look at its location, nature could not have assigned a more convenient or opportune place for the ear; situated near the mouth (the gateway for food and drink) and the workshop of speech, it has obtained a place equal in dignity. The ear is doubled so that if one is damaged, the entire sense does not perish. It is wide open so that it is always ready, and so that we might be awakened even in sleep when necessity arises. It is shaped in the manner of a <term>cochlea</term> <note>a snail shell</note>, so that the species of sound, united there, might present themselves more strongly to the sense by being multiplied through various reflections of the caverns. For this same reason, nature expanded the ear outward like a shell-shaped winnowing fan, so that the species of sound, gathered in this way, might strengthen the hearing. Hence, those who are hard of hearing curve their hand over their ears to hear better; for the sound, collected and multiplied there, flows more strongly into the organ. Yet, lest a more vehement sound bring some harm to the organ, nature...

# CHAPTER IX.
## On the nature of internal air, and where exactly hearing occurs; and whether it is propagated through a real or a notional being.

<margin>What is internal air?</margin>
That air is enclosed within the cavities of the petrous bone <term>petrous bone</term> <note>The hard, dense portion of the temporal bone that houses the delicate structures of the inner ear.</note> no one can deny, except perhaps someone who would admit the existence of a vacuum in the nature of things <note>The author refers to the traditional Aristotelian belief that "nature abhors a vacuum," meaning every space must be filled with some form of matter.</note>. This doubt alone might be raised: How is it present there? Is it distinct from the external air? What is its function? And how is it preserved? To free myself briefly from these questions: I say that this air was implanted within the ears themselves from the very beginning; hence the Philosophers call it "congenital," "implanted," and "built-in" <note>original: "congenitum, complantatum & inædificatum"</note>. It is no less a medium for producing sound than the external air; it is most pure, devoid of all sound, quiet and immobile, and finally, it is abundant and plentiful. Furthermore, we assert that this is not the same as the external air. For just as the air from without...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the propagation of sound, moving from the internal air of the ear to the philosophical debate over whether sound travels as a physical substance or a sensory "image." **Book 1. Anatomy of the Nature of Sound & Voice. 19**

...to be propagated, as some wish; some argue it travels only according to its notional being <note>original: "esse notionale" — a philosophical term meaning the thing exists as a concept or representation in the mind rather than a physical object.</note>; others assert it is propagated partly according to its real being and partly according to its notional being. We, holding the middle path, assert that sound is propagated through species <term>species</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "species" are the "forms" or "sensory images" of an object that travel through a medium to reach the senses, allowing us to perceive something without the physical object entering our body.</note>, as this is more agreeable to reason, since the propagation of sound in all things emulates the flow of visible species (if you except successive motion). For since visible species are ordered for the purpose of presenting a material object—which would otherwise be disproportionate to the power of the sense—through themselves as if through proxies of the object, certainly for the same reason audible species seem to have been instituted: namely, to carry the object of sounds to the power of hearing through expressed species of sound. 

Yet I do not doubt that sound is also carried and propagated to some extent according to its real and physical being, since sound takes its greatest strength from the continuous agitation of the air, as it is something without which it could not be propagated in any way, neither according to its real nor its notional being. Nor can it be proven by any reason that this quality of sounds diffuses its entire physical self into every part; nor is that necessary, since for their perception it is enough that species are emitted from them to the workshops of the senses—lest that which can be done by few means be done by many in vain, as the Philosopher <note>A traditional reference to Aristotle.</note> testifies.

But you will say: light diffuses itself into the medium according to its real being, therefore so does sound. I respond: the nature of sound is not the same as light in all respects; for the diffusion of light is instantaneous, whereas that of sound is <margin>The difference between the propagation of light and the propagation of sound.</margin> successive <note>Meaning sound takes time to travel from one point to another, whereas light was thought to be instant.</note>; luminous rays depend essentially on that from which they flow; but sound can exist even when that from which the sound flows no longer exists, as will be discussed in *Echologia* or *Phonocamptica* <note>The study of echoes and the reflection of sound.</note>. Sound and sight also differ in their radiation; the latter propagates its species in a straight motion, the former in a promiscuous <note>In this context, "promiscuous" means "spreading in all directions" or "mixed."</note> motion. For just as a wave pushes a wave, and a pebble thrown into a pond creates infinite circles from the proportionate pushing of the waves: so also sound is propagated through infinite circles of air agitated in a uniformly-difform manner; and it does not merely roll these along the surface, but promotes them as diffused spheres. For if we could see the motion of the air which the object of sounds produces, it would undoubtedly represent to us a most perfect system of "heavens," swelling always into larger and larger circles. The proposition is therefore clear.

# CHAPTER X.
## On the Nature and Genesis of the Voice.

**H**aving explained the nature of sound in general, it now seems appropriate to treat the voice as a species of sound, so that having wandered through various circles of compositions and resolutions, and having finally grasped the properties of individual things, we may rest sweetly in the center of truth. I believe that nothing in the world is better known, <margin>Praise of the human voice.</margin> nothing more familiar, and nothing more common than the voice, and that no one (unless perhaps deprived of the use of their ears) can be ignorant of it; for by the voice, all things in the world are carried out. The voice is the bond of the political world, the fosterer of human commerce, the communicator of faith and discipline, the teacher of the ignorant, the preserver of peace and justice, the protector of cities, and the sole conciliator of mortals. Without it, nothing would stand firm; indeed, it would be necessary for all communication in human society to perish. 

We now undertake to explain this; but although, as I said, nothing is more common, its cause is nonetheless utterly hidden. For who could easily explain such a great variety of the "striking" <note>original: "elisionis" — the physical process of air being expelled and shaped to create sound.</note> of the voice in animals? For we perceive the plaintive voice of the Owl, the mournful clangor of the kite, the complaints of the moaning turtledove, the "cuckooing" of the cuckoo, the warbling of the sweet nightingale, the chirping of sparrows, the crowing of roosters, the trumpeting of elephants, the bleating of sheep, the lowing of oxen, and we hear the barking of dogs—and in all of these, we marvel at the hidden expressions of love, hate, anger, indignation, and mournful sadness. But how these are formed in the throat, and by what proportion of the striking of the air they are born, is as obscure as these voices are clear and manifest to the hearing. Nevertheless, lest we seem to have surrendered in the face of such hidden matter, something must be dared; and if we are frustrated in our hope, it will be a consolation to have placed the effort in a praiseworthy light. That we may proceed with a consistent method, we begin the unfolding of the proposed matter with a definition of the voice in the usual manner, with the help of the good GOD.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of sound, transitioning from the general physics of sound to the specific definition and physiological production of the "voice" (vox), contrasting classical theories with an Aristotelian framework of causes.</meta>

# 20 Of the Great Art of Harmony and Dissonance

<margin>Epicurus said that the voice is a flow of atoms.</margin> It is remarkable how much dissonance exists among the most confused authors when assigning the genuine causes of the voice. Epicurus held that the voice is a "flow of atoms" which we see exiting the mouth as we speak; for he says this flow is emitted either by those calling out, sounding, or making a noise. When this flow encounters similar shapes, it is broken up, and when it falls upon the ears, the sense of hearing then arises. Democritus followed this same opinion, defining the voice as a "splitting of atoms into infinite parts," and he believed that hearing and sensation occur when these atoms are wound through certain circles all the way to the ears. Even some modern <note>original: "Neoterici"</note> pretentious philosophers follow these views; indeed, no opinion is so absurd that it cannot find applause among eccentric minds. The Stoics contend that the voice is produced by the force of air being struck into a fluctuating circle, while others devise different theories. But leaving each to his own opinion, we judge that the voice should be defined thus:

<margin>Definition of the voice.</margin> *The voice is the sound of a living creature, produced by the glottis from the striking of breathed air, for the purpose of explaining the feelings of the soul.* <note>original: "Vox est sonus animalis à glottide ex percussione respirati aeris ad affectus animi explicandos productus"</note> With these words, we explain the nature and essence of the voice so that all the causes pertaining to the constitution of the voice are revealed as if in an epitome. We establish "sound" as the <term>formal cause</term> <note>The "formal cause" is the essential nature or "shape" of a thing—what makes it what it is.</note> of the voice, "air" as the <term>material cause</term>, the "larynx" as the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent or tool that brings the thing into being.</note>, and finally, we determine the "intention"—by which we wish to signify something through the voice—to be the <term>final cause</term> <note>The "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note>.

<margin>Causes of the voice</margin> Therefore, "sound" rightly holds the place of the "genus" in the definition of voice; and since the voice is a specific kind of sound, we have rightly assigned "air" as its material cause, by the breaking of which it is produced. However, air is not the "matter" of the voice in just any state, but only as it is agitated and expelled outward from the lungs. The remote efficient cause of the voice is the body of a living creature—I say "living creature" because even if the sound of inanimate things is sometimes called a "voice," it is only to be understood metaphorically. For the sound of musical instruments—now intense, now soft, now deep, now high, and divided into voices by certain intervals like syllables—is transferred to the "true voice" only through a certain analogy. The proximate efficient cause and the most principal instrument of the voice is the Larynx. And specifically that part of the larynx which is called the glottis or epiglottis; for this, moderately covered and joined by certain muscles, produces the voice, as will be clear from the anatomy to be presented shortly. 

<margin>Cause of the voice.</margin> Therefore, the lung is not the cause of the voice, since the air which it blows out to form the voice has far too little impact; rather, it merely supplies air like a bellows. Neither the tongue, nor the throat, nor the lips, nor the teeth, nor the palate are properly the organs of the voice, since the office of these parts in humans is to pronounce the voice—already generated by the glottis—articulately and according to the legitimate sounds of syllables. Indeed, certain letters cannot be formed except by the lips, such as B, M, and P, so that it is impossible for one deprived of lips to pronounce them. Some are formed only by the tongue, like D, T, L, and N. Some only by the teeth, like Sch, Z, S, and R. Some only by the throat, like A, H, and A. Some can be pronounced only by the palate, like K, X, I, and G.

<margin>The glottis is the chief cause of the voice.</margin> You see, therefore, how the principal cause of the sound is the glottis, while the remaining parts of the mouth are nothing but instruments for the proper and better forming and pronouncing of the voice. The tongue, however, like a certain director <note>original: "Choragus" — the leader of a chorus or a stage manager.</note>, moderates and disposes everything conducive to the perfection of the voice. How the voice is formed through the glottis of the larynx will be discussed later.

Finally, the final cause is the intention to signify something. For the voice seems to have been instituted by nature in living creatures for no other end than to indicate the passions and feelings of the soul. <margin>Final cause of the voice.</margin> In humans, it is ordained for the declaration of the will; in brute animals, for the explanation of natural affections. <margin>The voice of a cat.</margin> For a cat, for example, has one voice while it is hungry, another when it is incited by jealousy, another while it flatters, and another when it burns with anger; and so it is with every other living creature, as has been indicated in the preceding pages.

->COROLLARY<-

<margin>Whether any sound whatever can be called a voice.</margin> From what has been said, it is clear that not every sound emitted by a living creature is a "voice," but only that which is made by the glottis with the intention of signifying something. Hence, the chirping of certain insects, such as cicadas and crickets, the humming of bees and wasps, and the hissing of snakes, are [not] voices...

### CHAPTER XI.
### Concerning the organ of the voice and its anatomy.

**C**um—Since we have said above that the Larynx is the organ of the voice, and all types of voice depend on this organ, it must be explained what its nature and structure are, and of how many parts it consists, so that the reasons for the genuine voice may better become known to the curious reader. The Larynx, therefore—which is the head or final part of the <term>rough artery</term> <note>The "rough artery" (*arteria aspera*) is the historical name for the **trachea** or windpipe, so called because of its ridged cartilaginous rings.</note>, or **Trachea**—is nothing other than an organ consisting of cartilages that bring forth the **glottis** and membranes, endowed with muscles and nerves, constructed primarily and properly for the sake of emitting the voice.

It is, moreover, a hard body, dense and thick, large and ample, possessing length, width, and depth, with a certain protuberance, prominent especially from the necks of men <note>This refers to the laryngeal prominence, commonly known as the "Adam's Apple."</note>, and is also round and circular, though with a certain obliquity. For in the front part it is exactly circular, but in the back, where it faces the **Esophagus**, it gradually falls away from the perfect figure of a circle and attains some length. Inside the body of this organ is a certain opening, which is called its fissure or **glottis**, whose elegance is no less than its utility, and is worthy of every praise. For the action of the larynx is entrusted especially to this part, and by it the voice (the proper action of this organ) is formed, specifically when the air passing through is compressed and struck, producing the voice in a truly wonderful way with the help of muscles. But since these things can be perceived by no better means than from its anatomy, we subjoin it here.

<margin>The constitution of the glottis.</margin>
You see, therefore, that two primary parts most worthy of consideration occur in the Larynx: the glottis and the epiglottis. The glottis is the membranous, fatty, and glandular substance of the Larynx, composed of a unique flesh and parenchyma <note>the functional tissue of an organ</note>, having at its end a slit like a pipe, resembling a tongue, as noted by the letter M. For just as the Retina is the seat of vision, and the parenchyma of the liver is the maker of blood, so we establish this membranous, fatty, and glandular body—anointed with a viscous and oily moisture—as the proper and genuine organ for producing the voice.

<margin>What is the epiglottis?</margin>
The epiglottis, however, is a certain part of the glottis that acts as a lid, overhanging it precisely to prevent any food or drink from flowing through the glottis into the larynx; hence it is called the door, the guardian, and the rampart of the larynx. By its opening we both breathe in and breathe out, and it has its own muscles assigned to it by nature, by which it may now be closed, now opened; but more on this in the following pages.

# CHAPTER XII.
## On the various differences of voices which are expressed by means of the Larynx.

<margin>Differences of voices from the constitution of the Larynx.</margin>
We have seen in the preceding chapter the structure of the organ of the voice; now let us see how it forms such a great variety of voices. For it is certain that, according to the varying constitution of the same organ, different variations of voices are born. It produces voices that are loud, soft, sharp, deep, smooth, rough, steady, trembling, strong, weak, thick, slender, clear, hoarse, cheerful, or mournful; furthermore, there is one voice for the sober, another for the healthy, and another for the insane; in a word, as many colors as there are, so many differences of voices can be conceived. To give the reasons for each of these would be a work of nearly infinite labor; therefore, we shall assign the causes for only some of them here, treating first the human voice, and then also the voice of brute animals <note>animals lacking reason</note>.

<margin>Threefold cause for the difference of voices.</margin>
Therefore, the differences of voices can be traced back to three causes: either to the natural constitution of the larynx, or to the air which is the matter and subject of the voice, or to the exhalation. Those which pertain to the larynx arise either from its temperament <note>The "temperament" refers to the balance of the four bodily humors: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> and the consequences of that temperament, or from accidental factors.

<margin>The quality of the Larynx.</margin>
The temperament of the Larynx, as with all its remaining parts, is either moist, hot, cold, or dry, or predominating from these mixed with one another either in good proportion <note>original: εὐκράτως (*eukratos*)</note> or in poor proportion <note>original: δυσκράτως (*dyskratos*)</note>.

<margin>Whence a dark and obscure voice.</margin>
A moist temperament of the Larynx without an inflow of humors <note>fluids within the body</note> produces a dark, obscure, and confused voice; if accompanied by an inflow of humors, it will create a hoarse voice. A dry temperament of the Larynx produces a melodious, clear, and resonant voice; and if dryness predominates, it creates a tinkling, shrill, and clanging voice, not unlike the calls of cranes.

Book I. Anatomical Study on the Nature of Sound and Voice. 23

...constricts and narrows it. A well-tempered <note>original: "εὐκρατον" (eukraton)</note> or moderate temperament of the larynx produces a voice that is sonorous, sweet, pleasant, charming, clear, transparent, and calm; and this pertains to the temperament of the larynx. Furthermore, the natural constitution of the larynx—which is based on its shape, size, position, passage, surface, and so on—gives birth to other differences in voices.

The internal shape of the larynx, being rounded lengthwise, makes the voice uniform, sonorous, and not distorted. <margin>What the shape of the larynx can contribute to the differences of voices.</margin> The passage does not produce different voices by itself, but in respect to its size; for if this passage is wide and ample, the voice is rendered deep and loud; if, on the other hand, it is narrow, the voice is thin and small; as is evident in pipes and flutes, and will be demonstrated at length in the section on musical instruments <note>original: "musica organica," referring here to the mechanical study of instruments as "tools" of sound</note>. The surface is either polished and smooth, or rough and uneven: from roughness, the voice will similarly emerge rough and unpleasant; from smoothness, it will be smooth, pure, sweet, and charming. The position or placement of the larynx emits a voice that is either diminished or distorted, or removes it altogether.

Air, also being the material cause of the voice, gives birth to its own differences of voices; for it is either thin or thick. <margin>What air can contribute to the differences of voices.</margin> The thickness of the air favors the depth of the voice, while its lightness favors sharpness <note>The author uses "sharpness" and "gravity" to refer to high and low pitch</note>; hence voices in winter are deeper than in summer due to the thicker constitution of the air. If the air is abundant and fast, it will produce a very sharp sound; if abundant and slow, a very deep sound; if sparse and fast, a moderately sharp sound; if sparse and slow, it will produce a tiny voice.

Finally, exhalation makes the voice either deep or sharp, small or large, high or thin. <margin>What exhalation contributes to the differences of voices.</margin> To these, it makes it constant, uniform, firm, and consistent and harmonious if the exhalation is constant, stable, and firm; or inconstant, weak, trembling, inconsistent, and dissonant if it is weak, inconstant, and trembling.

### FIRST COROLLARY.
### Concerning the Cause of the Loud and Small Voice.

But now it must be examined from where the loud and the small voice derive their origin. It is certain, therefore, that the various qualities of the matter are the causes of the various differences in the composite whole. Whosoever, therefore, perceives the loud and small voice to arise from large or small motion (as Plato did), or from the narrowness or width of the passage (as Galen <note>Galen was an influential Greek physician whose theories on anatomy and the "humors" dominated medicine for over a millennium.</note> did), or from heat and cold (as <term>Abenfina</term> <note>original: "Abenfina," referring to the Persian polymath Avicenna (Ibn Sina), whose medical texts were standard in European universities</note> did), they perceive correctly; for they assign to each the partial causes for forming a small and loud voice, which, when joined in one, constitute the adequate cause. This is evident in the loud sound of a trumpet, from which a loud voice necessarily emerges if it is large and joined with a forceful blowing. The size of the trumpet is capable of holding much air; and for the impelling of much air, the internal heat of the trumpeter is needed, in which the force and strength of the blowing is located. We experience the small sound of a trumpet from the opposite causes.

I say, therefore, that not only large or small air, heat and cold, or the width and narrowness of the windpipe <note>original: "asperæ arteriæ," the historical term for the trachea</note>, but most especially the width or narrowness of the slit or the <term>glottis</term> <note>The opening between the vocal folds; the author identifies this as the primary site of vocal modulation.</note> is required for the formation of a small or loud voice. <margin>How much the slit of the glottis contributes to the differences of voices.</margin> This, however, is made wider by heat and narrower by cold; it also intensifies the force of greater or lesser exhalation. Hence it follows that those who are warm by nature emit a loud voice, and those who are cold a small one; for the force of heat easily draws both breath and air to itself, all the more when it is more abundant. And just as heat strengthens respiration, so cold weakens it. Thus, from this the reason for the small or loud voice is most clearly revealed. For this reason, those who are greatly afraid are accustomed to emitting only a small and broken voice. For in such fear, the heat seeks the lower parts, leaving the upper parts behind; since these parts are deprived of heat, cold necessarily follows, and consequently weakness, and finally from this a small voice is born.

### SECOND COROLLARY.
### On the causes of deep and high-pitched voices.

<margin>Why children and women produce a thin voice.</margin> From this it is also evident that the same causes contribute to the formation of deep <note>original: "gravis," referring to low-pitched or bass tones</note> and high-pitched <note>original: "acuta," literally "sharp" or shrill tones</note> voices as those we previously mentioned regarding the formation of loud and soft voices. For in children and women, the formation of a high-pitched voice depends on the narrowness of the air passage. As these passages are gradually widened through age, the voice also necessarily shifts from high-pitched to deep; this continues until, in the elderly, the organ once again acquires a drier constitution, and the voice ends by shifting from deep back to high-pitched.

<margin>Why the voice changes during puberty.</margin> This is why a change of voice occurs in boys reaching puberty and as they mature <note>original: "femine turgentibus," literally "swelling with seed," reflecting the early modern belief that the onset of reproductive maturity redirected the body's vital fluids</note>, because of the great similarity and interdependence that the reproductive vessels <note>original: "vasa spermatica"</note> have with the vocal vessels. For when those reproductive vessels draw into themselves the heat and moisture intended for the vocal organs, the organs—deprived of those sustaining fluids—necessarily undergo another vocal conformation...

[Nature] constructed [the voice]; so too, for the same purpose, art—emulating nature—has devised and produced countless ducts and channels. Furthermore, just as a shape is carved into the base of the Larynx destined for forming various pronunciations of voices, so too do pipes have their own slits for producing different vocal variations; indeed, the pallets <term>palmulæ: small valves or keys in an organ</term> adapted for the hands represent the muscles, now opening and now closing the glottis.

The trumpet can also be aptly compared with the Larynx; for the Craftsman, to produce all kinds of sounds, has added various parts to the trumpet by which it can be prolonged and extended more or less. He flared the ends to diffuse the sound into the air without harshness, just as it is in the Larynx.

What else does the ringed trachea serve but the contraction and prolongation of the windpipe <note>original: "aspera arteria," literally "rough artery," the historical term for the trachea</note>, from which the intensity and weakness of the voice necessarily result? And just as the first opening corresponds to the glottis of the trumpet, so the other opening toward the lungs corresponds to the flared end of the trumpet. For air—the raw material of sound—is carried to the opening and struck; this same air, now intense and forceful, now abundant and slow, now sparse and swift, now weak with a lowering of strength, is drawn from the lungs by our will with the help of muscles and propelled into the opening of the trumpet. So too the multi-stopped flute <note>original: "Tibia polystoma," a flute with many holes</note>, or one pierced with many holes, resembles the windpipe in many ways. But since these things have been discussed extensively in *The Art of Making Organs* <note>original: "Muſurgia Organica"</note>, we refer the reader there.

### CHAPTER XIV.
### On the natural voices of animals and their anatomy.

Lest men should accuse nature of being a "stepmother" <note>An idiom suggesting nature is cruel or withholding, rather than a caring mother</note> in the provision of things due to each creature, she has provided for each in such a wonderful way that whoever <margin>The wonderful providence of God in the construction of animals.</margin> contemplates a little more deeply—especially those things which shine forth both in that wondrous order of the distribution of animal limbs and in the admirable structure of the senses—cannot sufficiently praise the divine goodness and majesty of the Creator as they deserve. Such is the order in all things, such the wise providence in all, such a great and incomprehensible workmanship in all. But since we have discussed these things at length in Book X of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Artis Magnæ Lucis & Vmbræ"</note>, Part 2, concerning the wonderful nature of things represented through microscopes and things recently discovered by us with their help, we refer the reader there. Therefore, in this place, we shall treat only of the nature and property of the voice of certain animals, lest we seem to have omitted anything in this our musical work.

#### §. I.
#### On the Voices of animals in general.

Animals can be considered here in three kinds: quadrupeds, birds, and insects. None of these are capable of musical melody or speech, unless you except some birds (which both soothe the ears of listeners with sweet melody and strike the hearers with amazement by their imitation of human speech). For since their tongue does not correspond to the Larynx, nor does it have any aptitude for pronouncing vowels and consonants—as is clear from their anatomy—it is no wonder that articulate pronunciation is also lacking in them. Content, therefore, with the natural voice granted to them by nature, <margin>Natural voices of animals.</margin> Cattle low, Sheep bleat, Dogs bark, Horses whinny, Elephants trumpet, Lions roar, Donkeys bray, Bears growl, etc.; although this sound is not so uniform and monotone <note>original: "ἰσότονος" (isotonos)</note> that it does not [reveal] some other [sounds] according to passions...

§. II.

Concerning the American quadruped animal which they call the Sloth, and the marvelous formation of its voice.

[Marginal note:]
Description of the animal Haut.

If Music had first been invented in America, I would certainly say it drew its beginnings from no other source than the voice of this miraculous animal. But before we declare its voice, let us first set down a description of the whole animal, which I received by word of mouth in this very year in which I write, from Father Juan Toro, Procurator of the Province of the New Kingdom <note>The "New Kingdom of Granada," roughly corresponding to modern-day Colombia.</note> in America, who both kept animals of this kind in his possession and performed very many experiments on their power and properties. The shape and nature of this animal are unusual; it is called "Sloth" <note>original: "Pigritia"</note> because of the slowness of its movement, being the size of a cat, with a loathsome face and claws protruding in the likeness of fingers. A mane existing on the back of its head veils its neck, and with the slow fat of its belly, it sweeps the very ground. It never rises onto its feet, walking so slowly that it can scarcely progress the distance of an arrow's flight in fifteen continuous days. Furthermore, it is not known what food it eats, for it is never observed to take any food. It lives mostly in the tops of trees, spending about two days in the ascent and just as many in the descent. Furthermore, Nature

[Marginal note:]
What are the weapons of this animal against external force?

seems to have equipped this animal with a double armor against beasts and animals hostile to it. The first is in its feet, to which Nature granted such strength that whatever animal it has seized, it holds so tightly that the creature is no longer able to free itself from its claws, but is compelled to die of hunger because of the long detention. The other is that this beast so moves men rising up against it by its appearance, that they refrain from molesting it, moved by an intimate compassion. For besides the tears which it sheds from its eyes, it strikes those looking at it with such a sorrowful aspect that it easily persuades them that one should by no means disturb what nature has made so defenseless and subject to such a miserable condition of body. To gain experience of this matter,

[Marginal note:]
Marvels of this animal.

the Father cited a little earlier took care to have one of these animals brought to the College of our Society in Cartagena <note>Cartagena de Indias, a major port in colonial Colombia.</note> of the New Kingdom; he also placed a long pole under its feet, which it soon gripped so tenaciously that it would not let it go at all. The animal, bound in this manner by its own voluntary suspension, was placed together with the pole between two beams in a separate place, where it hung for 40 whole days without food, drink, or any sleep, its eyes always fixed on those watching, whom it moved so much with its sorrowful look that there was scarcely anyone who was not touched by compassion for it. Finally, having been freed from this long suspension, they threw a dog to it; having soon seized the dog with its feet, it held it so strongly for four whole days until the wretched dog, destroyed by hunger, breathed its last. It perfectly reproduces musical intervals with its sound and voice.

They add, moreover (to return to our purpose), that a voice is not uttered by this beast except at night, and that voice is altogether prodigious. For with a voice interrupted by the duration of a single sigh or half-pause, it perfectly reproduces—by ascending and descending through those common intervals of six steps—the basic elements of music that beginners intone: *Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la; la, sol, fa, mi, re, ut* <note>The hexachord, the six-note scale used in medieval and Renaissance music theory.</note>. Thus, when the Spaniards first held those shores and perceived this kind of vociferation at night, they thought they heard humans imbued with the precepts of our Music. It is called **HAUT** by the inhabitants for no other reason than that it repeats this cry *Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha*, etc., through each step of the interval of the sixth. But so that you may better comprehend the figure of the animal together with its voice, it seemed best to place everything here before your eyes in one synopsis.

§. III.
**Concerning the Voices of birds.**

Furthermore, among the rest of the animals, birds have obtained the greatest power of singing and speaking—so much so that, what the elephant possesses in prudence and memory, the stag in fidelity, the ape in gesticulation, and the fox in cunning craftiness, the **Parrot** and the **Nightingale** excel among the winged animals in speech and song. lowing like a calf, bleating in the manner of a sheep, and sometimes whistling like a shepherd. and since there was a delay there according to local custom, the trumpeters, because they were pleasing, were ordered to prolong their songs. But there was no other cause except exercise and a vehement zeal for meditating, by which it might express the sound of those trumpets: for suddenly it shone forth again, producing nothing of its usual voices, but only the songs of the trumpets, which it imitated with such talent that it perfectly expressed all the changes and the ratios of proportions." Indeed, there is no other reason for this wonderful talkativeness in the magpie except the conformation of the **Larynx** and the tongue, and the bird’s most sagacious nature. Furthermore, all other birds that have the same constitution of the vocal organ emulate magpies, such as jackdaws and crows, regarding which consult the Ornithologists who treat them more extensively.

<margin>The ambitious nature of the nightingale and its love of praise.</margin>
The nightingale is not only *fond of music* <note>original: "φιλόμουσος" (philomousos)</note> but also *fond of glory* <note>original: "φιλόδοξος" (philodoxos)</note>: indeed, in solitary places, it modulates a simple song as if singing to itself or practicing without any elaborate display. But when it finds nearby listeners, then, as if displaying the riches of its voice, it fashions innumerable sounds with admirable variety. Now it draws them out evenly for a long duration; now it bends them; now it sings more delicately and concisely; now it twists and, as it were, curls the voice; now it intensifies it; then it relaxes it. It sings some long verses as if they were heroic <note>The author is comparing bird song to "heroic" dactylic hexameter, the meter used in epic poetry like the *Aeneid*.</note>; others short, like Sapphic verses; and sometimes very short ones like Adonic verses; it even possesses, as it were, musical games and scales. Furthermore, other younger birds meditate with themselves and try to imitate what they hear from the adults: the student listens with great attention, and one can perceive a corrected emendation and a kind of reprimand in the teacher. Moreover, who can sufficiently marvel at such a great voice in so small a body? Such 

<margin>Praise of the Nightingale, and the wonderful variety of voices.</margin>
a persistent spirit? While that sound of the throat is now drawn out long with a continuous breath, now varied by a bend, now distinguished by a cut, joined by a twist, sent forward by a recall, or darkened unexpectedly: sometimes it murmurs to itself; at other times a sound is affected that is flat, deep, sharp, rapid, extended, and where it seems best, vibrating; now at the highest, middle, or lowest pitch. In short, all the things that human art has devised through so many exquisite "tortures" of flutes <note>A metaphor for the complex mechanisms of wind instruments.</note> are performed by such narrow throats. And lest any art be lacking, there are many songs for individuals, and not the same for all, but each has its own; they compete among themselves, and a spirited contention openly arises, which often ends its life in death, the breath failing before the song; so that it may rightly be called the **Epitome** of all harmonic modulation.

But to return to our purpose: when I had frequently and with no small admiration attended to the wonderful power of this little bird’s modulation, a great desire seized me, not only to transfer those truly admirable musical phrases into musical notes, but also to perform an anatomy of the little bird, so that the cause of such great modulation might be more fully known; both of which have been done. For I have transferred the phrases of the modulations, caught from the mouths of singing nightingales, onto the musical scale, as will be seen shortly. I also took care to have an anatomy performed by Giovanni Trulli <note>Giovanni Trulli was a noted 17th-century Italian surgeon and anatomist, and a friend of the author.</note>, a distinguished anatomist, in my presence, so that I might exactly observe the individual parts of the larynx.

<margin>Anatomy of the Nightingale.</margin>

And indeed, we found first a very short tongue, but a larynx that was wonderfully fibrous and muscular; the remaining parts, however, shared no difference in their anatomy from other birds. From this I concluded that all this power of variety in voices proceeds from the innumerable fibers by which the glottis <note>The opening between the vocal folds in the throat.</note> is now tightened, now loosened, now pulled apart, now drawn in, and bent in every direction, with the tongue striking the individual voices like a plectrum <note>A small tool used to pluck the strings of an instrument like a lute or lyre.</note>. From this I also inferred that those "guttural diminutions"—which eunuchs <note>Referring to the *castrati*, male singers who maintained high vocal ranges and incredible agility.</note> form in the throat and call "trills"—are made not by the tongue, but immediately by the glottis, and are nothing other than a trembling of the throat produced by the exhaled air in the orifice of the glottis. But to encompass many things in few words for the sake of the curious Reader, I wished to exhibit here the musical voices of most of the more sonorous birds, represented from my own experience and observation, lest we seem to have omitted anything of curious interest.

<margin>What a "glottismus" is.</margin>
First, therefore, so that I might exhibit the individual chirps and trills, or the "chromaticisms" of the whistlings (which we shall hereafter call **glottisms**, because they are formed by the help of the glottis) according to the proper time, I took a cord one-and-a-half feet long, which in its swing and return would exactly represent the pulse of a healthy man. By means of this, I 

<margin>The Author's experiment performed on the Nightingale.</margin>
measured the time or duration of the "glottisms" of the nightingale. Furthermore, I attributed each two swings of the cord to one moderate measure of harmonic time (which the common people call the "beat," and the Italians call the *battuta*), so that one run of the cord, or a swing-and-return, would correspond to the *arsis* <note>The upbeat in a musical measure.</note> and the other to the *thesis* <note>The downbeat in a musical measure.</note>. Having observed these things properly, I began my observation very early in the morning in an appropriate place, and I found indeed that Nightingales arrange their whistling "glottisms" sometimes by semiminims <note>Quarter notes.</note>, sometimes by fuses <note>Eighth notes.</note>, and occasionally by semifuses <note>Sixteenth notes.</note>. But where they were adorning those smaller "glottisms," which the Italians call **Trills**, they performed them with such speed that they could by no means be rendered by semifuses, as those are too slow; therefore, trifuse or quadrifuse notes (that is, of which 32 or 64 constitute one beat) were necessary to express the property of the modulation. 

<margin>What a "pigolismus" is.</margin>
Truly, because I noticed that those "glottisms" were of many kinds, I have called those very clear "glottisms" modulated with a transparent and ringing voice **pigolisms**; but those which it renders through a certain kind of murmur, I call **teretisms** <note>These are technical terms coined by the author from Greek roots to categorize different styles of bird trills.</note>.

30 On the Harmony and Discord of the Great Art

<margin>What is a glazismus?</margin>
it seemed fit to call them *teretismos* <note>original: "teretismos"; refers to a specific type of chirping or trilling sound</note>; but those vocalizations which continue as if with an interrupted voice at the same interval, we call *glazismos*. Under these three terms, we include all the remaining species and differences of *glottisms* <note>original: "glottismorum"; refers to modulations produced in the glottis or throat</note>. Indeed, it seemed best to represent these species in Illustration III, lest we should appear to have omitted anything serving the curiosity of the Reader. Behold, these are the vocalizations that the Nightingale displays to us; besides these, we could not note others that were not the same regarding the inflection of the voice, though they are innumerable if we consider their mixture. For they exhibit these vocalizations with wonderful industry in each step of the *disdiapason* <note>An interval of two octaves</note> range; then they mix *pigolismos* <note>A term for a specific warbling or chirruping</note> with *glazismos*, and these with *teretismos* in such a variety that an infinite diversity of harmonic modulations emanates from them. Whoever, therefore, knows how to imitate nightingales by whistling and to perfectly express these turns of notes, let him know that he will perfectly express the song of the Nightingales <note>original: "Philomelarum"; a poetic name for nightingales</note> according to all rhythms and tempos.

->COROLLARIVM.<-
->[Corollary]<-

From what has been said, it is clear that the vibration of the glottis, by which the nightingale plays in these kinds of *pigolismos* and *teretismos*, is by far the most frequent. It equals (as I have also learned through experience) the vibration of a single string stretched to the weight of one pound, whose length was one pace and whose thickness was like a straw of hay, which used to vibrate almost infinitely when struck in the space of one second; and you will find that the glottis vibrates just as many times in forming a *pigolismo* or *teretismo*. This fact demonstrates the truly wonderful providence of God, who granted such a high level of music to this little animal destined for the relaxation of the human mind, that it not only surpasses all mechanical art of organs in speed, but also eludes the industry of all musicians in genius. For it affects not only the diatonic, but also the chromatic and enharmonic <note>original: "exharmonicam"; these refer to the three genera of ancient Greek music, with enharmonic being the most complex</note> method of singing in a wonderful way, as appears in the third vocalization: no instrument displays the chromatic-enharmonic steps more accurately than the nightingale with its throat. Nor do I doubt that this little bird, because of the suitable constitution of its vocal organ, is very capable of human speech; if there were a teacher, it could perfectly express other syllables by whistling. Regarding what Aldrovandi <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), a famous Italian naturalist</note> relates about the speech of three nightingales
<margin>Nightingales speaking with a human voice.</margin>
at Augsburg in a certain inn, who conferred with one another by day and night, many judge this to be a fable, or certainly they claim it could only have happened by some notable deception or the work of an intervening demon. But what we think about this, we shall indicate more opportunely in the following section.

->§. V.<-
->On the voices of the remaining birds.<-

I will add only one wonderful thing here, which I would never have believed if my own experience had not made me certain of the truth of the matter; and so the case stands: There is here in Rome, in the famous Monastery of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, the Very Reverend Father Master Damianus à Fonseca, a Portuguese man of great learning and authority, who has a little bird enclosed in a cage in his study, of that species of Larks which they call a Calandra <note>original: "Gallandram"; the Calandra lark, *Melanocorypha calandra*</note>. It was so skillfully taught by the brothers of the said Order that it not only pronounces the Litanies of the Saints as if with a human voice, but also chatters many other things that cannot be perceived without wonder. When the Most Reverend Lord Diego de Franchis, Abbot of Saint Praxedes, a man most refined in every kind of learning, first reported this marvel to me, I could hardly be induced to believe what was being reported until I was an ear-witness to such a marvel. And so, on March 16, 1648, accompanied by the mentioned Abbot and Father Jacobus Vivā, a distinguished Mathematician of our Society <note>The Jesuits</note>, I went to the said Father’s room. While we waited attentively in silence for the outcome, finally the bird, after the sweetest songs and various murmurs, clearly [spoke] many names of the Saints in the Italian language...

# Book I. Anatomical [Treatise] on the Nature of Sound and Voice. 31

...began to pronounce clearly and distinctly; now adding these words, "pray for us" <note>original: "ora pro nobis"</note>, now those, "Jesus Christ Crucified" <note>original: "Iesus Christus Crucifixus"</note>, and now various other names, up to 70 different ones, exhibited so wonderfully that hardly anyone could persuade themselves it was a bird whose tongue they perceived to be so similar to a human's. And although I remember reading many exotic things about various birds that mimic the human voice, as was mentioned a little earlier, I have found no historian who noted observing anything similar in a Lark <note>original: "Calandra"</note>. From this, I infer that Nightingales <note>original: "Luscinias"</note> are not as inept at forming speech as they are at song, as many believe; and thus that story of the Nightingales speaking in the Augsburg inn, according to the testimony of Aldrovandi, is not so impossible <note>original: "ἀδύνατον"</note> as anyone might persuade themselves. Indeed, I have no doubt that all birds which nature has equipped with a harmonious song are also capable of forming the human voice.

The Wren <note>Regulus</note> follows closest to the Nightingale; it borrows several phrases from the Nightingale in forming its trills <note>term: glottismus — a technical term for complex, rapid vocal warbling</note>, though less aptly and quickly. It also forms trills, but always in the same manner. The Finch, the Goldfinch, the Titmouse, the Flamingo, the Redbreast, the Lark, and as many singing birds as there are, none of them reach that variety of modulations which the Nightingale expresses.

The remaining birds certainly have a sonorous voice, but one adorned with none of the aforementioned types of trills; such as the Rooster, the Hen, the Cuckoo, the Swallow, the Hoopoe, the Owl, the Quail, and the like. Since their voice was not ordained for the delight of men, they express only that voice which suffices to explain the passions of the soul. But I thought I would not be acting out of place if I were to record the voices of some of them here in musical notation.

And indeed, the Rooster <note>Gallus</note> in particular emits various voices: one when he is moved by jealousy; another when he treads the hens; another when he indicates the time, which is the Rooster's own voice, whence the term "cock-crowing" <note>original: "gallicinium"</note>. He forms his voice, however, in nearly the manner expressed by the letter A in Illustration <note>original: "Iconismo"</note> III.

Where it is noted that the last syllable of the voice does not stay on the same pitch <note>original: "vnisono"</note>, but immediately declines from the same pitch by a third or a fourth.

The Hen <note>Gallina</note> similarly forms various voices; for she cries out differently when she calls her chicks, differently when she is laying eggs, differently when she burns with anger <note>original: "cholera"</note>, etc. While she is laying eggs, she makes a jump of a sixth from the starting pitch, as expressed by the letter B in Illustration III. The voice of one calling her chicks is indicated by the letter C in the said Illustration.

The Quail <note>Coturnix</note> always and repeatedly repeats the following twittering <note>term: pigolismus — a term used to describe the repetitive, rhythmic chirping of certain birds</note> in place of a song, as set forth by the letter D in Illustration III.

The Cuckoo <note>Coccyx or Cuculus</note>, having received its name from its voice, always warbles a two-syllable voice, not on the same pitch, but at the interval of a most perfect minor third, as appears in the notes under E in Illustration III.

The songs of all birds could be expressed in no other way, if anyone had the leisure to observe the process of each one in forming their voices. <margin>Natural / voices of / birds.</margin> For in each one, he will find a certain movement of the voice entirely distinct from the rest: thus Swallows "twitter" <note>original: "fritinniunt"</note>, Hoopoes "poop" <note>original: "pupizant"</note>, Thrushes "chatter" <note>original: "Kichlizant"</note>. Partridges "chirp" <note>original: "titibizant"</note>. The Sparrow "chirps" <note>original: "struthissat"</note>, the Magpie "chatters" <note>original: "Kittabizat"</note>, the Goose "cackles" <note>original: "gratitat"</note>, the Starling "whistles" <note>original: "pifitat"</note>, etc.

The Wren as well as the Bee-eater and the red-breasted Swallow are accustomed to "buzz" <note>original: "Zinzibilare"</note> with a similar song.

The Blackbird <note>Merula</note> expresses harmonic differences best of all, so that what the Parrot, Magpie, Raven, and Jackdaw can do in expressing the human voice, and what the Nightingale and other singing voices can do in expressing trills, the Blackbird can do among all other birds by singing, especially if it is instructed by a skilled master teacher. <margin>The Blackbird, / a distin- / guished singer.</margin> For there is hardly any kind of song so irregular <note>original: "heteroclitum"</note> that it does not learn it, pronouncing individual notes so exactly that it does not err in even the smallest semitone. There are, besides, other birds to which the ancients attribute great skill in singing, among which the Swan <note>Cygnus</note> occurs in the first place; <margin>Whether / the Swan / sings.</margin> there is a report that they sing most sweetly near their approaching death, whence the "Swan Song" is celebrated in all the monuments of the ancient poets and orators. And certainly, if we consider the organ of the voice in the Swan, nothing more wonderful occurs among all animals; <margin>Anatomy / of the / Swan.</margin> for the windpipe <note>original: "trachea"</note>, extended with various bends like a flexible trumpet, is seen inserted into the breastbone <note>original: "Sterno pectoris"</note>, received in a certain hollow—
