32 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

<margin>Why nature gave the Swan such a long windpipe.</margin>
...[re]ceptacle, emerging from there again, led around in another bend, it is finally inserted into the lungs with a bifurcated duct. Consequently, such an admirable constitution of the windpipe <note>original: *tracheæ*</note> suggests something divine in the formation of the voice. But he who knows nature’s hidden plan in the functions of organs will easily see that these various paths of the windpipe were given to the Swan not for music, but for other purposes. Since the Swan acts as a distinguished diver <note>original: *insignem vrinatorem*</note> and is frequently occupied for entire hours under water digging in the mud and seeking necessary food, it required a long windpipe first due to the length of its neck. Because this was not enough, nature inserted a concave receptacle in the breastbone <note>original: *sterni*</note> so that it might contain air necessary for breathing within it, as if in a certain pouch <note>original: *bursa*</note>, so that it would not be forced to emerge constantly and leave its food behind. Therefore, such a prodigious windpipe was given by nature so that the bird could carry the necessary air with it, as if in a womb. This can be seen in all fishing birds and divers. If indeed such a windpipe had been given to it for the sake of music, it is truly a wonder that nowhere and never has such a unique "Swan-song" harmony been perceived by anyone in these times. Thus, I consider this Swan-song to be entirely fabulous <note>meaning mythical or legendary</note>, introduced by Poets on the occasion of Nymphs, whom they called Swans because of their white brilliance. For nature does not always ordain the organs of voice in animals for the beautiful formation of sound, but for other uses necessary to the life of the living creature, as was evident in this organ of the Swan. Otherwise, the Pig, which by the favor of nature has been allotted a most beautiful Larynx, would sing the best and sweetest of all—which would be ridiculous, if not stupid, to assert.

## §. VI.
## Concerning the voices of certain insects, such as Frogs, Cicadas, Locusts, and Crickets.

<margin>The hiss of the Basilisk.</margin>
Insects also have their voices, established by a certain hidden plan of nature for the proper performance of their functions. Who does not know the hisses of serpents? The hiss of the Basilisk, if Pliny is to be believed, is so formidable that all animals flee, terrified by it. But leaving these things aside, we have undertaken to explain only two things here which bring no small amount of wonder to those who hear them: the croaking of Frogs and the chirping <note>original: *trillissinus*</note> of Cicadas, Locusts, and Crickets. Certainly, to reach such hidden causes of the voice, I have omitted no experiments. From this, I established a perfect anatomy of these small creatures, by which my desires were finally fully satisfied. For those things about which I first doubted, I soon learned through perfect and visual demonstration.

## §. VII.
## On the cause of the croaking of Frogs.

<margin>The *Ololigo* of the Frog.</margin>
Aristotle even doubted how Frogs produce that croak (which they call an *ololigo* <note>a Greek-derived term for a loud cry or croak</note>). For it is certain that they do not produce the voice with the glottis <note>the part of the larynx consisting of the vocal cords</note>, but with another part of the body. To find this, we will first exhibit its anatomy, so that the curious Reader may recognize how skillful, wise, and ingenious nature was in the factory of animals, and how admirably it behaved in joining all the parts together—both in the aforementioned animals and especially in the Frog, whose organ construction displays something divine.

<margin>Anatomy of the Frog.</margin>
First, therefore, look at Figure IV of Diagram II, where you will find the tongue is loose toward the throat, but is found to be immobile on the outside near the jaw. [A marks] the slit of the Larynx and the jaw of the Frog. BB are the cavities in which the two eyes rest, represented as two large oval-shaped swellings. The hole C follows next, marking the beginning of the throat...

# Book I. Anatomical [Discourse] on the Nature of Sound and Voice. 33

...denoting the cavity and the organ of the <term>croak</term> <note>Original: *coaxatus*; Kircher uses this term to mimic the 'co-ax' sound famously attributed to frogs by the Greek playwright Aristophanes.</note>. **D** denotes the **Larynx**, below which another opening, not unlike the first and resembling a small slit, is located nearby; this is the shape of the Larynx. **E** is the skin which covered the body of the tongue when it was naturally positioned inside; however, it has now been loosened from the interior and turned inside out by design, so that both the small slit and the shape, size, and position of the tongue might be made clear. **FF** refers to the lower jaw.

In the seventh figure, you indeed see the lungs filled with air and swollen, bearing an appearance like that of marble stones marked with various spots and colors. **A** is the membranous part covering the sections of the mouth. **B** is the <term>glottis</term> <note>The opening at the upper part of the windpipe</note>, whether in its shape or as the small slit of the Larynx. **C** is that slender body, namely the heart, while **DD** refers to the lungs.

Having established these points, I say that the croak is produced by the lip of the lower jaw, while the upper jaw remains motionless; for while it receives a small amount of water within the throat, the breath blown out from the lungs strives to penetrate the water held in the middle of cavity **C**; finally, as the lungs blow more vehemently, it passes violently through the small slit **D**.

He notes that the croak occurs when air from the lungs is forced through the larynx while the throat contains a small amount of water.</summary>

# 34 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

And if indeed, because of the animal's smallness and its delicate substance, the parts can scarcely be separated from one another unharmed even with the greatest diligence, they have nonetheless been arranged by us with such great industry that the individual parts can be discerned without difficulty, as appears from **Figure II**; in which **A, A** denotes the double <term>tympanum</term> <note>A drum-like vibrating membrane</note> lurking beneath a double scale. **B** is the double cave, in which the small membranes are hidden, by which the <term>stridor</term> <note>A high-pitched, creaking, or chirping sound</note> or sound is produced. **C** is the vault or chamber, where the enclosed air resonates when struck.

So that the organs that produce the chirping might be better exposed, we have arranged **Figure III**, in which **A, A** is the cave. **B** is the bract-like membrane, the maker of the sound. **C** is the yellowish membrane closing the vault in its upper part; if this is ruptured, the sound perishes. Truly, these things appear even better in **Figure IV**, where the animal rouses the membranes to sound, and **B** marks the vault.

We have seen the anatomy; now it is time for us to show the production of the sound. In this great apparatus of organs, therefore, those organs must be primarily considered by which this genus of insect produces that chirp, or that most acute sound. There is a double <term>tympanum</term> hiding under a double scale, a twin cave, and a vault; to which is added the bract, or membranes. I say, therefore, that this kind of animal, in the greatest heats (for it does not sing at any time other than in summer), is in need of cooler air. For this reason, while it shakes certain very hard membranes hidden within the <term>tympanum</term>, it agitates the air as if with a kind of fan, and by striking it against that bract-like membrane (marked with the letter **B** in Figure II), it excites the sound. Furthermore, the air is channeled into that concave chamber—whether you call it the cave or the vault—which that yellow bract-like membrane encircles. There, because of the cavity of the place (not unlike what happens in a struck military drum, the hollow of which is full of air), it effects that chirping or shrill tinkling. For this reason, those shaking membranes are not entirely closed by the shell which covers them, but a free entrance is always granted to the air. Whence also Nature bestowed two muscles upon it, with which it can agitate and fan those membranes by voluntary motion. The air, thus fanned and agitated more vehemently, is struck against the other yellow membrane stretched before the vault within the hollow, and finally produces the sound. Moreover, that little membrane is so suited for sounding that even when separated from the rest of the body, it gives off a certain tinkling when struck. Since the vault consists of the animal's very dry and almost bony constitution, it can easily produce such a tinkling. And this is the genuine cause of the voice of <term>crickets</term> <note>Kircher uses the term *grillus* (cricket), but his anatomical description of "drums" under "scales" describes what we now identify as a cicada.</note>: the <term>efficient cause</term> is the animal itself; the <term>formal cause</term> is the bract with the vault; the <term>material cause</term> is the struck air; and the <term>final cause</term> is the cooling of the animal, or perhaps even the flight of certain birds lying in wait for it, who are restrained by some hidden power of this sound. <margin>The cause of the sound of crickets.</margin>

From this it is clear how false the opinions of those are who think this chirp is formed by the animal's mouth; those also err who think this sound is produced only by the chirping of the wings, as happens in locusts. Truly, whoever desires to understand the matter more clearly, let him take an experiment in live anatomy (which is easy), and he will recognize in the thing itself that everything we have said is true.

The locust genus, however, produces sound with its wings, so that the wings move while placed upon one another. The inner part of the upper wing has a blackish, hard body placed transversely. The lower wing indeed has a small body of the same substance, placed on the edge of the upper border on the outer part; adjacent to this is a beautiful <term>tympanum</term>. By the mutual friction of these, that chirp is excited (indeed, even in dead ones by the touch of a <term>stylus</term>), and much greater in the living one, since more abundant air is trapped there. Hence the very tense wings strike the shaken air against that membrane, and hence the sound in the <term>tympanum</term>. See Figure II and V of <term>Schema II</term> <note>Kircher's term for his technical illustrations.</note>. <margin>The voice of locusts.</margin>

There are two species of crickets; for some are of the fields, and others are domestic, familiar to heated rooms, kitchens, and hearths. Both, however, excite sound in exactly the same way as locusts, wherefore we have decided not to dwell on them any longer. <margin>A double genus of cricket.</margin>

<margin>Problem 6.
Why do we not listen as gladly to a man mimicking a flute as to the flute itself?</margin>

**Sixth, it is asked:** Why do we not listen as gladly to a man who shapes his voice in the manner of a flute, as we do to the flute itself?

**The answer is:** Because that which belongs to nature is more pleasing than that which belongs to simulation. But as to why we listen to singers more gladly if flutes harmonize with them rather than lyres, the reason is that the flute, since it is driven to sound by breath, is more similar to the origin of the human voice. Thus, it better covers the errors of the voice; indeed, it perfects it and keeps it pure. This does not happen with the lyre, which is of a <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>Of a different kind or nature; here meaning the string-based sound is too different from the wind-based voice</note> nature; rather, the lyre detects all the errors of the voice. Therefore, since the sound of the flute blends better with the human voice, it is clear why we perceive singers more gladly when accompanied by a flute.

<margin>Problem 7.
Why dissonance is better perceived in a deep voice than in a high-pitched one.</margin>

**Seventh, it is asked:** Why is a <term>dissonance</term> <note>A harsh, clashing, or unharmonious sound</note> more easily perceived in a <term>Barytone</term> <note>original: "barytona"; a deep or low-pitched voice</note> voice than in an <term>Oxytone</term> <note>original: "oxytona"; a sharp or high-pitched voice</note> voice?

**The answer is:** Because a deeper or barytone voice is of slow motion and takes up more time, whereas a sharp or oxytone voice is of swift motion and consumes less time. Since slow things are better understood than swift ones, it appears that dissonance can be more easily noted in the former than in the latter.

<margin>Problem 8.
Why do those who yawn hear less?</margin>

**Eighth, it is asked:** Why do we hear less when we yawn?

**The answer is:** Because the sluggish breath, which we shake out from the depths of the throat, enters the ears and fills them, making a noise that obscures the sound coming from the outside. Added to this is the fact that in yawning, the <term>mandibles</term> <note>The jawbones</note> are pulled apart; by this distraction, a less free passage is granted to the external air to reach the ears.

<margin>Problem 9.
Why is sound better perceived inside a house than outside?</margin>

**Ninth, it is asked:** Why do those inside a house better perceive a sound usually made outside, while those stationed outside perceive less of a sound stirred up inside the house? 

**The reason is:** That a sound emitted outside the house, having found an open space, is dissipated and becomes weak, and for that reason is not as well perceived. However, an external sound that glides into a house is gathered together there, and consequently is presented more firmly to the ears.

Why we are more delighted by hearing than by reading.</margin>

<margin>Twofold sound: animate and inanimate.</margin>

Since the various qualities of the voice depend on the natural constitution of the acoustic organs; it is certain that from this an art can be discovered, by which, from the constitution of the human voice, we may arrive at the internal inclinations and passions of the soul; which we not inappropriately call **phonognomy** <note>A term coined by the author, meaning the "knowledge of character through the voice," similar to physiognomy</note>; and we have judged that it should be treated opportunely in this place.

It must be noted, therefore, that in this place we can consider sound to be twofold: animate and inanimate. Animate sound is again either rational or irrational. Rational sound is nothing other than the voice brought forth by an animal by means of the <term>rough artery</term> <note>original: "asperæ arteriæ"; the trachea or windpipe</note>, the larynx, and the epiglottis, with the intention of signifying something: by which last part we distinguish the human voice from that of brutes and from inanimate sounds, and those which occur without intention. Animate irrational sound is the voice of brutes, instituted to signify the passions of the soul. Inanimate sound, however, is the collision of any non-living bodies, such as thunder, the explosions of cannons, the crashing together of wood, metals, and other bodies, etc. Since, therefore, the sound of one body is <term>sharper</term> <note>meaning higher in pitch</note> than the sound of another body equal to it, it is necessarily concluded that the body with the sharper sound consists of a rarer <note>less dense</note> substance, and signifies a predominance of air or fire. But, so that you may proceed more safely in this art, take this experiment.

#### PHONOCRITIC EXPERIMENT.
#### Concerning the investigation of the nature of different kinds of wood, bones, and minerals through sound.

<margin>From sound, the density or rarity of bodies is gathered.</margin>

Let rectangular blocks or cylinders of equal size be made from every kind of wood previously properly dried, and strike them, suspended by a thread, with a <term>plectrum</term> <note>a small tool or pick used to strike an object to produce sound</note>, and you will perceive the most diverse kinds of sounds; for you will find some to sound a semitone, others a tone, a <term>ditone</term> <note>a major third</note>, or a <term>tritone</term> <note>an augmented fourth</note>, others a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>a perfect fourth</note>, a <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>, or even a <term>diapason</term> <note>an octave</note>, or otherwise; and once the proportions of the consonances are grasped, you will easily judge the natural construction of the bodies: namely, how much one is more compact than another, or how much rarer and more porous than the other. For since the density of any body arises from the greatest packing together of earthly and watery parts, one will be as much denser than another as its parts are more packed: and as much as a body is more packed, it will be so much heavier; as much as it is heavier...

the heavier it is, the more slowly it will be moved; and finally, the more slowly it is moved, the more deeply <note>original: "grauius" - referring to a low musical pitch</note> it will sound.
   Furthermore, the depth of sound in bodies is twofold: for some have a deep sound that is forceful, while others have one that is deep and dull. The former offers signs of an earthy and dry temperament; the latter of a watery, humid, and poorly compacted one. On the other hand, since thinness <note>original: "raritas" - the opposite of density</note> takes its origin from a highly porous substance and is capable of containing much air, bodies will be thinner the more porous they are; and the lighter they are, the faster they will be moved, and consequently they will sound higher and sharper in pitch.
   Note, however, that we are not speaking here of soft and liquid bodies, such as wool, feathers, liquids, and similar things that are not compact nor consist of solid substance, about which we will speak later; but of solid and hard bodies. Some of these will also have a sharp, forceful, and penetrating sound; others sharp indeed, but dull and weak. Just as the former provides evidence of porosity and lightness, so the latter provides evidence of porosity but of a flabbier substance. The same must be said of bones and metallic bodies of gold, silver, copper, iron, and lead. All of these you will find explained most extensively in our *Organic Musurgy* <note>A reference to Kircher's famous 1650 work *Musurgia Universalis*, specifically the section on instrument making</note>. Here, however, from what has already been said, we form the following Phonocritic Canons <term>Phonocritic: The art of judging the internal nature of an object by the sound it produces</term>.

### Canon 1. Phonocriticism of solid bodies.

<margin>The method of knowing the predominance of qualities in bodies through sound</margin>

IF the sound of some solid body, compared to the sound of another equal body, is deep and dull, it will give manifest evidence of a watery predominance, as happens for example in lead on account of its abundance of mercurial moisture. If, however, it has a sound that is deep but forceful, then you shall pronounce with certainty on a temperament of an earthy, light, and well-compacted body, as can be seen in iron and steel. If, furthermore, the sound of some solid body is sharp and thin, it will give signs of an airy temperament, and indeed of a porous and flabbier substance, as appears in tin. If, finally, the sound is sharp, forceful, and penetrating, then you will certainly conclude the body to be of a fiery temperament, or of a thin and extremely light substance, as we see in fiery things—for example, in the explosions of guns, etc.

### PHONOCRITIC EXPERIMENT.
#### Concerning the temperament of liquids.

<margin>Different liquids have different sounds.</margin>

TAKE three, four, or five glass chalices, all equal in shape and size, which you will fill with different liquids—for example, water, wine, and other distilled waters—in such a way, however, that they are all filled equally. This being done, rub the rim or edge of the chalice with a moistened finger for as long as it takes until you perceive a sound; this sound will indeed be different according to the diversity of the liquids. For the subtler a liquid is, the more sharply it will sound; and the thicker it is, the more deeply. Hence oil, since it is more compact and slow, will also sound more deeply; water will sound more deeply than "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vitæ" - concentrated alcohol or brandy</note>, and this more deeply than spirits or quintessences. Note, meanwhile, that oily liquids, although they are much subtler in substance than elementary water (being of an airy nature), nevertheless cause a somewhat greater depth of sound on account of their slowness and viscous substance. In other liquids lacking this stickiness, you will easily judge the elementary predominance according to the following canon.

**Rule 2. The discernment of liquids through sound.**

If the sound of a cup is heavy and dull, you may conclude from this that the liquid poured into it has a <term>watery temperament</term> <note>temperamentum: the mixture of qualities or "humors" (earth, air, fire, water) believed to compose all matter</note>, as is the case with spring water; nevertheless, spring water sounds sharper compared to swamp water, which has an earthy and dreggy nature. <margin>How the temperament of liquids can be discerned through sound.</margin> If the sound is sharp and thin, you have a sign of an <term>airy temperament</term>, as seen in all distilled waters <note>original: "aquis stillatitijs"</note>, which always have a sharper sound than any elemental water. Finally, if the sound is very sharp, subtle, and penetrating, it provides evidence of a <term>fiery temperament</term>, as appears in spirits and <term>quintessences</term> <note>the "fifth essence," the most refined and potent form of a substance in alchemy</note>; these, when placed in equal quantity in identical glass cups, produce a sharper sound than other liquids. Therefore, the sound itself will indicate how much more subtle one liquid is than another. For if one of them sounds at the <term>diapason</term> <note>original: "diapason" — the musical interval of an octave</note> compared to another, it is certain that it is twice as subtle as the other. However, on these matters, consult our *Musurgia* <note>The author refers to his own massive work on music and acoustics, *Musurgia Universalis* (1650)</note>, which treats all these things most extensively in the section on the magic of consonance and dissonance.

**Rule 3. The discernment of animal voices.**

Voice was granted by nature to brute animals for this purpose: that through it they might signal their passions, either to humans or to those of their own kind. For experience shows that birds, dogs, cats, and oxen form one kind of voice when moved by <term>choler</term> <note>yellow bile, the humor associated with anger and heat</note>, another during melancholy or phlegm, another when they love and fawn, another when they desire mating, or fear, or vehemently long for something. <margin>How the temperament of animals is known from sound and voice.</margin> For when they are moved by choler, it is certain they produce a sharper sound than when stimulated by hunger; for choler—being rare, subtle, and thin—sharpens the voice, while melancholy and phlegm, due to the sluggishness of the humor, dampen it. The boiling of the blood, however, renders it temperate. Therefore, if the passion is choleric, the voice will be more rapid and sharp, as can be seen in dogs and cats driven by rage; when they desire mating, they emit a sharp and moaning voice, a sign of fermenting blood. Thus, driven by one humor or another, they emit different voices. From this knowledge, a science could be formed by which one might understand the voice and language of animals, just as we read of <term>Apollonius of Tyana</term> <note>A first-century philosopher and mystic rumored to have the ability to understand animal speech</note>. We explain the language of these animals most extensively in our work entitled *The Tower of Babel* <margin>The book called *The Tower of Babel*.</margin>, where in due time the curious reader will find many rare and new things.

**Rule 4. The discernment of the human voice.**

Although the variety and multitude of voices in humans is no less than the variety of human faces, the inner affections of a person can perhaps be investigated more easily and certainly through the voice than through the diversity of faces. <margin>How the temperament of men can be known through the voice.</margin> Hence we read that Plato, when he desired to know the character of a certain youth, was accustomed to say: "Speak, so that I may see you." By this, he seemed to imply nothing other than the method by which he could know the inner character of the soul through the voice. The Sacred Scriptures also testify that Isaac recognized the difference between the brothers <note>Jacob and Esau</note> not by touch, but by voice. <term>Galen</term> <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> also knew the capacity of the chest through the voice when he said: those who have a strong voice, which they can continue without interruption, have a large chest. But here Galen speaks only of the strong voice, the cause of which is a wide and vast chest with large, ample lungs and strong muscles of the larynx and epiglottis. There are, however, other differences of voices which take their origin not so much from the chest, lungs, and epiglottis, as from the temperament: such as a voice that is slow, fast, sweet, harsh, distinct, confused, shrill, sharp, heavy, and deep, middling and temperate, etc.; all of which voices...

since the signs of different <term>temperaments</term> <note>In early modern science, a "temperament" was the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined a person's physical and mental nature.</note> are found in consonance and dissonance; they can easily be compared with colors, as was stated in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>Kircher refers here to his previous work, *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* (1646), where he discussed the relationship between light, color, and sound.</note>. ## §. I.
### On the intense and deep voice.

Those who shout loudly and deeply, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher Aristotle was a primary authority for Kircher; here he refers to the *Physiognomonica*, a work attributed to Aristotle that judges character by physical traits.</note> testifies, are compared to Donkeys. From this, they are inferred to be injurious, abusive, and petulant. <margin>Conjecture from the voice of a Donkey.</margin> For their petulant, injurious, and abusive nature when well-fed sufficiently teaches us that donkeys are scolders and insolent. Thus, Aristotle concludes: *The donkey has a very loud and deep voice; it is indiscreet, petulant, and abusive. Therefore, those whose voice is loud and deep are petulant, indiscreet, and abusive.* But it remains for us to see the reason for this. We see that a loud voice exists in those animals that have a large <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: "asperam arteriam"—literally the "rough artery," the common term for the trachea at the time.</note> and emit much air from it; they have a deep voice because they push much air slowly out of the pipe. <margin>Reason for the assertion.</margin> Therefore, animals that are large have a loud voice, since they also possess large vocal instruments. It is probable, then, that such men—who have a loud voice, a broad chest, a large windpipe, and a thick neck—are of a similar nature; for this indicates that the element of <term>earth</term> <note>Earth was considered the heaviest, coldest, and driest of the four elements.</note> dominates them in terms of their physical bulk. If, however, we perceive deepness joined with a loud voice (which the slowness caused by cold produces), it indicates a cold and dry temperament—that is, an earthy one. He who has acquired such a temperament is indeed greedy and fearful, yet also indiscreet and of a lowly mind. Furthermore, such people are intolerably insolent in prosperity, but more fearful than little hares in adversity—a nature which <term>Cornelius Tacitus</term> <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56 – 120 AD) known for his psychological insights into the Roman Emperors.</note> noted in the Emperor Caligula.

## §. II.
### On a voice that is deep at the beginning and ends in a sharp pitch.

Those who begin with a deep voice and end in a high or sharp pitch <note>original: "in acutum"—referring to a rise in musical pitch or frequency.</note> are categorized along with Oxen, as they are complainers, irritable, and sorrowful. This is the nature of oxen. Let us explain the reason for this in a few words. <margin>Conjecture from the bovine voice.</margin>
It is certain that in those who are sorrowful or suppressed by grief, heat is gathered from the extremities toward the center around the heart along with the <term>vital spirits</term> <note>Refined substances believed to flow through the body to facilitate movement and thought.</note>. Consequently, the upper limbs are deprived of heat and left in the cold. Because of the cold predominating in that area, the voice is usually slow and deep. Furthermore, the abundant heat around the heart requires abundant air; thus, the sorrowful draw in much air which, returning slowly, moves a great deal of external air. Consequently, a thick and deep voice emerges at the start. And since in speaking and complaining—to use the words of the Poet <note>A likely reference to Ovid, a favorite source for Latin authors of this period.</note>—
*Grief is poured out with tears, and is poured out again;*
It happens that through complaining talkativeness, the heat moved and released from around the heart exits and moves the air with great speed, which motion a high-pitched sound necessarily follows.

## §. II.
### On the small, soft, and relaxed voice.

Those who, **without passion**, possess a **small, soft, and relaxed voice**, are considered **mild** and **somewhat timid** <note>original: *timidiusculæ*</note>. <margin>The voice as a sign of mildness.</margin> Because their voice lacks the forceful expulsion of air associated with a bold or aggressive spirit, it is inferred that their internal <term>temperament</term> is similarly gentle and prone to retreat rather than confrontation.

Furthermore, those whose voices are found to be particularly **soft** <note>original: *mollem*</note> and **relaxed** are judged to be **effeminate** <note>original: *effæminatos*</note>. These qualities, **existing** <note>original: *existentis*</note> within a man, suggest a constitution that is more delicate and perhaps lacking in the "heat" and vigor traditionally associated with courage in this era's medical understanding. Just as a woman's voice is naturally higher and softer, a man with these vocal traits is thought to share in a more sensitive or less hardy disposition.

## §. VI.
### On the sharp and intense voice.

Those who, while they speak, emit a **sharp and intense voice**, are numbered among the **angry, the petulant, and the lustful**, and are compared to **Typhon** <note>In Greek mythology, Typhon was a monstrous giant associated with storms and chaos; in this context, he represents a wild, unrestrained, and shrill nature.</note> and to **goats**. <margin>The reason for the sharp voice.</margin> For the goat is an animal of a **hot temperament** verging toward **dryness**, and possesses <term>melancholy</term> <note>One of the four humors, associated here with a dry, earthy quality.</note> mixed with <term>phlegm</term>; because these do not harmonize well, they indicate a certain corruption of moisture within the dryness. This state is foul-smelling, as the odor they exhale sufficiently demonstrates.

Consequently, whoever possesses this nature will have both a voice similar to goats and the same impulsive inclinations. However, let no one think that we consider this inclination to be so violent that it cannot be corrected by the opposite acts of virtue; for no one is so malicious and perverse that they are incapable of virtue. I conclude, therefore, with the **Poet** <note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace.</note>:

*The envious, the angry, the lazy, the wine-bibber, the lover,*
*No one is so savage that he cannot be tamed,*
*If only he lends a patient ear to cultivation.*

## §. VII.
### On the thick and deep voice.

Those who emit a **thick and deep voice**, in the likeness of **oxen or bulls**, are considered **bold, rash, irritable, and fierce**. <margin>Character of the deep voice.</margin> This is because an abundance of heat and <term>vital spirits</term> <note>In 17th-century science, "spirits" were subtle fluids thought to circulate through the body to facilitate movement and thought.</note> dilates the passages of the breath, resulting in a sound that is heavy and powerful. Just as the bull is known for its physical strength and sudden fury, this voice signifies a spirit that is not easily governed and is prone to outbursts of anger.

## §. VIII.
### On the thin and weak voice.

Conversely, those who possess a **thin and weak voice** are generally regarded as **timid and fearful**, likened to the **hare** or the **deer**. <margin>The voice of the fearful.</margin> This indicates a "cold" temperament and a lack of internal heat, which causes the breath to be narrow and the vocal passages to contract. Such individuals are thought to lack the "spirit" required for bold actions, often preferring caution or flight over direct confrontation.

## §. IX.
### On the trembling and broken voice.

A **trembling voice** is characteristic of the **elderly** or those gripped by **intense fear**. <margin>The trembling voice.</margin> In the aged, it is a sign of the failing of natural heat and the weakening of the nerves that control the breath. In the fearful, it arises from the sudden retreat of the spirits to the heart for protection, leaving the vocal organs unsupported and unsteady.

## §. X.
### On the sweet and flexible voice.

Those endowed with a **sweet, flexible, and moderate voice** are judged to be of a **balanced and virtuous nature**. <margin>The harmonious soul.</margin> Such a voice reflects a perfect mixture of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and character.</note>, where neither heat nor cold, dryness nor moisture, exceeds its proper bounds. This harmony of the body produces a harmony of the soul, manifesting in a voice that is pleasing to the ear and indicative of a disciplined mind.

# CHAPTER I.
## On the Invention of Music.

<margin>The first principles and origin of Music.</margin>
**I**n this worldly theater of things, nothing is more common than sound; yet, just as it does now, it also provided the earliest race of mortals with various occasions and opportunities for its discovery. In the beginning, the whistling of the winds, as well as the hissing of certain animals—which those first mortals, scattered here and there through the fields, repeatedly perceived—gave the first occasion for the construction of **pipes**. These they fashioned after the likeness of nature from oat-straw, reeds, the leg-bones of cranes, and other hollow stalks of plants. Furthermore, the sound and noise of hollow bodies gave birth to the various equipment of **percussion instruments**, as will be seen later.

<margin>The first rudiments of pipes from reeds.</margin>
Since the first mortals for the most part devoted themselves to a rustic and pastoral life, and pitched their tents there where rich pastures were found and places watered by streams—and consequently filled with rushes, reeds, papyrus, and similar offspring of the stalk-bearing kind—it could not be that a people, who were idle for most of the day, would remain without some relaxation of the mind. It is likely, therefore, that these men first formed various **horns** <note>original: "lituos." A *lituus* was a curved trumpet used in ancient Rome; here Kircher uses it to describe early pastoral wind instruments.</note> for themselves from the aforementioned hollow stalks. Indeed, they did so with no less skill than we see shepherds and others living a rustic life today, and perhaps even with greater skill, as their minds were still more vigorous then.

Furthermore, since these same first mortals were mostly skilled in the **craftsman’s art** <note>original: "fabrilem artem." This refers to metallurgy and smithing, essential for early civilization.</note> (without which the society of the human race would perish), it could not happen that they did not occasionally produce various sounds and noises from the accidental collision of different bodies while working. From this, it is highly probable that they reached a knowledge of various percussion instruments by that very same reasoning that still occasionally happens to us today.

<margin>The origin of Musical Instruments.</margin>
Music, therefore, had the first origin of its invention not from the Greeks, or the Egyptians, or the Chaldeans, but from the first men before the Flood. Indeed, if all men were now removed from the world except for a few children ignorant of things, I have no doubt that, driven by necessity and through chance and experience over time, they could stumble upon various inventions necessary to the human race.

<margin>All inventions of things seem to have been accidental.</margin>
For the inventions of things are innate to man; they are not learned from books alone, but are drawn out by the intellect when some significant necessity compels it, or through chance, experience, or the suggestion of genius. Reason itself dictates, as I have said, that Music existed from the very beginning—quite apart from the fact that Holy Scripture clearly testifies to it. <note>Kircher refers here to Genesis 4:21, which identifies Jubal as the "father of all who play the harp and flute."</note> Certainly, in chapter 4, number...

<summary>Kircher argues that music originated not with ancient civilizations like the Greeks, but with the first humans before the Great Flood, who discovered sound by imitating nature and through accidental discoveries in craftsmanship. He posits that musical invention is an innate human response to the environment and the need for mental relaxation.</summary>

# CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the object of Music and its classification, and that 
### Music is a true speculative science.

**E**very faculty, by the order of nature, presupposes some object with which it is primarily concerned. The absolute and adequate object of Mathematics is "defined quantity." <note>original: "quantitas terminata." Kircher follows the Aristotelian tradition where mathematics is the science of quantity.</note> Just as quantity is twofold—continuous and discrete—so it gives birth to two Faculties: <margin>The object of Mathematics.</margin> Geometry and Arithmetic. Each type of quantity can further be viewed either absolutely (simply and by itself) or relatively (in relation to something else). The former constitutes the object of the "pure" mathematical sciences, while the latter constitutes the "mixed" mathematical sciences. Insofar as both types are considered in their physical substance, they provide a "material object" common to both pure and mixed sciences; <margin>The formal object of Optics.</margin> but insofar as they are considered by their form, they constitute a "formal object," <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "material object" is the general subject matter, while a "formal object" is the specific lens through which a science views that matter. For example, a body is the material object of both medicine and anatomy, but they view it through different formal lenses.</note> whose duty is to distinguish the science occupied with it from all others. In this way, the formal object of Optics is the visual line; the formal object of Music is the **sonorous number**; <note>original: "numerus sonorus." This refers to numbers expressed through sound, or musical ratios.</note> for no other faculty besides Optics and Music concerns itself with these specific properties. For although both Optics and Geometry have the "line" as their common material object, Geometry considers it under a different reasoning and formality than Optics: the former considers it as something extended, while Optics considers the line insofar as it is "visual." This formality is, as stated, the formal object of Optics, by which it is distinguished from Geometry and all other sciences. Similarly, both Arithmetic and Music have "numbers" as their common object. But Music considers them under a different formality than Arithmetic—namely, insofar as they are "sonorous," or as they represent certain proportions of sounds. Through this formality, Music differs from all other sciences as if by a formal object. However, what this "sonorous number" is must be explained more fully so that the nature of the formal object of this science may become clearer.

The "sonorous number," therefore, taken broadly, is nothing other than a number expressing a certain relation to voices and sounds, which is also found artificially in a sounding body. <margin>What is the sonorous number?</margin> But taken strictly, it expresses a relation only to **consonant intervals**, which are nothing other than certain proportions and forms of harmonies considered in the first place in Music. The first Musicians investigated these ratios on a single string, <note>Kircher is referring to the Monochord, a one-stringed instrument used to measure the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note> and they found that the quantity of the string's sound was equal to the number of parts into which it was divided. Thus, by knowing the length of the string and the parts into which it was cut, <margin>How the ancients investigated harmonic intervals.</margin> they formed an infallible judgment regarding the distance between a low and a high pitch. <note>original: "gravis & acuti." Literally "heavy" and "sharp," the standard Latin terms for low and high pitch.</note> So, in a certain string divided in two, by comparing the sound of one part to the sound of the whole string, they clearly came to know the interval or voice of the **diapason** (which they commonly call the **Octave**). They necessarily inferred that this consonance consists in a "double proportion" (specifically following the analogy of the divided parts), because it behaved as two to one.

Furthermore, since a low sound is born from slow motion, and a high sound from swift motion, they inferred another thing: namely, that the half-part of a divided string vibrates twice as fast as the whole, so that if the whole vibrates a thousand times, the half vibrates two thousand times. They formed the same judgment concerning all other <margin>Voices and sounds are the matter of harmony; numbers and proportions are its form.</margin> consonant and dissonant intervals, all of which I would examine more extensively here, had I not reserved them for the following books. And from this it is clear that just as voices and sounds are, as it were, the "matter" of harmonic intervals, so numbers and proportions are their "form." From their combination results, finally, the **sonorous number**, the true and formal object of Music. However, although all bodies are capable of producing sounds, they do not always...

<margin>Music is a subalternated science.</margin> And from this we first infer that Music is a <term>subalternated science</term><note>In the hierarchy of Aristotelian sciences, a "subalternated" science is one that "borrows" its mathematical principles from a "higher" or "subalternating" science (like Arithmetic) and applies them to physical matter (like sound).</note>; so that this may be understood, it should be noted that some sciences are "principal," while others are "less principal." The principal sciences depend on general principles known by the light of nature or the knowledge of the senses, from which they derive their conclusions; such as, for example, Geometry and Arithmetic, which are called "subalternating" sciences. The less principal sciences are those which, in addition to those principles known by the light of nature or acquired by the help of the senses, also take for their own principles the conclusions already demonstrated by a Principal science. And although they share the same common <term>material object</term><note>The "material object" is the general subject matter (e.g., numbers), whereas the "formal object" is the specific way that subject is studied.</note> with the Principal science, they nevertheless consider in this very subject or common object a certain perfection or "formality" from which they primarily receive their specific classification (as was said a little earlier regarding Optics in respect to Geometry), to which they are subalternated both by reason of their principles and their subject or object.

<margin>What is required for the subalternation of any science?</margin> This being established, it is also clear that Music is a science subalternated to Arithmetic; which is proven thus. Three things are required for the subalternation of any science, according to what has been said. First, that there be the same common material object for both the subalternating and the subalternated science. Second, that there be the same common principles for both to use in forming conclusions, and that, moreover, the subalternated science assumes as its own principles the conclusions made by the subalternating science. Third, that the subalternated science considers the common object as being affected by a certain perfection and formality, which is the foundation and basis of its specific classification. But these three things are found in Music; therefore, etc. For first, it considers "number," which is common to both Arithmetic and Music. Second, it uses principles received from Arithmetic. Finally, it considers number not precisely and by itself, but as affected by a certain perfection of <term>sonority</term><note>original: "sonoritas." Kircher means that while Arithmetic studies numbers in the abstract, Music studies "sounding numbers."</note>, or number shining forth in sounding bodies. This is seen when it exhibits sounds having any given degrees of highness or lowness; when, from any given sound, it finds others in a given proportion by varying the length, circumference, tension, and density of the sounding bodies; and when, finally, it counts, adds, subtracts, divides, and multiplies any given "sounding numbers." Furthermore, if this sonority is applied to lines that can be explained by number (as we have provided in our *Harmonic Geometry*), Music will be subalternated not only to Arithmetic, but also to Geometry, and it will have the "sonorous line" as its <term>formal object</term>, as will be proven more extensively in *Echosophia*<note>Kircher's term for the science of sound and acoustics.</note>.

<margin>Music can also be subalternated to Geometry insofar as it considers the sonorous line.</margin> It is clear, therefore, how Music is a subalternated science. It is also clear that it is not a pure mathematical science, but a "mixed" one, intermediate between Arithmetic or Geometry and Physics. Finally, it is clear that Music is properly and strictly called a Science, because it is subalternated, as was said, to Arithmetic and Geometry. Since, therefore, these subalternating sciences are properly called sciences (as Blancanus<note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit mathematician who wrote "Aristotelis loca mathematica."</note> learnedly and solidly demonstrates in his *Mathematical Passages in Aristotle*), it follows that the subalternated sciences are also such, since they use the same principles and, moreover, Music proceeds in a truly scientific manner. For it employs three types of principles—
<margin>Music is properly called a science.</margin> namely Definitions, Postulates, and Axioms—from which, finally, a perfect science is born, as the Philosopher<note>Aristotle.</note> proves at length in the books of the *Posterior Analytics*. And indeed, the definitions are perfect and essential, such as the definitions we proposed in the third book.

<margin>Definitions in Music.</margin> As, for example: *A harmonic interval is a space capable of tension and relaxation*, etc. *A double multiple interval, or the <term>diapason</term><note>The Greek term for an octave.</note>, is a harmonic space where the greater contains the lesser twice*, etc. *A triple multiple interval is a harmonic space where the greater contains the lesser three times*, and so on for the rest; these are essential definitions, and they cannot be otherwise; indeed, they are of eternal truth, as we demonstrate elsewhere, and they have a necessary connection with the nature of things. There are also Axioms or "Pronouncements" in the science of Music, which are propositions
<margin>Axioms in Music.</margin> known through themselves and by the light of nature. Such as: *Whatever harmonically measures another, also measures that which is measured by it*, etc. *A harmonic compound is resolved into the same simple elements from which it is composed*, etc. *Whatever measures the part taken away and the remainder, also measures the whole*; and many similar ones which we treat elsewhere by design. The Postulates are: *Given an equal string, as the proportion of space is to space,
<margin>Postulates in Music.</margin> so also is the proportion of sound to sound.* And similar ones, from which come the most certain conclusions, as in this whole work

### CHAPTER III.
### On the Division and Definition of Music.

<margin>Worldly Music.</margin>
Music, taken in its broadest sense, is nothing other than a discordant concord or a concordant discord of various things concurring to establish a single whole, concerning which we shall treat extensively in the final book; and it is either natural or artificial. Natural music encompasses the entire nature of things harmonically arranged, or what is the same thing, **Worldly Music**, containing the admirable harmony of the heavens, the elements, and mixed bodies. To this category, **Human Music** is also recalled, which consists either in the harmonic composition of the body, or in the wondrous order, disposition, <term>eukrasia</term> <note>original: "εὐκρασία" - a healthy balancing of bodily humors or qualities</note>, and concord of the senses, both internal and external, as will be discussed in its proper place.

<margin>Artificial Music is twofold.</margin>
Artificial music is either organic or harmonic. **Organic** contains the ingenious construction and use of instruments under a triple order: Wind, Stringed, and Percussion, concerning which we treat professionally in the entirety of Book V. **Harmonic Music** is that which, by means of sense and reason, considers the differences of sounds, modulations, and consonances, which we treat in various ways throughout four entire books, namely the Third, Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth.

<margin>What are speculative and practical Music?</margin>
Some divide Music into speculative and practical. Hence, the **theoretical musician** is said to be he who, excluding the senses, judges by reason alone whatever can occur in harmonic music. The **practical musician**, however, relying on sense alone, is ignorant of the cause of his operation as such; for which reason the theorist is as much nobler than the practitioner as science is more eminent than art; yet both are imperfect according to that saying:
*He is a beast, not a singer, who sings not by art, but by habit.*

<margin>Who is the perfect Musician?</margin>
Therefore, he alone is and ought to be called a **perfect Musician** who joins theory with practice; who not only knows how to compose, but can also give an account of the reason for every single thing. To perform this with dignity, however, a knowledge of almost all sciences is required: namely Arithmetic, Geometry, the Proportions of sounds, practical Music both vocal and instrumental, Meter, History, Dialectics, Rhetoric, and finally an absolute knowledge of all Philosophy. Thus, we define Music, taken in its rigor, as nothing other than *the perfect science of harmonic sounds occurring in any genre*, of which we place a certain archetype in this *Universal Musurgy* or *Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*. But having premised these things <term>katholikoteros</term> <note>original: "καθολικωτέρως" - more generally or universally</note>, let us now follow each in order, beginning with the various music of different Nations.

### CHAPTER IV.
### CONCERNING ANCIENT MUSIC
### And the Instruments of the Hebrews, and of what kind they were.

<margin>The multi-stringed Lyre before the flood.</margin>
Just as the invention of strings was easy, so also no one should doubt that it is most ancient and of primeval times. Since nothing is so necessary as the use of threads for binding various things together, and every extension of any threads whatever excites a certain pleasing sound, and from the varying tension of strings various sounds are born, nothing was easier for men skilled in music <note>original: "Musurgis"</note>, having first been taught by this experience, than to eventually invent instruments of every kind. Indeed, Sacred Scripture teaches us that the **multi-stringed Lyre** existed before the flood, and the Book of Kings and the Psalms teach that David used a **ten-stringed Psaltery**.

->**What kind of instrument was the Davidic Psaltery?**<- <margin>What was the Davidic Psaltery like?</margin>
No one has yet correctly defined what the Davidic Psaltery was; some believe it was not so much a specific instrument as a term denoting certain types of harmony and the modulation of the voice and sound. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> records that it had twelve sounds and was plucked with the fingers. Hilary, Didymus, Basil, and Euthymius <note>Prominent early Christian theologians and Church Fathers</note> call it the "most upright" of all musical instruments, containing nothing perverse or crooked within itself, because it was struck on the upper part. For this reason, it seems to have lacked the hollow shell [of a lute]; Augustine says it was carried by the hands of the player and had the "tortoise-shell" <note>original: *testudinem*; referring to the resonance box or vaulted soundboard</note> on the upper part—that is, the hollow wood upon which the strings rest to resonate—whereas the Citharas <note>ancient lyres or lutes</note> have this on the bottom. Jerome describes this instrument as being shaped like a square shield with ten strings. Hilary maintains it is the same as the *Nevel*, or *Nablium*. It is certain that the Psaltery was equipped with strings, and according to Suidas <note>author of a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>, the word for "playing the psaltery" <note>original: *psallendi*</note> means to pluck the strings with the tips of the fingers. A large portion of musicians attribute to it a likeness to our modern Harp, and they commonly depict it in its image with a triangular shape, which Apollodorus (as cited in Athenaeus) says was called the *magadis* <note>original: μαγάδιν; an ancient bridge-like stringed instrument</note>, and Aristotle calls the *trigonon* <note>original: τρίγωνον; literally "triangle"</note>; Suidas calls it the *Sambuca* <note>a triangular stringed instrument of Oriental origin</note>. Thus it follows that the strings in a psaltery were of unequal length, which Porphyry also records regarding the *Sambuca* in an ancient lexicon. Some say this psaltery and the *Nablium* are the same, based on those lines from Ovid’s third book of *The Art of Love*:

*Learn also to sweep the festive nablia with both palms,*
*They are suited to sweet melodies.* <note>original: *Disce etiam duplici genialia nablia palma / Verrere, conueniunt dulcibus illa modis.*</note>

This agrees with what Schilte <note>referring to Abraham Portaleone, author of *Shilte Ha-Gibborim*</note> asserts; for he says the *Nevel* was a stringed instrument and was divided into three octaves with twenty-two strings. The *Asur*, however, consisted of ten strings; the *Kinnor* of thirty-two; the *Machul* of six; and the *Minnim* of three or four strings. He claims the *Nevel* was constructed in the shape of a trapezoid, while the *Kinnor* was made in the likeness of the modern Cithara <note>likely meaning a lute or guitar-like instrument here</note>; the *Machul* and *Minnim* were like the Viola and the *Chelys* <note>original: *Chelym*; a lyre made from a tortoise shell</note>. However, lest I be too long-winded in reviewing the *Neginoth* <note>stringed instruments</note>, I have decided to share them here with the reader as drawn from an ancient Vatican manuscript, where the psaltery is shown under

-> [Hebrew: *Asur* / עשור] [Hebrew: *Nevel* / נבל] [Hebrew: *Kinnor* / כנור] <-
-> [Three illustrations of stringed instruments labeled A, I, and B] <-
-> A . . . . . . I . . . . . . B <-

form A, the *Kinnor* under B, the *Machul* under C, the *Minnim* under E, and the *Nevel* under I. <note>Note: Only A, I, and B are pictured in this specific woodcut section.</note> Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, a 17th-century polymath and music theorist</note> defines the new and ancient Cithara under a different figure. It appears that it bore a resemblance to our Harp, distinct with twenty-four strings across three octaves <note>original: *trisdiapason*</note>. What that mystical "ten-stringed instrument" <note>original: *decacordon*</note> was—representing the harmony of the triple world—will be described more fully elsewhere, as well as in our *Musica Hieroglyphica*.

The *Haghniugab* <note>likely *Agniugab*, a corruption of *Ugab*</note>, a stringed instrument (mentioned in the Targum <note>Aramaic translation of the Bible</note> of both Onkelos and Uziel), was not unlike the larger instrument commonly called the *Viola da gamba*, and it consisted of six strings. See Rabbi Hannase, chapter 10 of the *Shilte Ha-Gibborim*; it is frequently confused with the *Machul*, for they differ only in the number of strings.

50 On the Consonance and Dissonance of the Great Art.

§ I.
On the Percussion Instruments of the Hebrews.

The Hebrews used percussion instruments <note>original: "κρουστοῖς [kroustois] siue pulsatilibus"</note>, as testified by the *Shields of the Mighty* <note>original: "Schiltehaggibborim"; an encyclopedic work by Abraham Portaleone (1612) on Temple rituals</note>, where they are described in these words:

<note>Translation from the Hebrew:</note> "And they also knew the *Shoshanim* [Lilies], the *Machalat* [Dance instrument], the *Shushan Edut* [Lily of Testimony], the *Mashkirot* [Whistles], the *Kithros* [Lyre], the *Shavva*, the *Psanterin* [Psaltery], the *Simponiah* [Dulcimer or Bagpipe], the *Magrepha* of the Temple, the *Hydraulis* [Water organ], the *Tabla Guchana*, the *Ugav* [Flute/Organ], the *Taph* [Drum], the *Mena'ane'im* [Sistrums], the *Tseltselim* [Cymbals], and their like."

That is: Our fathers knew of the instruments: *Haschufanim*, *Hammechilath*, *Haschhusan-gnaduth*, *Mesbrakitha*, *Hakithros*, *Haschhabra*, *Hasphanderin*, *Hamingnanghin*, *Hasimphunia*, the *Magrepha* of the Talmud, the *Hydraulis*, the *Tabla gutgana*, the *Ugav*, the *Taph*, the *Mena'ane'im*, the *Hazalzaloth*, and similar ones, about each of which we shall speak.

I. On the Hebrew Drum called the *Toph* [תוף]. <margin>תוף</margin>

The author of the *Shields of the Mighty* states that the Hebrew drum had its origin among the Egyptians.

<note>Translation from the Hebrew:</note> "The Egyptian priests in particular used the drum in the temple of the 'Mother of All Gods,' who is called the goddess Vesta and represents the foundation of the earth; and our ancestors received it from them."

For the Egyptian priests used the drum especially in the shrine of the great Mother of the Gods, who is called the goddess Vesta and signifies the foundation of the earth. (Behold its form from the cited author;) Rabbi Abraham Portaleone <note>original: "Abraham Hannasè"</note> testifies that it had a different shape from modern drums. For he says it had the likeness of a ship or a skiff, which is why it was called a *Cymbalum* by the Greeks; for to the Greeks, a *Cymbalum* is nothing other than a musical instrument in the shape of a *Cymba* <note>a small boat or skiff</note>. He adds, moreover, that this instrument

[Illustration of a boat-shaped drum with two drumsticks, labeled with the letter N]

ment was covered with the skin of an animal, and then was struck with a plectrum like a pestle or a rod of iron or bronze, with a stroke now strong, now soft; with sounds now thick and frequent, and sometimes sparse and dull, just as is customary with our drums. Indeed, I have thought it best to include its likeness here, along with the citation from the author’s text:

<note>Translation from the Hebrew:</note> "The drum was called *Cymbalos* because of its shape, which was like a small ship called *cymba* in the Greek tongue; and it was called *Cymbalon* because it is like a small ship without a lid, made of metal such as copper or some other metal, long and narrow at its head and end, and wide and somewhat hollow in its middle."

...not a stringed instrument, but rather a percussion instrument <note>original: "pulsatile"</note> as he believes he has demonstrated with the most manifest arguments. For he says that this was the same as the Egyptian *Sistrum* or the Greek *krembalon* <note>a type of clapper or castanet</note>; he describes it as a circle surrounded by many small bells, usually made of iron, bronze, silver, or gold. But let us hear his own words:

<note>Translation from the Hebrew: "The Machol is a round instrument made like a hoop, with many bells fixed around it, and it is made of various metals..."</note>

->[Illustration: A circular metal frame with six small rings or bells attached to its outer edge.]<-
-><term>Machol</term> <note>Hebrew: מחול; traditionally meaning a dance, but interpreted here by Portaleone as a circular rattling instrument.</note><-

But perhaps, having made a comparison, we might better say that a *Sistrum* of this kind can be numbered among the instruments called *Zalzfaloth* <note>Cymbals</note> and *Minangnghinim* <note>Shakers/Rattles</note>—that is, among those which consist of many small bells.

For an instrument of this kind in no way corresponds to the *Sistrum* of the Egyptians. As we have shown at length in our *Egyptian Music* <note>A reference to Kircher’s own work, "Musurgia Universalis," or his studies on hieroglyphics</note>, the *Sistrum* was an iron instrument not equipped with small bells, but with iron rings on rods and a handle; when shaken, it produced a certain somber rattling sound from the collision of the iron rings both with each other and with the iron or bronze bars upon which they were threaded. You will find their form and mystical significance described most extensively in our *Oedipus* <note>Referring to "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," Kircher's massive work on Egyptology</note>, in the book on the Hieroglyphic Music of the Egyptians. However, I am led to believe that the Hebrew *Sistrum* or *Thoph* <note>A frame drum or timbrel</note> was manufactured in imitation of this, because young women everywhere used this kind of *Sistrum* for the dances <note>original: "tripudijs," a rhythmic three-step dance</note> performed at weddings, as we read in Exodus and the Book of Judges concerning Miriam, the sister of Moses, and the daughter of Jephthah. I have also learned from witnesses worthy of belief that the use of this *Sistrum* still persists in Palestine today.

### III. עץ ברושים Gnets Berusim.

I have found no one among the Rabbis who has correctly described what or what kind of instrument this was. Some confuse it with *Crotala* <note>castanets</note>; some wish it to be the same as the rustic instrument commonly called *Gnaccari* <note>likely "nakers" or small kettledrums</note>. Others confuse it with the *Sistrum*. Only Rabbi Hannasè <note>Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, the "Prince"</note> seems to have touched upon the truth when he describes it in these words:

<note>Translation from the Hebrew: "The Gnets Berusim are two pieces of fir wood that one strikes against the other to make a sound..."</note>

->[Illustration: A bell-shaped wooden or metal base being struck by a long, handled wooden mallet with rounded ends.]<-
-><term>Gnets Berusim</term> <note>Hebrew: עץ ברושים; literally "Fir Wood" or "Cypress Wood." Mentioned in 2 Samuel 6:5.</note><-

As far as I could determine, he says the *Gnets Berusim* were joined instruments, sounding with a clear tone, yet without harmony—as is usually the case with other stringed instruments <note>original: "fidicinis"</note>. In substance, they are nothing other than two pieces of fir wood. One of these is similar to a small mortar, the other similar to a small, long, round pestle, in the middle of which is a small handle, and on its two heads there were certain protruding nodes...

->### IV. <term>Minangnhinim</term> <note>Hebrew: מנענעים; from the root "to shake." Usually translated as rattles or sistrums.</note><-

There is no less controversy among authors regarding the meaning of this name. Some take it to mean a psaltery <note>a stringed instrument</note>, others a cymbal; many take it to mean children’s rattles. Hannase <note>Referring to Abraham Portaleone, author of "Shilte ha-Gibborim"</note> explains it best of all in the cited passage, with these words:

<note>Translation from the Hebrew: "The Minangnhinim is a square wooden board with a handle. Small balls of wood or metal are attached to it by chains or ropes. When shaken or struck, these balls hit the board and each other to create a loud, ringing sound."</note>

"This instrument," he says, "is a certain square wooden board, at the top of which is a handle suitable for gripping. On top of the board, here and there, are wooden or bronze globes <note>beads or small balls</note> attached by iron chains or even hempen strings stretched across the board; and when the board is struck, those globes emit a very clear sound, perceivable from a distance, both against each other and against the board."

->[Illustration: A wooden percussion instrument featuring a rectangular board on a handle. A horizontal bar at the top holds several dangling chains or cords ending in round metal balls. The letter 'R' marks the base of the handle.]<-

The <term>Magraphe Tamid</term> <note>Hebrew: מגריפה; literally "shovel," but here describing a Temple instrument used for the "Daily Sacrifice" or Tamid</note> was a different instrument from the *Magraphe* mentioned in the *Aruchin*. The former was a percussion instrument used to summon the people to the Temple, possessing a sound so powerful that Hannase says it could be heard as far away as the city of Jericho. No one, however, can explain its exact shape or how it produced such a portentous sound. They say, nevertheless, that it was placed in the courtyard of the Jerusalem Temple, and the place was so vaulted that the "voice" of this instrument, reflected and multiplied in various ways against the curved surface of the dome, produced a sound that could be perceived even in Jericho. It was an instrument instituted for summoning the Priests and Levites, and for signaling those who were impure to stand at the Temple gates. Certainly, if it is permitted to settle the matter with conjectures, I would suggest that this instrument had something in common with our larger bells, which are commonly known to be heard at a very great distance. What the *Magraphe* of the *Aruchin* was will be discussed shortly.

## Section III.
## On the Wind Instruments of the Hebrews.

### I. The *Mafrakitha*
The **Mafrakitha** <note>original: *Mafrakitha*</note>—so called from the whistling sound it produced—was an instrument of "many reeds" <note>original Greek: *polykalamos*</note>, which were bound together and fixed in a graduated fashion into a piece of wood shaped like a case. The reeds were open at the top, while the bottom was sealed with wood and a covering of skin. It was equipped with a handle, from which the wider box gradually narrowed into a smaller space. The instrument was applied to the lips, and by blowing into it while the fingers alternately closed and opened the holes on the side, various sounds were perceived according to the length, width, or shortness of the pipes, or even the intensity of the breath. From this, I conclude that this instrument was exactly the same as the **Syrinx** <note>The classic "Panpipes," named after the nymph Syrinx.</note> or the "seven-piped flute of Pan" <note>original Greek: *heptaulo Panos*</note>, as will be made clear shortly.

->משרוקיתא<-
<note>Hebrew/Aramaic: *Mashrokitha*, a term used in the Book of Daniel for a pipe or whistle.</note>

[Illustration: A set of panpipes mounted onto a rectangular wooden base with a handle.]

### II. The *Sāpunia*
The **Sāpunia**, a word corrupted from the Greek *symphonia* <note>original Greek: *symphonia*</note> if I am not mistaken, is mentioned (as was the previous instrument) in the third chapter of Daniel in these Aramaic words:

->*די בעדנא די תשמעון קל קרנא משרוקיתא קיתרס שבכא פסנתרין וסמפוניא וכל זני זמרא*<-
<note>Daniel 3:5: "That at the time you hear the sound of the horn, the pipe, the lyre, the sambuca, the psaltery, the bagpipe, and all kinds of music..."</note>

That is: *at the time when you shall hear the voice of the horn, the pipe (many-reeded), the lyre, the sambuca, the psaltery, and the symphony, and every kind of music, etc.* This corresponds to the Greek version: *Whenever you hear the sound of the trumpet, the pipe, the lyre, the sambuca, the psaltery, and the symphony, and every kind of music.* <note>original Greek: ὅτα ὡς ἂν ἀκούσητε τῆς φωνῆς τῆς σάλπιγγος, σύριγγος τε καὶ κιθάρας, σαμβύκης τε καὶ ψαλτηρίου καὶ συμφωνίας, καὶ πάντος γένους μουσικῶν.</note> Where the Aramaic says "horn," the Greek reading has "sound of the trumpet" <note>original Greek: *phōnēs tēs salpingos*</note>.

The **Sampunia** <note>An alternative spelling of *Sāpunia* used by the author.</note> is therefore understood not as a simple pipe, but as the *Shilte ha-Gibborim* <note>term: <term>Shilte ha-Gibborim</term> (Shields of the Heroes): An encyclopedic 16th-century work by Abraham Portaleone that attempted to reconstruct the musical instruments of the ancient Temple in Jerusalem.</note> describes it. It was a "double-pipe" instrument <note>original Greek: *diaulon*</note>, between which was placed a round bladder <note>original: *uter*</note> made from the skin of a ram or a wether. Two pipes were inserted into this bladder: one pointing upward and the other downward. When the upper channel was blown into, the bag filled with breath; when squeezed, it supplied air to the lower pipe, which produced various sounds through the openings of the holes arranged upon it, guided by the fingers. We provide its figure elsewhere. From this, it is clear that it was entirely similar to our small bagpipe <note>original: *utriculo*</note>, which shepherds and peasants use everywhere. Indeed, it is quite a marvel that in Italy to this very day, it is called by this name: the pastoral **Zampugna**.

[Illustration: A bagpipe featuring a leather bellows/bag with two wooden pipes attached.]

*Masra-* <note>Catchword for the next page: *Masrakitha*.</note>

Mention is made here and there in the Sacred Scriptures of various pipes; nonetheless, these can always be traced back to one of the three aforementioned types.

56 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance* <note>original: "Artis Magnæ Consoni, & Dissoni"; this is the title of the work, reflecting Kircher’s study of the harmony of the universe.</note>

...that is, in ten diverse types of instruments, they would praise God with instruments that served to express [1] difficult matters; second, matters pertaining to victory; third, Psalms to be recited to God; fourth, love songs; fifth, divine praises; sixth, prayer and the mind's trust in God; seventh, blessings; eighth, confessions; ninth, beatitudes; and tenth, those serving the joyful dances of the soul. To these, some add:

[Musical and poetic titles:] Protection, Memorial, Instruction, Do Not Destroy, Song of Loves, Young Voices, Golden Poem, Wild Rhythm, Flutes, Testimony, The Silent Dove of Far-off Lands. <note>original Hebrew: זינה זכירה משכיל אל השחת שיר ידידות עלמות מכתם שגיון נחילות עדות יונה אלם רחקים. These terms are found in the headings of the biblical Psalms and are believed to indicate specific melodies or instruments.</note>

<margin>Diverse instruments served diverse emotional states among the Hebrews. A great variety of Hebrew music.</margin> These names are indeed the titles of the Psalms; thus, different instruments were employed to stir different emotions in the soul. To stir divine praise in the minds of men, they employed every kind of pipe. For hymns of confession and thanksgiving, they used harps, psalteries, and similar instruments. To stir spiritual joys and dances, they used trumpets, the *Magrephah* <note>original: "Magrephis"; an ancient organ-like instrument used in the Temple to signal the priests.</note>, and cymbals. In the Temple, while solemn rites were performed, not everyone sounded their instruments together in a confused way; rather, the singers were distributed into choirs and sang together in alternating melodies.

For voices, as Kalonymus <note>A Jewish philosopher and translator, likely Kalonymus ben Kalonymus.</note> rightly says, were not mixed with certain instruments of greater noise and sharper sound (such as trumpets and trombones) or cymbals, lest the power of the words be lost, drowned out by the clamor of the percussion. Instead, voices were joined to harps and organs of a milder sound. Sometimes only stringed instruments were heard; at other times, only wind instruments; then again, *stringed melodies* <note>original Hebrew: נגינות (Neginot)</note> were perceived only by alternating choirs. Often, they competed together, mixed with voices to create a greater variety. The "Choragus" <note>A Greek term for a choir leader or producer.</note> of all these was the Royal Prophet himself, the author of the Psalms, some of which he sang with his own mouth. For there were, if we believe Sixtus of Siena <note>A 16th-century Dominican scholar and theologian.</note>, four thousand singers on instruments established by David. Among them, three were the most prominent, who sang the songs in the Temple alongside him on lyres, psalteries, and cymbals: namely Heman, Jeduthun, and Asaph. Ezra testifies that Asaph praised God "through the hands of King David," which is to say, using the Psalms written by King David’s hand.

<margin>The singers of David: Heman, Jeduthun, Asaph.</margin>

§. V.
Concerning the More Famous Musicians among the Hebrews.

**Asaph**, son of Berachiah, was the prince of the singers sounding brass cymbals and praising the Lord, ministering in the presence of the Ark. According to the interpreters, he is thought to have composed some of the Psalms himself.

**Heman the Ezrahite**, a singer and son of Joel from the sons of Kohath, was most skilled in cymbals and the trumpet. He was in some way equal to Ethan in learning and wisdom. He is thought to have composed the eighty-first Psalm, which begins, "O Lord, God of my salvation." Because he gave this to the sons of Korah to be sung, he inscribed it with both his own name and theirs.

**Ethan the Ezrahite**, son of Kushaiah from the sons of Merari, resounded with brass cymbals and was endowed with such wisdom that, according to the Book of Kings, no mortal was ever wiser than he, except for Solomon himself. There were also notable singers among the three sons of Korah—Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph—who were occupied with composing Psalms.

**Jeduthun** was an extraordinary singer and a most excellent player of the lyre <note>original: "Cytharædus"</note>, whom many confuse with Orpheus. <note>Kircher frequently draws parallels between biblical figures and Greek mythological heroes to show a unified history of music.</note> Since the directors of divine praise were of such quality and greatness—indeed, divinely imbued with the knowledge of singing and playing—it is only right that we believe they sang their hymns, composed with the highest artistry and genius, with a matching excellence of voice, rather than with a crude and unpolished confusion of sounds. No one should doubt that there were many others, especially in the <margin>The excellence of Solomon's music.</margin> time of King Solomon, who were most excellent masters of song <note>original: "phonascos"</note> in whose hands lay the power of the divinely instituted choir. For it was fitting for the wisest of mortals to have the wisest music, perfect in every rhythm, surpassing all the music of the Greeks and those who came after...
