### CHAPTER V.
### On the Music of David.

**H**aving prefaced these matters, it will at least be worth the effort to discuss a little more deeply in this chapter the style and mode observed by David in the composition of his hymns.

#### §. I.
#### Whether the Davidic Psalms were written in prose, or indeed in verse, and in what genre of verse?

<margin>David composed the psalms in a metric style.</margin> **P**hilastrius of Brescia <note>An 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies.</note> reports that there were heretics who asserted that David was a composer of profane and secular songs, an error also attributed to Paul of Samosata <note>A 3rd-century bishop whose teachings were condemned as heretical.</note>. In our own century, the Anabaptists say that the Book of Psalms was not written by David, but by certain more recent Jews after the death of Christ. However, the most holy Gospel of GOD, by quoting the psalms, easily refutes them. There are others who think that the metric style of writing <note>Writing in formal poetic meter rather than prose.</note> is soft, profane, and fit only for composing fables, or used to delineate various and impure emotions of anger or love; they cannot persuade themselves that any sacred books were ever written poetically. Indeed, for this reason, there were those who thought the Book of Job was not a true history, but a tragi-comic fiction of the Hebrews. However, it will be our task to utterly abolish this unfair judgment and to show, from every kind of erudition, that David composed his psalms in no other way than in a metric style.

First, there is no lack of irrefragable testimonies of Holy Scripture that clearly assert this: *The priests stood in their offices, and the Levites with the instruments of the Lord’s songs, which King David had made, singing the hymns of David with their own hands.* <note>Original Latin: "Sacerdotes stabant in officijs suis..." citing 2 Chronicles 7:6.</note> And the same is said in 1 Esdras 3 <note>Likely referring to the book of Ezra.</note>. In 2 Kings 23 <note>In the Vulgate, 2 Samuel is often titled 2 Kings.</note>, an elegant passage says: *These are the last words that David the son of Jesse said, the excellent psalmist of Israel.* And in Ecclesiasticus 47 <note>The Book of Sirach.</note> it is said of David: *He set singers before the altar, and in their voices he made sweet melodies.* There are those who think that whenever mention is made of "songs" in the Scriptures, it refers to the psalms of David, as in Ecclesiasticus 44: *Let us praise famous men, etc. and: Narrating the songs of the Scriptures in their youth.* For it seems that "youth" <note>original: "pueritia"</note> should be read there, not "skill" <note>original: "peritia"</note>, although the Greek word found there signifies both <note>The author is likely referring to the Greek word "paideia," which can relate to childhood training or education/skill.</note>. Saint David loved pious music from his cradle and from his youth (these are the words of Augustine, Letter 13, near the end) and he inflames us in the study of it more than any other author.

Second, this same point is concluded from the harmonious voice of the entire Church and the Fathers, asserting that David was a divine poet and his psalms are songs. Whence in the hymn on the Passion of the Lord (the author of which is the Christian poet Venantius Fortunatus), it is said:
*The things are fulfilled which*
*David sang in faithful song.*
And Sedulius, in his *Paschal Work*, says:
*Why should I, accustomed to Davidic songs, etc.*
Blessed Jerome, in the prologue of the Bible to Paulinus, speaks thus of David: *David [is our] Simonides.* <note>original: "Dauid Simonides"; Jerome is comparing David to Simonides of Ceos, a famous Greek lyric poet, to emphasize David's status as a master of religious verse.</note>

<note>original: "monides"</note> Simonides, our Pindar, and Alcaeus, as well as Horace, Catullus, and Serenus, sound forth Christ upon the lyre, and with the ten-stringed psaltery awaken Him rising from the dead, etc. St. Jerome <note>original: "Idem"</note> holds the same in his Preface to the books of Kings. And St. Ambrose, in his preface to the Psalms, speaks divine truths concerning David, the sacred leader of songs, and likewise concerning Moses, the composer of two songs. Regarding these same two, Eusebius in Book 11, *On the Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, says that their songs are in hexameter, trimeter, or tetrameter <note>Terms for different poetic meters based on the number of rhythmic "feet" per line.</note>; and that those things pertaining to style are most elegant, weighty, and pleasant. However, regarding their meaning, he says no human writing can be compared to them. St. Augustine, in Book 17 of *The City of God*, chapter 14, and in Letter 131 toward the end, also writes this. All these authors marvelously extol the songs of David and discuss the reasons that drove him to compose them. To these, add St. Athanasius, who speaks excellently of David in his *Synopsis*. Josephus, in Book 7, chapter 10, says: "David, having now completed his wars and dangers, and living in the deepest peace, composed odes and hymns in honor of GOD in various types of songs—partly in trimeter verse, partly in pentameter; and having prepared musical instruments, he taught the Levites to sing praises to GOD to their beat." Cassiodorus, in his Prologue to the Psalter, chapter 15, says that every mode of poetic speech took its beginning from the divine Scriptures, namely from David; just as all authors report that all other literature was derived from the Hebrews to the Greeks and Latins. Certainly, it is clearly evident that before the founding of Troy, before the voyage of the Argonauts, and before the beginning of the Olympiads, Moses, Deborah, the mother of Samuel <note>Hannah.</note>, and David had already observed the laws of song to the highest degree <note>original: "ad amussim," meaning with the precision of a carpenter's rule.</note> when they composed their Canticles according to metrical laws. Indeed, it is established by the testimony of Josephus, Justin, Origen, and Eusebius that profane <note>Non-religious or secular ancient authors.</note> authors borrowed much from here.

<margin>The Greeks learned Poetics from the Hebrews.</margin>

#### §. II.
#### On the titles of the Psalms.

<margin>The Psalms were composed to be sung with Instruments.</margin>
<margin>What does the phrase "Unto the end" in the titles of the Psalms mean?</margin>
<margin>In the titles of the Psalms, the instruments to which the Psalm was to be sung are noted.</margin>

The titles of the Psalms sufficiently declare that they were accustomed to be sung with organs and musical instruments. This is clear from the passages of Scripture and the Church Fathers already cited, but most especially from the titles of the psalms themselves. Many of these titles contain certain words that signify the musical instruments themselves to which such-and-such a psalm was to be sung. For example, the title of Psalm 4 is as follows: <note>original Hebrew: למנצח</note> *To the Chief Musician* <note>original: "La-menatzeach"</note>. *Unto the end, In songs, A Psalm of David.* The phrase "Unto the end" <note>original: "In finem"</note> is explained by the Doctors of the Church not in one way, but in various ways. St. Jerome translates it as "To the Victor." Others, such as Cajetan, translate it as "To the One Overcoming." However, "Victor" in this context signifies, as the Hebrews believe, the Prefect of the singers—the *Master of the Chapel* <note>original: "il Maestro di Capella"</note>. For in the choir during David's time, there was a leader and Master who directed the other singers, who possessed a more excellent voice and a more exact skill in musical matters; to him, David gave the psalms to be sung to musical instruments. Regarding this "Victor" (or whom we now call the Cantor, from singing; or the *Choragus*, being the head of the choir), there are those who think that in the title of the fourth psalm, that passage from Habakkuk 3 should be understood: *And the Victor will lead me upon my high places, singing in psalms.* Therefore, the "Victor" is the same as the Master Musician, or the leader of the singers.

What follows in the title of the same psalm, "In songs" <note>original: "In carminibus"</note>, greatly supports our view. For many among the Hebrews think the Hebrew word found there signifies a specific musical instrument designed for singing joyful and triumphant themes. Hence, where our version has the whole title as *Unto the end, In songs*, the Hebrews have *To the Prefect of the Singers, to musical instruments*. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, a medieval commentator.</note>, in his exposition of the title of Psalm 4, signifies by this title that effort by which the singers would strive to surpass and "conquer" <note>A play on the Latin "Victor."</note> one another in singing with joy; all of them singing psalms so heartily that they seemed to contend as if for a victory, etc. It cannot be denied, therefore, that the literal meaning implies the psalm itself is a song; and thus it is to be sung as a song in praise of GOD, even if in a spiritual and higher sense the phrase "Unto the end" signifies Christ (who is the end) and the mysteries of the Church which were to be carried out at the end of the ages.

**Book II. Philological [Treatise] on Hebrew & Greek Music. 59**

<margin>The titles of the Psalms indicate that the Psalms are songs.</margin>

Again, Psalm 5 reads: <note>original Hebrew: למנצח אל הנחילות מזמור לדוד</note> "To the leader, upon the flutes: a lyrical song of David." Regarding the term *hannehiloth* <note>A term often translated as "wind instruments" or "inheritances."</note>, the scholar Vatablus says: "It was a certain distinguished musical instrument," etc. This psalm of David was therefore entrusted to the most skillful master of the lyre-players, to be sung to the *hannehiloth*. Nicholas of Lyra <note>A prominent medieval Franciscan theologian.</note> is of the same opinion. Furthermore, the title of Psalm 6 is "for the <note>original Hebrew: השמינית</note> Eighth," that is, for the most intense tone and the clearest voice (the *hyperdiapason* <note>An interval an octave above the standard range.</note>). For this "eighth" voice, as we have shown elsewhere, is most suitable for children, women, and men alike; from this, it is evident that the use of the octave, which the Greeks call the *diapason*, was already in use long ago. This psalm was given to a very distinguished master of the musicians to be sung to the *Neghinoth* <note>A general term for stringed instruments.</note>, a musical instrument. Hence the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates it thus: "In praise for the singer, and a lyre of eight strings." In Psalm 9, the Hebrew reads: <note>original Hebrew: על מות לבן למנצח</note> "A Psalm for *Muthlabben*," that is, according to the melodies of a common song whose beginning was *Muthlabben* <note>Literally "Death of the son"; many scholars believe these titles refer to well-known tunes of the time.</note>. And in Psalm 21, the title has: <note>original Hebrew: למנצח על אילת השחר</note> "A song of David concerning the Hind of the Morning," meaning it was to be sung in the manner of a popular song whose beginning was "The Hind of the Morning." Thus says Vatablus; for St. Jerome also translates it as "For the morning hind," and Felix <note>Likely Felix Pratensis, a Jewish convert and scholar of the early 16th century.</note> as "For the hind of the dawn." All these things clearly express that the Psalms themselves are songs. Otherwise, we would have to admit that prose speeches were sung to musical instruments, which is almost unheard of and absurd among all nations. For it should be known that just as among Comic and Tragic poets, the type of instrument to which they were to be sung was marked immediately in the titles of the comedies (namely, with "equal pipes" or "unequal pipes," as in Terence: "Performed at the Megalensian games with two pipes"—a point also noted by Steuco of Gubbio in the title of Psalm 4, etc.), so in the titles of the Psalms, certain instruments are named to which they were to be sung, as we have shown.

<margin>The Wine-presses in the title of Psalm 8.</margin>

But the title of Psalm 8 must not be overlooked. For it says: <note>original Hebrew: למנצח על הגתית</note> "To the end, for the Wine-presses." Rabbi David <note>David Kimchi, also known as Radak, a medieval grammarian.</note> thinks that the Hebrew word found there, namely *Githith*, is the name of a musical instrument to which that psalm was to be sung. Others say it is the name of a Philistine city called Gath, either because David sang that psalm in that city, or because the instrument it was sung to was brought from that city—much like Pindar speaks of the "Dorian Lyre." For so says Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the most famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, as does Nicholas of Lyra here. Cardinal Cajetan adds here that this lyre had the shape of a wine-press (*torcular*), and that the etymology of the word is taken from "wine-press." Hence the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and St. Jerome translated it here as "The Wine-presses." Others say this psalm is called *Githith* because it was handed over to be sung by a certain singer, a son of Obed-Edom the Gittite. I believe it was named after the city of Gath where this kind of melody flourished, just as the Greeks spoke of "Dorian," "Lydian," and "Phrygian" songs after the peoples among whom they were in use; this practice still flourishes today. However, perhaps it also took its name from the wine-press because it was usually sung at the time of the wine-presses, during the Feast of Tabernacles, shortly after the crops were gathered and the grapes pressed in the wine-presses, as mentioned in Leviticus 23. Nor is it unfitting for this psalm to have been sung at the time of the wine-presses as a thanksgiving for the year’s fertility and the abundance of the vintages, along with Psalms 80 and 83, which are marked with the same title. All this is true provided that these also signify, in a mystical sense, the higher mysteries of Christ and the Church. I not only do not condemn this view but rather think that those who are content with the "husk" of the bare letter and feed on pods—rejecting the true food provided in the spiritual sense—should be most vehemently rebuked.

<margin>What the word "Selah," placed 73 times in the Psalms, signifies.</margin>

Furthermore, the word *Selah* often causes much trouble for the Doctors. First, this word is never found in the Hebrew codices (as Cajetan well notes on Psalm 3) except in the Psalms (and indeed seventy-three times) and once in the Prayer of Habakkuk, chapter 3. From this, the common opinion of the Hebrews becomes probable: that it is a word pertaining to the singing of the meter. Hence some say that the word signifies a change in meter...

for they express the force of this particle. The word *Selah* <note>A term found frequently in the Psalms, often interpreted as a musical or liturgical sign.</note> is derived from the root *Salal*, as Pagninus <note>Santes Pagnino, a renowned Hebraist and author of the *Thesaurus Linguae Sanctae*.</note> noted in his *Thesaurus of the Holy Tongue*, coming from the verbs *Sal* and *Salal*. In that work, following Rabbi Abraham, he says the word *Selah* is not significant of a specific meaning, but rather a directive for the singing, derived from the verb *Salal*, which means to exalt, to lift up, or to intensify. Regarding this, Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French humanist scholar.</note> says in his greater commentaries on Psalm 3: "Formerly, the singers were accustomed to raise their voices and cry out whenever this word occurred, as if they were saying: *Oh, what a heavy calamity! Let all our friends see and weigh it well.*" Cardinal Cajetan <note>Tommaso de Vio, a prominent Italian theologian and philosopher.</note>, commenting on Psalm 3, holds the same view and says that this word is "functional"—that is, it has the function of elevating and prolonging the voice. Rabbi Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a prolific medieval Jewish scholar.</note> asserts the same. From these sources, I gather that an elevation of the song and a certain intermission of silence are signified by this word, which in Italian songs is expressed by *piano* <note>original: "piano" (softly)</note> and *forte* <note>original: "forte" (loudly)</note>. Or, perhaps by this word we should understand the *arsis* and *thesis* <note>original Greek: ἄρσιν & θέσιν; the upbeat and downbeat that govern all music.</note> that moderate all musical composition; concerning which, you may see me discuss more extensively elsewhere.

### §. III.
### Concerning the Acrostic Verses of the Psalms.

<margin>Psalms composed and sung in alphabetical order.</margin>
I truly do not know what musical mystery lies hidden in the fact that several psalms are written in alphabetical order with remarkable skill. This style of writing via the letters of the alphabet—where each verse begins with a letter in its proper sequence—is a method specific to meters and poems. Indeed, Saint Hilary, in his commentary on Psalm 118, said there were only three acrostic psalms (that is, composed in alphabetical order): namely Psalms 110, 111, and 118. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Paula of Rome, added another to those three, namely Psalm 144.

<margin>There are seven psalms written alphabetically.</margin>
He even says those who think there are more such psalms are mistaken. However, the truth of the Hebrew Psalter shows that, besides those, there are also Psalms 24, 33, and 36—though the latter proceeds with an interrupted alphabet. This was observed by Cajetan in his commentary on those psalms, as well as by Titelmans, Jansen, Genebrard, and Sixtus of Siena in Book 1 of his *Bibliotheca* under the word *Psalterium*. The Lamentations of Jeremiah are also written in this alphabetical order, as is Chapter 31 of Proverbs, which is called the *Metropædia* <note>Instruction of a Mother</note> of King Samuel.

<margin>The reason for acrostic composition.</margin>
The reason (which seems to be the literal one for this acrostic composition) is that handed down by Rabbi David Kimchi and other Hebrew Doctors, as Sixtus and others note: it is familiar and customary for Hebrew poets to arrange poems dealing with illustrious subjects according to the series of the alphabet, so that they might be more easily impressed upon the memory and, once impressed, cling more tenaciously. It is also true, however, that Saint Jerome and other ancients (as Genebrard noted) believe these psalms were arranged in this series of letters not without great mysteries and Sacraments of the Church. See Jerome’s letter to Paula of Rome, which begins *Nudius tertius* <note>The day before yesterday</note>, in Volume 3, etc. But my interest now is not to pursue tropologies <note>Moral interpretations</note> or anagogies <note>Spiritual or mystical interpretations</note>, but to follow the "naked letter" <note>The literal, historical sense of the text.</note>.

Similarly, we have an example of this in the hymns of the Church; for the priest Sedulius composed a hymn alphabetically. For it begins with the letter A: *From the point of the sun's rising* <note>original Latin hymn: "A solis ortus cardine"</note>; then B: *Blessed author of the world* <note>original: "Beatus author seculi"</note>; and third, C: *The womb of the chaste mother* <note>original: "Castæ parentis viscera"</note>, etc. A part of this hymn is the one sung on the day of Epiphany: *O impious enemy Herod* <note>original: "Hostis Herodes impiè"</note>. And then I: *The Magi went the way they had seen* <note>original: "Ibant Magi quam viderant"</note>; then L: *The washing of the pure stream* <note>original: "Lauacra puri gurgitis"</note>; and so it proceeds all the way to X and Z in the uncorrected version of the hymn.

<margin>That in acrostic Psalms some letter is occasionally omitted.</margin>
But we cannot pass over what is touched upon by others: namely, what might be the cause for the alphabetical order being occasionally inverted in those seven Davidic psalms mentioned. For in Psalm 24, two letters are omitted: *Vau* and *Koph*, with no verse beginning with them. In Psalm 33, the letter *Vau* is again omitted. In Psalm 36, a double verse begins with each Hebrew letter, and sometimes a triple one; but *Hain* <note>The letter Ayin</note> is omitted, for no verse starts with it, and in its place *Zade* or *Tsade* is placed twice. In Psalm 144, the letter *Nun* is missing, and thus even in the Hebrew codex that verse is lacking which should have begun with that letter; although the Seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> added a verse of their own to correspond to that letter...

->§. IV.<-
->On the tropes and figures, and the poetic art<-
->hidden in the psalms.<-

**R**eperitur <note>This "R" is a large initial letter in the original.</note> Furthermore, an epitome of the entire poetic art is found in psalms of this kind; namely, the modes, tropes, figures, metaphors, hyperboles, allusions, personifications <note>original: "prosopopœiæ"</note>, silences <note>original: "aposiopeses"</note>, addresses <note>original: "apostrophes"</note>, exclamations <note>original: "epiphonemata"</note>, etc. of true poetry. And many other ornaments of speech or sentiment proper to poets and verses are found there. This is especially true of those that pertain to diction, which can hardly be done well without rhythm and meter. Since, therefore, they are done so well, so appropriately, and so exactly in the psalms of David, it must be said that the psalms themselves are true poems: and not only true, but the most elegant. For in the psalms there are many poetic figures. First, there is Repetition, as in Psalm 137 <note>original: "136" (Vulgate numbering)</note>: *Lay it bare, lay it bare.* <note>original: "exinanite, exinanite"</note> And that: *Who say to me, Aha, aha.* <note>original: "Euge, euge"</note> Psalm 35. *The king of the powers of the beloved, the beloved.* <note>original: "Rex virtutum dilecti, dilecti"</note> And Psalm 68. Poets use this figure similarly, such as Virgil: 
*The very woods sound: God, he is God, Menalcas!* <note>original: "Ipsa sonant arbusta DEVS, DEVS ille, Menalca."</note>

<margin>In the Psalms of David are found all the flowers and figures of the Poets.</margin>

<margin>Epizeuxis <note>the immediate repetition of words</note> in the psalms.</margin>

Likewise: the insertion of an intercalary verse <note>a repeated refrain</note>—to what kind of speech does this belong, if not to the metrical? As in Psalm 107 <note>original: "105"</note>: *Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men.* And: *They cried to the Lord when they were troubled.* These are repeated six times in that psalm. And Psalm 118: *I will confess to thee because thou hast heard me, and art become my salvation,* is repeated quite often. And Psalm 24: *Lift up your gates, etc.* is also repeated twice. Just as Virgil does six times in his *Pharmaceutria*:
*Begin with me, my flute, the Maenalian verses, etc.*
And: *Lead Daphnis home from the city, my songs, lead him, etc.*

<margin>Intercalary verse <note>a refrain</note>.</margin>

<margin><insert>Table II Day 3</insert></margin>

In the same way, he uses Apostrophe, or a turning of speech to a different person, as in Psalm 137: *O wretched daughter of Babylon, etc.* And Psalm 114: *What ails thee, O sea, that thou didst flee? etc.*
So the Poet <note>Virgil</note> says: *And Troy, you would now stand, and the high citadel of Priam, you would remain.*
He also employs Personifications <note>original: "Prosopopœias"</note> most frequently, such as: Psalm 19: *The heavens declare the glory of God.* And Psalm 98: *The rivers clap their hands, etc.*
So too the Poet: *Maenalus always has its tuneful grove and speaking pines; he always hears the loves of shepherds.*

Finally (to omit countless other examples), does the Reversion to the first line of the beginning, so that the last verse and the first of the psalm are the same, not argue that the psalm is metrical? As in Psalm 8: *O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name in the whole earth.* The epilogue <note>conclusion</note> is the same as the prooemium <note>introduction</note>. Homer does this as well in his hymns, as does Theocritus, as you will see in Eugubino <note>Augustinus Steuchus, a 16th-century scholar</note> on Psalm 8 at the end. Euthymius <note>a 12th-century commentator</note> believes these things were not done without mystery. For just as Christ (of whom Psalm 8 speaks), as if through a circle, returned to that place from whence he had come through the incarnation by his ascension: so the psalm, as if running back in a ring, ends in the very thing from which it took its beginning. For this reason, through the "closed Mem" (which, being brought back into a circle, lacks a beginning and an end), the perpetual kingdom of Christ is signified, contrary to the whole nature of that Hebrew element, which otherwise is always accustomed to be "open" at the beginning and middle of a word. See Isaiah, chapter 9, in the word <term>לםרבה <note>original Hebrew: *le-marbeh*, meaning "for the increase"</note></term>. But enough and more has been said regarding this proof.

§. V.

62 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

->§. V.<-
->On the various meters in which the Psalms were written.<-

[Marginal note:]
<margin>David as a Tragic, Comic, Satiric, Heroic, and Elegiac Poet, etc.</margin>

It is certain that David shows himself to be a Lyric, Tragic, Comic, Satiric, Heroic, Dramatic, Wedding-song <note>original: "Epithalamicum"; a poem written specifically for a bride and groom.</note>, and Elegiac poet in all things, according to the requirements of his subject matter. For at one moment he sings heroically of the kingdom of Christ, his victories, and the progress and glory of the Holy Church.
At another, he sings tragically, or rather weeps for the fall of Adam, the misery of the human condition, and the most cruel death of Christ, the most innocent lamb.
Then, satirically, he inveighs against the most corrupt morals of his age.
In an elegiac mode, he sounds forth the wedding song of Christ and the Church.
He stirs the memory of his ancestors and ancient events, chanting these in a heroic style.
Finally, he thunders divine praises and invites and rouses all mortals to them.
He also warns in a paranaetic <note>original: "paranæticè"; a style of speech intended to give moral advice or exhortation.</note> manner and imbues the reader with good morals. At times, he introduces different characters as if in a Comedy: now Adam with all his posterity, weeping for his lot; now Christ complaining about his persecutors; now the Holy Church, shaken on all sides by enemies, imploring heavenly aid; now the enemies themselves encouraging one another to shameful acts; now God avenging their crimes; now Christ triumphing gloriously over his enemies, and so on. Sometimes the author speaks alone, as Virgil does in the *Georgics* <note>A famous didactic poem by the Roman poet Virgil concerning agriculture.</note>; at other times, in a dramatic fashion (as happens in *Eclogues* <note>Short pastoral poems, often in the form of a dialogue.</note>), only the characters who are introduced speak. Sometimes it is a mixture of the Poet and those speaking with him, as occurs occasionally in the *Eclogues* and in the *Aeneid*. St. Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar.</note> enumerated these three genres at the end of Book 8, Chapter 7 of his *Etymologies*. At other times, David composed soliloquies in which he addressed and comforted his soul in silence, and with which he prayed to God in his mind. And so, no kind of poem or meter could ever be devised in which our prophet and heavenly poet David was not most diligently practiced.

[Marginal note:]
<margin>In what kind of verse the psalms were written.</margin>

But it is asked: in what kind of verse did he write these Psalms? Jerome, writing to Paula and Urbica in the Letter that begins *Nudius tertius* <note>Latin for "The day before yesterday," used here to identify a specific letter in Volume 3 of Jerome's works.</note>, says that certain psalms consist of iambic trimeter <note>A line of poetry with three pairs of "iambs" (a short syllable followed by a long one).</note>, and others of iambic tetrameter. He says the first two alphabets <note>The acrostic sections.</note> of the *Lamentations of Jeremiah* are written in something like a Sapphic meter; the third alphabet in trimeter, and so on. And in the Preface to the *Book of Job*, he says that from the third chapter of Job to the forty-first, the verses are hexameters <note>The standard meter of epic poetry, consisting of six rhythmic "feet."</note> running with dactyls and spondees. And at the beginning of his commentary on Psalm 118, he says: Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> reports that this Psalm and the song of Deuteronomy were composed in a single meter, and he thinks the Elegiac meter can be detected in both—namely, that the first verse consists of six feet, and the lower one, being one less, ends as a pentameter <note>A line of five poetic feet.</note>. Again, Josephus in Book 7 of the *Antiquities*, Chapter 10, says the Psalms of David were composed partly in trimeter and partly in pentameter verse. Furthermore, Eusebius Pamphili <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, an early Christian historian.</note> says: there are also among them (the Jews) most skillfully crafted poems, such as that great song of Moses and the 118th Psalm, which are composed in heroic meter, which is called hexameter. There are others also in trimeter and tetrameter; but those pertaining to diction are composed most elegantly, gravely, and pleasantly. Those that look to the meaning are to be compared to no other human writings, etc.
Again, St. Isidore asserts that all the psalms among the Hebrews were composed in metrical song. For in the manner of the Roman Flaccus <note>The Roman poet Horace.</note> and the Greek Pindar, he says some now run in iambics, now resound in elegiacs, now shine in Sapphics, moving along in trimeter or tetrameter feet. And these are the things I have been able to find among Jerome, Josephus, Eusebius, and Isidore, men outstanding in every kind of literature; for I did not think that the reasoning of more recent Doctors should be taken into account in this most ancient matter.

**Book II. Philological Treatise on Hebrew and Greek Music. 63**

Lest we should seem to have said nothing on a matter so obscure, it seemed to me worthwhile <margin>The author's opinion.</margin> to add to what has already been brought forward some things which might yet bring some light to these shadows.

I say, therefore, that it must not be thought that the Hexameter, trimeter, and Sapphic verses of the Hebrews are of the same kind as the poems of our own poets, or that they consist of the same quality, quantity, and arrangement of feet; rather, the arrangement, position, and order of the feet are different. This is because that ancient poetry of the Hebrews often admits other feet among the Dactyls and Spondees, sometimes even varying the order of the positions in which feet are usually placed among us. Indeed, Saint Jerome greatly favors this opinion of ours when, in his preface to Job, he speaks thus of Hebrew verses: *Because of the idiom of the language, they frequently admit other feet, not of the same syllables but of the same time-intervals; sometimes even the rhythm itself is sweet and tinkling, though freed from the strict measurements of feet; a thing which can be known only to poets.* <note>original: "Propter linguæ idioma crebrò recipiunt alios pedes non earundem syllabarum, sed eorundem temporum, interdum quoque rythmus ipse dulcis, & tinnulus numeris pedum solutis; quod Poëtis solis innotescere potest." Jerome was a 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin.</note>

To the point, then, I say that the Hebrews are accustomed to intersperse in their poems—contrary to the custom of our poets—certain unusual rhythms which the simple reader cannot understand, but only one most skilled in the metric art. Certainly, even among us, individual types of rhythms do not retain the same number of syllables and the same endings of poems, as we shall show in the *Panglossia Musurgica* <note>A reference to another section of Kircher's work "Musurgia Universalis" dealing with various languages.</note>. Nor indeed do the Hebrews employ this kind of poetry without reason; for it is wonderfully powerful in stirring up all kinds of emotions in the minds of men, as is clear enough from the Psalms of David. For he, by his poems, produced effects that were altogether admirable and almost incredible.

The stories of Amphion and Orpheus are fables and poetic inventions—that by the sound of the lyre they moved forests and rocks, stayed flowing rivers, tamed wild beasts, and that Orpheus recalled Eurydice from the underworld. Our other "divine Orpheus" <note>Referring to King David.</note> is the only one who truly performed greater deeds than those which they falsely fabled about the others. For he, with his harp, broke rocks, bent forests, and restrained the rivers of the passions as they glided most rapidly down precipices; he tamed the wild and monstrous characters of souls; he drove out and cast down the Evil Spirit <note>original: "Cacodemonem"</note> from the minds of many "Sauls." And he did not bring back only one Eurydice and immediately lose her, but he recalled countless souls of men, led away from the pit of the underworld, back into that golden life and light that is free from all hardship, etc.

But so that we leave nothing undiscussed, we shall give at this point a certain specimen, explanatory of all that has been said so far, in which it will be clearly evident both that the psalms were metrical and that they were sung in the Church of the Hebrews with metrical skill. This skill appears most clearly in Psalm 111, in which <margin>Psalm 111, of which the individual verses begin in the order of the alphabet.</margin> the individual verses are seen arranged according to the order of the letters of the Hebrew Alphabet; in which sometimes there are rhymes <note>original: "ὁμόφωνα" (homophona) - sounding the same.</note> and sometimes not; sometimes you will find trimeters, sometimes one or another kind of iambic, but it should suffice to have demonstrated the whole business by example. Thus, therefore, in the Psalms of David there are many poems of many kinds, many verses, and rhythms: which, however, can only be penetrated by those most skilled in the Hebrew language.

And from these examples, the reader will easily understand the system of Hebrew music, both ancient and modern. Nothing therefore remains except that, finally bringing an end to these lengthy discussions, we turn our attention to other matters.

### CHAPTER VI.
### Concerning the Music of the ancient Greeks, and their Instruments.

No one, except perhaps an unfair judge of history, can deny that just as all sciences were first transferred from the Hebrews partly to the Greeks and partly to the Egyptians, so also was music. Having been carried to them, it took on immense growth at all times and in both places. For who could restrain the most curious minds of the Greeks from traveling there? <margin>The Greeks drew many things regarding music from Solomon.</margin> The fame of the incomparable wisdom of both David and Solomon was scattered throughout the entire world. Who, I say, would not go to a place where there was such a magnificent display of wonderful things, such a multitude of male and female singers, such a variety of musical instruments constructed with the most exquisite skill, and finally, such an inexhaustible ocean of all arts and sciences—and most especially such an exact knowledge of natural things? There resided Solomon, the Oracle of all human wisdom. 

Certainly, I could easily demonstrate in this place that Orpheus, Linus, and Amphion—those first lights of Greek wisdom—drew everything they knew from there, had I not reserved this material to be treated with a more refined argument in my work on "Hieroglyphic Music" <note>Kircher likely refers to his forthcoming *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* or a later section of this work exploring the mystical origins of music.</note>. Therefore, we have decided to present in this place only the "husk" of Greek music and the instruments they used, while the "kernel" is reserved for the specialized treatises of this *Musurgia*. To the matter at hand, then.

Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De Institutione Musica" was the standard music theory text for a millennium.</note> reports from Nicomachus of Gerasa that the first musical instrument was invented by Mercury (whom many confuse with Hermes Trismegistus). <margin>The four-stringed Lyre of Mercury.</margin> As for who this Trismegistus truly was, since we discuss it at length in the *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher's work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (1652-54).</note>—a subject otherwise remarkably complex—I have decided to pass over it in silence here. This instrument, however, was equipped with four strings, according to the analogy of mundane and elementary music. By this, through a certain hidden reasoning, they denoted that **Harmonic Tetractys** <note>The *tetractys* is a Pythagorean symbol representing the number ten through the sum of the first four integers (1+2+3+4), symbolizing the harmony of the universe.</note> shining forth in the constitution of the four elements. At the same time, they displayed all the consonances by this same ingenious method: 

*   The first string to the second—that is, the **hypate** to the **parhypate**—sounded a **diatessaron** <term>Perfect Fourth</term>; 
*   The second to the third—that is, the **parhypate** to the **lichanos**—sounded a **tone** <term>Whole Step</term>; 
*   The third to the fourth—namely the **lichanos** to the **mese**—sounded another **diatessaron** <term>Perfect Fourth</term>; 
*   The **parhypate** to the **mese** sounded a **diapente** <term>Perfect Fifth</term>; 
*   The **hypate** finally to the **mese** sounded a **diapason** <term>Octave</term>.

Long after this Mercury, he was succeeded by Coræbus, son of the King of the Lydians, who added a fifth string to the four-stringed Hermetic lyre; later, Hyagnes the Phrygian, the father of Marsyas and the first author of the Pipes <note>original: *Tibiarum*—though often translated as flutes, these were double-reed instruments similar to an oboe</note>, added a sixth string. Finding this imperfect, Terpander of Lesbos added a seventh string to denote the harmony of the 7 planets; then Lycaon added an eighth, which joined the firmament to the 7 planets. Furthermore, Prophastus of Periota (or as some wish, Perinthus) added a ninth; Estiacus of Colophon the tenth; and finally Timotheus added an eleventh. The number of strings increased so much that later people, not content with the number of strings recorded so far, ascended to 36 or even 46 strings (as Epigonius of Ambracia is recorded to have done). From this nursery, as it were, emerged all kinds of Lyres, Citharas, Magades, Pectides, and Sambucas <note>various types of ancient harps and stringed instruments</note>, which we described in the sixth book. Hyagnes, the inventor of trumpets <note>original: *lituorum*—curved ritual trumpets</note>, gave others the occasion to discover innumerable kinds of multi-reeded instruments <note>original: *polycalamorum*, such as the Panpipes</note>; and these things briefly concerning instruments. He who desires more may see the seventh book, where we have treated them by profession.

§. I.
On the manner of singing used by the Greeks.

**T**he earliest musicians did not delight in the noise of many instruments sounding together, nor did they use the symphony <note>harmony</note> of several voices. Instead, they moved the souls of their listeners with a variety of vocal expressions, accommodated with great industry to the sound of the Lyre or the pipe, according to that saying:
*You to blow upon the light reeds, I to speak the verses.* <note>Quoting Virgil’s Eclogues</note>
<margin>The nature of ancient Greek music.</margin> In this manner, Homer introduces Achilles, Phemius, and Demodocus as singers. According to this tenor, they preserved a certain kind of music called the Rhapsodic style, and they were accustomed to recite and explain the verses of poets by singing. By this method, according to Plato, the verses of Homer were interpreted to the sound of the Lyre. Truly, the modulation was never performed by two voices at once, but by alternating intonations. Thus, in the works of Theocritus, the shepherds Daphnis and Menalcas, and in Virgil, Dametas and Menalcas, play with alternating voices. 
<margin>What is a chorus?</margin> Now, a **Chorus** was said to be a gathering of about 50 lyric poets singing both their own poems and the praises of the Gods, as well as those who had brought back a notable victory from the Olympic games. As a reward for the praises sung, they were presented with an ox. Phornutus also relates that rustic choruses, distributed for the fruits of the earth granted to them, paid their vows to Bacchus near an altar prepared with a sacrifice, to the sound of a flute-player. When the poets occasionally failed from too much mental exertion, a boy was substituted in the singer's place, as Livy testifies. From this, the custom of actors in theaters singing the verses of poets grew, according to that line of Horace:
*Thespis is said to have discovered an unknown kind of tragic Muse, and to have carried on wagons the poems which men, their faces smeared with wine-dregs, would sing and act.*
In the same way, while the Cithara-player sounded and the poet sang some poem, the others performed dances and choral rounds, according to Virgil:
*The Tyrians redouble their applause, and the Trojans follow.* And elsewhere:
*Some beat out dances with their feet and speak songs.*
And in this way they paid their praises.

# Book II. A Philological Study of Hebrew and Greek Music. 69

## §. II.

### Regarding the Odes of Lyric Poets, the Subject Matter of Poems, and Musical Laws.

The Pindaric Ode is divided into three parts: the first part of the Ode is called the *strophe* <note>original: στροφὴ, meaning "turning"</note>; the second the *antistrophe* <note>original: ἀντιστροφὴ, meaning "counter-turning"</note>; and the third is called the *epode* <note>original: ἐπῳδὸς, meaning "after-song"</note>. These are lyric verses, which were usually sung to the sound of the Lyre or Cithara. <margin>What are the strophe, antistrophe, and epode?</margin> It was called a *strophe*, however, because while that part was being sung, the dancers would move from the right toward the left; but while the *Antistrophe* was sung, the dancers would maintain the opposite movement in their dancing. When the *epode* sounded, they would rest for a little while as if tired, as if a certain pause had been placed between the movements. This manner of dancing endures among the Cretans even to this day. In such solemnities, the Arcadians used the Small Bagpipe <note>original: *Utriculo*</note>; the Sicilians used the Pectis <note>an ancient Greek lute or harp</note>; the Cretans used the Lyre; the Spartans used Pipes <note>original: *Tibijs*</note>; and the Thracians used Horns, and so on. <margin>Different instruments are used for different acts.</margin> Following these, the Romans, in presenting Comedies, used Pipes and Reed-pipes or whistles, which they called "right-handed" and "left-handed"; for by the use of these, they learned the specific character of the Comedy. For when the Comedy was about a grave and serious matter, the Flute-players <note>original: *Aulædi*</note> produced a grave and severe harmony with the left pipe; but when the Comedy was festive, joyful, and pleasant, the Flute-players sounded a harmony suitable to the material with the left pipe—namely, festive, joyful, pleasant, and so forth. Finally, they would sing mixed subject matter with a mixed harmony.

These types of pipes were also of two kinds: namely, the *Seranae* and the *Phrygian*. <margin>Serana and Phrygian pipes.</margin> The *Seranae* were called "equal" because of the equality of their holes; the *Phrygian* pipes, on the contrary, were called "unequal" because of the inequality of their holes. According to the testimony of Varro, the Phrygian pipe consisted of one hole, while the *Serana* consisted of two. According to Pliny, some used water-reeds or canes, which they would cut at a certain time of year around the setting of the star Arcturus; after a three-year drying process, they would finally fashion them into *Auloi* <note>Greek double-reed pipes</note> and whistles. <margin>The ancients fashioned reeds into pipes.</margin> They seemed to be invited to do this by nature itself, which arranged the parts between the nodes in the reeds so that when they were cut through the nodes and adapted into pipes, they differed in sound just as they did in length. Indeed, they differed in such proportion that the first or longest pipe varied by exactly one tone from the next, but sounded a *diapason* <note>an octave</note> compared to the eighth, and so on for the others in between. But concerning these, consult Book 7, where these matters are treated by design.

Furthermore, some themes of ancient music were Verses composed with the greatest art and genius in praise of the Gods (such as, for example, the hymns of Orpheus); others contained the praises and Encomiums of illustrious men distinguished by victories in the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games (such as the Pindaric Odes). Others exhibited loves in Wedding Songs <note>original: *Epithalamios*</note> (such as the poems of Catullus); others provided the material for funerals and the mourning of Dirges <note>original: *Neniarum*</note>, such as the *Epidimiae* instituted to drive away pestilential contagion, and so on. Others, finally, sang of tragic and comic subjects, and other similar themes full of gravity and severity. In this way, Demodocus composed the glorious deeds of most celebrated men: the contention of Ulysses with Achilles, the Fable of Venus and Mars, the Trojan Horse, and so forth. Phemius <note>written as *Foemus*</note> sang of the adultery of Mars and Venus in song, intended not to incite but to avoid luxury. Following their example, the wicked Nero (as Suetonius relates) <margin>Nero's insolence in comedies.</margin> sang the Mythology of Niobe while covered by a mask to the sound of the Cithara; and with various tragedies mixed in, he would now represent Canace in labor, now Orestes the matricide, or Hercules in his madness, and so on. In a word, the material which the Ancients recited by singing were histories of all those admirable things which had happened from the origin of the world even unto their own times.

In these matters, they were not indiscriminate or unthinking; rather, they moderated the emotions of mortals with rhythms and verses suitable to the harmony. From this, the rules of such harmony...

70 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

<margin>Why harmonic modulations were called "laws."</margin> These modulations were called "laws" <note>original: *nomi*, from the Greek *nomoi*</note>—and not without great reason and mystery—because it was not permitted to change them under the severest penalty. They were established for the purpose of being played to the sound of the cithara or lyre to stir the soul with their harmony and to rouse the memory of the listeners so they might remember them more firmly. There were three types: some were sung to the cithara or lyre; others to the pipe <note>original: *tibia*</note>, or to reeds and whistles; and the last were performed with a harmony common to both. Furthermore, these aforementioned modulations received various names, either from the people among whom they flourished—such as Ionic, Aeolic, or Boeotian; from their rhythms and verses—such as Orthian or Trochaic; from their modes—such as the "Sharp" <note>original: *Acutæ*</note> or "Four-seated" <note>original: *Tetraædiæ*</note>; from their inventors—such as the Terpandrian or Hieracian; or from an event, such as the Pythian, and so on. The Pythian Law was a composition whose theme contained the contest of Apollo with the serpent Python, which gives the story its name. The name of the song was *Delona*, because Apollo was a native of the island of Delos. According to Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a Greek grammarian and sophist</note>, this Pythian law was divided into five parts: the first was called the "Preparation" or "Exploration"; the second, the "Challenge"; the third, the "Iambic"; the fourth, the "Spondaic"; and the fifth and last, the "Triumph" <note>original: *Tripudium*, a ritual triple-beat dance</note>. In the first part, Apollo explored the serpent's hiding places and the suitability of the ground for fighting. In the second part, he performed the manner in which he challenged the serpent to battle. In the third part, the actual contest was sung to the sound of the pipe, which they called "the gnashing" <note>original: ὀδοντισμὸν (*odontismon*)</note>, in which the hissing of the formidable serpent and the clashing of its teeth were imitated. In the fourth part, Apollo’s victory was narrated. Finally, in the last part, the festivals, dances, and triumphs of Apollo for the victory he achieved were established. Additionally, there was a "Satyric" law called the *skirtos* <note>original: σκιρτὸς, a leaping dance</note>, which Bacchus instituted after he returned from subjugating India; this was a law for the pipes in which the rhythms, melodies, gestures, and harmony were changed according to the nature of the subject matter.

<margin>The Pythian Laws.</margin>

<margin>What the music of the Ancients consisted of.</margin> From all that has been said so far, it is clear enough that the music of the ancient Greeks consisted of rhythm, meter, instrument, poet, and dance, which sometimes all concurred in a single composition, and at other times the greater portion of these things, etc. It is also evident that the Poet and the Musician were one and the same person; Orpheus, Linus, and Amphion joined poetry to music. Hesiod was accustomed to sing his poems to the specific sound of a laurel branch, which, according to Pausanias, he produced by striking the air. That Pindar was both a Poet and a Musician is clear from the inscription which Alexander the Great ordered to be written on the doors of Pindar's house during the destruction of Thebes, in these words: *Do not burn the roof of Pindar the music-maker* <note>original: Πινδάρου τοῦ μουσοποιοῦ τὴν στέγην μὴ καίετε</note>.

<margin>Poet and Musician meant the same to the ancients.</margin>

§. III.

Regarding the Musical Instruments of the Ancients.

<margin>The invention of the Lyre and Cithara according to the Greeks.</margin> The constant and unanimous opinion of almost all mythologists is that the first inventor of the Lyre or Cithara was Mercury, the son of Atlas and Maia. He is said to have restored a tortoise shell <note>original: *Testudinem*</note> found after the flooding of the Nile by adding strings to it, thus turning it into a Lyre. He gave the finished instrument to Orpheus, or as others say, to Apollo, in exchange for which he is said to have received the Caduceus <note>the herald's staff carried by Mercury</note>. Although the story is described differently—yet most ingeniously—in Homer, the reader may consult it there, as these matters are common knowledge and we shall not dwell on them.
Regarding the shape of this lyre, certainly in such darkness of antiquity I think hardly anything certain can be established. However, if we are to rely on conjectures, I would say it was of such a shape as we find almost always inscribed under the same form on the ancient monuments of the City of Rome, and on the surviving coins and medals of the ancients. We can see it even now in the Farnese, Mattei, Sallustian, Pincian, and Borghese gardens, and in the Justinian Antiquarium, sometimes in the hand of Apollo, sometimes in that of Mercury. Hyginus, however, presents a different shape for it. Others make it different not only in shape, but also in the number of strings; among these, some make the same instrument three-stringed, others four-stringed, and others seven-stringed. Some confuse it with the lyre of Amphion, Orpheus, and Linus; but...

### Section IV.
### On the subject and perfection of music among the ancients, and on harmonic signs and notes.

Furthermore, later music-makers <note>original: *Musurgi*</note>, seeing that the music established by the early sages of Greece was quite imperfect, worked seriously to bring it to some level of perfection. Pythagoras of Samos acted as the leader <note>original: *Choragum*, referring to the director of a chorus</note>; he was the first to hand down the proportions of harmonic movements based on the weights of hammers <note>A reference to the legend where Pythagoras discovered musical ratios by listening to the different sounds of blacksmiths' hammers</note>, which he also demonstrated with numbers, and he was the first to reveal the "harmonic world." He was followed afterward by Aristoxenus, Timotheus, Euclid, Hippasus, Archytas, Aristotle, Plato, Timotheus, Thales of Miletus, <margin>Ancient Musicians.</margin> Philolaus, Eubulides, Nicomachus, and countless others, whom you may find in the works of Plutarch. These men, refining the precepts handed down by Pythagoras, raised music to that degree of excellence which we read flourished among the Greek musicians of that age with great admiration. For these men, exploring harmonic proportions through various divisions of strings <note>likely using a monochord, a single-stringed scientific instrument</note> according to the sense of hearing, finally presented music with very exact rules. 

They were the first to separate consonant intervals from dissonant ones and gave names to individual intervals. They discovered the triple genus of music—diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic <note>These represent the three ways of tuning a tetrachord, or four-note scale segment, in Greek theory</note>; they established the variety of tones or modes <note>original: *troporum*</note>, and performed countless other things with such subtlety of genius that we still look up to and admire them to this day. However, since we describe the method of their procedure in each of these at length in the following books, we only wanted to indicate it briefly here. They were followed by Quintilian, Ptolemy, Plutarch, Albinus, Boethius, Augustine, and others, both Greek and Latin, who excellently amplified the science in various and most subtle volumes, as will be clear as this work progresses.

The curious reader will undoubtedly desire to know what method and manner the cited ancient musicians of Greece maintained in marking harmonic proportions. For it is certain that they indicated their harmonic intervals with specific notes, just as is the custom in our own century; and according to these notes, they both sang the melody and played the instruments. Various authors have handed down various signs for this, but they have been poorly understood, as will be seen later. I certainly, in order to penetrate that mystery, left nothing untried. Having searched through both the Vatican and other libraries, I finally discovered various manuscripts on this subject. One was a Greek manuscript in the Vatican by the philosopher Gaudentius. Another I found in our own library by the very ancient musician Alypius. From a comparison of these, I have finally, with no small labor, "dug out" that ancient system of musical notation <note>original: *characteristicam*</note>. I present it to you in its entirety in Book 7, Inquiry IV; please consult that section.

## CHAPTER VII.
## On the Modern Music of the Greeks.

The Greek Church not only cultivated music wisely established by the ancients, but also handed down its widely diffused offspring to posterity. For since there was praise in the Church of the Saints, and choirs of religious men were established everywhere, incessantly praising God day and night, they employed music as a perfect standard <note>original: *amussim*, a carpenter’s rule or level; used here to mean a precise method</note> for singing psalms. Indeed, lest they should seem to yield in the fervor of psalm-singing to their pagan <note>original: *Gentilibus*</note> predecessors—who sang to the empty powers of gods—they devised other notes to perform music in church choirs with great decorum. Through these, they might make ecclesiastical chants both better and more suitable for offering praises to GOD. It is our purpose in this present chapter to interpret this kind of notation, so that the reader might not find anything lacking in this *Musurgia* <note>Kircher’s term for his comprehensive musical work, meaning "the art of music-making"</note> regarding curious matters; thus, if he should ever come across musical books written with such notes, he may have a key by which to reach the music contained in those books. Indeed, I have taken this entire method of singing from the books...

### Concerning the cadences of the Tones.

Moreover, the modern Greeks have certain terms with which they explain all harmonic modulation <margin>The Greek style of singing.</margin>, which corresponds exactly to our Solmization <note>Solmization is the system of attributing distinct syllables to the notes of a scale, similar to the modern "do-re-mi" system.</note>. There are specifically eight: *Ananes*, *Neagie*, *Aanes*, *Neeanes*, *Aneanes*, *Neanes*, *Nana*, and *Agie*. Once these have been cycled through, they return to the same harmonic step from which they started. These are the eight governors of the tones. *Ananes* corresponds to the first tone. If you descend one step from it, you will find the fourth plagal <note>A "plagal" mode is a derived or "sideways" version of a primary musical mode, typically starting a fourth or fifth below the primary (authentic) version.</note>, that is, the fourth; if you descend one step from that, you will find the *barys* <note>meaning "heavy" or "deep"</note> or third; and if you descend one step from that, you will find the second plagal, that is, the second; and if you descend one step from that, you will find the first plagal, the first. If you then ascend one step from that, you will find the second tone; and if you ascend one step from there, you will find the third tone; and finally, if you ascend one step from there, you will have the fourth tone, and the following step will give the first tone, and so on for the rest.

It should be known, however, that if you descend from any tone, a change of tone occurs in that voice. In this manner, there are eight tones demonstrating individual voices, and voices arising from the change of tones. For if you descend five steps from the *tetraphonia* <note>An interval of a fourth.</note> or from the first [tone], you will find the fourth plagal or fourth tone. Four are called "Authentic" <note>original: κύριοι (kyrioi), meaning "lords" or "proper."</note>, meaning proper, and four are "Plagal" <note>original: πλάγιοι (plagioi), meaning "oblique" or "subsidiary,"</note> as has been said. The signs of the eight tones follow.

Book III. On the Doctrine of Harmonic Numbers: 81

### Definitions in Music.

1 **UNISON**, or *equal-sounding* <note>original Greek: "ἰσόφωνος" (isophonos)</note> is the same in Music as the monad or unity is in Arithmetic, the point in Geometry, or the center in a circle; it is incapable of any tension <note>term: "tension" — the tightening of a string to raise pitch</note> or remission <note>term: "remission" — the loosening of a string to lower pitch</note>.
2 **INTERVAL** is a certain mutual relationship between the spaces of a low and high sound, or the *distance* <note>original Greek: "διάστημα" (diastema)</note> between a high and low sound.
3 **HARMONIC SPACE** is what we call a string, a cord, a piece of wood, a pipe, exhaled air, or any other thing from which we draw out a sound when compared to another similar body that is more tense or more relaxed.
4 **MULTIPLE INTERVAL** occurs when a larger space contains a smaller one multiple times; such as double, triple, or quadruple.
5 **HARMONIC PART** is that which, when taken a certain number of times, measures the whole itself.
6 **SUPERPARTIENT INTERVAL** is when a larger space contains a smaller one, plus several aliquot <note>term: "aliquot" — a portion that is contained an exact number of times in a whole, like 2 is to 6</note> parts of that smaller space.
7 **SUPERPARTICULAR INTERVAL** is when a larger space contains a smaller one, plus one such aliquot part of it.
8 **HIGH SOUND** <note>original Latin: "sonus acutus" — acute sound</note> is the frequent and very swift vibration of air compressed by the collision of bodies.
9 **LOW SOUND** <note>original Latin: "sonus gravis" — grave sound</note> is the slow and sluggish vibration of loose air from the collision of bodies.
10 **PHTHONGUS** is a *melodic* <note>original Greek: "ἐμμελής" (emmeles)</note> inflection of the voice, that is, a sound suited for the voice at a single pitch.
11 **CONSONANCE** is a mixture of high and low sound reaching the ears in a sweetly uniform manner.
12 **DISSONANCE** is a harsh and unpleasant striking reaching the ears, consisting of two sounds that mix with one another only with difficulty.

### Axioms and Postulates in Music.

1 Whatever measures another, also measures that which is measured by it.
2 A harmonic compound is resolved into the simple elements from which it is composed.
3 The part of any number is the unity named by that number <note>For example, "one-third" is the unit derived from the number three</note>.
4 Unity, when multiplied by any number, produces that same number.
5 Whatever measures a part taken away together with the remainder, also measures the whole.
6 Things that are equal to one and the same thing are also equal to each other.
7 Whatever transcends something twice over must necessarily be beyond half of that thing.
8 For those things whose wholes are equal, their halves will also be equal.
9 Whatever, when doubled, does not fulfill the whole, does not contain the half either.
10 Every whole is greater than its part.
11 Given an equal string, the proportion of space to space is the same as the proportion of sound to sound.
12 Between harmonic numbers differing only by unity <note>such as 2 and 3, or 3 and 4</note>, no mean <note>term: "mean" — a middle value or ratio</note> can be intercepted.
13 To divide any space into any number of equal parts.
14 The harmonic whole compared to its part, like the relaxed string to the tense one, produces a lower sound.
15 Every proportion is as number to number.
16 A part produces a higher sound compared to the whole.
17 By the addition of movements to a low sound, the pitch is sharpened; by the subtraction of movements from a high sound, the pitch is lowered.
18 As magnitude is to magnitude in similar material, so is sound to sound.
19 A high sound consists of more movements than a low one.
10 <note>Note: This is likely a typographical error in the original for Axiom 20</note> A tone cannot be harmonically divided into two equal semitones.

# CHAPTER I.

## On Proportions, their definition, and division.

So that the power and nature of Music might be more exactly perceived, order seems to require that we speak in the first place about the ratio <note>original Greek: "λόγῳ" (logō) — meaning reason, word, or proportion</note> and analogy of numbers. Thus Euclid, in the Definitions of Book V, defines Ratio as follows. *Ratio (or what is the same thing, Proportion) <margin>What Ratio is.</margin> is a certain relationship of two quantities of the same kind, however large they may be, of one to the other.* And so that we may now—for the sake of avoiding wordiness, having omitted various divisions of quantities—deal only with the Ratios of numbers, we first set down the definition of Ratio as follows: *Ratio is a certain relationship or comparison of one of two numbers to the other;* that is: any number can be compared with another, and is found to be either equal to it or unequal. If it is equal, such as 4 to 4, the Ratio will be called one of equality, which we reject as being unsuitable for music <note>Kircher rejects equality because music requires a "distance" or interval between notes to create melody or harmony; a unison (1:1) provides no movement.</note>. If, however, it is unequal to it, the Ratio will be called one of inequality, of which kind two species are counted, namely the major ratio...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher introduces the mathematical concept of ratios as the foundation of music, citing Euclid to define how numbers relate to one another. He distinguishes between ratios of equality (which he deems musically uninteresting) and ratios of inequality, which form the basis of musical intervals.</summary>

The term comes from the Latin *super* (above) and *bipartient* (dividing into two parts).</term> ratio. And it has species that are truly infinite. For if the larger contains [the smaller] once, and additionally two thirds, it will be called the **superbipartient-thirds** proportion; if it further has two fourths, or fifths, sixths, sevenths, or eighths, it will be called the **superbipartient-fourths, -fifths, -sixths, -sevenths, -eighths**, etc. Again, if the larger contains the smaller once, and additionally three, four, five, or six sevenths, eighths, ninths, etc., it will be called a **supertripartient, superquadripartient, superquintupartient, or supersextupartient**-sevenths, -eighths, -ninths, and so on to infinity, as in the example.

## II.

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of mathematical proportions used in music theory, moving from definitions of complex ratios to practical methods for calculating multiple and superparticular ratios.</meta>

84 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance* <note>original: "Artis Magnæ Consoni, & Dissoni"</note>

Finally, the **multiple superpartient proportion** <term>multiple superpartient: A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number multiple times, plus two or more fractional parts (e.g., 8:3, which is 2 and 2/3).</term> is a number which, when compared to another, contains it more than once and still contains several of its fractional parts; this can occur in infinite ways. For if one number contains another more than once—specifically twice—and additionally two-thirds of it, it will be called a **double superbipartient-thirds**, as is evident in the second example, and so on. From these examples, if I am not mistaken, the origin <note>original: "genesis"</note> of any proportion whatsoever is more than sufficiently clear. However, lest any difficulty remain for students <note>original: "Tyronibus," meaning beginners or novices</note>, we shall here present the origin of each one separately through paradigms.

### Proposition I.
#### To find a multiple proportion.

**M**ultiply both terms—having first found the smallest terms of the proportion—by 2, and you will have the second proportion; if multiplied by three, you will have the third; if multiplied by four, you will have the fourth, and so on to infinity. For example, let the **sub-double** <term>sub-double: The ratio of 1 to 2; the inverse of a double (2:1).</term> proportion 1 to 2 be extended; the terms will be multiplied by two, and you will have 2 and 4 as the second term of the double proportion. If you triple these again, you will have the third term of the double proportion, 3 and 6, and so on to infinity. If, however, the first and smallest terms were in a **triple proportion**, such as 3 to 1, each term multiplied by 3 will give the remaining triple proportions in order to infinity. The same must be said for the rest of the multiple proportions increasing to infinity.

| All doubles. | All triples. | All quadruples. | Quintuples. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 8 | 12 | 16 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 |
| 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 3 | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

### Proposition II.
#### To find and multiply a superparticular proportion.

**T**ake the number that names the fractional part expressed in the proportion; for the next larger number—which is to say, the one that exceeds it by one unit—compared to it, will give the first **superparticular proportion** <term>superparticular ratio: A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2, 4:3).</term>, such that it cannot be explained in smaller numbers. If these terms are doubled, or multiplied by any proportion, numbers of the same proportion will necessarily be produced. For example, let the **sesquitertian** proportion <note>original: "sesquitertia," the ratio 4:3</note> be proposed to be multiplied and extended to infinity. The first term named in the proportion will be 3, and the immediately following number, 4, will be the larger term of the desired sesquitertian proportion, which cannot be expressed in smaller terms than 3 and 4. Therefore, if you multiply this proportion by 2, the second proportion will result; if you triple it again, you will produce the third proportion, and so on to infinity. In the same way, you will increase the **sesquialter**, **sesquiquartan**, **sesquiquintan**, **sesquisextan**, and infinite others.

### Proposition III.
#### To continue a superpartient proportion.

<term>superpartient proportion: A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number once, plus two or more fractional parts of that number (for example, 5:3, which is 1 and 2/3).</term>

### Proposition V.
#### *To find multiple superpartient proportions.*

<term>multiple superpartient proportion: A complex ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number multiple times (double, triple, etc.) plus two or more fractional parts of that smaller number.</term>

**M**ultiply the denominator of the proposed fractional parts by the whole number of the multiple proportion; then, add the number of the parts to that product, and you will have the first ratio of the series being sought. For example: if one seeks all the **quadruple super-eight-partient elevenths** <note>original: "quadruplæ superoctupartientes vndecimas"; this refers to a ratio of 4 and 8/11, or 52:11.</note> proportions, we multiply the denominator of the eleventh parts (which is 11) by 4 (the number of the quadruple proportion). To the resulting product of 44, we add 8 (the number of the eight-partient). The resulting number, 52, compared to the denominator of the parts (11), gives the first sought-after ratio. Doubling these numbers will give 104 to 22 as the second ratio, and so on to infinity, as is clear in the example.

# CHAPTER II.
## On proportionalities.

**A**nalogy, or the proportionalities defined by Euclid, are divided into several kinds. However, the three principal types—which mathematicians call "means"—are the **Arithmetic**, **Geometric**, and **Harmonic**. Although our primary business here is with the last of these (the third type), we believe it necessary to briefly treat each one in this place so that the difference by which the Harmonic is distinguished from the preceding two may be understood.

<margin>What is Arithmetic Proportionality?</margin>

**ARITHMETIC** analogy <note>original: "ἀναλογία" (analogia); the Greek term for proportion or relationship.</note> or proportionality (or the arithmetic mean) occurs when three or more numbers proceed by the same difference. For instance, in these numbers: 4 | 7 | 10 | 13 | 16, each number exceeds the one before it by three. These are said to constitute an arithmetic proportionality. It is, moreover, of two kinds: **Continuous** and **Discrete**. It is Continuous when there is no interruption in the progression of the numbers, but each is compared with the one immediately preceding it, as in the example just given. It is Discrete, however, when an interruption occurs in the progression of numbers, so that they are compared only in pairs, and not [interconnectedly]...

<summary>This page concludes the calculation of complex "multiple superpartient" ratios and begins a new chapter defining the three types of mathematical means—Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic—focusing first on the Arithmetic mean.</summary>
<keywords>multiple superpartient proportions, arithmetic mean, Euclid, musical mathematics, ratio sequences, continuous vs discrete proportionality</keywords>

*Book III. On the Doctrine of Harmonic Numbers.* 87

...but not just any number with its immediately preceding one, as happens in these numbers: 4, 7; 8, 11; 30, 33. For the same difference <note>The difference is 3.</note> exists between the pairs 4 & 7, 8 & 11, and 30 & 33, but not between 4 & 7 and 7 & 8, and so on.

**GEOMETRIC** proportionality or **Mean** exists when three or more numbers have the same ratio. This is properly called "proportionality" or "analogy," whereas the previously mentioned type [Arithmetic] is so called improperly, since the ratio is not always the same between its terms. Thus, they are more correctly called "Means" because of the middle terms which are placed between the extremes according to a certain rule. For example, these numbers 2, 4, 8, 16 constitute a geometric proportionality because each has the same double ratio to its predecessor. This type is also twofold: **Continuous** and **Discrete**. Continuous is seen in the numbers just cited. Discrete, however, is seen in these six: 2, 4, 12, 24, 30, 60. Here, only the pairs always have a double ratio between them, but not every number to its immediate predecessor.

<margin>What is a musical proportion?</margin>
**MUSICAL** or **Harmonic** proportionality or mean exists when three numbers are so ordered that the ratio of the largest to the smallest is the same as the ratio of the difference between the two larger numbers to the difference between the two smaller ones. For example, consider these three numbers: 3, 4, 6. The ratio of the largest (6) to the smallest (3) is double [2:1]. The difference between the largest (6) and the middle (4) is 2, while the difference between the middle (4) and the smallest (3) is 1. Since the ratio of these differences (2 to 1) is also double, they constitute a musical or harmonic proportionality. That this proportionality is truly "harmonic" is clear from the fact that it produces the three principal consonances: the <term>octave</term> <note>original: "diapason"</note>, the <term>fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente"</note>, and the <term>fourth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>. In this example, 6 to 3 represents the octave, 6 to 4 the fifth, and 4 to 3 the fourth. The same rule applies to the rest. But let us now proceed to the specifics of harmonic proportionality.

### Proposition I.

#### *To find three numbers in harmonic proportionality.*

Three harmonic numbers are found from any three numbers of an arithmetic proportionality in this way: Multiply the first term by the second, then the first by the third, and finally the second by the third, and you will have what is sought, as follows.

Suppose there are three arithmetic proportional numbers: 1, 2, 3. To derive three harmonic proportionals from these: multiply 1 by 2 and then 1 by 3; this produces the first and second terms of the harmonic proportionality: 2 and 3. If you then multiply the second arithmetic term by the third (2 times 3), it will produce 6, the third harmonic proportional.

| 1. 2. 3 Arithmetic |
| :--- |
| **2. 3. 6 Harmonic** |

**Alternatively:** Multiply the middle term of the Arithmetic proportionality by the extremes, and the extreme harmonic terms will be produced; meanwhile, the arithmetic extremes multiplied by each other produce the middle term of the harmonic series.

| 1 | 2 | 3 | Arithmetic |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **2** | **3** | **6** | **Harmonic** |

as is clear in the cited example. From this, it is evident that the extreme terms of the harmonic proportionality (and their differences) maintain the same ratio as the extreme terms of the arithmetic proportionality from which they were derived.

# Proposition 2

### To assign a harmonic proportional mean between any two given numbers.

You may find the <term>harmonic proportional mean</term> <note>The harmonic mean is one of the three classic mathematical means, alongside the arithmetic and geometric; in music, it is used to determine the proportions of strings that produce harmonious intervals.</note> between any two given numbers in the following way. Multiply the number representing the difference between the given numbers by the smaller of those numbers; then, divide the product by the sum of the original numbers. Finally, add the resulting quotient to the smaller number, and the resulting total will be the mean you seek. 

For example: let the two proposed numbers be 15 and 60. To find the harmonic mean, multiply their difference (45) by the smaller number (15), and divide the resulting product (675) by their sum (75). If you add the quotient (9) to the smaller number (15), you will produce the middle term, 24—as is evident in this example: 15, 24, 60. 

You will find the same mean if you multiply that same difference (45) by the larger number (60) and divide the product (2700) by their sum (75). The quotient (36), when subtracted from the larger number (60), will leave the same middle term: 24.
