### CHAPTER IV.

### Division of the Monochord according to the chromatic genus.

What the Chromatic genus consists of has been shown above; therefore, it would be superfluous to repeat its description in this place. I will say only this: since the <term>Tetrachords</term> <note>Four-note segments that were the building blocks of ancient Greek scales.</note> of this genus proceed by two semitones and one <term>trihemitone</term> <note>An interval equal to three semitones, or a minor third.</note> or <term>semiditone</term> <note>Another term for a minor third.</note>, you will easily divide the chromatic monochord by the following method.

Since in the preceding diatonic monochord, the outermost strings of the tetrachords are fixed in place and always remain the same, you will divide the monochord of this genus very easily if you ignore the points E, H, P in the previous division. For if line DB is divided into 16 equal parts, and three other parts are added to these toward A so that they become 19, they will give the sought-after semiditone or trihemitone. But let us clarify the matter with an example. Therefore, to divide the monochord chromatically—since a tetrachord of this genus consists of two semitones and a semiditone—you will determine these in each individual tetrachord as follows.

#### The Lowest Chromatic Tetrachord.
<note>original: "Tetrachordon hypaton Chromaticum"</note>

First, while the string remains with its endpoints of the tetrachords common to both the diatonic and chromatic divisions, let the string DB be divided into 16 equal parts, and to these let three equal parts be added. You will then have aB divided into 19 parts, and the interval aD will be a semiditone, or a Trihemitone, or a minor third. aB will be the 3rd sought-after string. Since in the preceding Four-fold Monochord, we established the first interval of the Tetrachords as a minor semitone, here the interval CF, joined with Fa, will constitute two semitones; aD, however, will constitute a semiditone or 3 other semitones. By dividing the string DB into 16 equal parts and adding 3 other equal parts to them, the first semitone CF will emerge, the second semitone Fa, and the semiditone or Trihemitone aD, forming the sought-after Chromatic Tetrachord. This is also evident from the following: if we subtract the minor semitone between CB and FB from the <term>sesquitertial ratio</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, which produces the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> or <term>diatessaron</term>, from the Trihemitone aD in the <term>supertripartient 16 ratio</term> <note>The ratio 19:16.</note>, there will necessarily remain the semitone Fa of the <term>superquintupartient 76 ratio</term> <note>The ratio 81:76.</note>, as 76 is to 81.

#### The Middle Chromatic Tetrachord.
<note>original: "Tetrachordon meson chromaticum"</note>

If you wish to determine the other middle chromatic tetrachord, let GB be divided into 16 equal parts and let 3 others be added to these toward b, so that they become 19. bB will be the third added string, dividing the middle chromatic tetrachord DI into the first semitone Ib, the second semitone, and bG into the sought-after Trihemitone or semiditone.

#### The Disjunct Chromatic Tetrachord.
<note>original: "Tetrachordon diezeugmenon chromaticum"</note>

Let string LB be divided into 16 equal parts and let 3 others be added to these, and you will have the semiditone LC. Then follow the two semitones CN and Ne. eG will be the whole tone (or two semitones) separating the Middle Tetrachord from the Disjunct Tetrachord.

#### The Highest Chromatic Tetrachord.
<note>original: "Tetrachordon hyperboleon chromaticum"</note>

Let OB be divided into 16 equal parts and let three other parts be added to them, and you will have the Trihemitone dO, which is then followed by 2 semitones dQ and QL, which taken together constitute the Highest Tetrachord.

#### The Chromatic Conjunct Tetrachord.
<note>original: "Tetrachordon Synnemenon Chromaticum"</note>

Let MK be divided into 16 equal parts, and to these let 3 other equal parts be added; the interval MN will then be a <term>trihemitone</term> <note>a "three-half-tone" interval, or a minor third</note>, while the two following semitones will be KR and RG, and the <term>Synnemenon</term> <note>The "conjunct" or connected tetrachord in the ancient Greek system</note> Tetrachord will be completed.

You see, therefore, that in the Chromatic Monochord nothing else is required except that a third string be added to the diatonic Tetrachords. This is achieved if—following the examples of EB, HB, and PB from the diatonic Tetrachords—the remaining fixed strings DB, GB, LB, and OB are each divided into 16 equal parts and 3/16 are added to each. For these additions will transform the <term>diatonic</term> <note>The standard natural scale</note> Monochord into a chromatic one, while both the names and all the numbers remain the same, except for those that correspond to the third added string, or the strings marked with the letters a, b, cc, and d. ### CHAPTER V.
### Division of the Monochord according to the Enharmonic genus.

<margin>Lowest Tetrachord</margin>
<margin>Middle Tetrachord</margin>
<margin>Disjunct Tetrachord</margin>
<margin>Highest Tetrachord</margin>
<margin>Conjunct Tetrachord</margin>

Since the first, second, and fourth strings—that is, the <term>hypate hypaton</term> <note>the lowest note of the lowest tetrachord</note>, <term>parhypate hypaton</term> <note>the "next to the lowest" note</note>, and <term>hypate meson</term> <note>the lowest note of the middle tetrachord</note> marked with the letters C, F, and D—of every diatonic tetrachord division are fixed for the enharmonic tetrachords and are essential to them, we shall transform the diatonic monochord into an enharmonic one with almost no trouble, in this way: Since an enharmonic tetrachord consists of two <term>dieses</term> <note>very small intervals, roughly a quarter of a tone</note> and one <term>ditone</term> <note>a major third</note>—that is, it proceeds from the low pitch through a diesis, a diesis, and a ditone or major third—nothing else is needed except that the semitone of the diatonic genus intercepted between C and f be divided in half at point f, creating 2 dieses. Thus, Cf will be the first diesis, fG the second, and FD the ditone. What is done in the "lowest" (hypaton) tetrachord should also be done in the remaining tetrachords. Thus, the semitone DI in the diatonic monochord, divided into two dieses through point g, together with the ditone IG, will give the <term>middle</term> (meson) enharmonic tetrachord; and the semitone KI in the diatonic monochord, divided in half into two dieses through point h, together with the ditone LM, will give the <term>disjunct</term> (diezeugmenon) enharmonic tetrachord. Likewise, LR divided in half through point I (that is, into 2 dieses) together with the ditone QO will give the <term>highest</term> (hyperboleon) tetrachord. Finally, the <term>conjunct</term> (synnemenon) tetrachord will be produced by GR divided into two dieses through point K, together with the ditone RM, as is most clearly evident in the figure.

#### Corollary I.

1. You see, therefore, that by rejecting E from the diatonic lowest tetrachord and a from the chromatic, and by dividing CF in half, the enharmonic <term>hypaton</term> <note>lowest</note> tetrachord CfED is established.
2. By rejecting H and b from the diatonic and chromatic middle tetrachords and dividing DI in half, the enharmonic <term>meson</term> <note>middle</note> tetrachord DgIG is established.
3. By rejecting M and C from the diatonic and chromatic <term>diezeugmenon</term> <note>disjunct</note> tetrachords and dividing KN in half, the enharmonic diezeugmenon tetrachord KhNL is established.
4. By rejecting the strings P and d from the diatonic and chromatic <term>hyperboleon</term> <note>highest</note> tetrachords and dividing L in half, the enharmonic hyperboleon tetrachord LIQO is established.
5. By rejecting N and h from the diatonic and chromatic <term>synnemenon</term> <note>conjunct</note> tetrachords and dividing GR in half, the enharmonic synnemenon tetrachord GKRM is established.

<note>This diagram maps out the "Enharmonic" genus of ancient Greek music theory as understood in the 17th century. The numbers represent the length of a vibrating string; the larger the number, the longer the string and the lower the pitch. The scale is divided into "tetrachords" (four-note groupings). Unlike our modern scale, the Enharmonic scale uses very small intervals called "dieses" (roughly quarter-tones) and very large gaps called "ditones" (major thirds). This system was considered the most difficult and refined of the ancient musical styles.</note>

# CHAPTER VI.

### Regarding the "String-Cutter" instrument, by which we are able to divide any given line or string into the voices appropriate to individual strings in the Chromatic-enharmonic style faster than can be said.

We include here, by way of a <term>finishing touch|Greek "coronis," a flourish or concluding mark</term>, a noble instrument in which we encompass, as if in a certain <term>recapitulation|Greek "Anacephalaeosis," a summary or summing up</term>, everything that has been said so far. It is constructed as follows: 1. Take two rulers, AB and CB, which you will join exactly at the center B with a hinge, so that the outer lines AB and BC extend perfectly from the center, and both legs can be opened or constricted to any interval at the user’s pleasure, just as is usually done in <term>proportional compasses|An early calculating tool used by engineers and musicians to scale measurements</term>. 

2. Using a compass, transfer all the intercepted divisions of the diatonic monochord explained above, beginning from A <term>proslambanomenos|The lowest note in the ancient Greek musical system</term>, from the center B of the instrument onto the lines DB and EB of both legs. Then transfer the individual divisions of the chromatic monochord from the center B of the instrument onto lines HB and GB of both legs. Finally, transfer the divisions of the enharmonic monochord in the same manner onto lines IB and LB of both legs from center B, and you will have the instrument prepared.

### Use of the Instrument.

If you first desire to have the division of the diatonic monochord on any given line, place the instrument upon a table and intercept the length of the given line with the legs of a compass at the final points D and E. Then, leaving this instrument in the exactly unmoved position that you see here; if you transfer the points of the strings on both legs (which are marked with the same letters) onto the given line or string, you will have a string proportionally divided according to the diatonic system. If, however, you do not wish to determine the whole string but only a specific <term>consonance|An interval that sounds pleasant and stable</term> on a given string—for example, a <term>diapente|A perfect fifth</term>—if you transfer the space noted between the legs at DD onto the given string, you will have a marked fifth...

Book IV. On the Geometrical Division of the Monochord. 205

### CHAPTER VII.

#### On the geometrical division of any interval into two or even more equal parts.

Division, in the broad sense used here, is either rational or <term>irrational|In 17th-century music theory, rational divisions are those that can be expressed as whole-number ratios (like 2:1 or 3:2). Irrational divisions involve square roots or other values that cannot be written as simple fractions, often required for perfectly equal temperament</term>; the latter is not considered by the Musician except by accident, while the former is considered under a threefold perspective: arithmetic, geometric, or harmonic. 

Therefore, a consonance is divided according to **arithmetic proportionality** when its extremes are divided by a middle string point in this way: the larger part of such a division is perceived between the middle and the high <note>original: "acutam"</note> pitch, and the smaller part between the middle and the low <note>original: "grauem"</note> pitch. 

However, according to **harmonic analogy**, the extremes are judged to be divided in this way: the larger part of the division is felt toward the low pitch, while the smaller part is felt toward the high pitch—a reasoning entirely contrary to the first method. Thus, an <term>octave|original: "diapason"</term> arithmetically divided into a <term>fifth|original: "diapente"</term> and a <term>fourth|original: "diatessaron"</term> has the fifth situated above and the fourth below; but when harmonically divided, it has the fifth disposed below and the fourth above.

A consonance divided according to the laws of **geometric proportionality**, however, favors equality; that is, from the middle point of division, there is as much toward the low as toward the high...

<summary>Kircher explains the three ways to divide a musical interval: arithmetically, harmonically, and geometrically. He specifically notes how arithmetic and harmonic divisions flip the placement of the fifth and fourth within an octave.</summary>

Similarly, it is established that AD, AE, and AC are proportional. Therefore, all four will be in proportion, which was to be demonstrated.

### Proposition III.
#### To find a line that bisects a given interval into two equal parts.

Let there be two given lines representing a <term>diapason|The Greek and Latin term for an octave (ratio 2:1)</term> or octave, labeled AB and EF, between which it is necessary to find a <term>mean proportional|The geometric middle point; in music, this represents the exact frequency that sits halfway between two notes in a logarithmic scale</term>. If these lines are joined in a straight line, and the mean proportional is sought according to the preceding method, I say that the discovered mean proportional—which we here designate as CD—is the line that divides the double ratio of AB to EF into two equal ratios. Consequently, it divides the octave into two equal intervals, for the ratio of CD to EF is the same as the ratio of AB to CD.

Furthermore, if one now wishes to find other mean proportionals, one between AB and CD, and another between CD and EF:

A ---------------------------------------- B
<note>Line representing the lower note of the octave</note>

C -------------------------- D
<note>Line representing the middle point (the "tritone" or augmented fourth in equal division)</note>

E --------------- F
<note>Line representing the higher note of the octave</note>

Then join AB and CD in a straight line, and a semicircle drawn from the midpoint of the joined lines will determine a line drawn perpendicularly from the point where the two lines meet; this creates a mean proportional, just as was done before. In the same way, you will find the mean proportional between CD and EF, and countless others that can be placed between those newly discovered.

### Proposition IV.
#### To find the mean proportionals that bisect the whole tone and the semitone.

Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who argued that musical intervals should be judged by the ear and divided into equal parts, rather than strictly by the whole-number ratios favored by the Pythagoreans</note> and his followers, as seen in the preceding pages, were accustomed to dividing the <term>tone|A whole step</term> into two equal semitones, and one <term>semitone|A half step</term> into two equal <term>dieses|Small musical intervals, often less than a semitone</term>; which...

# Book IV. On the Geometrical Division of the Monochord: 207

...which they demonstrated by the following reasoning. Let there be two strings, A and C, in a **sesquioctave ratio** <note>original: "proportione sesquioctaua"; a 9:8 ratio, which defines a standard Pythagorean whole tone</note>, forming a whole tone. Let the mean proportional B be sought according to the preceding proposition. I say that the line or string B will divide the given tone into two equal parts, namely into two equal **semitones of Aristoxenus** <note>Aristoxenus of Tarentum was an ancient Greek theorist who argued that the ear, rather than mathematical whole numbers, should judge intervals; he was an early proponent of dividing the octave into equal parts</note>. For as A relates to B, so B relates to C; but A to B and B to C will sound as two equal semitones because of the equality of the proportion. Therefore, the point is proven. But if one finds two other mean proportionals between AB and BC, he will have three mean proportionals, which will divide the tone into four equal <term>dieses|The smallest intervals in ancient Greek music theory, often used to describe quarter-tones</term>.

->[Diagram: Three horizontal lines representing string lengths. Line A is at the top labeled 1, Line B in the middle labeled 2, and Line C at the bottom labeled 3. A large number 2 is positioned to the right, indicating the division of the interval.]<-

**Proposition V.**
***To divide an octave into 12 semitones by means of 11 mean proportionals.***

This can be achieved in two ways: the first is geometrical, the second mechanical. In the first method, you will proceed as follows: let there be two given strings in a **double ratio** <note>original: "dupla proportione"; a 2:1 ratio, which creates the musical interval of an octave</note> A to B. Find the mean proportional C between them. Then, through the second proposition, find two mean proportionals I and L between C and A, and two other mean proportionals M and N between C and B. The given interval will then be divided into 6 equal parts by 5 mean proportionals. If you then find further mean proportionals between each of these, you will have the mean proportionals between the two extreme strings A and B by which the interval is divided into 12 exactly equal semitones.

**A system of 11 mean proportionals by which the octave is divided into 12 equal semitones of Aristoxenus.**

## CHAPTER VIII.

### On the Dichotomous Instrument, by which we can geometrically divide any consonance into 2 equal parts more quickly than can be said.

### Proposition I.

->To divide a tone, major third, fourth, fifth, sixth—in a word, the whole system—into two equal parts.<-

We showed it to be impossible <note>original Greek: "ἀδύνατον"</note> arithmetically with fixed numbers and rational ratios <note>The author is referring to the mathematical fact that you cannot find a rational number (a simple fraction) that perfectly bisects most musical ratios, like the 9:8 whole tone</note>. You shall construct the instrument as follows: let any given straight line AV on a wooden or bronze plate be bisected at point B. ### Corollary.

From these demonstrations, it follows by what method one can divide the intervals of any entire system <note>A "system" refers to a complete scale or a sequence of musical notes</note> into two equal parts using this instrument. This is achieved if one transfers the intervals of the entire system onto the line **B V** of the Instrument, and then proceeds as previously described.

And these are the matters we thought necessary to discuss regarding the division of the Monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships between musical intervals</note>. All of these points could have been deduced at much greater length, but for the sake of brevity, we have judged these alone to be sufficient for an understanding and knowledge of musical Geometry.

He who desires the more hidden secrets <note>original: "arcaniora"</note> of this musical geometry should consult the sixth and ninth books of this work. There, he will find many things—which could not be presented here due to the nature of the subject matter and the order of the work (such as those things pertaining to Geometric and Static music <note>In this context, "Static music" refers to the study of musical ratios as they relate to weights and the physical properties of objects</note>)—delivered with as much variety as possible.

Since these things have been handed down, as it were, in a theoretical sense <note>original: "speculativè"</note>, nothing now remains except that we reduce all those principles to human uses—that is, to **practice**. This we shall perform hereafter, with divine grace assisting us.

Book V. On the Crafting of Harmony. 213

...but in vain; for we speak here of **Melothesia** <note>The art of "melody-making" or setting text to music.</note>, or of composition, by which we report harmonic motifs properly ordered in different voices. I am not ignorant indeed that at all times there has been some natural **Counterpoint** <margin>Whether the ancients used music of several voices.</margin>, by which two or more singing together affect a diversity of voices, of the kind one may hear among sailors, reapers, and others; I am also aware that in the many-stringed instruments used by the Ancients, harmony was constituted from the harmonious vibration of different strings, as all Ancient authors on Music show. But we do not speak of these; the question is only whether the Ancients had the **Symphonetic** <note>The art of polyphonic or "symphonic" harmony.</note> art or music, as it is used today or something similar, constituted from several voices?

But before this controversy is decided, three things occur to us to be examined first. **First**, how did the ancient Ecclesiastical <note>Early Christian or Church-related.</note> Musicians mark their harmonic steps? **Second**, what signs did they use? **Third**, whether they composed for several voices? And although we have handed these things down extensively in our various writings on Music, it seemed fit to repeat a few things from many in this place, lest some doubt arise for the curious reader in the course of reading.

Most people ascribe the invention of the entire musical business used today (by which we constrain the ascent and descent of voices through notes of different value within five-line staves, or, to speak more clearly, within five linear spaces) to **Guido of Arezzo**. <note>An 11th-century monk regarded as the father of modern musical notation.</note> But when I had more diligently searched the hidden corners of older libraries, I finally found that those linear spaces by which we represent harmonic intervals were in use much earlier. For on my journey to Malta, while I was surveying the library of St. Savior in Messina, which is very well equipped with Greek Manuscripts, a manuscript book of Hymns was shown to me by those monks, written about 700 years ago, in which many Hymns were seen expressed in musical notes; and eight lines had been drawn, to which at the beginning as many letters corresponded; on the lines, however, the ascent and descent of the voices was observed by black dots, or rather little circles, as the following Diagram teaches.

Book 5. On the Art of Composition. 215

...was sung; and let the same judgment hold for others; all of which I would treat more extensively in this place if they were not already clear from the basics of practical Music, which we presuppose here. But so that Guido <note>Guido d'Arezzo (c. 991–1033), a Benedictine monk and music theorist.</note> might proceed more successfully, he placed dots within 5 lines, each of which corresponded to individual <term>clefs</term> <note>Symbols used to indicate the pitch of written notes.</note>, with the syllables placed below them; according to the intervals of those dots, the harmonic intervals were also arranged. As appears in the following Example.

-> [ A musical staff with five lines and a clef ] <-
-> ut mi fa sol la sol fa mi la sol fa sol <-

While I was treating these matters, the Most Reverend Abbot Don Diego de Franchis <note>A 17th-century Benedictine historian.</note> informed me that very ancient <term>antiphonals</term> <note>Books containing the chants or "antiphons" sung during the liturgy.</note> are kept in the Monastery of Vallombrosa, which were in use before the time of Guido. In these, instead of musical notes, they used dots placed above or below a single line according to the cadences of the hymn or antiphon. He gave me the following example, where the descent and ascent of the dots represent the intervals of the Antiphon *Salve Regina*.

-> ———————————————————————————————————————— <-
-> . . . . . . . . . . . . <-
<note>In the original text, these dots are placed at varying heights above and below the single horizontal line to indicate pitch.</note>
-> ut mi fa sol la sol fa mi la sol fa sol <-

From this is known that species of composition which to this day we call **Counterpoint**, in which, while we place notes against notes, we use "points" or dots.

For it is certain that Guido did not use the musical notes common in our time; <margin>Jean des Murs, inventor of musical notes.</margin> therefore, in the Guidonian invention, a method for measuring time in song was lacking, until about 300 years later, a certain distinguished musician, **Jean des Murs** of Paris <note>A 14th-century mathematician and astronomer who developed "mensural notation," which allowed for specific rhythmic durations.</note>, putting the finishing touch on Guidonian music, devised notes by which the duration of time could be shown. That Guido himself discovered the syllables <note>The solmization syllables: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la.</note> is asserted in a certain letter to Brother Michael, a monk of the same Order, cited by Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian.</note> in the year 1022; in which letter he complains greatly about the malice of certain people, as can be seen there.

It is added in the same place that Pope Benedict VIII sent three messengers to him in Arezzo to lead him to Rome for the purpose of publicly explaining the recently invented method and logic of singing. Once the message was received, Guido was conducted to Rome by his Abbot and the chief Canons of the Church of Arezzo and presented himself to the Pope. The Pontiff received him most kindly and would not let him leave until he had learned to sing one of the verses from his Antiphonal. He wrote a book about his invention which he called sometimes the *Introductory* and sometimes the *Micrologus* <note>original: *Micrologum*</note>, dedicated to Bishop Theobald of Arezzo, where in the dedication he promises a skill in singing within the space of a month which, in the old style, even a person of great talent could scarcely achieve in many years. He finally ends the book with these words: *The end of the Micrologus of Guido, aged 34 years, under Pope John XX, etc.*

Furthermore, Guido, not yet content with this new method of singing, was the first to devise a <term>symphony</term> of many voices, unheard of before this time. He was also the author of <term>polyplectric</term> instruments <note>Instruments with many "plectra" or jacks, essentially keyboard instruments.</note>, such as harpsichords, clavichords, and the like, which the already cited dedication implies, as he used a certain harmonically constructed **monochord** for singing. <margin>Guido, inventor of polyphonic music.</margin> From these things, therefore, I conclude that Guido stood out as the Inventor of **polyphonic Music**; since before his time, it cannot be gathered from any monuments of the Ancients that this kind of Music was in use among them.

<summary>Kircher credits Guido d'Arezzo with the invention of the musical staff and polyphony, while noting that Jean des Murs later added rhythmic notation. The text highlights a transition from ancient single-line "dot" notation to the multi-voice structures used in the 17th century.</summary>

### CHAPTER III.
### On Plainchant.

**Plainchant** <note>Original: *Musica plana*. Also known as Gregorian chant; a monophonic, rhythmically free style of church music.</note> does not weigh the duration of time, but rather the differences between high and low pitches, because none is more suitable for divine worship; for it contains solemnity along with clarity, and it inspires devotion wonderfully. It is divided into Boethian, Gregorian, and Aretinian types.
**Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on music served as the standard textbook for a millennium.</note>, imitating the Greeks and **Pythagoras**, established 15 divisions on the <term>monochord</term> <note>A single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals mathematically.</note> (that is, within the <term>disdiapason</term> <note>A double octave, the standard range of the "Greater Perfect System" of Greek music theory.</note> or greatest system), whom Saint **Ambrose** and Saint **Augustine** followed among the Latins.
Moreover, they divided these 15 strings or positions into 4 <term>tetrachords</term> <note>Four-note scales used in ancient Greek music theory.</note>, or into 5 fourths, which allowed a semitone between the first and second points. But since these were treated extensively at the beginning of the 3rd book, I did not wish to be longer here; a simple inspection of the diagram placed there is sufficient.
Afterward, **Saint Gregory the Great** introduced 7 letters—A B C D E F G—around the year 594 of the Lord, repeating these up to the number 15. Finally, **Guido of Arezzo** enriched the "hand" or musical scale with 20 letters and 6 syllables: *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la* <note>The origins of modern solfège (do, re, mi...); *ut* was later replaced by *do*.</note>, as was shown and is clear from the Manual scale. In this, you will especially consider these things:

<margin>
Things to
consider in the
musical scale.
</margin>

**First**, the Scale with <term>clefs</term> and voices cleverly arranged.
**Second**, the letters with signs divided in many ways into lines and spaces, so that $\Gamma$ *ut* <note>The lowest note of the medieval system, "Gamma Ut."</note> occupies a line, while A *re* occupies a space.
**Third**, the Clefs are divided into low, high, and super-high pitches. For the first 8 letters with signs are low, the following 7 are high, and the last 5 are super-high.
**Fourth**, the letters are also divided into 7 <term>deductions</term> <note>Also called hexachords; a series of six notes starting on different pitches (G, C, or F).</note> and distributed as if into colonies; the locations of the deductions are always situated with the voice *ut*, to which the other 5 notes *re, mi, fa, sol, la* are added to complete the <term>hexachord</term>.
**Fifth**, the deductions are governed by 3 properties: by the <term>natural</term>, the <term>hard B</term> (represented by the square $\natural$ symbol), and the <term>soft B</term> (the flat symbol ♭). The hard B property enjoys three deductions, by which the letter G ascends; namely F *fa, ut*; G *sol, re, ut* (low), and G *sol, re, ut* (high). Those sung through the soft B are F *fa, ut* (low) and F *fa, ut* (high).
**Sixth**, only 3 principal Clefs are considered, depicted by the 3 following notes: F *fa, ut*; C *sol, fa, ut*; and G *sol, re, ut*. F *fa, ut* is noted with this sign [stylized F-clef symbol]. They denoted C *sol, fa, ut* with this sign [stylized C-clef symbol], which held the seat they also called "natural." The 3rd letter, G, was signed and had its seat in the same clef. And with these, they marked the entire harmonic system; where one must also note the mutations <note>The process of switching between hexachords to reach notes outside a six-note range.</note> in *ut, re, mi* when ascending, and in *fa, sol, la* when descending. Note also that the distance between each of the 6 singable syllables is a whole tone, except in *mi* and *fa*, which are a semitone apart, as has been shown extensively elsewhere.

**Mensural Music** <note>Original: *Musica Figurata*. Music where the shape of the note dictates its specific rhythmic value, unlike the free rhythm of plainchant.</note> is *the diverse quantity of notes and the inequality of shapes, which are increased or diminished according to the requirement of mode, time, and prolation* <note>Technical terms for the rhythmic relationships between different note levels (longs, breves, semibreves).</note>.
In this, the following are considered:
1. The lines on which musical figures are written, and the spaces between them. They call the lowest line the first "string," the following the second, and so on for the others. And each pair is distant...

As for what pertains to the signs, the <term>prolation</term> <note>The relationship between different levels of rhythmic duration, essentially the "time signature" of the era.</note>, and the value of the notes, take note:

There are eight notes or "singable figures" which, when placed on the lines, distinguish the short and long durations of time to be spent in singing. 2. The value of these is such that one is always double the next. Hence, a **Maxima** is worth two **Longs**; a **Long** is worth two **Breves**; a **Breve** is worth two **Semibreves**; a **Semibreve** is worth two **Minims**; <margin>The value of musical notes.</margin> a Minim is worth two **Semiminims**, and so on for the others. This follows the rules of <term>imperfect time</term> <note>In early music theory, "perfect" time was triple meter (based on the Trinity), while "imperfect" time was duple meter (where notes divide into two).</note>.

3. They used to assign certain properties to these notes, which they expressed with these words:
The **Maxima** *sleeps*; the **Long** *reclines*; the **Breve** *sits*; the **Semibreve** *strolls*; the **Minim** *walks*; the **Semiminim** *runs*; the **Chroma** *flies*; the **Semichroma** *vanishes*. <note>This was a popular mnemonic used by music teachers to help students visualize the relative speeds of the notes.</note> Much could be said in this place regarding time, prolation, and the signs of the notes. ### CHAPTER V.
### On the Parts of the Art of Composing Harmony.

**Harmony** is the union of diverse tones reduced to a concord. For it does not only admit a simple melody in higher or lower sounds, proceeding from interval to interval with faster or slower motion according to the time prescribed in the notes—as happens in **Plainchant** or **Gregorian chant**—but it also possesses other voices that create a concord and sound together as "accidents." From these, as if from limbs or parts, harmony is composed. These parts can number 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and so on—however many the composer desires. Nevertheless, there are always only four principal parts...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of musical composition from the previous section on notation and note values, now moving into the specific characteristics and roles of the four primary voice parts: Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass.</meta>

218 *Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

<margin>Characteristics of the highest voice.</margin>
The voices are called **Soprano**, **Alto**, **Tenor**, and **Bass**: 1. The **Soprano** (which is also called the *Discant* or the *Superior* part, the *Soprano* by the Italians, the *Haut-contre* <note>original: "Hautcōtie" (Haut-contre). While usually meaning a high tenor today, Kircher uses it here for the highest part.</note> by the French, and the *Netodus* <note>original: "Netodus," from the Greek "nete," the highest string of the lyre.</note> by the Greeks) is the highest voice of any harmony, mostly suited to the voices of children. It especially delights in moderate intervals, such as thirds, fifths, and sixths; it shrinks wonderfully from larger leaps, such as frequent octaves—especially when descending—and it always completes the Tenor (which it respects as the leader and "choir-master") both in its harmonies and in the logic of its fugues and cadences. In the nature of things, it represents **fire**, which does not know how to be contained at the bottom.

<margin>Characteristics of the Alto.</margin>
2. The second voice is the **Alto**, called the *Paranetodus* <note>original: "Paranētodus," from the Greek "paranete," the string next to the highest.</note> or *Contratenor* by the Greeks, so called because it rarely meets in harmony with the Tenor; for the most part, it holds a fourth above the Tenor. It is common for this voice, not infrequently, to be shaken out of and exiled from its proper place. Many times, it must also yield its place to rests to avoid the <term>tritone</term> <note>An unstable interval of three whole tones, often called "the devil in music" in this period.</note> and the diminished fifth. On the other hand, when it takes the opportunity to "raise its crest," it stirs up a certain ambition regarding the seat of the highest voice during the formation of cadences. In the nature of things, it corresponds to the element of **air**, which is composed of both high and low, just as air is both hot and moist.

<margin>Characteristics of the Tenor.</margin>
3. The third voice is the **Tenor**, called *Mesodos* <note>original: "Mesodos," from the Greek "mese," the middle string.</note> by the Greeks; so called from "holding" <note>original: "a tenendo."</note>, because proceeding with a constant pace between the low and high intervals, it "holds" the melody, as it were. This is not only because it has more elegant consonances with the Soprano, but also because it holds the circuit and limits of the entire harmony, not permitting the other voices to break out above or below them. Judgment of the <term>mode</term> <note>The underlying scale or "tone" of the piece.</note> must also be made from the Tenor, and it is usually an octave apart from the Soprano. This voice is common to almost everyone except boys and women; for with this voice, men perform Plainchant or Gregorian chant. When boys and women sing it, they sound an octave higher, as was shown elsewhere. In the nature of things, it holds the place of **water**, established with a certain even weight.

<margin>Characteristics of the Bass.</margin>
4. The fourth voice is the **Bassis**, commonly called the **Bass**, and *Hypatodus* <note>original: "Hypatodus," from the Greek "hypate," the lowest string.</note> by the Greeks; so called because all voices lean upon it as if upon a base or foundation. For when that voice is less firm in a concert, all the remaining voices waver and falter, nor can they have any majesty. This voice is therefore properly the lowest voice of any concert, the support and pillar of all the other voices. It delights in lower and larger intervals, such as the fourth, fifth, and octave. In the nature of things, it corresponds to the **Earth**.

<margin>Which of the four voices is more worthy.</margin>
Furthermore, there is great controversy over which of these four is the more worthy voice. Some prefer the *Netodus* or **Soprano**, while others prefer the *Hypatodus* or **Bass**. We say that each, considered in its own kind, is most worthy, since neither has dignity without mutual correspondence. Thus, one who hears the **Bass** alone desires, by a certain natural instinct, to hear either the **Soprano** or the **Tenor**; and one who perceives the **Soprano** alone immediately desires the **Bass**, without which the upper voice deservedly vanishes or is rendered unpleasant. For since harmony is a certain "composite," and every composite (as the physicists say) consists of "matter" and "form," certainly both parts conspire toward the perfection of the whole. The **Bass** concurs as the *matter*, while the **Soprano** acts as the *form* of the musical composite. Just as matter is the subject for the form and all other qualities, so the **Bass** stands under the remaining voices. Just as matter is prior to form in its origin (as that which receives the form), so too is the **Bass**. Yet, just as form surpasses matter in essence, nobility, and dignity, so too does the **Soprano** exceed the **Bass** in the speed of the voice, as well as in its subtlety and ornamentation <note>original: "diminutione."</note>. For since a thing is more excellent the more it is in motion, certainly the **Soprano** voice must be judged more excellent than the **Bass**, which has less motion and is closer to rest. But to embrace many things in few words: each prevails in its own dignity, which then acquires its fullness when both are united with the rest to complete the perfection of the harmony. But consider here the notation of the individual voices.

Book V. On the Art of Composition. 221

## Section I.
## On the Division of Consonances.

Various authors have held various opinions concerning **consonances** <term>consonance</term> <note>From the Latin *consonantia*, meaning "sounding together." In music theory, it refers to intervals that sound stable and pleasant to the ear.</note>. The ancients listed fewer, while the moderns recognize more; however, among the most esteemed authors, there are no more than six simple consonances, according to **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose work *De institutione musica* was the standard music theory textbook for a thousand years.</note> in Book 2, Chapter 6. **Glareanus** <note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563), a famous Swiss music theorist.</note> also testifies to this in Book 1, Chapter 9. Furthermore, although some music writers judge any harmony beyond the **double octave** <note>original: "di diapason"</note> to be fruitless—because higher sounds do not allow for a **blending** <term>crasis</term> <note>original: "crasin," a Greek term for "mixture." Here it refers to the way two notes fuse together into a single harmonious sound.</note> and are perceived with greater difficulty by the judgment of the ears—nevertheless, in our age, the range extends not only to two octaves, but to three, and indeed even to four. Whence:

Consonances are first generally divided into **perfect** and **imperfect**; and into **simple** and **compound**.

**Perfect consonances** are those concluded within these first four numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4. <margin>Which intervals are perfect Consonances.</margin> They are based partly on **multiple proportions** and partly on **superparticular proportions** <term>superparticular</term> <note>A mathematical ratio where the larger number is exactly one more than the smaller (e.g., 2:1, 3:2, 4:3).</note>, such as the double, the one-and-a-half (*sesquialtera*), the one-and-a-third (*sesquitertia*), triple, and quadruple. These correspond to the **octave, fifth, fourth, twelfth,** and **fifteenth**. They are called "perfect" either because of the perfection of the numbers themselves, or because they alone perfectly satisfy the hearing; thus, whoever hears them appropriately coordinated perceives nothing discordant or incongruous. The reason for this is nothing other than the simplicity of the numbers producing such consonances.

**Imperfect consonances** are all those that occur after the number four, such as 4, 5, and 6. <margin>Which are imperfect Consonances.</margin> These include the **major third** <note>original: "sesquiquarta," the ratio 5:4.</note> and the **minor third** <note>original: "sesquiquarta" [Note: This is likely a typo in the original Latin for *sesquiquinta*, the 6:5 ratio].</note>. When these are joined to the **fourth** <note>original: "diateſſaron."</note>, they generate the **major and minor sixths** <note>original: "hexachordon maius & minus."</note>. They are called "imperfect" either because they do not fall quite so gratefully upon the ears, or because the proportions that constitute them are a greater distance from unity. For they are partly of superparticular proportion, like the two thirds, and partly of **superpartient proportion** <note>A ratio where the larger number is more than one unit greater than the smaller (e.g., 5:3).</note>, like the two sixths. **Simple consonances** are those contained within a single octave, such as the Third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and octave. **Compound** or **Replicated consonances** are those that occur beyond the octave.

Some divide consonances into three classes: some are **simple** or primary; <margin>Consonances divided into 3 classes.</margin> others are **compound** and secondary; and finally, others are **doubly compound** or triplicated. Properly speaking, there are only four **Primary** consonances: both Thirds, the Fifth, and the Sixth. To these, some add the **Unison** and some the **Fourth** (which, as I have said, is not considered a consonance when viewed in a certain way, yet it produces consonance).

There are four **Compound** consonances: the Octave, tenth, twelfth, and thirteenth. Indeed, an **Octave** is nothing other than two unisons, one low and the other high. A **Tenth** is nothing other than a Third joined to an octave. An **Eleventh** is nothing other than a Fourth added to an octave. A **Twelfth** is nothing other than a Fifth joined to an octave. And a **Thirteenth** is nothing other than a Sixth joined to an octave.

**Triplicated** consonances are those that arise from the simpler ones being tripled, and they are four: the Fifteenth, Seventeenth, Nineteenth, and Twentieth. A **Fifteenth** is nothing other than three unisons: low, high, and very high. A **Seventeenth** is nothing other than a Third joined to a Fifteenth. Likewise, a Fifth joined with a Fifteenth constitutes a **Twentieth**, as seen in the following:

| | | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Primary or Simple | 1 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| Secondary or Compound | 8 | 10 | 11 | 12 | 13 |
| Triplicated or Doubly Compound | 15 | 17 | 18 | 19 | 20 |

| **Simple or primary** | | | | | **Secondary or compound** | | | | | **Triple or complex** | | | | |

**A**nd these are the harmonies that musicians use everywhere; there can certainly be many more, as is the case with clavichords, organ pipes, and other instruments to be explained in the following book. In those instruments, it often happens that the voices extend across four **octaves** <term>octave</term> <note>original: "octauas." An interval spanning eight notes of a scale.</note>, as can be seen from the **tables** <note>original: "Abacis," referring here to musical charts or diagrams.</note> placed there. However, just as the human voice rarely ascends beyond three octaves, musicians likewise have no need for more harmonies than these.

<margin>Why certain harmonies are called perfect.</margin>

There are truly five perfect harmonies: the 5th, 8th, 12th, and 15th <note>These correspond to the Fifth, Octave, Twelfth, and Double Octave.</note>. Two are [Musical staff notes labeled 'A'] simple and just as many are compound. They are called perfect because, as I have said, they produce a perfect sound without any **harshness** <note>original: "displicentia," literally "displeasure" or "dissatisfaction." In music, this refers to dissonance.</note>. For this reason, a **semitone** <term>semitone</term> <note>The smallest interval in traditional Western music; a half-step.</note> is not found within them; if a semitone is added to them, then a perfect fifth becomes a **diminished fifth** <term>semidiapente</term> <note>original: "semidiapente." A dissonant interval also known as a tritone.</note>, or an imperfect 5th consisting of two whole tones and two semitones. This is the distance from *mi* to *fa* <note>In the solfège system of the time, the semitone always occurred between the syllables *mi* and *fa*.</note> across a fifth, and it is a forbidden interval. Wherever it occurs, the *mi* is usually changed into *fa* <note>This refers to the practice of *musica ficta*, where performers added accidentals (sharps or flats) to avoid harsh dissonances not written on the page.</note>, as demonstrated by the letter A in that section. Again, if a semitone is added to an octave, the perfect **octave** <term>diapason</term> <note>original: "diapason," the Greek term for an octave.</note> becomes a **diminished octave** <term>semidiapason</term> <note>original: "semidiapason." An octave shortened by a semitone, which sounds highly unstable.</note>, which is the distance of *mi* to *fa* across an octave. This is a forbidden interval; when it occurs, the *mi* is usually changed to *fa* so that a perfect octave is created.

You see, therefore, why these harmonies are called perfect; they are certainly endowed with such power that, in whatever way they are arranged among themselves, they always produce a harmony. Both the beginning and the end of musical compositions usually start with them. They do, however, maintain some difference in perfection among themselves; for the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> is more excellent than the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, and the Fifth more than the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, and so on for the rest, as has been shown more extensively elsewhere.

<margin>Why other harmonies are called imperfect.</margin>

Imperfect harmonies, on the other hand, are those that do not perfectly satisfy the judgment of the ears. They are called imperfect because they do not stand as proven according to the doctrine of mathematical proportions; many of the same species follow one another immediately, whether ascending or descending. There are six of them: the 3rd, 6th, 10th, 13th, 17th, and 20th. They are called imperfect because, as I said, they produce an incomplete sound and have little **pleasantness** <note>original: "gratiam," literally "grace" or "charm."</note> unless they are mixed with perfect ones, or at least joined to perfect ones at the end. And because imperfect harmonies can become perfect by means of **chromatic ratios** <term>chromatic</term> <note>original: "ratione chromatis." This refers to using sharps or flats to alter the quality of an interval, such as making a minor third major.</note>, semitones can be conveniently placed within them. This allows a perfect interval to be made from an imperfect 3rd or 6th, and vice-versa, depending on the nature of the **hard or soft song** <note>original: "cantus duri vel mollis." This refers to the system of hexachords: *cantus durus* used B-natural, while *cantus mollis* used B-flat.</note>; about which we shall speak in a specific treatise. But now let us follow each one individually.

When two or more voices or instruments sound the same pitch.</note> is therefore the foundation of all harmony; it is a "self-sounding" voice <note>original: "ἀυτόφωνος" (autophonos)</note>, or sounding the same, lacking any interval. It is the same thing in Music as a **point** is in Geometry, or **unity** (the number one) is in Arithmetic. ## 226 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

### § II.
### On dissonances, or dissonant intervals, and their nature and quality.

**Dissonant intervals** are those that strike the ears unpleasantly. These are, primarily: the **second** (or tone), the **tritone** <note>An interval of three whole tones, notorious in early music for its perceived harshness.</note>, the **diminished fifth** <note>original: "semidiapente"</note>, the **seventh**, the **diminished octave** <note>original: "semidiapason"</note>, and their various compounds.

The **Tone**, or **second**, is a dissonance and the first composite musical interval, formed by two voices and one whole step. It occurs between any two adjacent strings <note>In this context, "strings" or "chords" refers to the notes of a scale or the physical strings of a monochord.</note> arranged by tone, except for the steps E–F and B–C, and in other notes affected by the signs for flat (b) and sharp (♯). It is twofold: **major** and **minor**. The minor consists of the **sesquinonal** proportion <term>sesquinonal</term> <note>The mathematical ratio 10:9.</note>, while the major consists of the **sesquioctaval** proportion <term>sesquioctaval</term> <note>The mathematical ratio 9:8.</note>.

-> **Major, minor, and major tones** <-
[Musical notation on a five-line staff showing three intervals labeled "Major Tone", "Minor", and "Major".]

Furthermore, the **Tone** is divided into two **semitones**—specifically the **major** and the **minor**—as we have shown elsewhere. However, there is no small dispute and contention among authors regarding which semitone—the major or the minor—is the constituent part of the species of the **Fourth** and **Fifth**. We assert irrefutably that it is the **major semitone**, and that it consists of 5 **commas** <term>comma</term> <note>A very small interval, the "atom" of musical measurement, representing the tiny difference between two nearly identical notes in different tuning systems.</note>. It is, however, called the "lesser interval" of the diatonic genus; for this reason, some were perhaps deceived and thought it should be called the "minor semitone," as we have shown at length on page 102.

This **major semitone** is the space and primary interval found naturally between the musical syllables or strings ***mi-fa*** or ***fa-mi***. It consists in the **sesquidecimafifth** proportion <term>sesquidecimafifth</term> <note>The ratio 16:15, the standard measurement for a diatonic semitone.</note>, having the ratio of 15 to 16. It is the **soul of all music** and the **rule of all harmony**, insofar as it constitutes the entire diversity and variety of harmonic intervals. Consequently, if it is found in the first interval [of a scale], it constitutes the first species; if in the second, the second species, and so on for the rest, as we showed on page 148. In that section and elsewhere, we have followed the opinion of the ancients and called this semitone sometimes "major" and sometimes "minor" interchangeably. However, having considered the matter more carefully, we have decided that henceforth it should always be called the **major semitone**. This is because it is indeed larger, as is evident from the form of its mathematical proportion, and it consists of 5 commas. I am not unaware that some posit a threefold semitone (major, medium, and minor); but since we have dealt with those above, and they do not occur in practical use, I have judged it superfluous to treat them more extensively. The genuine expression of this major semitone in musical notes is as follows:

-> **Major Semitone** <-
[Musical notation on a five-line staff showing four pairs of notes, labeled below as "mi fa", "fa mi", "mi fa", "fa mi".]

The **minor semitone** is the space and interval found on the string of **B-flat** and **B-natural** <note>original: "b fa b mi"</note>, by the power and force of the flat (b) and sharp (♯) signs. It does not occupy different strings <note>Meaning it occurs on the same letter-name note, like C to C-sharp, rather than C to D-flat.</note>, as is evident from the diagram at the side. The duty of this minor semitone is to diminish a major consonance and render it minor, and vice versa. It is found between the notes *trite synnemmenon* and *paramese* <note>Greek terminology for B-flat and B-natural.</note>, as was said above. These signs are the markers that distinguish **natural song** from **accidental song**—or, what is the same thing, **hard** (*durus*) from **soft** (*mollis*). Many people somewhat thoughtlessly confuse the flat (b) with the sharp (♯), but they would do better if they marked each type of song with its appropriate sign—

<margin>The minor semitone.</margin>

## CHAPTER VII.
## On Tones or Modes, and Their Number and Quality.

A Tone or Mode is nothing other than a certain and determined method of forming a harmony <note>original: "concentus"</note>, as was shown at length in Book III. It is of such great weight in our *Symphoniurgia* <note>The art of composing harmonious music.</note> that if anyone attempts to compose a melody <note>original: "Melothesiam"</note> without a certain and determined mode, he will undoubtedly have made a "syllogism without a figure." For just as the three operations of the intellect, with which Logic (for example) is concerned, serve no discourse unless they are skillfully directed through syllogisms under certain and determined "figures" <note>In traditional logic, a "figure" refers to the specific arrangement of terms in a logical argument. Without a proper figure, the argument has no valid structure.</note>; so too a harmony will be judged deservedly confused, imperfect, rash, and bound by no laws of harmonic rhythm if it is not made under a certain and determined mode. Therefore, although we have treated this most necessary business of all music very extensively in Book III, we have nonetheless decided to bring it back to the anvil here, lest there be anything that might hinder the beginner <note>original: "Tyronē"</note> in the successful progress of their composition. We shall treat first of the number of Tones; second, of their division; third, of their various constitutions; and fourth, finally, of the nature and property of each.

### §. I.
### On the number of Modes or Tones.

There is such great disagreement among authors regarding the number and quality of tones that you can hardly discern which view to support. Some want exactly 14, following the seven species of the octave <note>original: "diapason species"</note> doubled. Others want only 12, following the seven species of the octave but rejecting two because of the "square b" <note>original: "b quadrum." This refers to B-natural, which can create the "tritone," an interval historically avoided in church music for its harshness.</note>, as was shown at length in Book III. Certain others established eight, as do all those who perform the Divine Offices and the Psalms, Introits, and Antiphons in churches, ordering them according to their own tones. Others, considering the first and the eighth to be one, have placed only seven, according to the seven species of the octave. From these, others have defined only six, rejecting one species because of the B-natural. The Greeks establish only four: "first, second, third, and fourth" <note>original: "πρῶτον δεύτερον τρίτον τέταρτον"</note>; so that it is truly a marvel that in a matter of such great importance, authors have been so dissonant. We, as we showed in Book III, judge that 14 tones can definitely be established if we consider them according to their full breadth <margin>14 Tones can be correctly established</margin>. For from the seven species of the octave, considered according to both harmonic and arithmetic division <note>These are mathematical ways of dividing the octave into a fifth and a fourth to create different modes.</note>, exactly 14 result. However, because two are for the most part unsuitable for music, 12 tones are received by the unanimous consent of the better class of musicians.

<summary>This page concludes the study of dissonant intervals and introduces the theory of musical modes, comparing the necessity of modes in music to the necessity of logical "figures" in reasoning. The author discusses historical debates over whether there are 4, 8, 12, or 14 musical modes, concluding that 12 are practically useful.</summary>

As for those who establish seventy-two tones, we assign them not to practical musicians, but to the Metaphysicians <note>Kircher is likely dismissing complex microtonal systems—such as those proposed by Nicola Vicentino—as being too abstract for the actual practice of music.</note>.

## §. II.
## On the Harmonic and Arithmetic Division and Arrangement of Tones.

<margin>Division of Tones into Authentic and Plagal.</margin>
The first division of tones is into the authentic and the plagal. The second is into the Mixed, Neutral, and Foreign; we shall deal with the first division first. But before we proceed further, it must be noted that the requirements of tones consist in octaves and numbers. If these are rightly arranged, the harmonic and arithmetic arrangement will flow from them. For just as it was shown in the preceding pages how octaves are made from Fourths and Fifths, so too from the tones and semitones of Fourths and Fifths is born that arrangement of which we speak, the Harmonic and Arithmetic, through their *eutaxia* <note>original: εὐταξία; meaning "good order" or "right arrangement."</note>.

A **Harmonic arrangement** is when, in an octave, the fifth is placed below and the fourth is placed above; from this arrangement are born six odd-numbered Authentic tones. It is called "harmonic" because the fifth always renders the fourth placed above it consonant.

An **Arithmetic arrangement** is when the fourth is placed below and the fifth is placed above; and from this constitution flow the even-numbered tones, which they call *plagios* <note>original: πλάγιος; meaning "sideways" or "oblique."</note> or plagal—that is, "inverted." For the arrangement of the octave is inverted: the Fourth, which in the Authentic was above the Fifth, now falls below it. It is called "Arithmetic" because, just as among Arithmeticians a larger number is placed in the higher position and a smaller in the lower <note>In the mathematical ratios of intervals, a Fifth (2:3) involves "smaller" numbers than a Fourth (3:4), but Kircher is referring to the division of the string length or the "arithmetic mean" where the smaller interval (the fourth) occupies the lower structural position.</note>, so in this arrangement the Fifth occupies the upper place and the Fourth the lower. And so, from each species of octave, two Tones arise: the Authentic and the Plagal.

An **Authentic tone** is a mode harmonically arranged—that is, it has the fifth below and the fourth above—and it is of an odd number. Its specific quality is to possess a greater and freer authority for ascending above the final key than the plagal; namely, it dominates within its own range up to the octave and even beyond with a certain bold license, adding or subtracting as it pleases. Whence the rule:

**Every song that completes its octave above the final seat is to be referred to the Authentic.**

Hence, among the Greeks, it is not inappropriately called *authentes* <note>original: αὐθέντης; meaning "Author" or "Master."</note>, meaning "Author" and "Lord." Musicians call harmonies established under this system "loud" and "masterly" <note>original: "clamosos & heriles"</note> because of their effect, as they complete the melody’s harmony in a direct ascent up to the 8th and 10th notes in respect to the final note, and they do not drop down more than a single step. There are six of these, as I said, of the odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. Whence the Verse:

*The tone from an odd number is Authentic,*
*Whose melody leaps high from its own seat,*
*Reaching the octave, from which it is scarcely permitted to descend.*

Or otherwise: *The odd number gives the Authentic, the even gives the plagal.*
*Call the Authentics the "masters" and the plagals the "servants";*
*The Authentics climb upward, and the servants downward.*

A **Plagal tone** is a mode arithmetically arranged—that is, it has the fourth below and the fifth above. Its specific quality is to descend below the final; it accepts increase and decrease beyond the sound. Whence the rule:

**A song having its octave so arranged that it has a fourth below the final and a fifth above the final must be assigned to the plagal tones.** These things, however, are to be understood of plainchant rather than figured <note>polyphonic or rhythmically complex</note> music, in which the key of either the plagal or the Authentic tone suffices.

There are six of these of the even numbers. Whence the Verse of the Ancients:

*The plagal tone wants to be of an even number,*
*Descending from its own region to the depths of the fifth,*
*Though it is granted to rise to the fifth, and rarely to the sixth.*

But the figure placed here will declare all things more clearly than many words:

Six

...or <term>subjugated</term> <note>original: "subjugales"; these are the Plagal modes, which are considered secondary or "under the yoke" of the Authentic modes</note> modes. It is called an **Arithmetic arrangement** because the fourth, being placed below, does not possess that same sweetness of harmony that it has when it follows the fifth. It is called "arithmetic" based on the relationship of the numbers 12, 9, and 6.

<margin>Why one is called Harmonic, and the other Arithmetic.</margin>

For just as 12 exceeds 9 by the same number—three—that 9 exceeds 6, so too in this arithmetic division of the <term>octave</term> <note>original: "diapason"</note>, the middle term is distant from the two extremes by an equal number of units. In contrast, the **Harmonic arrangement** is based on the numbers 12, 8, and 6. Here, the middle number 8 exceeds the lower 6 by two, while it is exceeded by the upper 12 by four. This is called "harmonic" because these proportions (12 to 8 being a Fifth, and 8 to 6 being a Fourth) reflect the natural resonance of musical strings.

<margin>The difference between the arrangements.</margin>

To state it simply:
1. In the **Harmonic arrangement** (Authentic modes), the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente"</note> is on the bottom and the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron"</note> is on top.
2. In the **Arithmetic arrangement** (Plagal modes), the **Fourth** is on the bottom and the **Fifth** is on top.

From these two arrangements, the twelve modes of music are constructed. The odd-numbered modes (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) are called **Authentic**, as they follow the harmonic division. The even-numbered modes (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) are called **Plagal** (or "oblique"), as they follow the arithmetic division. 

<note>The author is using Pythagorean number theory to explain why some scales feel "stable" (Authentic) and others feel "secondary" (Plagal). In the 17th century, music was seen as a branch of mathematics.</note>

### On the Tones and their Intervals

It is further required that we recognize the specific boundaries of these modes. Every mode is contained within the space of an octave, but they differ by where that octave begins and ends on the scale, and where it is "cut" by the middle note. 

*   **The First Mode (Authentic)**: Ranges from D to D, divided at A.
*   **The Second Mode (Plagal)**: Ranges from A to A, divided at D.

Even though both use the same notes, the "center of gravity" changes because of where the Fourth and Fifth are positioned.

A **Neutral** or **imperfect mode** is one that does not complete the <term>octave</term> <note>original: "diapason"</note>; it does not ascend beyond the sixth note, nor descend beyond the third. Hence the verse:
*The mode that does not rise by the law of the Authentic,*
*Nor is lowered by the rule of the Plagal, is rightly called Neutral.*

The **Foreign Mode** <note>original: "Tonus Peregrinus"</note> is so named, not because it belongs to foreigners, but because it is very rare and "alien" in our harmonies, <margin>What is the Foreign Mode?</margin> and is used for nothing except the psalm *When Israel went out of Egypt* <note>Psalm 114, traditionally sung to this unique "wandering" melody</note>. However, we shall show in what follows that it is properly the 9th mode, which the Ancients knew little about, as the eight <term>intonations</term> <note>standard melodic formulas used to start a chant</note> used until now were sufficient for them. The Aeolians used it most frequently, which is why it is also called the **Aeolian**. But let us return to the **Authentics** and **Plagals**.

An **Authentic** mode is therefore composed of 8 notes ascending by steps, or by leaps, or by a mixture of steps and leaps. A **Plagal** mode, however, consists of the same 8 notes, but descending by steps, leaps, or both. They have this in common: each pair of "neighboring" modes <note>an Authentic and its related Plagal</note> ends on one and the same letter or <term>key</term> <note>original: "clave"; here referring to the "final" or home note of the mode</note>. Thus, the 1st and 2nd modes end on **D**. The 3rd and 4th on **E**. The 5th and 6th on **F**. The 7th and 8th on **G**. The 9th and 10th on **A**. The 11th and 12th on **C**. All these are natural and <term>diatonic</term> <note>using the standard notes of the scale without sharps or flats</note>, as follows:

By the same logic, all those melodies that are marked with a <term>B-flat</term> <note>original: "b molli" or soft B</note> are categorized in exactly the same way and follow the same order—namely, according to the sequence of these six letters: **G, A, C, D, E, F**. These are called **accidental**, or "as-if" accidental and chromatic modes.

No mode ends on <term>B-natural</term> <note>original: "b quadro" or square B</note>. Consequently, no mode can be placed there unless it is supported by the help of <term>chromatic signs</term> <note>sharps and flats</note>. Yet, these signs cannot be applied to all modes in such a way that this problem does not occasionally intervene.

So, if you were to transpose the third mode to the fifth—that is, from E to B—instead of the true and standard intervals, prohibited and monstrous ones present themselves: a <term>semidiapente</term> <note>a diminished fifth, often called a "false fifth"</note> instead of a perfect fifth, and a <term>tritone</term> <note>an interval of three whole tones, historically nicknamed the "devil in music" for its harsh sound</note> instead of a perfect fourth. ### Section V.
### On the arrangement of Modes, and how they can be recognized in any melody.

Having established the composition and transposition of the <term>Tones</term> <note>original: "Tonorum"; here referring to the church modes like Dorian or Phrygian</note>, we now follow with the distinction by which the modes are most clearly discerned. This is found in the variation and change of the semitone within the Fifths and Fourths from which the octaves of the Modes are composed. As I have said before, this is of such great importance that if you were to remove the semitone from music, you might rightly be judged to have removed music entirely. For this reason, one mode usually differs from another by the placement of just a single semitone. Therefore, the primary types of Fifths must be carefully observed; for their arrangements and changes, due solely to the different placement of the semitone, produce the diversity in the modes. For example, consider the seventh and first, or the second and eighth; even if they are contained within the same octaves, because the semitones change their place within the Fifths, they produce notably different modes, as was demonstrated in the chapter on the species of the octave.

The Modes can therefore be recognized in six ways: from the beginning, the middle, and the end; from the species of the octave, fifth, and fourth; through the keys of the <term>clausulae</term> <note>original: "clausularum"; formal melodic endings or cadences</note> in individual modes within choral chant; and finally, they are most often recognized by their <term>Tropes</term> <note>distinctive melodic formulas or patterns</note>. <margin>How the Modes are discerned.</margin>

<margin>Modes are recognized in six ways.</margin> At the **beginning**, a mode is recognized by this rule common among the Ancients: Every song ascending from the final note to the fifth at the beginning is <term>Authentic</term> <note>The "higher" version of a mode, ranging from the final note to the octave above</note>; but that which goes below the final note is <term>Plagal</term> <note>The "lower" version, which ranges from a fourth below the final to a fifth above</note>. However, this rule is arbitrary and not a matter of law, for any note may take its beginning in any space, provided it is contained within the certain limits of its mode. Hence, the **Moderns** <note>original: "Neotericos"; referring to 17th-century composers</note> now take no account of this.

In the **middle**, they are recognized in two ways. First, by the **Range** <note>original: "Ambitu"</note> or course of the melody. Second, by the **Repercussion**. Regarding range, it should be noted that there is a fixed rule demonstrating how much a song ought to ascend above or descend below the final note; or rather, it is the circuit of the octave depicted in two different figures of letters of the same name. For instance, the range of the first mode is between two D's, as follows:

[Musical notation: A four-line staff with a C-clef on the second line from the bottom, showing a range from D to D with a diamond-shaped note on A.]

Hence, the proper and true range of any mode is completed within an octave, though the license of modern musicians frequently oversteps this.

**Repercussion** is nothing other than a certain and specific interval. For each Mode has its own cadences or courses, by which they can be distinguished by ear alone. Hence the Verse:

*Re, la,* belongs to the first; *re, fa,* gives the rule for the second;
*Mi, mi,* the Third has; the Fourth seeks *mi, la* for itself,
*Fa, fa,* the Fifth has; *fa, la,* the Sixth adopts for itself.
The Seventh has *ut, sol*; *ut, fa,* the last shall have. <note>These Latin syllables refer to the "characteristic" melodic intervals of each of the eight modes. For example, the 1st mode (Dorian) is characterized by the interval between D (Re) and A (La).</note>

It should be noted here in passing that one should not always cling to these repercussions; for that would be quite ungraceful. Instead, they should be represented occasionally through <term>fugues</term> and sweet cadences, as will be seen later.

From the **end**, the Mode is recognized according to that common proverb: *In the end, it will be seen what Mode it is.*

Whether the melody be in **Hard Song** <note>original: "cantus duri"; the system using B-natural</note> or **Soft Song** <note>original: "mollis"; the system using B-flat</note>, its Mode will be recognized from the final keys as follows:

# CHAPTER VIII.
## On the Modes of chant, both Ecclesiastical (or Gregorian) and Figurate.

<margin>The Authors of Ecclesiastical Chant: Ambrose and Gregory.</margin>

Two types of singing have been used in the Catholic Church up to this point: Ecclesiastical chant, also known as <term>cantus firmus</term> <note>literally "fixed song," the foundational melodic line of traditional church music</note> or plainchant; and secondly, <term>figurate chant</term> <note>elaborate music with varied rhythms and multiple parts, essentially early polyphony</note>. We do not inaccurately refer to these as **monodic** and **polyodic**. The former is called **monodic** because everyone sings the same melody using the same intervals; the latter is **polyodic** because it is sung by several different voices arranged harmonically. The founders of monodic or Ecclesiastical chant were those great lights of the Church, Saint Ambrose and Saint Gregory the Great, from whom it is called "Gregorian" even to this day. For these holy men of God—driven not so much by their own will as by divine instinct so that the offices and praises of God might be performed everywhere in the churches with decorum and majesty at the appointed times—left nothing undone. In imitation of the ancients, they sought out certain new modes of singing well and skillfully; that is, they adapted ecclesiastical songs to specific <term>tones</term> appropriate to the meaning of the words. They did this so that not only would the ears be stirred by the sweetness of the divine praises, but also so that, through the power of the melody, the soul might be caught up in God, resting as if in a center of sweetness, and might cling solely to the Best and Greatest God. 

From this, the custom and habit of singing the psalms with alternating intonations of voices in the choir has grown down to our own times. Hence, they composed <term>Antiphonaries</term> <note>books containing the choral parts of the Divine Office</note>, the <term>Introits</term> of the Masses, and other hymns with such great artistry, such appropriate harmony, such an ingenious arrangement of the Tones, and such a marvelous adaptation of the harmonic melodies to sacred matters, that they seem to have received the method of Ecclesiastical chant not from men, but as something <note>original Greek: θεόπλαστος (theoplastos)</note> "divinely fashioned," brought down from heaven itself. 

For among the <term>musurgi</term> <note>Kircher's term for musical craftsmen or composers</note> of today, who could compose anything similar? Following in their footsteps were many others afterward, who at all times strived to promote the dignity and preeminence of Ecclesiastical chant. I will say no more; but he who diligently examines the Antiphonaries and books of hymns, and correctly perceives the artistry and genius in the adaptation of the tones, will be forced to admit that in these times nothing similar has been done, nor can be done. The reason for this is nothing other than the fact that almost all musicians, having looked down upon the **monophony** <note>single-voiced music</note> of this chant, affect **polyphony**, that is, the harmony of many voices. However, what should be thought regarding the excellence of each will be discussed elsewhere. 

And this is that **choral** or **monastic** chant, which everyone calls **Gregorian**, some call **plain** (because it lacks the harmonic intervals of diverse voices), some call **firm**, others call **choral** (from the Choir), and others **monastic** (from the Monks). If it is performed correctly and with majesty, nothing can be more powerful in stirring the emotions. Furthermore, churchmen in the choir primarily use eight modes or tones, by which they regulate all their songs. I have decided to place their intonations or <term>Euauoæ</term> <note>a mnemonic word used in liturgical books consisting of the vowels from the phrase "saeculorum. Amen," used to indicate the ending of a psalm tone</note> here, so that the difference of each one may be more clearly known.
