### CHAPTER IX.
### On the division of Counterpoint.

**Music-making** <note>original: "Melopoeia"</note> or the **Craft of Harmony** <note>original: "Symphoniurgia"</note> is divided into Counterpoint and composition itself. **Counterpoint** is the skillful arrangement of a plainchant <note>the traditional, unadorned chant of the Church</note> proceeding with various melodies, or the setting of notes against one another; and this is of many types. One type is **Extemporaneous** <margin>What counterpoint is and how many types there are.</margin> or natural and common, which many barbarously call *fortisation* <note>original: "fortisationem"; likely a corruption of "fauxbourdon," a technique of improvised harmony</note>. Another is **Artistic** or **Florid**, which others call "composition," but which we entitle by the better names of *Melothesia* <note>melody-setting</note> or *Symphoniurgia*. The former is called extemporaneous because it is performed on the spot, not by premeditated reason or through the guidance of art, but with nature as its leader and dictator. This is the kind used by societies of miners, tailors, shepherds, and similar people laboring together, who use it to banish the weariness of their toil.

**Artistic counterpoint** is the fit and skillful joining and comparison of consonances <note>harmonious intervals</note> among themselves. As stated above, it is called counterpoint from "counter-positioning," because according to reason and rules, they set other notes against the existing consonances to produce a sweet and pleasant melody for the ears. It is also so called because a harmony emerges from voices set against each other, or as you might say, "point against point," because the notes of the Cantus, Alto, Tenor, and Bass are opposed to each other on the musical staff <note>original: "pentagrammo Melothetico"</note> like soldiers in a battle line. Or, as was shown earlier, because the ancients used points instead of notes.

Artistic counterpoint is threefold: **Simple**, **Florid**, and **Colored**. To these, some add free, bound, and syncopated counterpoint, though all of these can be conveniently reduced to the florid and colored styles.

**Simple artistic counterpoint** is that in which there is no variety of rhythm or note value; rather, point is placed against point—that is, note against note—with an equal measure of time. <margin>What simple counterpoint is.</margin> This occurs in the common singing of the psalms, or when individual opposing notes are of the same kind, quantity, and value, as is clear in the following example.

Hh [Counterpoint] <note>Catchword for the following page.</note>

But **florid** or **broken** counterpoint is when we adapt species of notes—decorated as if with paintings and the colors of various figures—to a Gregorian or choral chant, or to any subject whatsoever. We call it "broken" <note>original: "fractum"</note> because the notes of the remaining voices, which are applied to the choral chant, are resolved into smaller note shapes, as if they are broken and crumbled into fragments <note>original: "minutias"</note>, as follows in the subsequent example, in which the same subject of simple counterpoint is changed into florid.

### Diminished or florid counterpoint.

[Musical notation for four voices in florid counterpoint]

You see, therefore, how in this example it is no longer "note against note," but the notes of the lower voice are, as it were, broken and diminished; by which **diminution** <note>the division of long notes into many shorter, faster notes</note> not only is a remarkable variety achieved, but a peculiar sweetness and a certain majesty of harmonic song is won. For this reason, it has always been held in great esteem by the ancient Church fathers following Aretinus <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the medieval monk credited with inventing modern musical notation</note>.

...rather one should know that this is of such great importance, and involves such great difficulties, that it might make even the most skilled Masters sweat—especially if it is to be perfected with discernment and completed in every detail. We now intend to assign the rules for this here. Since every art and faculty is supported by certain specific rules—so that, namely, the Craftsmen may proceed with a good method and certainty, by which they avoid errors and slips, and finally, being directed according to the rules <note>Original: *canonicè*, meaning according to the "canon" or established law of the art.</note>, may reach the goal of the art—so too does the Composition of Harmony, being the most orderly of all, seem to claim these rules for itself as if by a certain right. Thus, the composers <note>Original: *Musurgi*</note> may attain the goal of the art, which is either the Praise of GOD, or the delight of oneself and others.

Therefore, let the rules be simple, by whose direction we proceed in this Musical Composition; they are both General and Particular. The General rules are those which teach us the general method to be preserved in Music; the Particular rules, indeed, show what must be observed by us in each specific type of Counterpoint. We shall treat both briefly.

**The first precept:** For the ease of Composition <note>Original: *Melothesias*, from the Greek for "placing a melody."</note>, the Beginner <note>Original: *Tyro*, a term for a recruit or apprentice.</note> should prepare for himself a reusable tablet <note>Original: *palimpsestum*, referring here to a slate or erasable surface for drafting music.</note> on which four musical staves <note>Original: *pentagramma*, literally "five-lines."</note> are drawn, and for each staff its own voice should be accommodated, in the manner which we proposed above, and finally propose here.

->Alto<-
->Tenor<-
->Bass<- <note>Original: *Basis*</note>

[The notation displays four numbered systems of clefs and signatures:]
1. Soft natural <note>Original: *mollem naturalem*, usually indicating a B-flat in the signature.</note>
2. Hard natural <note>Original: *duram naturalem*, indicating the use of B-natural.</note>

4. Hard transposed

We have marked in these staves the individual voices with various clefs, not because they must all be placed at once, but so that the composer may choose for himself the signature which is most suitable for the proposed purpose. Hence, we have placed the first signature as soft natural, the second as hard natural, the third as soft transposed, and finally the fourth as hard transposed.

**The second precept:** It is necessary for the Composer to know the doctrine of the tones <note>Original: *tonis*, referring to the musical modes like Dorian or Phrygian.</note> which we sent shortly before, lest he err in the range <note>Original: *ambitu*</note>, the "repercussion" <note>The characteristic intervals or melodic formulas of a mode.</note>, the keys of the cadences and fugues, and the remaining requirements of the tones.

**The third precept:** The Composer should first aptly join the Bass and the Soprano, and then the other voices in order. And indeed the Bass, according to its nature as the place of the foundation, should be deep <note>Original: *grauis*</note>, and it should enjoy larger intervals, such as 4ths, 5ths, and octaves; it should flee the unison and thirds as much as possible. For whatever the Bass is like, such will be the fabric of the whole; if that is beautifully proportioned, neat, and graceful, the whole fabric of the composition will be such. If that is harsh, consisting of unformed intervals, it is necessary that such a harmony also arises in the remaining voices. The Soprano <note>Original: *Cantus*</note> should also proceed with motions contrary to the bass; it should enjoy the smallest intervals and use diminutions <note>Rapid, decorative notes that "divide" a longer note value.</note> of the voices frequently. For since it represents fire, it is appropriate that you represent its agitations. The remaining voices should proceed by middle ways and motions.

**The fourth precept:** The nature and property of the Text or words must be diligently considered, for the various affections of the soul—joy, mourning, the weeping of pain, fear, wailing, anger, laughter, pity, love—must be so bound to the notes that the process, expressed with variety, may rejoice or exult by the very diminution of the notes; but in Chromatic places, the syncopation of the notes...

248 **Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance**

The harshness and hardness of syncopations <note>In this context, syncopations refer to suspensions, where a note is held over from a previous chord to create a temporary dissonance before resolving.</note> seem to express a certain grief; regarding these individual emotional affects, however, see the various examples at the end of Book VII.

**The fifth precept:** The Composer <note>Original Latin: *Melotheta*, literally "one who sets a melody."</note> should diligently observe the movement of the harmony. There are, moreover, various movements of notes expressed by the voices. Some voices proceed in a straight order; some seek each other with contrary movements; others delight in oblique movements. This is done either by steps—whether "ladder-like" <note>Original: *climacticos*, referring to stepwise motion up or down a scale.</note> movements or by leaps—or by cadences. Or to put it better, every progression of notes is fourfold: it is done either by conjunct steps <note>Moving to the very next note in the scale.</note> or by disjunct steps <note>Skipping notes in the scale.</note>; and by either similar or contrary movements.

->**The Variety of Harmonic Progression**<-

| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Direct motion** | **Direct motion by conjunct steps** | **Direct motion by disjunct steps** | **Simple oblique motion by conjunct steps** | **Oblique motion by disjunct steps** | **Motion by contrary steps** | **Motion by leaps** |

<note>This table describes the "Grammar" of how two musical lines can move in relation to one another. Note that Kircher's terminology differs slightly from modern theory; for example, what he calls "oblique" (both moving in the same direction) we now call "parallel."</note>

You see in this example that **direct motion** occurs when the notes of two voices are found on the same string <note>Meaning they remain on the same pitch.</note>, as the first example teaches. Truly, **direct motion by conjunct steps** occurs when, with the base voice fixed, the other voice ascends or descends step by step, as the second example shows. **Simple oblique motion by conjunct steps** occurs when both voices ascend or descend step by step according to the fourth example. **Direct motion by disjunct steps** occurs when one voice is fixed and the other ascends or descends intermittently by disjunct steps <note>Leaps larger than a second.</note> according to the third example. **Oblique motion by disjunct steps** is when one voice moves obliquely and the other, moving by a leap, similarly ascends or descends by leaps or interrupted steps, as the fifth example teaches. Truly, **motion by contrary steps** is when two voices tend toward opposite parts by ascending or descending through conjunct or disjunct steps according to the sixth example. **Motion by leaps** is when both voices proceed by leaps, as the seventh example proves. Finally, from all these movements an **eighth** results, which we call **mixed**, as it is composed of the rest. And deservedly, all Music consists of these movements, which I would wish the Composer to fix deeply in his mind before he applies himself to the perfect system and method of composing.

### Particular Precepts.

1. A praiseworthy beginning of harmony carries a great deal of weight when it consists of perfect consonances <note>The Unison, Fifth, and Octave.</note>; for these strike the mind of the listener better than imperfect ones, although some people may think otherwise.

2. Two consonances of the same species—such as two unisons, two fifths, and two octaves, along with their compounds the 12th and 15th—should not follow each other immediately in similar descent or ascent without the intermission of other intervals. See the examples below in the "Cautions to be employed by the composer in artistic composition" <note>This is the classic rule against "parallel fifths and octaves," which was thought to make the independent voices sound too much like a single thickened line.</note>.

3. However, consonances of different species are permitted to follow each other immediately, both in ascent...

<summary>This page defines the various types of melodic motion between voices (direct, oblique, contrary, and mixed) and begins listing the specific rules for composition, including the famous prohibition against parallel perfect fifths and octaves.</summary>
<keywords>melodic motion, counterpoint rules, conjunct motion, disjunct motion, parallel fifths, perfect consonances, musical affects, syncopation</keywords>

--- Page 287 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Particular Precepts" of musical composition from the previous page, concluding the ten general rules for counterpoint before moving into practical exercises for part-writing.</meta>

Book V. On the Composition of Harmony. 249

...both in ascent and descent, as with 5ths and 8ths, and likewise for equivalents <note>Referring to compound intervals, like a 12th being equivalent to a 5th.</note>, as will be stated later.

4. Multiple perfect consonances of the same species are permitted if they are sounded on the same note <note>Original Latin: *chorda*, literally "string," but referring to a repeated pitch.</note>.

5. Multiple consonances of the same species are permitted if they move from the same note through contrary motions into different parts. Nothing is more common or well-worn in eight-voice works distributed into two choirs, as we shall see later.

6. From perfect consonances to imperfect ones, the transition is made by contrary, oblique, direct, or conjunct motion, provided one part makes a leap of a major 3rd. Conversely, transitioning to perfect consonances by contrary motion provides a better effect than by direct or oblique motion alone.

7. In Composition <note>Original: *Melotheſia*, the art of setting a melody.</note>, multiple imperfect consonances can follow each other immediately, whether of the same or different species, as will be shown in the cautionary rules. Although it is better to use two thirds following each other—one major and the other minor—than two minors or two majors; the same is to be said of sixths.

8. Music has a great kinship with Poetry. For it is considered a greatest fault in a Composer <note>Original: *Symphoneta*.</note> if he makes a short syllable long, or conversely a long syllable short; for such a pronunciation would be inept on the word *amare* <note>Latin: "to love."</note> in the following notes: ♩ 𝅗 ♩ <note>The original shows diamond-shaped notes where the middle note on the accented syllable is higher in pitch but short in duration, which would feel unnatural.</note> But regarding these, more will be said in *Poetic Musurgy*.

9. In the composition of many voices, it is not considered a fault if certain voices often meet in unison, provided it is done discreetly and with judgment.

10. The end of a melody should be taken from perfect consonances. Finally, the entire art of composing—to embrace much in few words—consists of three things: the knowledge of the Tones <note>Referring to the musical modes.</note>, the exact knowledge of consonances and dissonances, and finally, the imitation of good authors. Innumerable precepts could be added here, but because we have reserved them all for their proper places, I have thought it best to put forward only these general ones here.

### CHAPTER XI.

### On the practice of simple Counterpoint and any other 
### simple composition.

What Counterpoint is, and what composition is, has been said in the preceding sections; therefore nothing else remains but that, finally putting our hands to work, we teach how to join voice to voice skillfully by the placement of one note against another; which we will perform through the following Problems.

#### Compositional Problem I.

#### Given any composed bass, to build the remaining voices—Tenor, Alto, and Soprano—or to add them compositionally.

Having placed the four-voice staves <note>Original: *pentagrammis*, referring to the five-line musical staff.</note>, and marked them correctly with clefs according to the third precept as you see; and having placed the Bass as a subject (which subject can be taken from plainchant or composed at will), let it be, for example, according to the second precept in the sixth tone. With this placed, you will build the remaining three voices with this industry: namely, with the aid of only the three simple consonances: the third, fifth, and octave.

First, distinguish the individual notes of the subject or bass with their letters as you see; then, against the first note of the bass, which is marked with the letter F, you will place the notes of the remaining voices in this manner: Seek the letter F in the individual scales of the staves for the Tenor, Alto, and Soprano, and mark it diligently as you see has been done.

<meta>This page continues the practical instruction on "Melothesia" (the art of musical composition), specifically demonstrating how to construct four-voice harmony by calculating intervals from a given bass line. It then transitions into the specific rules for two-voice composition.</meta>

# 250 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

From this <note>referring to the base note on the previous page</note> you will calculate a Third, a Fifth, or an Octave separately for all the other voices on the five-line staves. For example, from the F-clef of the Tenor, we have calculated a Fifth, and at that interval, we have placed a note corresponding to the base note. In the Alto, we counted an Octave from the F-clef, and there in the Octave (that is, on F), we placed a note regarding the base note. Finally, in the Soprano <note>original Latin: *Cantus*</note>, counting a Third from the F-clef, we located a note responding to the base note. Having thus assigned the consonances proper to each voice, we proceed to the second note of the bass, marked **B**, by counting a 3rd, 5th, or Octave upward in each voice, just as was done before. Once those consonances are assigned, you proceed note by note to the third bass note, which you will find on **G**. From **G**, we will count upward in each voice either a Third, a Fifth, or an Octave, as was done before. You will then have the desired result, with the numbers of the proper consonances assigned to each note. In this way, you will proceed in order for the remaining notes, placing note against note, until you have finished the entire song. All of this is clearly and lucidly revealed in the following Example <note>original: *Paradigmate*</note>, so that it seems entirely superfluous to speak further on the matter.

### Example of Musical Composition via simple consonances: 3, 5, 8.

| Voice | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |

| **Alto** | 8 (F) | 8 (B) | 8 (G) | 8 (D) | 8 (A) | 8 (B) | 8 (F) | 8 (C) | 8 (F) |
| **Tenor** | 5 (C) | 5 (F) | 5 (D) | 5 (A) | 5 (E) | 5 (F) | 5 (C) | 5 (G) | 5 (C) |
| **Bass** <note>original: *Basis*</note> | **F** | **B** | **G** | **D** | **A** | **B** | **F** | **C** | **F** |

You see, therefore, with what ease you can construct any musical settings <note>original: *Melothesias*</note> or simple counterpoints from any given subject through only these three simplest consonances.

### Diphony, or the Musical Composition of two voices.

No one should think it is easier to compose a Diphony <note>original: *Dyphonium*, from the Greek for "two sounds"</note> or two-voice counterpoint than a Tetraphony <note>four-voice composition</note>; for diphony also has its own rules, distinct from other harmonies of many voices.                                             §.  II.
                         *On Three-Part Composition, or Three Voices.*

**T**he rules for this do not differ from the rules of the previous section. This only must be noted: just as every <term>proportion</term> <note>In the Pythagorean tradition, musical intervals were expressed as mathematical ratios</note> is completed in three terms, so too the perfection of the entire harmonic proportion consists in three voices. For as appeared in the preceding examples, since there are only three simple <term>consonances</term> <note>Combinations of notes that sound stable and pleasant to the ear</note> that complete all harmony—namely the Third, the Fifth, and the Octave—and since these three are assigned to the voices, it is self-evident that any remaining voices added beyond three are merely certain <term>replications</term> <note>Repeated notes at a higher or lower octave</note> of these consonances. 

You shall proceed in composing <term>Tryphonia</term> <note>Compositions for three voices</note> in this manner: any subject can be chosen, whether taken from <term>Gregorian chant</term> <note>The traditional monophonic sacred song of the Roman Catholic Church</note>, or from your own imagination, or arranged in any other way. Once you have this, you shall proceed according to the rules prescribed for two-voice compositions, and a <term>Tryphonium</term> will be produced that is perfect in every respect <note>original: "omnibus numeris absolutum"; literally "absolute in all its numbers"</note>, as follows:

### §. III.

### On Tetraphonies, or compositions for four voices.

**A**lthough we have already shown the composition of four voices in the first place, nevertheless, because certain things worthy of consideration occur, I have decided to treat it more extensively here. First, in the preceding <term>tetraphony</term> <note>A musical composition for four voices</note>, we used only 3 simple <term>consonances</term> <note>Stable musical intervals</note>—namely the 3rd, 5th, and 8th <note>The Octave</note>. <margin>4-voice composition corresponds to the 4 elements.</margin> Here, however, we also use <term>sixths</term>, as well as <term>Thirds</term>, both minor and major. Otherwise, the rules are exactly the same as those we prescribed in the preceding sections. Moreover, the four-voice composition is the noblest and sweetest of all, notwithstanding that the Octave is found among these three; for this very replication <note>The doubling of a note at a higher or lower pitch</note> possesses a certain majesty for stirring the emotions of the soul. Whence, just as the entire harmony of things consists in the perfect mixing of the four elements <note>The classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, so too the Tetraphony is constituted of four voices as if of so many elements, as was indicated above. Since these things are so, we will place a Tetraphony here, so that from it you may recognize, as if in a model <note>original: "ἐν τύπῳ" (en typō); meaning a pattern, type, or representative form</note>, the perfection of simple harmony in simple <term>counterpoint</term> <note>The technique of combining different melodic lines</note>. And let this Paradigm <note>An example or model</note> serve in place of many rules.

->### Fourth Four-Voice Composition<-
<note>original: "Tetraphonium IV."</note>

[A musical score consisting of four systems of notation. Each system contains two five-line staves using diamond-shaped mensural notes. Numerical sequences, such as 5, 8, 3, 6, 8, 5, 8, are written above the notes to indicate the intervals between the parts.]

You see in the first Four-Voice Composition <note>The author is likely referring back to the first of the series of examples starting on page 254.</note> a remarkable skill in the arrangement of harmonies; whereby the Bass <note>original: "Basis"</note> and the first note of the Soprano <note>original: "Cantus"</note> harmonize aptly in a minor tenth, where you also see the measure divided by a fifth, a fourth, and a minor third. You also see in the second note how skillfully the twelfth is divided by an octave and by a minor third doubled <note>original: "semiditonum siue tertiam minorem replicatam"</note>; and so it is with the other following harmonies, which we submit to the examination of experts.

We have placed in this spot another Four-Voice Composition, following a process different from the first. For the Bass begins from the note D <note>original: "d la, sol, re"; a name for the pitch D according to the medieval hexachord system.</note> and ends on G, a twelfth away from that D. Secondly, it contains certain cadences which are permitted, though not usually common, such as those found in the 11th and 12th notes, which are a minor tenth apart. Thirdly, at the beginning, the Bass sounds in a higher register, with the Tenor taking its place; this was done to show that it is not always necessary for the Bass to remain below the other voices. Rather, according to the nature of the lyrics or the emotion, the Bass can occasionally exchange roles <note>original: "clypeum mutare"; literally "to change shields," a Latin idiom for switching places.</note> with the Tenor, and indulge the playfulness <note>original: "lasciuię"</note> of the higher voice. To make this bolder ascent of the Bass easier to recognize, we have marked the notes of the Tenor and Alto that descend below it with the number 1.

The third Four-Voice Composition also has its own peculiar craftsmanship. You see how aptly the minor third is placed in the Tenor above the Bass, and how fittingly the minor sixth is placed in the Alto above the Tenor, as well as the minor tenth in the Soprano above the Tenor. Or, what amounts to the same thing: how well the twelfth of the Soprano, the octave of the Alto, and the third of the Tenor harmonize with the Bass. You see also that in the harmony of the notes occupying the third position, almost all consonances are found, as is clear from these numbers: 1, 8, 12, 17. For the major seventeenth is divided by two intermediate notes, 2 and 3, which are placed between 1 and 5. Even though this division is not "harmonic" <note>In the Pythagorean or Zarlinian sense, a "harmonic" division refers to specific mathematical proportions (like the harmonic mean).</note>, it is nevertheless entirely natural; it acquires a certain harmonic quality from the very ratio of the numbers increasing toward the high pitch. However, these matters are discussed elsewhere. You also see in this last Four-Voice Composition the use of the Fourth in the 11th note of the Tenor, where you see the Fourth, surrounded and tamed by perfect harmonies, reduced to proper order.

### Section IV.

## On Five-Voice Compositions, or Simple Five-Voice Counterpoint.
<note>original: "De Pentaphonijs siue contrapuncto simplici 5. vocum."</note>

After the four-voice compositions <note>original: "Tetraphonia."</note>, we now come to Five-Voice Compositions <note>original: "Pentaphonia."</note>, or songs to be arranged for five voices. In these, one voice—whether it be the Soprano, the Alto, the Tenor, or the Bass—is always doubled, according to the nature of the musical subject and the judgment of the composer <note>original: "Melothetæ," a Greek-derived term Kircher uses for a creator of melody or a composer.</note>. Furthermore, in the composition of these five-voice pieces, the exact same rules must be observed as those given in the preceding sections. Therefore, nothing else remains to explain the matter, except for the present example <note>original: "paradigma."</note> in which you may behold, with the greatest skill, the harmonies of the individual voices placed in counterpoint against one another.

### Section VI.
### Concerning Seven-Voice and Eight-Voice Compositions.

We call compositions of seven or eight voices a "musical setting" <note>original: "Melothesiam," from the Greek word for the arrangement of melody and harmony.</note> in which there is no difference from the preceding methods in the way voices are composed or the notes are adapted. Therefore, we shall be content with providing only an example and gradually progress to other topics. Regarding songs for eight voices that are distributed into two separate choirs, we shall speak more extensively in the sections that follow.

### Compositional Problem II <note>original: "Problema Melotheticum II."</note>

**Given any two voices, to skillfully connect the remaining voices to them.**

In the preceding sections, we demonstrated the method by which—given a bass or a subject of a musical setting <note>original: "Melothesias," from the Greek for the arrangement of a melody</note>—we can skillfully connect as many remaining voices as we wish through the three simple consonances: the Third, the Fourth, and the Octave. In this section, however, we shall show the method by which, given any voice whatsoever, you may be able to join the remaining parts to it; and so that the entire business may proceed methodically through rules... <note>The text continues on the following page with the specific rules mentioned here.</note>

...so that you may better understand them when methodically arranged. It should be noted that two voices always meet either in a unison, or a Third, or a Fourth, or a Fifth, Sixth, or Octave; therefore, given two voices agreeing in one of these consonances <note>A consonance is a combination of notes that sounds pleasant or stable to the ear.</note>, let us see how you may connect the remaining voices.

### Rule I. Concerning the Unison.

1. Whenever the Soprano <term>original: "Cantus," the highest melodic part</term> is in unison with the Tenor; the Bass will have a Third below, and the Alto will have a 5th or 6th above the Bass as follows.

[Musical notation on four staves]

| Soprano | Alto | Tenor | Bass |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 Unison | 5 or 6 above the Bass | 1 Unison | 3rd below the Tenor |

2. Whenever the Soprano is in unison with the Tenor, the Bass will have a Fifth below the Tenor, while the Alto will have a Third or a Tenth above [the Bass] as follows.

[Musical notation on four staves]

| Soprano (C.) | Alto (A.) | Tenor (T.) | Bass (B.) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Unison | 3 or 10 | 1 Unison | 5 below the Tenor |

3. When the Soprano is in unison with the Tenor, if the Bass has a Sixth below the Tenor, the Alto will have a Third or a Tenth above the Bass as follows.

[Musical notation on four staves]

| Soprano (C.) | Alto (A.) | Tenor (T.) | Bass (B.) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 Unison | 3 or 10 above the Bass | 1 Unison | 6 below |

4. When the Soprano is in unison with the Tenor, if the Bass is an Octave below the Tenor, the Alto will be a 5th, 6th, 10th, or 12th above the Bass, as follows.

[Musical notation on four staves]

| Bass (B.) | Alto (A.) | Tenor (T.) | Soprano (C.) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 8 below | 10, 12, 6 | Unison | Unison |

5. When the Soprano is in unison with the Tenor, if the Bass is a 10th below the Tenor, the Alto will be a 5th or 12th above the Bass, as follows.

[Musical notation on four staves]

| Bass (B.) | Alto (A.) | Tenor (T.) | Soprano (C.) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10 below the Tenor | 5 or 12 | 1 Unison | 1 Unison |

## Melothetic Problem II.

Therefore, first let the **Tenor** and **Bass** harmonize in a <term>Fifth</term><note>An interval of five scale degrees</note>; then look in the middle transverse compartment for the column **H E** (Fifth). This column shows the upper numbers 3, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17, which correspond to the remaining voices to be built above the two voices (that is, the **Tenor** and **Bass** harmonized in a Fifth, as was said), as appears in the first example.

Again, for the second example, let the **Bass** and **Tenor** (or any other voice) harmonize, for instance, in a <term>Fourth</term>. Then look in the transverse section for (Fourth). The numbers placed in the upper column will serve for building the remaining voices above the two first composed in a Fourth. Note, however, that in the second and fifth compartments of said column, two numbers are always contained: in the second, 6 and 5; in the fifth, 13 and 12. These signify that the operation can be established in two ways. For if you take the number 6 from the right side of the second compartment, know that in the fifth compartment, the corresponding number to be taken is 13, not 12. And if you take the number 5 on the left side (the left side in this table is **CD**, the right is **AB**), the corresponding number 12 must be taken in the fifth compartment, so that two numbers of the same side are always taken as corresponding to each other. For if the numbers were taken crosswise—6, for example, with 12, or 5 with 13—the <term>Composer</term><note>original: "Symphoneta"</note> would expose himself to the greatest error. All of this must also be understood regarding the doubled numbers in the remaining compartments.

To return to the proposed example: if, having placed two voices harmonizing in a Fourth, you wish to build the rest, you will take 6 from the fourth column for the **Alto**, and for the **Soprano** either 13, or 8, 10, or 15, as is clear in the second example. However, in this example, a major sixth will sound better than a minor one, and the latter better than a fifth. The same should be said of the derivatives of these simple <term>consonances</term><note>intervals that sound pleasing or stable</note>; for among the doubled numbers, those on the right are always better than those on the left.

Again, let the **Bass** and **Tenor** harmonize in a <term>Sixth</term>. If it is a major sixth, a major third follows it, and one 4th above the Bass between the Tenor and Bass, as the IV example teaches. But if it is a minor sixth, a minor third must be placed between this and the first note of the Bass; the same must be observed regarding the remaining <term>replications</term><note>intervals expanded by an octave, like a 10th being a replicated 3rd</note>.

Again, if the **Tenor** harmonizes with the **Bass** in a <term>Seventh</term>, you will build the remaining voices upon these in three ways: first, if you place a fourth within the seventh, which resolves with a major third...

Here you see the ratio of the Fifth is 2 to 3; if it has a fourth <term>diatessaron; the interval of a perfect fourth</term> above it, it necessarily presupposes an octave below, which 1 to 2 represents, since no other number occurs before or after 2 that constitutes an octave except 1. In a similar way, you see that 4, which 3 precedes, constitutes an octave with 2, as was clear a little later in the notes; so much so that the lower sound of a Fifth always has an octave above it. If, however, one takes the higher sound of the Fifth, it must necessarily presuppose either a Fourth above or a twelfth <term>duodecimam; an interval of an octave plus a fifth</term> below; the same happens in all other consonances, since they always presuppose and require consonances expressed by the numbers either immediately preceding or following them in the sequence.

Since, therefore, the ratio of the Fourth is 3 to 4, if you wish to know which consonances it presupposes both before and after, let four numbers be written in their natural order: 2, 3, 4, 5; that is, 2 before 3 and <margin>The secret of the number six and...</margin>

## On the precautions to be taken in composition and the errors to be avoided.

**First Precaution:** Two or more perfect consonances <note>Perfect consonances include the unison, the fifth, and the octave; they are considered "stable" sounds.</note> of the same kind and proportion can follow each other immediately neither in steps nor in leaps, not even in the smallest notes. For if someone were to continue two or more unisons, or two fifths or octaves in descent or ascent, he would commit a very essential error in Music, as seen in the example.

->Succession of Octaves | Succession of Fifths | Succession of Fifths and Octaves<-
[Musical notation with the following interval ratios:]
8 8 8 8 8 8 8 8 | 5 5 5 5 5 | 8 5 8 8 8 5 5 8 8
<note>This refers to the famous rule against "parallel fifths" and "parallel octaves," which was thought to destroy the independence of the musical parts.</note>

**Second:** So great is the force of successive fifths and octaves that they cannot be removed even if dissonances intervene or smaller <term>pausis; rests</term> are used; as is clear in the following example.

->These movements are illicit.<-
[Musical notation with the following interval ratios:]
5 6 5 5 4 5 5 5 5 5 5 5 8 8 8
<note>original: "Hi processus illiciti."</note>

**Third:** A succession of unisons can in no way be prevented by an intervening second <note>An interval of a second is a "step" on the scale, usually considered a dissonance.</note>, as is clear in the first example; nor is a succession of octaves removed by the interposition of a seventh or ninth, as in the second example; nor can a succession of fifths be prevented by any means by the intercalation of a sixth or fourth, as the third example shows. We understand this, however, to apply to rests and <term>minimis; half notes or "minims"</term>; not to <term>semibreuibus; whole notes or "semibreves"</term>.

You see therefore in the first <term>phrase; clausula</term> that the highest and lowest voices begin with the same motion to tend upward from the octave; yet with such skill that, even if they follow each other at unequal times, nothing seems to prejudice the first phrase. The same appears in the second phrase in which you see both the upper and lower voice descending from an octave through <term>conjunct motions; motus coniunctos</term> <note>Stepwise movement, rather than leaping.</note>, which method of composing is not only not illicit, but is accustomed to provide the greatest grace to the harmony.

The third way is when smaller notes are employed, which, moving by steps or even by leaps, interpose a 10th or a 6th into the octave, and thus remove the forbidden succession. However, I would want this to be understood regarding the harmony of several voices, not of two voices, in which [forbidden successions] should be avoided as much as possible.

### CHAPTER XII.
### On the use of imperfect consonances.

**Imperfect consonances** are Thirds, Sixths, and their derivatives or compounds—the 10th, 13th, 17th, and 20th—as can be seen in the following table. They are called "imperfect" because they produce a more imperfect sound and have little grace unless they are mixed with, or at least joined at the end by, perfect ones; however, they are primarily called "imperfect" because they undergo great variation due to the increase or decrease <note>Referring to the difference between major and minor intervals.</note> that is evident in minor and major sixths and thirds.

#### On the Rules or use of Thirds.

### §. II.
### On the Rules for the Use of Tenths.

**Rule 1.** Tenths are "replicated" <note>In music theory, a "replicated" or compound interval is one that has been expanded by an octave. ### §. III.
### On the Rules or Use of Sixths, or Hexachords.

<margin>How the major and minor sixth are to be placed.</margin>
**Rule 1.** The Sixth is twofold: Major and Minor. We shall declare the use and movement of both in this place; for if these are placed correctly and with artful judgment, they possess no less grace in compositions than thirds. Indeed, it will be discussed at length in Book 7 that sixths possess a great power in stirring the emotions <note>original: "affectibus concitandis." Kircher refers to the *Affektenlehre*, the theory that specific musical intervals and structures can physically move the listener's "animal spirits" to feel specific emotions.</note>.

Therefore, a sixth can be placed sweetly when the voices are arranged as much as possible in steps and in contrary motion, with a perfect consonance always preceding the imperfect ones; as is clear in the following example. This can be done as much by step as by leap, as much by ascending as by descending, provided that the voices move by legitimate intervals. Thus, a unison moves more often into a minor third, and more rarely into a major one; and more often into a minor sixth, and more rarely into a major one. Look for the reason for this in *Musical Physiology* <note>Kircher's term for the study of the physical nature of sound and its effect on the human body.</note>, but take the following example of what has been said.

[Musical notation on two staves. The first staff has figured bass numbers: 3 3 1 3 6 3 6 8. The second staff has numbers: 1 3 5 8 6 5 6 8.]

You see in these two examples how a return is made from a unison or an octave, through thirds and sixths, back again into an octave by contrary motions.

# CHAPTER XIII.
## On dissonances and their manifold use in composition.

God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "DEVS Opt. Max." or Deus Optimus Maximus, a common title for the Divine.</note>, has arranged this entire universe in His immense wisdom by this law: that good things are seen to be connected to evil, fertile to sterile, hard to soft, weak to healthy, sweet to bitter, life-giving to poisonous, virtues to vices, and adversity to prosperity by an inviolable law. They perform the same function in the world as dissonances mixed with consonances do in music. For just as harmony can in no way obtain its perfection except through the mixing of dissonances, so the world cannot be preserved without both evil and good things. Since we have spoken of these matters at length in our section on "Worldly Music" <note>This refers to the *Musica Mundana*, the ancient concept that the movements of celestial bodies and the elements follow harmonic proportions.</note>, we refer the reader there.

Dissonances, therefore, are no less necessary to the musician than consonances, for by these, melodies acquire all their grace, and they perform the same function in harmony as the skillful use of shadows does in a painting.

There are, moreover, three simple dissonances: the second, the fourth, and the seventh. There are as many compound ones derived from these: the 9th, 11th, and 14th; and the triplicate ones: the 16th, 18th, and 21st, as the following table demonstrates.

**Book V. On the Composition of Harmony. 279**

The value of these notes is such that one is always double the next following it. Hence, a **maxima** is worth two **longs**, a **long** is worth two **breves**, a **breve** is worth two **semibreves**, a **semibrevis** is worth two **minims**, and so on.

The **Rests** <note>original: "Pausæ"</note> correspond to these in the same order. A Rest is a skillful omission of the voice, invented both for the rest and breathing of the singers and for the sweetness and charm of the song; specifically, so that the continuous sound of a single voice does not dull the listener, but rather that the sense of hearing—which is otherwise quite easily distracted—might be refreshed. Therefore, if they are applied to a song at the right moment, they bring no small amount of delight. For as it is rightly said, "that which lacks alternating rest is not lasting" <note>original: "quod caret alterna requie durabile non est," a quote from the Roman poet Ovid.</note>, the first composers <note>term: "Musurgi," from the Greek for "makers of music."</note> skillfully found these "negative signs" to free the singer from the continuous intensity of the voice.

For this rest repairs the strength and relieves the weary limbs. We have assigned as many rests as there are notes in the preceding diagram, all of which are marked crosswise—that is, by lines drawn from the upper parts downward through the lines lying flat on the plane, as you see. [Diagram of musical staff with various rests]

1. The **Rest** reaching across 4 lines corresponds to the **maxima** note, as it fills 8 measures of time in silence.

2. The **Long Rest** is so called because it corresponds to the **long** note; it occupies the space of three lines and completes 4 measures of time in silence, being double the previous one.

3. The **Breve Rest**, named after the **breve** note, is a line normally terminating between two lines of the five-line staff <note>term: "pentagrammi," Kircher's term for the musical staff.</note>; it completes two measures of time in silence.

4. The **Semibreve Rest**, or **half-rest**, is a small stroke drawn normally from a line downward to the middle of the interlinear space, equivalent to one measure of time, as the number written above it demonstrates; thus.

5. The **Minim Rest**, also called a **semi-minim**, is a small stroke drawn normally from a line upward to the middle of the interlinear space; it is the opposite of the previous one, filling half a measure of time, thus.

6. The **Semiminim Rest**, also called a **Sigh** <note>original: "suspirium," a poetic term for a short rest.</note>, correctly expresses the likeness of a hook and denotes a fourth part of the time to be spent in silence.

7. The **Fusa Rest**, or **Half-Sigh** <note>original: "semisuspirium"</note>, expresses the likeness of an inverted hook and notes 1/8 part of the time, thus:

8. The **Semifusa Rest**, or as others prefer, the **double color** <note>original: "chroma duplicatum"</note>, refers to a double inverted hook and notes 1/16 part of the time. The value of all these is shown in the preceding diagram.

It must be noted, however, that the value of both notes and rests is governed by a regular measure which the Greeks call **Metron**, the Latins call **Tactus**, and the Italians call **la Battuta** or the **pulse**. Every beat or measure of time consists of two movements, which the Greeks call **Arsis** and **Thesis**.

<margin>The **Semibreve**</margin>
[Diagram of a semibreve note]
<margin>The Greek letter **Lambda** (Λ)</margin>
<margin>**Arsis** (Lifting): 1/2 minim</margin>
<margin>**Thesis** (Lowering): 1/2 minim</margin>
<margin>What **Arsis** and **Thesis** are.</margin>

**Arsis** and **Thesis** <note>In modern terms, the "upbeat" and the "downbeat."</note> is the measure of time to be applied in the placement of a **semibreve** note; it is nothing other than the Beat, or the measure of time considered according to the lifting or lowering of the hand. For if the hand is lowered while uttering a semibreve, this depression will be called **Thesis**; if it is lifted, this lifting of the hand will be called **Arsis**. **Thesis**, or the lowering of the hand, measures one **minim** note, and the lifting measures another **minim** note; these two notes are equivalent to one **semibreve**, as is clear in the margin. And this **Arsis** and **Thesis** is of such great importance in placing dissonances appropriately that the entire logic of dissonances seems to depend upon it; for if you have rightly adapted the dissonances to this, you will create harmony.

It occurs when a semibreve or minim is placed between two other semibreves or minims, or any others; or even when a minim rest is struck through the aid of the arsis or the lifting of the hand. It is very familiar in song and brings great charm if one uses it correctly. It is most especially used in the interplay of two voices with great pleasure for the ears, but no less so in three or more voices. It is not necessary to give many rules or examples of this, since they are encountered everywhere and are known to everyone. However, one must be careful that the separation of the notes is not awkward, which would happen if it were either too long, or delayed by rests, or expressed through notes that are too large.
  The rule for this is as follows: The semibreve and the minim are the only notes that support syncopation.

->### §. II.<-
->**Concerning the Prerequisites of Reconciling Dissonances.**<-

Since, therefore, dissonances are most necessary for the composer <note>original: "symphonetæ"</note>, both for ornament and for bringing variety to the harmony, he should strive to have the greatest knowledge of them. For even though harmony is primarily made of consonances, because consonances alone produce satiety and boredom if they are continued too long, it happens that this kind of distaste is removed by mixed dissonances, just as by a variety of foods. For just as day delights most after darkness, sweetness after bitterness, and good after evil, so, as has been said, a consonance usually possesses greater grace after a dissonance.

Now, in this place we consider dissonances either in themselves and absolute, or accidental and relative. **Absolute dissonances** are those which have no place whatsoever in harmonic use, such as if a breve or long note were found in a two-voiced composition <note>original: "concentu dyphonio"</note> in the 2nd, 4th, 7th, or other unsuitable places.

It must be noted that the semitone <note>original: "hemitonium"</note> is of such great importance in all things that the ancients rightly called the interval of the major semitone, *mi-fa*, the whole of Music. <margin>Great consideration must be given to the semitone.</margin> The chromatic signs B, ♭, and ♯ must also be considered with the greatest diligence.

To do this, it must be known: the natural sign <note>original: "b quadrum"</note> or "hard" B, in "soft" song <note>original: "cantu molli," referring to the hexachord system</note> mostly surrounds that key which can receive the syllable *mi*; <insert>Example I.</insert> [Musical score] but the flat <note>original: "B molle"</note> in "hard" song surrounds that key which can receive the syllable *fa*. In hard song, however, the natural sign on the string B-fa B-mi is superfluous, just as the flat is on the string B-fa in soft song. The sharp sign <note>original: "♯"</note>, however, except for the note *mi*, can be placed in any other location. <insert>Example II.</insert> [Musical score] Furthermore, the flat, wherever it is placed, lowers the sound by a semitone, while the sharp sign raises it by the same distance. And so, with the addition of a flat, the interval becomes larger in relation to the higher sound, but smaller in relation to the lower sound, as is clear in the first example. Conversely, the sharp—which almost always has the following note ascending—diminishes the interval in relation to the higher sound and increases it in relation to the lower, as is clear in the second example; concerning these things, take this rule.

In leaps or larger intervals, a sharp [$\sharp$] cannot be continued unless the voice that provides the foundation proceeds from a major sixth to a third.

[Musical notation on two staves with numbers 6 7 6 3 8 6 7 6 3 8 below the first staff]

Relative or "accidental" dissonances are those which, at first glance, do not seem to differ from consonances. But because they either exceed or fall short by a minor semitone, if you pay close attention, they easily reveal themselves; those that exceed by this minor semitone are called **augmented** <note>original: "superflua," literally superfluous</note> intervals; those that fall short by a major semitone are called **diminished** intervals. <margin>Which intervals are augmented and which are diminished.</margin> Thus, a fourth is called augmented when, with a minor semitone added to it, three whole tones are produced, which is why they also call it a **tritone**. This tritone, or augmented fourth, occurs either ordinarily or extraordinarily. It occurs ordinarily if you proceed upward from F to B or from B to E, as is evident in the first and second examples; for intervals of this kind are tritones, or augmented fourths. It occurs extraordinarily, however, if you mark the highest note of any fourth with this sign $\sharp$, or the lowest with a round b <note>the flat sign: $b$</note>, as the 3rd, 4th, and 5th examples show.

<margin>Augmented and diminished fifths.</margin> The dissonant fifth is likewise twofold, augmented or diminished. It is augmented when the sign $\sharp$ is added to the upper note of the interval, as is clear in examples 6 and 7. There you see that from C to G-sharp <note>original: "G. cancellatum," referring to the cross-hatched look of the sharp sign</note>, and from A to C-sharp, an augmented fifth is similarly born. But from B <note>original: "h," the German notation for B-natural</note> to F; likewise from C-sharp to G, or from G-sharp to D, a diminished fifth is born, as examples 8, 9, and 10 indicate.

In no different way is the octave twofold, augmented and diminished. It is augmented when its upper note is marked with this sign $\natural$ <note>Kircher uses the natural/square-B sign here to indicate a sharpening of the pitch</note> as examples 11 and 12 show. <margin>Augmented and diminished octaves.</margin> It is diminished when the lower note of the same is marked with the same sign $\sharp$ or even a soft b <note>flat</note>, as the final example shows. From these, the following rule results:

### CHAPTER XIV.
#### On the placement of dissonances so that they are rendered consonant.

Although it is clear from the very name <note>etymology</note> that nothing disturbs harmonic melody as much as dissonant intervals, nevertheless, by the skillful industry of musicians, it has been brought about that they are not only mixed into harmonies, but are even necessary for establishing and composing cadences <note>original: "clausulis"</note>.

### Section 1.
### On the use of the Second, Ninth, Sixteenth, and Twenty-Third.

**Rule 1.** Whenever a second is placed between two thirds, it always produces a good effect, as is evident in the first example. <margin>Rule on the placement of the second.</margin>
**Rule 2.** Whenever one voice moves by step from a unison while the other voice remains stationary on the unison, the second will sound consonant, as is evident in the second example.
**Rule 3.** Whenever the second is included between a major third and a unison, and the first voice is in syncopation <note>In this period, "syncopation" typically refers to what we now call a suspension—holding a note over from a previous beat to create a temporary dissonance that then resolves.</note>, it will be rendered consonant, as is evident in the third example.
**Rule 4.** The ninth—which is a "doubled" second—placed between a minor tenth and a fifth, will sound consonant, as the fourth example teaches.
**Rule 5.** A second, ninth, or sixteenth that is syncopated will always produce a most sweet effect, as is evident in the fifth example.

### Section 2.
### On the use of the Fourth.

There is a great controversy among authors concerning the Fourth; should it be numbered among the consonant intervals or the dissonant? <margin>How the Fourth may be dissonant or consonant.</margin> We respond briefly: the fourth arranged harmonically within the octave is consonant, but arranged arithmetically within the octave is commonly considered dissonant <note>This refers to the mathematical division of a string. An "arithmetic" division (where the string is divided into equal parts, e.g., 2, 3, 4) often resulted in the fourth being treated as a dissonance in the counterpoint of this era, whereas a "harmonic" division treated it as a stable interval.</note>, although in the following pages we shall show it to be absolutely consonant. And we discuss this especially in this place: how it might become consonant when placed arithmetically, and what position it ought to take among the consonances so that it sounds well; and how the same fourth must be "tied" <note>Prepared as a suspension</note> to cast off its dissonant harshness, as will be learned from the following rules.

**Rule 1.** Since sixths usually receive a middle tone so that they are divided into a fourth and a major or minor third, it has been found by experience that a minor sixth conveniently has the fourth in the upper position and the third in the lower. A major sixth, however, keeps the opposite order, except in those places where, by the formation of a cadence, it passes into a fifth; there, it usually retains the minor third in the upper position. From which we form this rule:

**Rule 1.** Whenever a major sixth is positioned such that it has a fourth below it and a minor third above it, then the fourth becomes simply and absolutely consonant, just as it does when it is placed within an octave above a fifth; as is clear in the first example, and appears brightly in the harmonic table proposed above in Problem 3. See what we have pursued at length there regarding the position of the fourth.

**Rule 2.** When the lower voice undergoes the fall of a fifth <note>A common movement in a cadence, such as G to C</note>, the fourth will be a consonant middle syncopation <note>A suspension where a note is held over from a previous chord</note> between two breves <note>Double whole notes</note> or semibreves <note>Whole notes</note> of the upper voice, as is clear in examples II, III, and VI. The use of this fourth is so frequent that there is hardly any song in which it is not found. But more on this at length in the chapter on Syncopation.

**Rule 3.** Whenever two voices set at the interval of a third move—specifically the first voice by step or conjunct motion in minims <note>Half notes</note> or semiminims <note>Quarter notes</note> while the other remains still—the second minim or semiminim will be a consonant fourth, as examples III and IV teach. Furthermore, how the Fourth can be placed at the beginning, middle, and end as a consonance by a new artistry will be demonstrated at length in Book 7.

## §. III.
## On the Use of the Seventh.

The Seventh is a pure dissonance; yet, when it is placed with the customary artistry in both cadences <note>original: "clausulis" — the concluding phrases of a musical section</note> and in syncopation, it is rendered consonant.

**First Rule:** The use of the Seventh is primarily in cadences; most frequently in minims <note>half notes</note>, rarely in semibreves <note>whole notes</note>, and never in breves <note>double whole notes</note>. For dissonances are very often permitted under these conditions. <margin>Rule regarding the positioning of the Seventh.</margin>

For whenever the first note is consonant in a series of semiminims <note>quarter notes</note>, the second will indeed be dissonant by its own nature, but because of the speed of the motion—being hemmed in by the first and third consonants—it is rendered consonant. In the same way, a Fourth is rendered consonant when it falls between a 3rd and a 5th. No differently, the 6th and 7th, when positioned between a 5th and an 8th <note>an octave</note>, produce a praiseworthy harmony. However, all these things will shine forth more clearly in Examples I, II, III, and IV.

**Second Rule:** The Seventh is also rendered consonant through syncopation; specifically if, while the lower voice remains still on a breve or semibreve, the other voice moves from a third to a fourth through a syncopated semibreve. This use of the Seventh is most frequent and is employed everywhere. See the following Example.

### §. IV.
### On the Use of the Tritone, or Augmented Fourth, and the Semidiapente, or Diminished Fifth.

<margin>How the Tritone is represented on the scale.</margin>

What the Tritone is, what the Diminished Fifth <note>original: "Semidiapente," also called the "false fifth"</note> or "diminished fifth" is, and also what the "Half-Octave" <note>original: "Semidiapason"; Kircher identifies this here with the diminished seventh</note> or diminished 7th is, has been sufficiently discussed in the preceding sections. For although the Tritone usually occupies four degrees <note>i.e., four letter-names like F to B</note> on the scale, while the Diminished Fifth occupies five <note>i.e., five letter-names like B to F</note>, they are nevertheless one and the same dissonance as far as the ears are concerned. This is evident from the harmonic system to be presented shortly, since both contain 6 equal semitones within an octave divided into 12 equal semitones. Following this division, we have divided the individual octaves of the keyboard layout <note>original: "abaci Clauecymbalorum" — referring to the arrangement of keys on a harpsichord or organ</note> into 12 semitones; please consult those.

§. VI.
Rules regarding the Syncope, commonly called the syncopation of dissonances.

*Syncope* <note>original Greek: Σύγκοπις</note>, or in the common style *Syncopation*, is a Greek word adapted for Latin use from the verb meaning "to strike" or "to beat" <note>original Greek: συγκόπτω</note>. This is because notes expressed and sung in this way against the beat <margin>What syncopation is.</margin> seem to "strike" or "beat" the person measuring the time. For while the beat <term>Tactus|the physical movement of the hand or finger used to keep time in Renaissance and Baroque music</term> is measured equally, syncopated notes are not measured equally, but are, as it were, broken against it. Therefore, a syncope is the irregular application of a note to the beat, caused by a preceding smaller note-shape. A syncopated note becomes twice as large, either in actuality or in potential, as the note immediately following it into which it is resolved. It is considered larger in potential when a syncopated semibreve <note>a whole note</note> is taken with two semiminims <note>quarter notes</note> in place of a breve <note>a double-whole note</note>, or a minim <note>half note</note> with a dot and two fusas <note>eighth notes</note> in place of a semibreve. As in this example:

[Musical notation on a single staff]

Syncopation occurs in two ways: First, without the mixing in of dissonances, which is strictly speaking syncopation in name only. Second, it occurs through the intervention of dissonances, which is governed by the following rules.

**Rule 1.** When, after a second, two voices fall from a third into a fifth or an octave, and the second is covered by cadences, then a fitting syncopation of notes is made, as the first example shows.

For Rule I. For Rule II.

**Rule 2.** When the fourth is covered in cadences—namely, when after the syncopation or "mutual reverberation," two voices fall from a third into a fifth or an octave—syncopation occurs as is evident in the example.

**Rule 3.** When the diminished fifth <term>semidiapente|an interval of a diminished fifth, considered a "soft" dissonance</term>, the major sixth, and the ninth are covered by cadences, the syncopation obtains a successful result. The same occurs when a seventh is covered by cadences, and after the seventh, two syncopated voices fall from a sixth into an octave.

### *The syncopated second, when continued, is rendered most sweet.*

<margin>Syncopation is the soul of dissonances.</margin>

### *The syncopated fourth, when continued, is rendered most sweet.*

### CHAPTER XV.
### Concerning the lawful and unlawful progression of consonances and dissonances, by which they move from one to others.

We shall deal in this chapter with the progression of consonances and dissonances, and how one may lawfully pass to another. This is a matter of great importance in *musical composition* <term>Melothesia|the art of composing a melody or harmonic structure</term>; indeed, I consider it **impossible** <note>original Greek: "ἀδύνατον"</note> for anyone who is ignorant of this to achieve anything worthy of praise in this art. Certainly, among the nearly countless authors whose works come to light daily, you will find scarcely a few who have not struck this precipice and suffered a "shipwreck" of their composition.

<meta>This page continues Chapter XV from the previous page, where Kircher began discussing the "laws" of musical motion. He is moving from general warnings about musical "shipwreck" into specific, technical rules for how voices should move between intervals.</meta>

292 *Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance.*

<margin>Musicians expose themselves to great errors if they do not have knowledge of harmonic progressions.</margin> For as long as they have no regard for the logic of lawful or unlawful harmonic progression, and commit everything to the fallacious judgment of the ears—accepting unlawful movements as lawful—they testify throughout their books how meager their knowledge of this art truly is. While I was observing these things, before we proceeded to the composition of **Florid Counterpoint** <note>A complex style of composition where voices move in varied rhythmic patterns against a simpler melody</note>, it seemed right to demonstrate in this Chapter, from the principles of infallible science, which progressions are lawful and which are unlawful.

<margin>Twofold progression.</margin> It should therefore be understood that progression can be considered in two ways in this context: first, insofar as all consonances included within an octave move from a unison to individual intervals contained within that octave, both upward and downward. Second, insofar as a transition can be made from the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, or 5th to all other intervals.

It should be understood secondly that not all progressions can be used in every kind of vocal composition. For there are some that have a place only in **two-voice works** <term>dyphonis|compositions for two voices</term>, some only in **three-voice works** <term>triphonis|compositions for three voices</term>, and some only in **four-voice** <term>tetraphonis</term> and other **multi-voice works** <term>polyphonis</term>. However, the common rule is this: progressions that are good for two voices are also good for any other compositions of many voices, but the reverse is not true.

§. I.
*Concerning the transition or progression from a unison to a 2nd.*

<margin>Progression from 1 to 2 occurs in 2 ways.</margin> This kind of progression can occur in two ways: first, on the **downbeat** <term>thesis|the naturally "strong" part of a musical measure</term> in syncopation, while one voice moves by step and the other remains still, as is evident here. Second, on the **upbeat** <term>arsis|the naturally "weak" or "lifted" part of a musical measure</term> without a **ligature** <note>original: "ligatura" — a slur or connection between notes</note>; namely, while one voice moves by step and the other remains still without syncopation, and this occurs in three voices, as is shown in the margin.

for 2 voices.    for 3 voices.

<margin>Progression from 1 to a minor 3rd occurs in 3 ways.</margin> The second progression, from a unison to a **minor third**, occurs in three ways. First, at the start of a measure by contrary and joined movements on the downbeat, or with each voice moving by step. Second, on the upbeat of the measure, with one voice moving by a leap of a minor third while the other remains still. Third, on both the upbeat and downbeat, while one voice moves by step and the other by a leap of a fourth, and this occurs in three-voice compositions. Furthermore, all the following progressions are lawful and can be used without any hesitation in any composition of any number of voices.

# Book V. On the Art of Composition. 301

## CHAPTER XVI.
## On Florid Counterpoint.

We call it **Florid Counterpoint** when we adapt notes of various shapes and figures—as if they were painted and adorned—to a Gregorian chant or any other melody that serves as the <term>subject</term> <note>original: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon). The underlying musical theme or "cantus firmus" upon which the counterpoint is built.</note> or basis of the musical composition. Since we have already dealt quite extensively with the rules and requirements for perfect composition, nothing remains but to apply those previously delivered rules to Florid Counterpoint.

<margin>Florid Counterpoint is varied.</margin>

Florid counterpoint is entirely varied and encompasses all the methods of the art of **Musical Composition**. One type of florid counterpoint is **simple**, another is **double**; there is one that proceeds through the artistic weaving of note shapes, and another that moves through the ingenious exchange of harmonic motions. We must speak of each of these and their ornaments individually.

### §. I.
### On Simple or Diminished Florid Counterpoint.

<margin>Diminished Florid Counterpoint.</margin>

**Florid** or **diminished** counterpoint is nothing other than a specific kind of musical composition that admits not only consonant numbers but also dissonant ones—not in just any fashion, but with remarkable industry and singular skill—using notes that differ in value from the notes of the subject, as well as notes concealed by <term>syncopation</term> <note>original: "syncopsi." The rhythmic technique of shifting the accent from a strong beat to a weak beat.</note>.

It should be noted, therefore, that just as in **Simple Counterpoint** a note placed against a note renders a simple harmony; so now in **Florid** or **diminished counterpoint**, the notes we intend to arrange above the chosen subject are different in value. That is, as many notes may be taken as the composer has need of for his purpose, provided that they are equivalent to the value of one measure of time in the subject or the chosen voice. Hence, for every **semibreve** <note>In the notation of this period, a semibreve is roughly equivalent to a modern whole note.</note> there correspond either two **minims** <note>half notes</note>, as in the first example; or 4 **semiminims** <note>quarter notes</note>, as in the second; or 4 **fusae** <note>eighth notes</note> with a minim, as in the third; or 8 **fusae** or <term>bearded notes</term> <note>original: "pogoniæ." These are notes with multiple flags, similar to 16th or 32nd notes, so called because of their "beards" or tails.</note>, as is evident in the fourth example. Regarding these, therefore, observe the following rules.

| I. Example | II. Example | III. Example | IV. Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| <note>The notation here illustrates a single long note in the bottom voice (the subject) against which the upper voice plays increasingly faster divisions: first two notes, then four, then a mix, then eight.</note> | | | |

<margin>How dissonances become consonances.</margin>

**Rule 1.** Whenever **Minims** or **semiminims** begin from a unison, a 3rd, or a 5th according to stepwise motion and on the <term>downbeat</term> <note>original: "thesin."</note>, then the alternating notes—that is, the 2nd and 4th—will necessarily sound as dissonances by their very nature; however, the 1st and 3rd notes, or those which are sung on the <term>upbeat</term> <note>original: "arsin." Kircher is describing what we now call "passing tones," where dissonant notes are allowed on weak beats if they are framed by consonants on strong beats.</note>, will be consonant. Thus, whatever dissonances are contained between the downbeat and upbeat are rendered consonant by the neighboring consonances of the 1st, 3rd, and 5th intervals that surround them, as has been declared in the model.

**Rule 2.** Whenever the lower voice consists of a **breve** <note>A long note value, equal to two semibreves.</note>, the flow of notes from a unison to an octave should not be made of mere semiminims, but from a mixture of these and fusae; yet in such a way that up to the 5th they are semiminims, and from there to the octave there are 2 fusae, as is clear in the following example. Since indeed...

Kircher provides specific rules for how many fast notes can replace a single slow note and how to properly place dissonant notes on weak beats.</summary>
<keywords>florid counterpoint, diminished counterpoint, rhythmic values, semibreve, minim, fusa, arsis, thesis, passing tones, dissonance, musical composition</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Florid Counterpoint from page 301, focusing on the specific rhythmic and harmonic rules for "diminution"—the technique of breaking down long notes into shorter, decorative figures while maintaining harmonic propriety.</meta>

For if [notes] should concur after the 5th, 6th, and 7th, and the 7th falls on the **arsis** <note>original: "arsin." In Kircher's terminology, the arsis refers to the strong beat or the "lifting" of the hand in conducting, which usually requires a consonance.</note>, it is impossible for a good harmony to be produced, since the arsis always requires consonant notes; hence it happens that **eighth notes** <note>original: "fusæ." The smallest standard note value in this period, equivalent to a modern eighth note.</note> placed with such speed so absorb the **seventh** [dissonance] that its harshness can in no way be perceived. Furthermore, due to the speed of the eighth notes, the eighth occurrences fall on the arsis, and thus all are rendered consonant. The same thing happens if a leap is made from the octave through two eighth notes into the fifth, and from there through **quarter notes** <note>original: "semiminimas."</note> into the unison, as is evident in the example. We propose this rule in shorter words as follows: With the base remaining immobile, for example, on a **double-whole note** <note>original: "breui."</note> upon the note D, the remaining voices can lawfully run through the 5ths, ascending or descending. First, the **Soprano** <note>original: "Cantus."</note> from D through F into A by ascending; the **Tenor** or **Alto** on the other hand from A through F into D by descending, or even through the octave; yet with this caution: if the running notes are quarter notes reaching the fifth, the two following notes should be eighth notes, and the last should terminate in a **half note** <note>original: "minima."</note>, while the base remains at rest in a double-whole note.

**diminutions** 
are made in 
**polyphony**.
</margin>

**Rule 3.** Whenever a flow of quarter notes is made from the 1st or 8th [interval] such that the ninth note is a **whole note** <note>original: "semibreuis."</note>, then the lower voice will have a whole note corresponding to the 4 quarter notes in unison, as happens in example I; and it will have another whole note corresponding to the remaining 4 quarter notes at a fourth below, as in example II; truly, the third whole note placed in the ninth degree will respond to the whole note either at the octave, or at the 3rd or 5th below, and a harmony will be produced as follows in example III. If indeed a descent is made through quarter notes from the octave into the unison, so that the note placed in the ninth position is at the unison or octave with the lower voice; then the whole note of the lower voice will be distant below the first note of the upper voice by an interval of a fifth, as in example IV; and the second whole note will be at an interval of a fifth below the fifth note of the upper voice, as in V; and the third whole note will be in unison or an octave with the ninth note, as is taught in example VI.

[Musical notation: Six examples labeled I through VI showing the coordination of moving quarter notes in the upper voice against slower whole notes in the lower voice, maintaining specific harmonic intervals.]

<margin>A syncopated dot must be consonant.</margin>

**Rule 5.** Whenever the first note is lengthened by a dot, a singular grace of harmony is achieved, as this dot undergoes a kind of **syncopation** <note>original: "syncopen." In this context, it refers to the suspension or "holding over" of a note from a weak beat to a strong beat.</note>; however, the dot itself must always be consonant—that is, if a separate note were placed where the dot is, that note would have to be consonant. ### On Formal Cadences in Florid Counterpoint.

<margin>What a formal cadence is in music.</margin>

A **formal cadence** <note>original: "Clausula formalis." In Baroque theory, a "clausula" or cadence is the melodic and harmonic formula used to conclude a musical thought.</note> is nothing other than a brief, skillful, and pleasing agreement and sweet joining of different voices into perfect consonances through the introduction of a dissonance. It is called a *clausula* from "closing" <note>original: "à claudendo."</note>, because it is seen to close the harmonic periods. It corresponds to the skillful and emotionally moving **period** in Rhetoric; for this reason, they are called "commonplaces," natural inflections, and musical phrases. For the more practiced one is in these, and the greater the store of them one has acquired from the best authors, the sweeter and more skillfully crafted melodies he will compose. Since, therefore, cadences are extremely necessary in every kind of counterpoint, we will first teach how these are to be skillfully constructed.

<margin>What is required for establishing cadences.</margin>

**Rule 6.** In cadences, three notes are considered: the last, the penultimate, and the antepenultimate. In a cadence, the **Soprano** <note>original: "Cantus."</note>, in respect to its penultimate note, will always have its last note move upward. The **Tenor** will have its last note move downward in respect to its penultimate. The **Bass** will either drop the last note of the cadence to an **octave** below the Tenor, or it will harmonize with the Tenor at a **third** below the Tenor's last note, or it creates a **unison**. The last note of the **Alto** is arbitrary, for it is placed according to the arrangement of the bass.

Soprano — Alto — Tenor — Bass

[Musical notation: A four-part musical example showing the standard movements of each voice in a formal cadence.]
