<margin>The notes *mi* and *fa* are of great importance in music.</margin>

**Rule 7.** In the formation of cadences, the penultimate note of the **Cantus** <term>Soprano or highest voice</term> must necessarily form a **sixth** with the Tenor; the **Basis** <term>Bass voice</term> should be a **fifth** below the Tenor; and the **Altus** <term>Alto</term> should occupy a **fourth** above the Tenor, unless the cadence is established on the note *mi* <note>original: "in mi constituatur." This refers to a Phrygian cadence, where the resolution moves by a half-step (mi to fa) in a way that requires different harmonic intervals.</note>. The first part of the antepenultimate <note>The third-to-last note.</note> note in the Cantus is indeed consonant, but the latter part is joined in a **seventh** with the Tenor, for cadences are joined through **syncopation** <note>A suspension, where a dissonance is prepared and then resolved.</note>; the Bass is placed a fifth below and the Alto a fourth above, unless perhaps a cadence on *mi* requires a different arrangement of the Bass, as we shall soon describe. Furthermore, when the Bass is a fifth below the Tenor, it resolves into a sixth under the antepenultimate note, as will be clear to those comparing the Tenor with the final note of the Bass.

<margin>A new method for skillfully arranging cadences.</margin>

Just as there is a specific logic for the notes *mi* and *fa* in every musical matter, so too does it claim a unique formation for itself in a cadence. For although the same method of joining the final, penultimate, and antepenultimate notes is preserved in the Tenor and Cantus, the final note of the Bass does not descend to the **octave** as happens in others, but to a **fifth**; sometimes it is even placed at a **third** below the Tenor’s final note. From this, the Alto also takes on the form of the cadence—otherwise, the Alto voice would have to be arranged according to the Bass's structure. Indeed, the penultimate and antepenultimate notes of the Bass are located not a fifth below the Tenor, but at a third; and the Alto claims a convenient place for itself at a third above the same Tenor. Thus, a single cadence can be varied in many ways, as is evident in the following paradigm.

[Musical notation on four staves showing various four-part vocal arrangements of cadences.]

<margin>Variation of different cadences.</margin>

Finally, these notes in a cadence are not infrequently changed—so that the uniform repetition of them does not cause boredom, and so that the text can be better applied—as you see in the following examples.

[Musical notation on two staves showing melodic variations of cadence formulas.]

**Rule 8.** Furthermore, in cadences, it must first be observed that they are constructed from the best consonances and with a singular elegance of the voices; therefore, great diligence and care must be applied in constructing them. Second, the final note of a cadence should fall especially at the start of the **major tactus** <term>the primary downbeat or pulse</term> or in the following beat, specifically at the beginning of the next **distinction** <note>A phrase or section of the text.</note> in the musical period. Master composers are accustomed to observing this with the greatest study, and they usually judge the skill of a composition by it. However, so that the reader may have diverse material for musical exercise, he may see various cadences composed according to every rigor of the rules in Book 7.

<margin>Various species of cadences <term>original: "clausularum," the technical term for a musical ending or cadence</term>.</margin>

There are, moreover, various species of cadences: simple, diminished, florid, and fugal. A **simple** cadence is one whose parts proceed with standard notes without syncopation <term>the shifting of a rhythmic accent from a strong beat to a weak one</term> and without dissonances. A **diminished** <note>In this context, "diminished" refers to "diminution," the practice of breaking long notes into shorter, faster ones.</note> cadence is one whose parts proceed with dissimilar notes with syncopation—both diminished and whole—and through consonant notes mixed with dissonant ones, as is clear in the following example.

**Rule 11.** Florid cadences are also made, "dancing" <term>original: "tripudiantes"</term> with the shortening of note values; it is remarkable how much grace of harmony and emotional stirring in the listeners they achieve, especially if they are aided by various syncopations in the manner of fugues <note>where voices imitate one another in succession</note>, as follows:

Florid cadences. | Syncopations.

## CHAPTER XVII.
## On Melothetic Styles.

### MELOTHETIC PROBLEM I.
### Given a subject, to compose a florid counterpoint for two voices in the Ecclesiastical style.

We call "florid counterpoint in the Ecclesiastical style" that which is constructed upon an underlying basis <note>original Greek: ὑποκείμενον (*hypokeimenon*), meaning the foundational subject or "cantus firmus"</note> or subject taken from Gregorian or Ecclesiastical chant. It is produced by the following method:

Let the musical subject be the lower voice, upon which you wish to skillfully adapt another voice; proceed as follows:

First, observe the nature and property of the Tone <term>Mode: the specific scale or melodic character of the chant</term> which the subject follows. Then begin the Counterpoint according to the rules handed down in the preceding chapters, always starting with a perfect consonance. Use elegant "diminutions" <term>diminutions: the technique of dividing long notes into groups of shorter, faster notes to create a "florid" or decorative effect</term>, as well as the syncopations and ligatures <term>ties: notes held across beats to create tension and resolution</term> prescribed previously. Avoid improper melodic movements and intervals with all your effort. It will suffice to have demonstrated the matter by an example in the following two-voice piece.

->Two-voice counterpoint in the Ecclesiastical style.<-

<margin>The Ecclesiastical Style</margin>
The **Ecclesiastical Style** differs from the **Motetic Style** in this: the former is, for the most part, founded upon some subject taken from Gregorian Chant; the latter, however, coordinates the remaining voices at will over an artificially composed bass. This can be seen in those songs commonly called **Motets** <note>original: "Motectas"</note>. Since these are most often based on a text from Sacred Scripture or a Hymn on the lives of the Saints, and are usually longer than average, the composer <note>original: "Symphoneta"</note> does not insist upon the subject with such rigor, nor is he forced with such scrupulousness to adhere to the chosen tone; rather, he is able to wander in various ways and indulge his harmonic genius as much as the words and the craft of composition <term>Melothetic art</term> permit.

First, therefore, let the lower or higher part lead (it does not matter which), and let the other follow after the prescribed rests. Let the process be carried out according to the rules of **diminutions** <term>diminution: the breaking of a long note into many fast notes</term> and the syncopations of voices handed down in the preceding sections; special account should also be taken of the text and the words. However, since these matters occur everywhere in all authors, the reader may consult them.

<margin>The Theatrical Style</margin>
The **Theatrical Style** is threefold: **Recitative**, and this is properly suited to one or two persons; **Choric**, which takes the place of an interlude and is most often called a Chorus, and it is <unclear>sweetly</unclear> modulated. The third is **Festive**, **hyporchematic** <note>original Greek: ὑπορχηματικός (*hyporchematikos*), referring to music for dancing and singing</note>, or **saltatory** (dance-like). This category includes other types which are commonly called *Canzones*, *Allemandes*, *Gaillards*, *Passamezzos*, *Duplas*, and *Sarabandes*, which are most in use among the French and Germans; regarding these, more extensive material will be given in Book 7.

The **Recitative style**, however, belongs to only one voice with its bass—that is, it is performed by two voices for the most part, one of which expresses the words, while the other takes the place of the bass, performed on an instrument. Whoever has a mind to know this style more extensively should consult the countless authors of this kind published in Italy since the time of **Giulio Caccini** (who first restored this method of singing, which was very common among the ancients). For an exact example, composed according to a rigorous balance, see Book 7; one should also consult the musical opera <note>original: "Comœdiam musicam"</note> of **Claudio Monteverdi** titled *Arianna*; and the *Life of St. Alexis* by **Cardinal Barberini**, which was once performed musically and published in print. Since he treats the method of the recitative style exactly and perfectly in that work, the curious reader will find there material in which to exercise himself.

### Section II.
### On Triphonies, or the setting of music for three voices according to multiple styles.

->Composing three-voice pieces in the Ecclesiastical style.<-

For once the student <note>original: "Tiro," referring to a novice or recruit in the art of music</note> has exercised himself for a short while in two-voice pieces <term>dyphonia: compositions for two voices</term>, he shall proceed to the composition of three-voice pieces <term>triphonia: compositions for three voices</term> according to the rules handed down. And first, indeed, he shall exercise himself in florid counterpoint <note>a style of composition where the voices move in varied rhythmic patterns against each other</note>, or the Ecclesiastical style. So that he may perform this with greater success, he should take as his subject any Plainchant <term>cantus firmus: a "fixed song" or pre-existing melody used as the foundation of a polyphonic work</term>, or another melody of his choosing. In the motet style, however, he shall proceed differently.

We call it the Motet style when we do not adhere to a subject of Plainchant, but rather the composer <term>symphoneta: a creator of polyphonic harmony</term> adorns the song with freedom or a certain artistic diligence. What a motet actually is has already been stated in the preceding sections.

First, therefore, either all the voices should begin together, or the lower voice should proceed with a unique artistry, followed by other voices after some pauses <note>this refers to "imitative entry," where voices enter one after another repeating a similar theme</note>. The **Theatrical style**, what it is and its various types, has been discussed in the preceding pages, and will be explained more extensively in the seventh book; but now, let us see by what reasoning and method it is to be established.

This style consists, therefore, in a movement of the voices that is suitable, pleasant, delightful, and prepared for dancing <note>original: "ad saltum," implying a rhythmic quality suitable for choreography or jumping/leaping movements</note>: for which reason care must be taken that it possesses a beautiful proportion—namely triple or sesquialtera <term>sesquialtera: a musical ratio of 3:2, where three notes are played in the time of two, creating a lilting, triple-meter feel</term>—which are judged the most suitable of all for theaters and dances. ### §. I I I.
### On Tetraphonies, or compositions for four voices.

We come at last to **Tetraphonia**, or the composition <note>original: "μελοθεσίαν" (melothesia), the art of composing melody or setting music to text</note> of four voices. Just as this is constituted from four voices, like the four elements of the harmonic world, so it deservedly holds the chief place among polyphonic works; indeed, whatever is added beyond four-voice composition is rightly considered a mere replication <note>Kircher views the four-voice texture—Soprano, Alto, Tenor, Bass—as the complete "harmonic body," with any additional voices simply doubling these core roles</note>. And although we have shown the logic and method of composing these in the preceding sections, it seemed appropriate here to demonstrate the "flowering" practice of Melothetic counterpoint. Because this practice differs from simple counterpoint by many miles <note>original: "multis parasangis," a Persian unit of distance; Kircher uses it idiomatically to mean "by a great deal"</note>, we will present its rules in this place, so that what must be observed by composers in any style might become clearer than the noonday sun.

**Rule 1.** Just as a perfect mixing of elements constitutes the harmony of the elemental world, and this mixing arises from contrary qualities—where, to speak with Ovid <note>original: "Nasone," referring to Publius Ovidius Naso</note>:

->...in one body<-
->Cold things fought with hot, moist with dry,<-
->Soft with hard, things having weight with those without weight.<-

So exactly the composer, looking to the example of nature, shall mix dissonances with consonances with such industry that the whole symphonic body breathes forth a focused harmony. This will be achieved if he has a thorough knowledge of three things. First, the logic of **harmonic progressions**. Second, a knowledge of **Syncopations**, or the binding of notes <note>original: "σύνδεσμον" (syndesmon), referring to ligatures or tied notes</note>. Third, an exact understanding of **measuring time**, or what is the same thing, a distinguished knowledge of the rise and fall <note>original: "arsios, & thesios," the upbeat and downbeat</note> of the measure. Since these three things have been discussed in the preceding pages, I have judged it unnecessary to dwell on them any longer.

**Second**, just as a Logician about to demonstrate a concept of his mind first seeks a syllogistic figure under which he may skillfully direct his reasoning; so a Musician, before all else, shall seek a **harmonic figure** suited to the harmonic concept—that is, the **Mode** or **Tone**, under which he may fitly and appropriately produce the harmony conceived in his mind. Then he shall look around to see what action the composition is intended to serve; if for the Church, let him use the **Ecclesiastical style**, selecting for his subject a **Plainchant** or **Cantus Firmus** <term>cantus firmus: a pre-existing melody, usually from Gregorian chant, that serves as the foundation for a polyphonic composition</term>...

### Problem Three.
### Tetraphony in the Ecclesiastical style.

<margin>The true standard of the Ecclesiastical style.</margin>

First, let the following hymn, *Ave maris Stella* <note>original: "Hail, Star of the Sea," a medieval plainchant hymn to the Virgin Mary</note>, serve as an example of the most perfect form. In this, the Tenor holds the subject of the plainchant <note>original: "Cantus plani," the traditional Gregorian melody</note>, while the other voices are interwoven so skillfully and strike each other so sweetly that nothing more pleasing seems possible for the ears. The harmony itself is swelling, grave, full of substance, and imprints a certain impulse of piety upon the soul. This is the true standard of the Ecclesiastical style, which I would earnestly desire our musicians of this time to imitate, as it is most suited for divine praises.

The first strophe of the hymn exhibits the artistry of a simpler "obligato" counterpoint; the second strophe provides the same, but in a higher style than the first; the third strophe varies further, pressing the subject of the *Cantus Firmus* <note>The "fixed song" or pre-existing melody used as the basis for a polyphonic composition</note> in a still more sublime style, as will be clear from an examination of the strophe itself. Finally, the fourth strophe, through a change of tempo, devises a thoroughly ingenious context of fugues <note>referring here to imitative polyphony where voices "chase" one another</note> founded upon the *Cantus Firmus*, as is apparent. 

But all these things will be better revealed to the diligent composer <term>Musurgo</term> <note>Kircher’s term for a skilled music-maker or composer</note> through the inspection of the example itself than by any idle description of mine in many words; for you will see that the melodic artistry of this hymn is completed through four stages, as it were, each always more sublime than the last. 

Whoever intends to pursue the Motet style in four-voice harmony should read among the ancients: Orlandus Lassus, Josquin des Prez, Arcadelt, Jodocus of the Meadows <note>original: "Iodocum pratensem," another name for Josquin des Prez</note>, and Palestrina <note>original: "Prænestinum"</note>. Among the moderns: Giovanni Battista Grillo, Jean Maillard <note>original: "Inmetetum Gallum"</note>, Morales, Suriano, Troiano, Nanino, Cifra, and countless others. For authors of the Madrigal style, let him consult Agostino Agazzari, Scipione Dentice, the Prince of Venosa <note>Carlo Gesualdo, famous for his expressive and chromatic madrigals</note>, Orazio Vecchi, and many others.

## §. II.
## On Polyphonic Voices.

We have said in the preceding sections that perfect harmony consists in a consort of four voices, and that any additional voices are merely repetitions of the original four. If, therefore, anyone delights in polyphony <note>From the Greek *polyphonia*, meaning "many sounds" or multiple independent voice parts.</note>, he may create a five-voice composition by doubling one of the four; a six-voice by doubling two; and a seven-voice by doubling three. However, because a unique artistry—distinct from four-voice writing—shines forth in five-voice compositions, we shall present here, for the sake of the curious musician, a five-voice piece in the Ecclesiastical style <note>original: *stylo Ecclesiastico*. This refers to the "strict" or "sacred" style of the Church, as opposed to the more free "theatrical" style.</note>, composed according to every rigor of the rules. In this piece, the emotions <note>original: *affectus*. In Baroque music theory, this refers to the "Doctrine of the Affections," where music is crafted to evoke specific spiritual or emotional states.</note> expressed by the words are beautifully rendered with remarkable harmony, so much so that everything we have said regarding the art of composition <term>Melothesia <gloss>The technical art of composing a melody or a complete musical work.</gloss></term> up to this point is contained within it, as if in a summary.

### CHAPTER XVIII. ###

#### On a new and admirable system and method for arranging Counterpoint through various combinations. ####

**Note:** After we have discussed the commonly used rules of Counterpoint, perhaps more extensively than was necessary, we will now, for the sake of the curious musician <note>original Latin: *Musurgi*. Kircher uses this term to describe a creator or inventor of music.</note>, attempt something more sublime. In this section, we shall provide a truly wonderful artifice by which any Counterpoint may be adorned with the greatest ease and an almost infinite variety. From this, it will be clear how many secrets flow from harmonic Arithmetic, and what inexhaustible depth the power of musical combination possesses. And although Silverio Picerli <note>original Latin: *Picerlus*. Referring to the author of *Specchio primo di musica* (1630).</note> attempted something similar before us in his practice of composition, he barely explained himself; I have therefore considered it my duty to bring the fruit of the seeds he sowed to a more fertile cultivation.

But leaving aside digressions, let us begin our intended task. In this context, we call the **Subject** <term>Subject: The *Subjectum*, a foundation of Counterpoint usually taken from plainchant (Cantus Planus).</term> that which is the foundation of the Counterpoint. We call the **Counterpoint** that voice which is expressed through various "diminutions" <note>Diminution refers to breaking long notes into shorter, more decorative notes.</note> of notes above the subject, serving as its foundation and base. 

In this musical undertaking of ours, Counterpoint can be considered in two ways: it is either **solo counterpoint** or **replicated counterpoint**. Solo counterpoint is two-fold: it is placed either above the subject or below it. When it is placed below the subject, it is called the **first descending counterpoint** <note>original Greek/Latin: *hypobatos*, meaning "going below."</note>; and whenever it is placed above the subject, we then call it the **first ascending counterpoint** <note>original Greek/Latin: *hyperbaton*, meaning "going above."</note>. In the first case, the subject is called "ascending," and in the latter counterpoint, it is called "descending." See the example provided of both.

Counterpoint I. florid, Ascending.
[Musical notation on a five-line staff with a C-clef on the first line]
Subject I. common, Descending.
[Musical notation on a five-line staff with an F-clef on the fourth line]
Subject I. Ascending.
[Musical notation on a five-line staff with a C-clef on the fourth line]
Counterpoint I. florid, Descending.
[Musical notation on a five-line staff with an F-clef on the fourth line]

From both types of Counterpoint—the descending as well as the ascending—twelve different Counterpoints are born. In the replication of all of these, there are different methods, different observations, permissions, laws, and so on.

<margin>The Third-Interval <note>original Greek: *Diatritos*.</note></margin> 1. The first is called the **Third-Interval Counterpoint**, because the second voice of the replicated counterpoint stands apart from the first by a third, either above or below.

### §. I. ###
#### On Counterpoint of the Third. ####
<note>original Latin: *diatrito*</note>
**Problem 1. To compose a counterpoint of the third.**

If you wish to consider the various logic of this counterpoint, take the subject or fixed song <term>Cantus firmus: A foundational melody, often drawn from plainchant, around which other voices are composed.</term>, which we marked a little earlier with the letter B; over which you should establish the florid counterpoint, namely voice A.
If you replicate this voice A one third below, you will have a "hypotriton" counterpoint, which can be replicated or varied in six ways. First, if, as I said, you replicate the upper voice A at an interval of a third below. Second, if you replicate the same a tenth below. Third, if you replicate the same first voice a twelfth below. Fourth, if you replicate the first voice a sixth above it. Fifth, if you replicate the same an octave above it. For the logic of all these, see the end of this chapter, where everything will be demonstrated arithmetically.
When this continuation of replication is completed, six entirely different polyphonies will be established, which can be sung not only in their natural order, but—what is wonderful—in any retrograde order <note>Retrograde: Playing or singing a melody backward from the last note to the first.</note>, as will be seen later.
Indeed, not only is the florid counterpoint (or "diminished" voice) replicable and singable in so many ways, but the subject itself is as well; however, it is done by a certain contrary logic, so that through those same consonances by which the first counterpoint (or first voice) was replicated below, the subject may be replicated above through the same intervals described just before, as can be seen in the example placed below.

Tt Colum- <note>This is a catchword, indicating the start of the next page.</note>

And this is a double paradigm; the first of which teaches, given a <term>subject</term> <note>the main melody</note> and a <term>diminished counterpoint</term> <note>a secondary melody using faster note values than the main subject</note>, in what manner and by what logic those parts may be replicated according to the intervals assigned to each. The second example, or third column, gives another example of counterpoint in which it is replicated by the 3rd, 10th, and 12th above the first voice, and by the 6th and 8th below the same, using a logic contrary to the first counterpoint. ### A Melodic Corollary.

**E**rom which things, when properly compared with one another, there follows a varied method of polyphony <note>original: "polyphoniorum ratio," referring to the logic or system of multi-voiced music</note>. For the subject of the counterpoint is common to all the replicated counterpoints, to such an extent that as many two-part harmonies <note>original: "dyphonia"</note> are born as there are replicated counterpoints. For each of them, when sung with the subject, constitutes a different two-part harmony. By the same reasoning, <margin>Two-part harmony from counterpoint in the third <note>original: "hypotrito"</note></margin> the subject, together with the principal counterpoint, constitutes as many distinct two-part harmonies as the subject itself is replicated, as the second column shows, where each subject sung with the common counterpoint *hypobatus* <note>original: "hypobato," meaning descending or lower-stepping</note> at the foot of the column constitutes a distinct two-part harmony.

2. It is shown that one can arrange not only different two-part harmonies from the said replication, but also three-part harmonies <note>original: "triphonia"</note>—that is, singing with three voices—in six ways.

The **First Three-part Harmony** will be formed by the first and second counterpoint together with the common subject.
The **Second Three-part Harmony** will be formed by the third and fourth counterpoint together with the common subject.
The **Third Three-part Harmony** will be formed by the first and third counterpoint together with the common subject.
The **Fourth Three-part Harmony** will be formed by the second and fourth counterpoint together with the common subject.
The **Fifth Three-part Harmony** will be formed by the second and sixth counterpoint together with the common subject.
The **Sixth Three-part Harmony** will be formed by the fifth and sixth counterpoint together with the common subject.

Again, if you combine the replicated subject with the principal counterpoint, another five-fold three-part harmony will be produced.

The **First Three-part Harmony** will give the first and second subject with the common principal counterpoint at the foot of the second column.
The **Second Three-part Harmony** will give the first and third subject with the common counterpoint.
The **Third Three-part Harmony** will give the third and fourth subject with the common counterpoint.
The **Fourth Three-part Harmony** will give the first and fifth subject with the common counterpoint.
The **Fifth Three-part Harmony** will give the fifth and sixth subject with the common counterpoint.

Note, however, that not every combined voice is distinct, but some coincide in unison. Combinations to be avoided are shown in the following table.

| Voices of the replicated counterpoint | Voices of the explained subject | The same thing must be said about the counterpoint of the second example, and about all others that can be arranged above a given subject in <term>hypotritus</term> <note>A technical term from Greek meaning "under the third," referring to counterpoint generated at the interval of a third.</note>. This thing is truly marvelous, and I do not know if it has been noted by any musician until now. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 & 6 } | 1 & 6 } | |
| 2 & 3 } are in unison. | 2 & 5 } are in unison. | |
| 3 & 5 } | 2 & 3 } | |

### Summary Practice of Counterpoint in the Third.

**Q**henever, therefore, anyone wishes to arrange a counterpoint in the <term>third</term> <note>original: "hypotritum"</note>, he shall first establish the aforementioned subject as the principal counterpoint. Having done this, [he replicates] the first voice or principal counterpoint according to the numbers placed here at the side...

**Problem III. To compose counterpoint at the fifth below.**
<note>original: "hypodiapente"</note>

Let the subject remain, as before, always the same; then let the principal Counterpoint be made over it. Once these are set:

If you replicate the first voice below by a fifth, you will have the second voice; if you replicate the first again by a twelfth below, the third voice will come forth. If further you replicate the first voice above itself by a fourth, the fourth voice will come forth; if finally you replicate the same first voice above itself by an octave, you will have the fifth voice. By a similar reasoning, if you replicate the subject above itself by a tenth, a fifth, and a twelfth; then by a fourth and an octave below, five variations of voices will come forth. Each of these, if sung with the principal counterpoint, will constitute five different *dyphonia* <note>original: "dyphonia," a term for two-part compositions or intervals</note>. Likewise, if each of the five voices of the Counterpoint are sung with the common subject, the same number of two-part harmonies will result. However, the following paradigm will clarify the meaning better.

In this counterpoint, the sixth, octave, thirteenth, and fifteenth are prohibited at the outset. For in replication, they become dissonances. Likewise, a second resolved with a unison is forbidden, as are the seventh and ninth resolved with the octave. ->### §. IV.<-
->### On Counterpoint at the Sixth.<-
<note>original: "Diabex," likely a typographical error for "Diahex"</note>

We call this counterpoint "at the sixth" because the second voice is replicated a sixth below the first voice of the counterpoint. In this counterpoint, the following rules must be observed.

<margin>Cautions in counterpoint at the sixth <note>original: "diahex"</note></margin>

First: in this style, the third, fifth, two sixths, and two tenths are prohibited as illicit intervals. Likewise, the twelfth and two thirteenths are forbidden, as they produce dissonances somewhere during replication.

Second: The second and fourth joined with thirds, and several sevenths joined with sixths, are prohibited. So too are the ninth joined with the tenth, and finally several fourteenths resolved with sixteenths, since they turn into dissonances in one of the replicated voices. However, the Unison is permitted...

### §. V.
### On Counterpoint at the Seventh <term>hypohebdomus</term> or <term>diahepta</term>.

**C**ounterpoint is called <term>hypohebdomus</term> <note>from the Greek for "under the seventh"</note> because the second replicated voice stands apart from the first by the interval of a seventh, both in the subject and in the counterpoint. It is twofold: either <term>hypohebdomus</term> <note>seventh below</note> or <term>hyperhebdomus</term> <note>seventh-above</note>. We shall provide a paradigm for both. In these two voices of the subject and counterpoint, this must be noted: whenever the counterpoint is a seventh below, its subject must be established as a seventh above; and whenever the counterpoint is a seventh above, its subject must be established as a seventh below, as is also clearly evident from the preceding sections.

## § VII.
## On Counterpoint at the Twelfth Below (*Hypodiadecatos*).
<note>original: "Hypodiadecato," from the Greek for "under" and "twelve." This refers to counterpoint where a voice is transposed a twelfth—an octave plus a fifth—downward.</note>

That counterpoint is called **hypodiadecatus** in which the second voice is replicated a tenth below; in this, one must avoid two thirds, two sixths, two tenths, and the thirteenth, as well as two seconds resolved with a third. Likewise, the fourth and the seventh, two ninths, and two elevenths occurring on tenths. However, one third, sixth, and tenth are permitted. Also, a second resolved with a third, and a ninth and eleventh resolved with tenths.

### Problem VII. To compose counterpoint at the twelfth above (*hyperdiadecaton*).
<note>original: "hyperdiadecaton," referring to the twelfth interval transposed upward.</note>

Let a subject be made, as is evident in the paradigm [example], above which a first counterpoint is constructed at the octave above, as appears below.
Once this is completed, you will replicate this counterpoint below by the 10th, 12th, and 3rd, and by the 8th above. Again, by the 10th, 12th, 3rd, and 5th below, and finally by the 6th above the subject; from the given octave and the lowering by the 10th, ten <term>dyphonia</term> <note>compositions for two voices</note> will be produced from the first counterpoint. If you establish this replication in the subject by the same reasoning, another ten two-voice pieces will be produced. If, indeed, they are sung in retrograde order <note>backwards, from the end to the beginning</note>, just as many two-voice pieces will come forth in both the voice of the counterpoint and the subject; and so, from this simple combination, forty different <term>dyphonia</term> will emerge. But let us demonstrate the matter through a paradigm.

### §. VIII.
### On Counterpoint at the Lower Eleventh
<note>original: "hypodiacendecato," a term derived from Greek roots meaning "under the eleventh."</note>

This counterpoint is so named because the second voice descends an eleventh below it; in which only the thirteenth, fifteenth, and the fourteenth resolved with the thirteenth are allowed, while the rest are forbidden.

#### Problem VIII. To compose counterpoint at the eleventh.
<note>original: "diedenca," likely a shorthand or variation for the eleventh interval.</note>

### §. XI.
### *On Counterpoint at the Twelfth Below.*
<note>original: "De Contrapuncto hypodiadodecato." "Hypo-" means below, and "diadodeca" refers to the interval of a twelfth.</note>

We call this Counterpoint by this name because the second voice stands at a full twelfth below the first voice. In this, I would have you avoid the sixth, thirteenth, and fifteenth; likewise, the second resolved with the unison; the seventh resolved with the sixth; the ninth resolved with the octave; and the fourteenth resolved with the thirteenth. However, the unison, 3rd, 5th, 8th, 10th, and 12th are allowed. Likewise, the second and fourth resolved with the third, and the ninth and eleventh resolved with the tenth.

**Problem 9. *To compose counterpoint at the twelfth.***

Let the subject remain as before, and let a Counterpoint be made an octave above, as appears below in the Example. Once this is done, you will replicate this Counterpoint below the first voice by a 12th, 3rd, 8th, and 10th, and a 6th above the first voice. In like manner, the subject is replicated—namely, by a 12th, 3rd, 8th, and 10th above, and a 6th below the first voice of the subject. From this completed replication, six two-voice textures immediately arise, both in the Counterpoint and in the replicated Subject. If individual Counterpoints are sung with the common Subject, and individual parts of the subject are sung with the principal counterpoint, you have six three-voice textures in each replication, in this manner:

      ⎪ 3 & 4 ⎪ will give a       ⎪ 4 ⎪   the Subject, you will find four
      ⎪ 4 & 5 ⎪ three-voice piece ⎪ 5 ⎪   Four-voice textures.
      ⎩ 4 & 6 ⎭                   ⎩ 6 ⎭

If indeed  you compose 1 & 4 counterpoint with 1 & 3 ⎫                   ⎫ 1
If again   you compose 3 & 4 counterpoint with 1 & 5 ⎬ Subject, you will ⎬ 2
If also    you compose 4 & 5 counterpoint with 3 & 4 ⎬ have a four-voice ⎬ 3
If finally you compose 1 & 6 counterpoint with 1 & 5 ⎭ piece.           ⎭ 4

### §. X.
### On Counterpoint at the Thirteenth.
<note>original: "De Contrapuncto diatredecato." The term "diatredecato" is derived from the Greek "dia" (through) and the Latin "tredecim" (thirteen), referring to the musical interval of a thirteenth.</note>

In this style of Counterpoint, the second voice, when transposed <note>original: "replicata"</note>, stands apart from the first by the interval of a 13th; it is from this that it takes its name. It is performed in this manner:

**Problem X. To compose a counterpoint at the thirteenth.**

Let the same subject remain, above which a counterpoint is constructed at the octave <note>the interval of an 8th</note>, as is shown below. This counterpoint will then be transposed below by the 13th, 4th, 6th, 7th, 10th, and 15th; and also by the 8th, 5th, and 3rd above the aforementioned first counterpoint. The subject will be transposed across various intervals, but always—as has been stated—in inverse proportion, as the example teaches. Forbidden in this counterpoint are thirds and fifths, and two consecutive sixths. Also forbidden are tenths and twelfths, and all kinds of tied <term>dissonances</term> <note>clashing notes that are held over from a previous beat to create tension</note>, except for the second resolving into a unison, the ninth resolving into an octave, and the fourteenth resolving into a thirteenth. However, a single sixth, an octave, a thirteenth, and a fifteenth are allowed. Indeed, all these matters will become clearer from what will be demonstrated shortly. For the process is the same for all in every respect, with the same permissions and laws; therefore, it should suffice to have demonstrated the matter with an example.

### §. XI.
### On Counterpoint at the Fourteenth.
<note>original: "De Contrapuncto diatetradecato"</note>

This Counterpoint takes its name from the interval of the 14th <term>Diatetradecaton: a compound musical interval spanning an octave plus a seventh.</term>, by which the second voice is replicated below or above the first. You will possess every variety of this Counterpoint if you proceed by this industrious method.

#### Problem XI. To compose counterpoint at the fourteenth.

<margin>Replication of Counterpoint at the fourteenth.</margin>

Let the same Subject remain, above which the Counterpoint is established at the interval of a fifth. If, therefore, you replicate this first Counterpoint below by the 14th, 3rd, 5th, 10th, 12th, and by the 8th, 6th, 4th above the same, you will have the Counterpoint called *diatetradecaton* <note>counterpoint at the fourteenth</note>. If, however, through the same intervals you replicate above the Counterpoint composed below the subject—as is clear in the second example <note>original: "Paradigma"</note>—you will have the Counterpoint at the fourteenth; the same must be said regarding the subjects of each Counterpoint. But let us demonstrate the matter with an example.

§. XII.

On Counterpoint at the Double Octave.
<note>original: "disdiapason," a Greek term used in music theory to denote an interval of two octaves.</note>

Counterpoint at the double octave is so named because the second voice stands apart from the first by an interval of a fifteenth. You will possess every variety of this counterpoint if you proceed according to this method.

Problem XII. To compose counterpoint at the double octave.

Let the same subject <note>The "subject" or *cantus firmus* is the fixed melody used as the foundation for the harmony.</note> remain, above which a counterpoint is composed at the interval of an octave. If this Counterpoint is then repeated <note>original: "replicetur"</note> below the first voice at the 15th, 6th, 8th, and 10th, and at the 8th and 3rd above the first voice, you will have the sought-after counterpoint. From this, seven two-part harmonies <note>original: "dyphonia"</note> will be produced if you sing the individual replicated voices with the subject; likewise, seven other two-part harmonies will result if you sing the individual replicated voices of the subject with the first counterpoint. Indeed, you will have twelve three-part harmonies <note>original: "triphonia"</note> in both, in this manner:

360 *Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

->Use and Explanation of the Table.<-

<margin>Various uses of the table.</margin>
**T**here are 12 columns in this table, each of which contains one of the 12 counterpoints <note>A melody written to be played alongside another melody</note> as the titles show. Four transverse series of notes signify the double counterpoint, both <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>original: "hyperbaton"; from Greek, meaning "stepping above," referring to a melody transposed to a higher register</note> and <term>hypobaton</term> <note>original: "hypobaton"; from Greek, meaning "stepping below," referring to a melody transposed to a lower register</note>, along with the subject appropriate to each, as the side title shows. Thus, the musical notes in the 1st and 4th columns show the beginning of the double counterpoint, both upper and lower. Series A shows the beginning of the principal counterpoint in each column. Series B shows the beginning of its subject <note>The primary theme or melody upon which the counterpoint is built</note> over which it is constructed in each column. Series C shows the beginning of the subject for the other counterpoint, and transverse series D shows the beginning of the lower counterpoint, which is constructed over the subject contained below the transverse series C.

From this arrangement, it is clearly evident that whenever a counterpoint is "hyperbatos"—that is, moving above the subject—then the subject is called "hypobaton"—that is, moving below—as can be seen in series A and B. You see the opposite in the other counterpoints C and D.

Within the remaining space in each column, two numbers are arranged. The first, written in Roman numerals, signifies how many voices can be replicated. For example, in column 1, these numbers I, II, III, IV, V, VI indicate that the <term>diatriton</term> <note>A specific harmonic interval, likely the third, or a shorthand for this specific column's structure</note> counterpoint of this column can be replicated six times—that is, it can have six replicated voices. The remaining corresponding numbers (5, 3, 10, 12, 6, 8) indicate through which harmonic intervals the principal voice ought to be replicated, either below or above. For example: Voice I (the first counterpoint), which has the number 5 placed in its row (in this fashion: I. 5.), indicates that the first note of the principal counterpoint is a fifth away from the first note of the subject; and so on for the remaining numbers contained in the same transverse series in each column, all of which indicate how far the note of the first counterpoint is from the first note of the subject. The remaining numbers indicate, as I said, the intervals through which the other voices must be replicated, above or below the counterpoint. For example: in the first column, these numbers II. 3. show that the second voice of the upper counterpoint ought to be replicated a 3rd below itself. In this same way, the remaining numbers III. 10. and IV. 12. indicate that the first upper counterpoint can be transferred below by a 10th and a 12th. <margin>A wonderful transposition of the table.</margin> Indeed, the lower counterpoint can be replicated above itself by those same intervals. Likewise, the subject of the upper counterpoint can be replicated above by the same intervals; truly, the subject of the lower counterpoint is replicable below by the same intervals, as was clear in the paradigm. However, the numbers 5 and 8, corresponding to voices V and VI below the transverse line of the first column, show that a contrary method of <term>Melothesia</term> <note>The art of composing melody</note> or replication must be established. For when the upper counterpoint is transferred below in voices I, II, III, and IV by the intervals 3, 10, and 12 below, then voices V and VI must be transferred above by a 6th and an 8th. Likewise, in the upper counterpoint, voice V must be transferred below by a 6th and an 8th.

From this, it is clear: 1. The upper counterpoint with the upper subject preserves the same method of replication and <term>metathesis</term> <note>rearrangement or transposition</note>; just as the lower counterpoint and lower subject preserve exactly the same order of replication. Therefore, whatever has been said regarding the numbers of the first column must also be understood regarding the numbers in the following columns.

<margin>The wonderful power of combination and its prodigious effects.</margin>
From this truly marvelous artifice, a certain wonderful power of combination shines forth, which increases to such an extent that from the diverse transposition and replication of these 12 counterpoints alone, there emerge over 136,000 pieces—partly <term>diphonia</term> <note>two-voice compositions</note>, partly <term>triphonia</term> <note>three-voice</note>, and <term>tetraphonia</term> <note>four-voice</note>. If indeed you take the notes as combinable in any way you please, there will emerge from this single subject of 5 notes combinations or mutations of diverse voices as follows: 126,739,456—that is, one hundred twenty-six million, seven hundred thirty-nine thousand, four hundred fifty-six different counterpoints. This number is so great that no abundance of books would suffice to contain them. I urge all composers and musicians to exercise themselves diligently in these matters. For if they drink these things deeply into their minds, they will no longer suffer from any lack of inventions, but will reach a point where they can [compose] anything in music...

Book V. On the Making of Polyphony. 361

...they might boast that they can provide for the musical craft. But so that it may be clear to the curious reader upon which principles we have founded the wonderful system of the aforementioned counterpoints, it seemed best to demonstrate this from its foundations here before we proceed further.

### An Arithmetic Demonstration of the aforementioned Counterpoints.

**S**o that the curious reader may more deeply inspect the inexhaustible riches of arithmetic, it seemed best to demonstrate each thing said so far from its sources. This is so that Musicians may know how important it is to be imbued with mathematical rules for penetrating more deeply into the nature of counterpoint, and how nothing worthy of praise can be performed in this business without them. From this, I hope it will happen that musicians who are ignorant of such things will cease to bark against theoretical matters, and will learn to venerate in silence those things which they do not grasp. There is an inexhaustible ocean of things <margin>The Musician must be a mathematician.</margin> hidden under mathematical veils, which consequently only a few—those whom God and nature have made fit and capable—can penetrate. Thus let it be:

**Lemma I. The process of harmonic numbers is infinitely replicable, according to the consonant numbers contained within any given System.**

Numbers, as has also been demonstrated in the preceding sections, contain all artificial harmony when disposed in their natural order. For if you place their individual numbers in natural order before or after the forms of consonances expressed as numbers, a certain wonderful harmony and concord of voices will immediately flow from the comparison made between each individual number. Whoever knows how to apply this combination correctly will undoubtedly stand upon an infallible foundation for making parts agree through appropriate consonances. Thus, given any motion or process of numbers of a counterpoint composed over some subject; I say that as many musical arrangements <note>original: "melothesias"; from Greek, meaning the composition or setting of a melody</note> can proceed in a certain parallel motion of numbers either above or below the subject as there are consonant numbers contained in the natural series of numbers from 1 to 15—that is, the <term>disdiapason</term> <note>original: "disdiapason"; a scale of two octaves</note>—and further to 22—that is, the <term>trisdiapason</term> <note>original: "trisdiapason"; a scale of three octaves</note>. Since all those numbers are consonant both to the subject and the counterpoint, necessarily two, three, or four will perfectly agree with it. For if they do not agree, they will therefore be dissonant; but they cannot be dissonant, since by hypothesis they are consonant. They will therefore be consonant, and that from the nature of numbers implanted in them; since all things unite themselves perfectly according to those things demonstrated in the 4th book. And therefore, that they should not agree is impossible <note>original: "ἀδύνατον"</note>. Let this, then, be the first foundation.

**Lemma II. As many musical arrangements are necessarily replicable above a subject as there are parallel motions feasible over a subject through combination.**

Let a counterpoint be constructed over some subject, movable by any process of numbers; I say that it is replicable in as many ways as consonant motions parallel to it can be ordered through combination. And so, through "combinatory music-making" <note>original: "musurgiam"</note>, there are as many combinable harmonic motions parallel to the first counterpoint as there are harmonic numbers contained within any harmonic System according to the preceding lemma. For since these processes of numbers are founded upon the concords within the natural series of some system of octaves <note>original: "διαπασῶν"</note>, all harmonic processes disposed above the first counterpoint will necessarily be consonant. For the union of harmonic strokes will join them so perfectly that even if the music is the same regarding the harmonic process and progression, it is nevertheless made diverse and concordant by that miraculous efficacy of numbers. For that parallel motion has this specific property: that at whatever consonant interval it is ordered below or above the counterpoint,

...[from the previous page] they exhibit, from the perfect union of harmonic proportions or ratios, a perfect agreement of voices through a process of notes of this kind. This occurs because it is impossible for them not to coincide in either a 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, or 8th <note>octave</note>, or in one of the intervals replicated from these. Since these are consonant by our initial assumption, they will necessarily harmonize. Therefore, as many notes are necessarily repeatable above a given subject of **composition** <term>melothesia: the art of composing melody and harmony</term> as can be arranged in parallel motion above a given subject; which was to be demonstrated.

Having thus established these fundamental lemmas, let us now see how they are to be arranged in practice.

### Problem: To construct an Arithmetic-harmonic Abacus which exactly exhibits all motions of harmonic processes.

<margin>The harmonic abacus, showing the causes and reasons of counterpoint for individual parts.</margin> Let the numbers from 1 to 15 be arranged in their natural order; for beyond this number, such processes are for the most part useless. Let the numbers be arranged in this order: let the top of the **abacus** <note>In this context, a table or calculation grid</note> be marked by the natural sequence of numbers from 1 to 15; then let the base of the abacus follow the same sequence from 1 to 15. Let the right side proceed downward with the same sequence, while the left side proceeds upward from the base with the same sequence, but in contrary motion. Let the intermediate numbers proceed so that all the "1s" occupy the diagonal line of the abacus, from which they then move now upward, now downward, in natural order, as appears in the abacus provided below. In this table, take note that the numbers marked with little stars or asterisks denote **consonant intervals**, while the remaining numbers lacking stars denote **dissonant intervals**.

From these things it is clear how numbers demonstrate the process of things in nature, and how the natural order of numbers beautifully exhibits the degrees of beings in the universe through the order of their consequences; and how, joined together, they conspire into the perfect harmony of the whole. Indeed, if you were to transpose even a single number from this table, you would bring about the greatest dissonance and **disorder** <note>original Greek: *ataxian*</note> to the whole. From this it is also clear how that saying of Aristotle—when he says "the essences of things are like numbers"—is to be understood. Moreover, the universe observes these laws of numbers not only in the arrangement of the principal heavenly bodies, but this numerical process is most especially seen in the elemental order of the world: in the generation and corruption of things, in the composition of mixtures, in the increase and decrease of quantity, and in the intensification and weakening of qualities. Since there is copious material for speaking of these things elsewhere, we shall remain silent for now.

Wherefore, let us return to the specifics of our undertaking.

364 of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Column B D shows the replication of the subject over the counterpoint, or even the replication of the counterpoint over the subject to be established, as will be shown later. Indeed, the numbers A B show the arrangement of the subject below the counterpoint; the numbers C D, however, denote the disposition of either the counterpoint below the subject or the subject above the counterpoint. Furthermore, the Greek names show the 12 types of counterpoints, each corresponding to its own column. Their numbers show the arrangement of the subject below the counterpoints; just as the upper numbers, descending downwards, show the arrangements of the said counterpoints below the subject, so the lower numbers, ascending upwards, show the arrangements of the counterpoints above the subject, as is clear from the use of the table.

A table is called "immobile" <note>original Latin: *Immobilis tabula*</note> when this table is described on separate slats or small columns, by the combination and transposition of which the work proceeds according to the mind of the Composer <note>original: *Musurgi*, referring to the skilled musical architect</note>. For if someone joins the first column with a column of one of the 12 counterpoints which he intends to arrange, he will be able to dispatch the business with the greatest ease; I would wish this to be understood also for the columns verging upwards from below. But since these things are clearer from the preceding examples of the 12 counterpoints, as well as from those which will follow, than if I were to describe them in many words, I have decided to refrain from explaining them more diffusely.

You see, therefore, the abacus arranged with such skill that there is almost nothing so hidden in the art of composition <note>original: *Symphoniurgia*</note> that it does not encompass. But lest we seem to mock the reader with empty, bombastic words, let us demonstrate the matter demonstratively. If, therefore, given a subject and counterpoint, you desire to add any voices below or above, you shall proceed from the preceding table as follows: see of what species the counterpoint is—whether it is a third <note>original Greek: διατρι'τα (diatrita)</note>? or a fourth <note>original: διατεσσάρωv (diatessaron)</note>? or if it is from any other marked at the head of the table—and carefully note its column. Having done this, if you wish to replicate the counterpoint, take in the first column A C the intervals through which you wish to replicate the other counterpoints; for these, in the common cell of the assumed counterpoint column, will show the number according to which you can replicate it below the subject.

But we will show the matter with an example. Let there be, for example, the first counterpoint, a lower-third <note>original: *hypodiatritus*</note>, the form of which we gave in Problem I; and you wish to know in how many ways it is replicable. First, you will compare the individual numbers of the column with the numbers of the third column, that is, of the "lower-third" counterpoint; and if in the intervals of this column there occur dissonant <term>dissonant: sounds that create musical tension or "clash," like seconds or sevenths</term> numbers such as 2, 7, 9, 11, 14, know for certain that replication under these is not possible at all. Since all these numbers are dissonant, it will be a sign to you that replication cannot be made.

Under the remaining consonant intervals, however, the said replication will be very easily dispatched, provided the cautions we handed down in the cited place are observed. For example: if you wish to replicate the assumed counterpoint by a 3rd below, you will look for the third in column A. C., and the common cell in the column of the "third" counterpoint <note>original: *diatriti*</note> will give 1, which indicates that the replicable counterpoint ought to begin in unison with the subject. If, however, you wish to replicate it by a 5th, the number 5 in column C. A. will show the number 3 corresponding to it in the third column, which indicates that the counterpoint is replicable at the 3rd below the subject. In this way, a counterpoint replicable at the 10th above shows an 8 in the third column, by which it is shown that it is replicable at the octave below the subject; and so on for the rest.

And this is indeed the case if you make a comparison of the replication below the subject; but if you establish a comparison of the replicable counterpoints to the first note of the principal counterpoint, the individual numbers in the first column—3, 10, 12—will show the beginnings of the replication of the counterpoints below the principal counterpoint. However, so that you may have the voices to be replicated above the principal counterpoint, subtract 3 from 10 and 12, and 7 and 9 will remain; from which, if a unit is subtracted, they will leave 6 and 8. If, therefore, you replicate the counterpoint at the 6th and 8th above, you will have two other counterpoints; all of which are clearly demonstrated in the first "third" counterpoint, which we proposed in the 10th problem. If, however, you again establish a comparison of the principal counterpoint with the subject, you will find the first note of each to be a 5th apart; you will therefore seek column 5, and in it the numbers corresponding to the aforementioned numbers of the replication of the counterpoints—for example, 3, 10, 12 in the first column correspond to 3, 6, 8 in [the table...]

Book V. On the Creation of Symphonies. 365

The **fifth column**, whose two latter numbers, **6** and **8**, show—as previously stated—that the replication <note>original: *replicationem*, referring to the repetition or transposition of a musical line</note> of the counterpoints must be established **below the subject** according to these numbers. Just as with the earlier numbers **3, 10, and 12**, the replication must be established below the counterpoint that is not the subject; the two latter numbers, **6** and **8**, simultaneously show that a replication can also be made according to these **above the counterpoint**. Or, what is the same thing, through **10** and **12** above the first note of the subject. 

For if you add **3** to **6**, and **3** to **8**, the results will be **9** and **11**; if a unit <note>the number 1</note> is added to each of these, they will constitute **10** and **12**. Thus, if you subtract **3** and then **1** from the numbers to be replicated below the counterpoint, the intervals will be produced by which the counterpoint is to be replicated below the subject. If, however, you add **3** and **1** to the numbers of the counterpoints to be replicated below the subject, the numbers for replicating counterpoints above the subject will be produced. This matter is utterly marvelous, and I suspect it has never occurred to any other musician.

But if you wish the subject to be replicated while the counterpoint remains immobile, this will be done with the same numbers **3, 10, and 12** in the first column, to which the last two numbers **10** and **12** in the fifth column correspond as **6** and **8**. This is done in such a way, however, that through the first **3**, the replication is established **above the subject**; through the latter two, however, the replication is made **below the subject**, as clearly appears in the first example of the <term>Hypotritus</term> <note>A specific species of counterpoint in Kircher's system, likely involving the interval of a third</note> counterpoint in Problem I. 

Furthermore, if someone should compose a <term>Hyperbaton</term> <note>A style involving displaced or transposed intervals</note> subject in an inverted style, such as the second example of the **Hypotritus** counterpoint represents, he will learn the replications of this from the abacus in this way. Since the first note of the counterpoint is a fifth <note>original: *per quintam*</note> distant from the first note of the subject, and you wish all replications to be made **above the principal counterpoint**, the fifth column—or the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fifth</note>—at the base of the abacus will give you all the replications tending upwards, having a position contrary to the previous ones: namely **3, 10, and 12**. These show that the replication is to be established by **3, 10, and 12** above the counterpoint. Since in the fifth column of the base of the abacus, **6** and **8** correspond to the last two, **10** and **12**, it signifies that the replication is to be established by **6** and **8** below, in a manner contrary to how it was done in the previous counterpoint. You will also have these two numbers if you first subtract three, and then a unit, from **10** and **12**. 

The reason why we have chosen only **3** from the first column is that in the **Hypotritus** counterpoint, all the remaining replications are either faulty, or in unison, or dissonant, as will be clear to anyone examining the matter more skillfully.

Truly, time would fail me if I wished to bring forth all the mysteries of this <term>Abacus</term> <note>The grid-based calculation tool for music</note>; it is enough that we have indicated its use in a few words. Since we have shown its use in the preceding pages through twelve different counterpoints, the sagacious reader will perceive my meaning better from the explanation of a single example than from many words. Hence, at the top and the bottom of the abacus, we have annexed the names of the **12 counterpoints** appropriated to the individual columns, so that each column might teach how the replication in each species of counterpoint is to be performed. 

Specifically, the first column **A C** teaches the replications of counterpoints **below the principal counterpoint**; the intermediate columns, however, teach that the replications of the same counterpoint are to be established not below the principal counterpoint, but **below the first note of the subject**. Conversely, if you wish to replicate the counterpoint above, you will use the same numbers in column **B D**; the corresponding numbers in the intermediate columns rising upwards from the base **C D** will show the replications to be made **above the subject**. The numbers of the base **C D** will serve then either when the subject is to be replicated while the counterpoint remains immobile, or when the subject is **Hyperbaton** and the counterpoint is **Hypobaton** <note>Meaning "lower" or placed beneath</note>. The upper **A B** columns will serve when the counterpoint is to be replicated while the subject remains immobile, or when the subject is to be replicated while the counterpoint remains immobile. All of these things are most clearly evident from the twelve examples of counterpoints. Thus, nothing else seems to be required for the penetration of this mystery than a diligent comparison of the replicated counterpoints with the **Abacus**.

366 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

#### On the harmonic Figures or Tropes to be observed in songs.

Figures in our *Musurgia* <note>Kircher's term for the art of musical composition, as well as the title of this work</note> are the same and perform the same function as the colors, tropes, and various modes of speaking in Rhetoric. For just as the Orator moves the listener now to laughter, now to weeping, presently to mercy, and sometimes to indignation and wrath—now to love, piety, and justice, and at other times to the opposite of these emotions—through the skillful arrangement of tropes, so too does Music through the skillful arrangement of harmonic clauses or periods. Certainly, that Music is "soul-bending" <note>original: *flexanimem*, a term implying the power to turn or influence the mind</note> is confirmed by the consensus of all authors everywhere; indeed, the records of historians are full of the wonderful effects it causes. However, since we have undertaken to treat these matters extensively and by profession in Book VII, I have judged it superfluous to linger on them longer here; therefore, let us return to our purpose. There are, then, two types of figures to be considered by musicians: the Principal and the Less Principal.

The **Principal figures** are the *commissura*, Syncopation, and Fugue. The **Less Principal figures** are twelve: the Pause, Repetition, Climax, *Complexum*, Anaphora, Catachresis, *Noema*, *Prosopopæia*, *Parrhesia*, *Aposiopesis*, *Paragoge*, and *Apocope* <note>Kircher is borrowing these terms directly from Greek and Latin rhetoric to describe musical gestures like pauses, sudden silences, or repeated themes</note>. We must speak of each and every one of these in order, so that nothing regarding our *Musurgia* remains hidden, nor that it should seem to yield to Rhetoric in any way.

#### §. I.
#### On the Principal Figures.

<margin>What a *commissura* is.</margin>
The Principal figures are three: *Commissura*, Syncopation, and Fugue.
A *commissura* <note>literally a "joining" or "seam"</note>, which is also called a *symbasis* <note>original Greek: σύμβασις, meaning a meeting or agreement</note> or "celerity," occurs when small notes—even if they are dissonant—nevertheless enter the harmony skillfully without offending the ears; or, it is when dissonances are committed in the smaller notes of counterpoint and on the upbeat <note>original: *eleuatione tactus*, the "lifting" of the hand in conducting</note>. All smaller notes are admitted in a *commissura*, such as minims, semiminims, fusae, and semifusae <note>these correspond to half, quarter, eighth, and sixteenth notes</note>; a semibreve <note>whole note</note>, however, is not admitted because it is too slow. Furthermore, the *commissura* is of two kinds: direct and falling. The former occurs when a dissonance is perceived by the sense of the ears on the *thesis* <note>the downbeat</note> of the measure, yet is admitted because of the following concordance; more recent composers call this by the suitable name "Resolution." This is because a breve or semibreve is "resolved" into smaller parts, both consonant and dissonant, of which very full and frequent mention was made in the preceding treatise on counterpoint.

A "falling" *commissura* occurs when the first part of the beat is consonant and the latter is dissonant—that is, it happens on the upbeat, not on the downbeat. This is positioned for the sake of the following note, and thus the dissonance is rendered good by the [following] consonance; it happens most often in larger notes while ascending or descending, as appears in the following example.

The second figure is Syncopation, concerning which I have dealt most abundantly in another specific chapter; I think it would be superfluous to repeat those things here, since you can easily understand my meaning from the examples already provided.

# §. I I.
# On Fugued Composition, or
# On the Artful Arrangement of Fugues.

<margin>The excellence of Fugues.</margin>
The principal figure among musicians is the Fugue, which is held in such high regard that a song is not considered artful unless it is packed with the most laboriously crafted fugues. And just as the genius of a rhetorician shines through the artful arrangement of figures in the art of Oratory, so too must the happy genius of a musician be judged by a beautiful and extensive series of fugues.

<margin>What is a Fugue?</margin>
<margin>What is the *phonagogus* voice?</margin>
<margin>How many types of fugue?</margin>
A fugue is a certain successive repetition and artful distribution of one and the same musical phrase <note>original: *clausula*</note> in different parts of a song. The first voice is called the *Phonagogus* <note>from the Greek for "voice-leader"</note> or the "Leader" <note>Latin: *dux*; Italian: *la guida*</note>, also known as the "antecedent" voice; the other is the "consequent." Generally speaking, a fugue is of two types: total and partial. A "total" fugue is when two or more voices, starting from the same theme, continue from the beginning to the end of the harmony according to some specific rule; some call this a "bound fugue" <note>original: *fuga ligata*</note>, or commonly a "returned fugue." This is again of two types: set either upon the same pitch or different pitches. If it is set upon the same pitch or the same key, it is called a "fugue in unison." If it is set upon different pitches, it takes its name from the harmonic interval by which it is distant from the first voice. For if the second voice begins a fourth above, it is called a fugue in the *hyperdiatessaron*; if below, a fugue in the *hypodiatesseron*. <note>Kircher uses these Greek-derived terms to specify the interval: *hyper* (above) or *hypo* (below) combined with *diatessaron* (a fourth), *diapente* (a fifth), or *diapason* (an octave).</note> Likewise, if the second voice starts a fifth above or below, it will be called a fugue in the *hyperdiapente* or *hypodiapente*; the same is said for a fugue in the *hyperdiapason* and *hypodiapason*. These kinds of fugues are most often called "canons" because of the regular path by which the voices follow one another; we call them *peridromas* <note>meaning "running around"</note> or "periodic symphonies" because they go in a circle. There is no other difference between a total fugue and a canon except that a fugue usually distinguishes its voices from one another, whereas here, several voices are drawn from one and the same written line through appropriate signs for the beginning and end of each voice, as will be shown later in great detail. These canons are again diverse: some proceed in straight order, others in retrograde order (which they call <term>cancrizantes</term> <note>literally "crab-walking," where the melody is played backwards</note>). Some are straight, others inverted.

<margin>Various subdivisions of fugues.</margin>
A "partial" fugue, or a "free and loose" fugue, is one where the follower says the same notes as the leader, not from the beginning to the end, but only for a certain distance. These are again manifold: simple and double. Simple ones are repeated only once; double ones are repeated frequently. Again, they are regular and irregular. Regular fugues are when they are arranged on the same pitch; irregular when on different pitches. They are called "authentic" when they ascend and "plagal" when they descend. They are called "imitating" when they are replicated in different places; they are "imitated" when they are made upon the notes and harmonic progression of some *cantus firmus* <note>a "fixed song" or pre-existing melody, usually from plainchant</note>, which is then repeated—such as the books of Antiphons, Introits, and Hymns composed by various authors. For example, when one wishes to arrange a fugue over the *Salve Regina*. There are furthermore "inverted" fugues, namely when one voice ascends by the same intervals by which the other descends. However, we place this entire classification before your eyes in the following single, simple example.

### §. III.
### On partial imitating fugues.

**F**ugues that are "partial" or "imitating" are those which are constructed over the notes of some plainchant <note>traditional church chant</note>, or <margin>Rules for the composition of fugues.</margin> over another indifferent subject <note>a basic melodic theme</note>; a countless multitude of these occurs everywhere and in all places. The rules of this Counterpoint are as follows: First, the fugue must be established either upon the same pitch <note>original: *chordam*, literally 'string'</note>, or upon different ones. If it is on the same pitch, the fugue is said to be "in unison"; you may then arrange this either by <term>conjunct steps<note>melodic motion where notes move to their immediate neighbors in the scale, rather than leaping</note></term> or by separate intervals. Furthermore, these can be placed either below or above the subject, but let us assign the rules for composing them.

**Rule for a partial fugue in unison, above and below the subject.**

I. Two <term>consonances<note>intervals that sound stable and pleasant to the ear</note></term> are not made by conjunct steps, such as a 5th and a 6th.
II. The first note must always be a perfect consonance <note>such as a unison, fifth, or octave</note>; or at the very least, a major imperfect consonance <note>such as a major third or sixth</note>. The second note, however, can be a 2nd, 3rd, 5th, or 8th; it will be all the better the less frequently it strikes the same pitch.

III. The first note of the **following voice** <note>original: *vocis consequentis*; the voice that mimics the theme</note> must be led so that it responds to the **leading voice** <note>original: *antecedenti*</note> in the measurement of the upbeat <term>arsis<note>the upward stroke in a musical beat, often signifying the "weak" part of the measure</note></term>, or the lifting of the beat; that is, it must begin after a rest of a <term>minim<note>a half-note, which in Kircher’s time was often the standard unit for a half-beat</note></term>, which is 1/2 of a "time" <note>original: *temporis*; a full musical measure or tactus</note>, or a whole beat.

IV. The second following voice must correspond to the first following voice, just as the first followed its leader: namely, after a rest of a whole beat. Finally, the third following voice must correspond to the second, just as the second did to the first, and that one to the leader—starting, of course, after a full-and-a-half measure of time. And so, if there were countless voices, each would anticipate the next by a half-measure of time. It is enough to have composed only one voice over the subject, which the remaining voices then repeat after the aforementioned rests.

This counterpoint can first be sung both without a subject and with a subject. In this context, we call it a **subject** when an inferior <note>lower</note> or superior <note>higher</note> voice rests upon a single key—as seen here in C below and in G above—while the remaining voices follow each other in exactly identical progression after a proportional measure of time. ### Section IV.
### On unison fugues with a subject moving diatonically <note>original Greek: *diatonos*; moving by steps</note> upward and downward.

We call these **diatonic fugues** when the subject upon which they are established proceeds by whole tones and steps, as is evident in the following pedagogical example. This kind of fugue can be considered in two ways according to the movement of the subject: it either moves by **diatonic descent** or by **diatonic ascent**. When it ascends, we call it **ascending** <note>original: *anophatum*</note>; when it descends, we call it **descending** <note>original: *catophaton*</note>. (We accept the term "diatonic" here not precisely in the way we defined the "diatonic genus" earlier, but insofar as the subject proceeds from tone to tone). Furthermore, the diatonic fugue itself can be established in four ways: namely, in unison, in the fourth, in the fifth, or in the octave.

#### Rules for establishing a diatonic fugue in unison.
In this class of fugues, the subject either ascends or descends **diatonically** <note>original: *diatonos*</note>. In both cases, the first of the remaining voices must be established as the **leader** <note>original: *dux*</note> by using the third, sixth, and fifth. That is, for every note of the subject, there must be a corresponding note in the first leading voice at the third above. Thus, if the notes of subject **A** are **semibreves** <term>semibreve<note>the equivalent of a modern whole note</note></term>, the first note in the leading voice **B** must be a **minim** <term>minim<note>a half note</note></term> at the third above. It begins at the **downbeat** <term>thesis<note>the start or "fall" of a musical measure</note></term> of the measure, while the first of the other voices begins at the **upbeat** <term>arsin<note>the "lift" or weak part of the beat</note></term> at the sixth above, and so on, as the numbers indicate. The second voice **C**, which follows the leader immediately, should be preceded by a **semiminim rest** <term>semiminim<note>a quarter note</note></term>. The third voice **D** should be preceded by a **minim rest**; thereafter, they proceed in exactly the same tenor as the first voice **B**, which is the leader or **conductor of voices** <note>original Greek: *phonagogos*</note>.
