You see from this example, if I am not mistaken, clearer than the midday sun, how a fugue in unison—whose subject moves diatonically <note>original Greek: *diatonōs*; by steps</note> whether ascending or descending—is to be constructed using 3rds and 5ths. For if you begin the notes of the *phonagogus* <term>phonagogus<note>From Greek, literally "voice-leader"; Kircher’s term for the melodic line that guides the counterpoint</note></term> above the individual notes of the base (or subject) starting at the 3rd on the **thesis** <note>the downbeat or stressed part of the measure</note> so that the second part of the measure falls on the **arsis** <note>the upbeat or unstressed part of the measure</note> at the 5th, you will have completed the composition of the leading voice, as you see. 

If you then transcribe this voice twice more and place the appropriate rests before each—namely, a [semiminim rest] and [minim rest] part of the measure (or what is the same, a semiminim rest for the first following voice and a minim rest for the second following voice)—you will have completed a fugue in unison. This is achieved by means of 3rds and 6ths when the subject moves diatonically <note>original: *diatonōs*</note> upward, and by means of 3rds and 5ths when the subject moves diatonically downward; which is what was to be done. If you again compose a leading voice over an ascending subject using 8ths and 6ths, and over a descending subject using 8ths and 5ths, you will have another fugue. I could bring forward many other combinations here, but I remain silent on them for the sake of brevity.

<margin>What is a fugue in unison?</margin> Note in this place that by "fugue in unison" we do not mean the subject, but the leading voice and the remaining following voices. These proceed in unison—that is, upon the same string or key—and if the rests were removed, they would all sound the same, for they would be mere octaves, as the expanded example sufficiently declares. However, when we say a fugue in unison is perfected by means of 3rds and 6ths or 3rds and 5ths, this must be understood as referring to the relationship between the subject and the leading voice, for these are composed from the said intervals as the example teaches. 

Furthermore, we call it an **expanded example** when all the voices are divided and written out separately. We call it **contracted** when two, three, or four voices are contained within a single voice by way of a **canon** <term>canon<note>A rule-based composition where one melody is performed by multiple voices starting at different times</note></term>, the starting points of which are demonstrated by certain signs, as will be seen later. I wished to explain all these things at length here before I proceed further, so that nothing might delay the reader in what follows.

## Composition Lesson II. On the rules for establishing a fugue at the fourth.

**R**ule I. This fugue is so named because the first following voice <note>original: *consequens*</note> rises a fourth above the leader <note>original: *antecedentem*</note>; the rules of which follow. You will have the first <term>voice-leader<note>original: *phonagoga*; the primary melodic line that guides the counterpoint</note></term> or antecedent, if you begin on the first part of the measure's time by moving from the 5th to the 3rd above the first note of the ascending subject **B**. However, ensure the second part of the measure ends on the 3rd. Then, on the second note of the subject, the first part of the measure at the **thesis** <note>the downbeat</note> should begin on the 3rd, and the other part at the **arsis** <note>the upbeat</note> should end in unison: as the first example teaches. <margin>What a fugue at the fourth above is.</margin>

Rule II. If, however, the voice of the subject descends, two minims in the leading voice **D** will correspond to each semibreve in the subject. The first of these will begin on the 5th and the second will end on the 6th, and you shall proceed thus with the rest. <margin>Fugue at the fourth above with a descending subject.</margin> Furthermore, if you repeat this leading voice a fourth higher, you will have a three-voiced fugue <note>original: *Triphonam*</note>. This fugue at the fourth above <note>original: *hyperdiatessaron*</note> can still be established in two other ways: namely, if the two minims of the leading voice are on the 5th and 8th during the subject's ascent, and in the subject's descent those same minims are placed on the 3rd and the unison above. Finally, if you repeat the following voice a fourth above, you will have what you seek.

## Composition Lesson IV. On the partial fugue at the octave above.

The beginning of the 2nd voice.

A **fugue at the octave above** <note>original: *Fuga hyperdiapason*</note> is so called because the following voice transcends the leader by an octave; it is completed with the help of the following rules.

**Rule I.** If the subject **H** ascends, a leap shall be made in the leading voice **I** from the 3rd to the 6th. This is done so that the first part of the measure begins at the 3rd above the first note of the subject on the **downbeat**; the other half of the beat should end on the 6th note on the **upbeat**, or rather, finish on the 5th at the lifting of the hand. You shall continue these same intervals until the final note of the subject, over which you will then repeat the second following voice at the octave above the leader, preceded by a minim rest <note>original: *pausa minimæ*</note>, as the example shows.

**Rule II.** If, however, the voice of the subject descends, the first note **M** of the leading voice or **voice-leader** shall begin at the sixth above the first note of the subject, and you will complete the measure of time by moving through the third to the fourth. This progress will then be continued until the final note. If you then repeat the following voice over the leader one octave higher after a **short rest** <note>original: *suspirio*; literally a "sigh," referring to a minim or crotchet rest</note>, you will have the sought-after fugue at the octave <note>original: *fugam hypodiapason*—though the context suggests an octave relationship, *hypo* usually means "below"; Kircher may be referring to the relative position</note>, the example of which follows.

->### Musical Composition V. On the fugue in which the voice-leader is placed below the subject. <note>original: *Melothesia V. De fuga, in qua vox phonagoga infra subiectum constituitur*</note><-

In the preceding sections, we have shown by what method fugues are to be established in unison with the subject placed below the voice-leader <note>original: *phonagogam*</note>; now let us reveal how the same are to be established with the subject placed above the voice-leader.

**Rule I.** If subject **A** in the highest voice ascends, you will place the voice-leader **B** (also called the leading voice <note>original: *ductricem vocem*</note>) below the subject in this manner. The leading voice **B** should descend stepwise from the 3rd to the 5th, and then to the octave, and from there to the 4th; for here there are 4 numbers: the 3rd and 5th correspond to the first note of the subject; the octave and 4th correspond to the second note of the subject, as is clear in the example. Furthermore, if you then repeat this voice, continued by these intervals, in the two following voices **C** and **D**—with a quarter-note rest <note>original: *pausa semiminimæ*</note> preceding in **D** (the first following voice) and a half-note rest <note>original: *pausa minimæ*</note> in the second following voice **G**—you will have the sought-after fugue.

**Rule II.** If, however, the highest voice descends, as is shown in **V**, the voice-leader **X** below will begin at the octave, from which it will run stepwise to the sixth, and from there to the 3rd and 5th; however, in such a way that the first two numbers respond to the first note of the subject, and the later numbers respond to the second note of the subject. You shall maintain this method of proceeding until the very last note. You will have the completed following voices if you repeat the said voice-leader below in unison, with a quarter-note rest preceding the first following voice and a half-note rest preceding the second following voice. Indeed, the examples will teach all these things most clearly.

**Rule II.** You shall compose a **fugue at the fifth below** <term>hypodiapente; from the Greek 'hypo' (under) and 'diapente' (fifth)</term> in three ways. Note, however, in this place that the following voice <note>the "comes" or following voice</note> must be repeated below the voice-leader at the interval of a fifth; for it is from this that a fugue of this kind is called a "hypodiapente." The same must be said regarding the preceding fugue. But examples will show all these things more clearly than the sun.

§ V.
**On fugues whose subject ascends not stepwise, but by leaps.**

The third kind of partial fugues is that in which the subject does not move by tones <note>stepwise</note>, as in the previous section, but ascends or descends by **leaps** <term>saltus; melodic intervals larger than a second</term>. Moreover, leaps of this kind can be by a 3rd, a 4th, a 5th, or an 8th; we shall treat each of these in order.

**Pattern I. A fugue at the unison in which the subject ascends or descends by a 3rd.**

If the ascending subject moves up by a third, you can create the voice-leader in the first mode if, from the 3rd, the leading voice is conducted through the unison and through 4 **quarter notes** <note>original: *semiminimas*</note> or **eighth notes** <note>original: *fusas*</note> mixed, until it runs to the 5th below the subject, and then ascends to the 4th above. And indeed, the first two numbers correspond to the first **whole note** <note>original: *semibreui*</note> of the subject; the latter two numbers truly correspond to the second note of the subject, as the example clearly teaches. The following voices, however, will be repeated: the first indeed after a quarter-note rest, the second following after a half-note rest.

If, however, the subject descends by a third, you will allow the voice-leader to run from the 5th below through the 3rd, and another 3rd again into the 5th, so that the first two numbers always correspond to the first note, and the following two to the second note of the subject; the remaining following voices are truly repetitions of the first, with rests placed before them as previously, as the example clearly teaches.

### Example II. Of a fugue in unison, whose subject is **disjunct** <term>hyperbaton; a Greek term used here to describe melodic motion that leaps rather than moves by step</term>, and proceeds from third to third.

The progression of the highest voice **descends** by a third, and the **voice-leader** positioned below will proceed, first from the 12th to the 8th below the subject, and then from the 3rd to the 5th. This is done so that the first two numbers correspond to the first note of the subject, and the two later numbers respond to the second note in the subject. This voice-leader should then be repeated below in unison after two preceding rests—a quarter-rest and a half-rest—and you will have what you seek, as the example teaches.

The remainder of the measure will begin from the 6th and end on the 4th.

### Another example of a three-voice fugue at the upper fourth <term>hyperdiatessaron; the interval of a musical fourth above the starting note</term>.

### CHAPTER XIX.
### On Harmonic Canons, or
### On Periodical Symphonies.

All those harmonies are called **Canons** which, being enclosed in a single voice, yield different voices through diverse starting points and many-voiced <note>original: *polyphona*</note> proportions. They are called **Canons**, which is to say "rules," because they must be followed with the utmost rigor as prescribed. They are of two kinds: first, loose and free; second, restricted and bound <note>original: *obligati*</note>. Those of the first kind are again twofold: either with absolute freedom or conditional freedom. The first type applies to all those [compositions] handed down so far, except that these are sung as if enclosed under one voice-part. Bound Canons are also of various types. We must deal briefly with each.

### §. I.

384 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

### § I.
### On Canons in Unison.

<margin>A singular secret.</margin>
I will reveal in this place a musical secret known to few, if any; by which anyone can compose a canon of any number of voices with admirable ease. We begin first with the canon in unison, for as this is the easiest of all to create, it is appropriate that it holds the first place. It is established according to its harmonic periods. In this context:

<margin>What a harmonic period is.</margin>
A harmonic period is nothing other than one member of a Canon, or that phrase <note>original Latin: *clausula*</note> which exists between the end of the first voice’s entry and the beginning of the second; in like manner, the second harmonic period is called that phrase which lies between the end of the second voice and the beginning of the third. And so on for the others. To explain myself briefly: if someone composes a phrase <margin>A short and easy method of composing Canons.</margin> for three voices, and then extends those periods into a single long melody or voice, he will have completed a Canon of three voices in unison. Similarly, if someone composes a phrase of four voices and extends those phrases into one long voice, he will have a Canon of four voices. Thus, a composition of five phrases extended lengthwise will produce a canon of five voices; six phrases will produce six voices, and so on to infinity. Let there be an example:

**Paradigm I of an expanded Canon.** | **Paradigm II expanded.** | **Paradigm III expanded.**
--- | --- | ---
3rd Voice phrase [Musical notation] | II. [Musical notation] | III. [Musical notation]
2nd Voice phrase [Musical notation] | [Musical notation] | [Musical notation]
1st Voice phrase [Musical notation] | [Musical notation] | [Musical notation]
1st Voice phrase.

Here we have given three paradigms. In each one, you see a composition of three voices; these three voices are nothing other than three phrases which, when placed in a straight line or extended lengthwise, will produce three canons. In these, one voice follows the other by the same duration of time that the phrase itself lasts. We present the three individual canons here in expanded form, and below in contracted form <note>In an "expanded" canon, all voices are written out; in a "contracted" canon, only the main melody is written with marks indicating where subsequent voices should enter.</note>, as is evident.

->Contraction of the first expanded Canon into one voice for three parts <note>original Latin: *tryphoniam*, a term derived from Greek meaning "three-voiced"</note> after 8 beats <note>original: *tempora*</note>.<-
[Musical notation]
Ca.

<summary>Kircher reveals a "musical secret" for easily composing canons in unison by dividing a multi-voice phrase into sequential periods and then lining them up into a single continuous melody. He demonstrates how a three-part harmony can be "unrolled" into a single-voice canon where each new voice enters after the duration of one phrase.</summary>

We have presented here three divided Canons along with the periods <note>In this context, a "period" refers to a specific segment or phrase of the melody</note> of each. The first has two periods and is consequently "dyphonic," that is, for two voices. The second, consisting of three periods, is "triphonic," that is, for three voices. The third consists of four periods and is "tetraphonic," that is, for four voices. Moreover, the first following voice begins once the first voice has finished its period; the second begins once two periods are finished; the third once four are finished. And so, finally, when all periods are finished, a *peridromus* <note>original: *peridromus*, a Greek-derived term meaning a "running around" or circular recurrence</note> occurs—that is, a return to the first period—and thus the continuation of the Canon becomes perpetual in a circle.

*Obligated Canon, whether strict, or unison in unison.*

Let the voice-leader <note>original: *phonagogus*</note> begin to ascend step by step, whom the rest follow from the same clef after a whole rest. One must, however, diligently observe that nowhere do two fifths or octaves, or dissonances occur, which must be avoided. If the first period is so arranged on the writing-tablet <note>original: *palimpsesto*, likely referring to a reusable slate used by composers for drafting</note> that the remaining periods or circular returns are placed directly beneath it, then every error will be easily avoided, as was explained in the preceding examples.

### On Syncopated Fugues.

Syncopated fugues <term>Fugæ Syncopatæ; a style of imitation where the rhythm is shifted against the beat, creating a "syncopated" or driving effect</term> are so named because the leading voice <term>phonagogus; the "leader" or first voice in a fugue or canon</term> proceeds through continuous syncopations in the second, fourth, or fifth interval, while the subject <note>the main melodic theme</note> ascends either by steps or by leaps...

<summary>This page demonstrates a specific canon at the lower fifth composed by Emilio Rossi based on the Lament of David, and begins defining the rules for syncopated fugues.</summary>
<keywords>Hypodiapente, Emilio Rossi, Loreto, Absalom, canon resolution, syncopation, phonagogus, counterpoint</keywords>

--- Page 428 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of syncopated fugues from the bottom of page 389, detailing specific rules for their construction based on the melodic intervals of the subject.</meta>

390 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

... proceeds. This is fourfold; for first, either the subject proceeds by steps, or by thirds, or by fourths, or by fifths. These are the rules for each.

**Rule I.** Whenever the subject rises by seconds <note>i.e., by step-wise motion</note>, then the fugue conveniently follows at the fifth <term>diapente; the musical interval of a fifth</term> either above or below the subject, provided, however, that the following voice <term>consequens; the second voice in a fugue that "follows" the first</term> also proceeds through syncopated steps. For example, if the subject rises in semibreves <note>equivalent to modern whole notes</note>, the first note of the following voice at the fifth above will begin as a minim <note>a half note</note>; then, all notes until the last will be semibreves, while the final note will be a minim like the first. It will thus have a syncopated fugue at the fifth above or below as you please. Therefore, nothing is easier than to create syncopated fugues by neighboring steps <term>gradus coniunctos; melodic movement where notes are right next to each other on the scale</term>. If you set the first and second [half] of the following voice as half the value of the first note of the subject, and the remaining middle notes at the same value as the subject's notes, you will have the desired result. Likewise, if the notes of the subject are minims, the first and last notes of the following voice should be semiminims <note>quarter notes</note>, and the middle ones minims. Alternatively, rests <note>original: *pausæ*</note> can be used in place of those notes.

### Examples of Diatonic Syncopated Fugues.

->**Syncopated voice at the 5th below.**<-

**Rule II.** Whenever the subject rises by thirds, the fugue is made at the fifth above or below, using this method: the start of the following voice begins after a rest equal to half the value of the first note of the subject; the remaining middle notes are continued with syncopation until the last, which ends with a rest equal to the first. This applies when the following voice is above the subject. However, when the following voice is below the subject, the opposite path is taken: for the beginning of the follower starts not with a rest, but with a note half the value of the first note of the subject, and similarly ends with a rest half the value of the last note of the subject. Then, in descending, it begins from a similar rest and ends in a note of equal value. But an example will clarify the matter better.

**Rule III.** Whenever the subject rises by a fourth <term>diatessaron; the interval of a fourth</term>, the following voice <term>consequens; the second voice in a fugue</term> will be set either a fifth or an octave above or below the subject. If you choose the former—that is, a fifth above—the beginning of the following voice will be made with a note of half the value <term>subdupla; half the rhythmic duration</term> of the first note of the subject, and it will end with a rest equal to that half-value. The opposite is done if you wish the following voice to proceed below the subject. If you choose the latter—that is, if you wish to raise the following voice an octave above the subject—the start of the following voice will begin with a rest half the value of the first note of the subject, and it will end with a note equal to that half-value rest. The opposite is done if the composition is established an octave below the subject.

**Rule IV.** Whenever the subject <term>subiectum; the primary melody or "leader" in a fugue</term> ascends by fifths <term>diapente; the musical interval of a fifth</term>, the fugue shall be made in a similar manner at the fifth or the octave, above or below. This occurs if it begins with a rest of half the value <term>subdupla; a rhythmic duration half that of the preceding note</term> of the first note of the subject, and ends on a note equal to that half-value. If the following voice is placed a fifth below, you shall establish the opposite arrangement: that is, it will begin with a half-value note and end its ascent on a rest of equal half-value; then it will begin again on a rest and end on a note. If, however, you place the following voice an octave above, a rest will precede it and it will end on a note of equal value. If it is placed an octave below, the following voice will begin with a note and the song will end with a rest.

### CHAPTER XIX.

### On free and imitative fugues.

**Free or imitative fugues** are those called such because they are not held by such rigorous laws as the "bound" fugue and canons (which we will discuss in the following sections); rather, they wander here and there at will, following one another now at the beginning, now in the middle, and sometimes at the end. And these are the most common of all, found in the works of every Author. They can be established in various ways and in any number of voices, though the artistry shines most clearly in four-voice compositions <note>original: "tetraphoniis," referring to four-part harmony.</note>. In these, sometimes two and sometimes all the voices follow the paths of the leaders <note>original: "phonagogæ," a term Kircher uses for the leading voices that "guide the sound."</note>. These kinds of fugues are made through various intervals: some through steps close together <note>original: "gradus coniunctos," or conjunct motion where notes move up or down the scale one step at a time.</note>. Some move by the interval of a third, some by a fourth, and many by the fifth and eighth; to give examples of all of these would be a work of infinite labor. Therefore, leaving those aside, it seemed best to provide only the rules in this place.

#### Rule for a multi-voiced, free, and loose fugue through conjunct steps.

**First, this kind of fugue** can be established for any number of voices; I remember having occasionally composed them for 12 voices <margin>How a 12-voice fugue is made</margin> in this manner: let the voices of the first choir follow one another from one and the same key in unison, or at the octave; this will be done easily if the progression of the voices happens tone-by-tone into the fifth. For with the song preceding in quarter notes <note>original: "semiminimas."</note>, let the second voice follow from the same key after a half-note rest <note>original: "pauſam minimæ."</note>, and the third after a whole-note rest <note>original: "pauſam ſemibreuis."</note>, and the fourth after a rest of a whole-note and a half-note combined. If indeed the first voice of the second choir, starting from the key where the bass of the first choir ended, moves into another fifth, and the rest of the voices follow with the same timing, we will then have a fugue of 8 voices. If finally the first voice of the third choir, starting from the key where the bass of the second choir rests, begins to run into the fifth, and the remaining voices follow in the stated order of rests, a fugue of 12 voices will be had, into which you can afterwards insert beautiful cadences <note>original: "clausulas."</note> and harmonic formulas.

*Rule for the free diatonic fugue.*

If the first note of the first voice, arranged at the interval of a tone, is a breve, and the second is a semibreve, while the remaining notes follow at will, the second voice shall proceed with the same note value and progression after a rest of three beats. The third voice will indeed follow with the same progression and value of notes after a rest of eight beats; finally, the fourth voice will follow with the same tenor and value of notes after a rest of eleven beats, as the following example teaches. And this method is most highly praised in Church Music, and is characteristic of Palestrina and Morales, and other authors of the higher rank.
<note>Palestrina (original: "Prenestini") refers to Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, the most famous composer of the Roman School. "Moralis" refers to Cristóbal de Morales, a leading Spanish composer of the Renaissance.</note>

## The free and loose fugue: dimorphic or two-formed.

There is also another type of free four-voice <term>fugue</term><note>In this period, "fugue" refers generally to imitative counterpoint where one voice "flees" and another "follows," rather than the strict formal structure known in later Baroque music.</note>, in which two voices follow each other with one progression and at certain intervals, while the remaining two follow each other with a different progression and at other intervals. This fugue is, moreover, very easy, and it is nothing other than a certain repetition of the first two voices; its rules are these:

### 396 *Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

## *Free and loose fugue in the madrigal style, from the second into the third.*

There is also another type of <term>fugue</term><note>In this context, a fugue refers to imitative counterpoint where voices enter one after another with the same melody.</note> that falls from the second into the third; it is graceful and full of harmony, and is frequently used by the most learned <term>Palestrina</term><note>Kircher refers to Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (c. 1525–1594), the most famous composer of the Roman School of Renaissance polyphony, whom Kircher held up as the gold standard of sacred music.</note>. In this style, the second voice follows the first at the interval of a fifth above after one <term>measure</term><note>Latin: *tempus*. In the musical theory of this time, a *tempus* was a primary unit of rhythmic measurement.</note>. The third voice maintains the progression of the first after a rest of three and a half measures; the fourth voice follows this after a rest of four and a half measures, maintaining the progression of the second. ### A paradigm of fugal <term>Melothesia</term><note>From the Greek *melothesia*, meaning the art of melody-making or musical composition.</note>, established according to every rigor of the rules.

In regards to these compositions—where fourths, seconds, and sevenths may be found wandering here and there without <term>resolution</term><note>The movement of a dissonant note to a consonant one, which "resolves" the tension.</note> or <term>ligature</term><note>Also known as a suspension; a technique where a note is held over from a consonant chord into a chord where it becomes dissonant, before resolving downward.</note>—I would not wish an unskilled musician to pass judgment. Let him first consult reason, and thereafter he should also consult the ears.

## On retrograde canons, also known as "crab-like" canons, or similarly, those proceeding in forward and backward order.

Composers not infrequently create certain Canons which they call <term>cancrizantes</term><note>original: "cancrizantes," meaning "crab-like." Just as a crab is thought to walk backward or sideways, these musical pieces are designed to be played from the beginning to the end and from the end to the beginning simultaneously.</note> from the backward movement of the crab; for the first voice begins the melody in the forward order, while the second begins from the end in backward order. Since this matter produces no small wonder in the unskilled, I will briefly show by what method and ingenuity they are to be established; for the feat is not as great as the common people think, nor so difficult that it cannot be fashioned with the same ease as the previous ones. Therefore, observe these rules in constructing them.

### Rule I.
<margin>What are retrograde canons, and how are they constructed?</margin> If someone first wishes to compose such a piece for two voices: He will satisfy his desire if he composes a <term>diatritos</term> counterpoint <note>original: "diatritos." This refers to a specific rhythmic or harmonic ratio (3:4) discussed in earlier chapters.</note> (which we have treated extensively in Chapter 1, Section 2) according to the rules delivered there. For this will be sung in forward and backward order. The same can be done in several of the other twelve types of counterpoint delivered in that same place.

### Rule II.
Let there be, for example, a Canon of eight measures; first you compose half the part of the canon, then you compose the other part below the first part, so that the notes of the second voice are properly adapted to the preceding voice. Once this is done, if you connect this second part to the first in such a way that the first notes are the last, and the last note is the first—coinciding with the previous last note in <term>unison</term><note>Where two voices sing the exact same pitch at the same time.</note>—you will have a perfect crab-like canon. An example follows.

Eee Ca- <note>Catchword for the next page, likely beginning the word "Canon."</note>

## CHAPTER XIX.
## On the more secret method of Canons.

In order for you to look more closely at the inexhaustible riches of Music, we will provide certain examples in this place in which the musical business of combination will seem to achieve a certain incomprehensible infinity. Unless these could be demonstrated from the hidden science of numbers, I would think that no one could truly be induced to believe it. Yet they are certain and devoid of all falsehood. Of this kind is the Canon which the distinguished musician Pier Francesco Valentini <note>Pier Francesco Valentini (c. 1570–1654) was a Roman composer famous for his complex "puzzle canons" that could be realized in thousands of different ways.</note>, a Roman, proposed to us in an entire work; and it is the following:

### The Multiform Canon.
<note>original: "Canon Polymorphus."</note>
[Musical notation on one staff]

And this is that wonderful Canon, variable in a thousand, nay, infinite ways. It contains ten <term>tempora</term> <note>original: "tempora," referring here to musical measures or primary beats.</note>, one rest, and seventeen notes. This can first be sung in more than two thousand ways—not only in two, three, or four voices, but also in five voices in more than two thousand ways, and in six voices more than three thousand times. Nay, by combining each part with the others, it deservedly extends itself into an infinite variety. We would gladly expand upon all of these here at length, did not the sheer mass of the combinations prevent it.

For so great is the multitude and variety of this combination that ten entire volumes could be adorned from its innumerable variety alone. But here we will show at least some ray of this combination, so that from it we may understand the rest. Therefore, if you sing the aforementioned subject—the first and principal voice of the Canon placed just above—in retrograde order, the second voice will be born, which you might deservedly call the second subject, as follows.

### The second voice of the subject is the retrograde of the first.
<note>original: "Subiecti secunda vox retrograda primi." Retrograde means the melody is played backward from end to beginning.</note>

[Musical notation on a five-line staff]

Furthermore, if you make the first subject proceed again with contrary motions, a third subject or third voice will be born, as follows.
<note>By "contrary motions," Kircher refers to melodic inversion, where an upward interval becomes a downward one of the same size.</note>

### Third subject, or the third voice, the inverse of the first, or proceeding with motions contrary to the first.

[Musical notation on a five-line staff]

If finally you sing this third voice in retrograde order, a fourth voice or fourth subject will result, as follows.

### The fourth voice, retrograde to the third.

[Musical notation on a five-line staff]

You see, therefore, how from a single subject, four others are born, each of which is again capable of infinite combination. 

First, these four voices are resolved simply—that is, each is capable of being a <term>fugue<gloss>A musical technique where a theme is introduced by one voice and then imitated by others.</gloss></term> with itself; then, they can be made into fugues with one another. <margin>The power of combination in this canon is infinite.</margin>

Second, this Canon can be varied almost infinitely by the power of replication or transposition, which each voice admits either above or below according to whatever <term>consonances<gloss>Intervals or chords that sound stable and harmonious.</gloss></term> are made, in exactly the same manner we showed in the preceding sections regarding the combination of Counterpoint.

Third, this Canon can be varied almost infinitely when some voices sing using <term>semiminims<gloss>Equivalent to modern quarter notes.</gloss></term>; others through notes of smaller value, that is, <term>minims<gloss>Half notes.</gloss></term> and semiminims under the same <term>minor imperfect time<gloss>A rhythmic meter, similar to modern 2/4 or cut time.</gloss></term>; or while under the same time certain voices sing <term>semibreves<gloss>Whole notes.</gloss></term> to semibreves, with others singing through minims and semiminims, and semiminims to the <term>breve<gloss>A double whole note.</gloss></term>.

Fourth, by reason of pauses; for this Canon admits pauses in every place, just as it admits a beginning, middle, or end of any other voice in every place.

But time would fail me if I wished to reveal all the mysteries of this Canon; therefore it is enough in this place to have suggested the artistry in summary to wise and skillful Musicians. For those who resolve this Canon—just as the aforementioned Pier Francesco Valentini ingeniously resolved it in two thousand ways—will see that what we have said is true.

## On the Musical Labyrinth.

Thus, 96 voices with 24...

408         *Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

Having examined this "Knot" <note>original: "Nodum"; a term for a complex musical puzzle or canon</note> more deeply, I have finally discovered that this same canon can be sung not only by 96 voices, but by a total of 512 voices, or what is the same thing, distributed into 128 choirs. Thus, just as in the previous version there emerged 24 Sopranos and as many Altos, Tenors, and Basses; so here there emerge 128 Sopranos, 128 Altos, 128 Tenors, and 128 Basses.

[Musical notation for four voices: Soprano, Alto, Tenor, Bass]

For these four long notes of 16 beats can be sung by the highest voices, or 128 sopranos <note>original: "discantibus"</note>, always repeated on the same string <note>meaning the same pitch or melodic line</note>; and the four long notes corresponding to the Alto are likewise singable by 128 Altos.
  First: The four long notes corresponding to the Tenor will be singable by 128 Tenors, and finally the four lowest long notes corresponding to the Bass voice will be singable by 128 Basses; which, multiplied by 4, constitute 512 voices. Furthermore, the said Canon shall be sung by this rule: that 16 choirs, following a sequence of 16 beats or whole rests in the manner of a fugue, sing the four long notes.
  Second: It shall be sung by the rule that 16 Choirs sing the 4 long notes through syncopation, so that one always begins after another at the middle of a whole beat, or at the half-stroke <note>original: "medio tactu"; referring to the conductor's beat</note>.
  Third: 16 other Choirs shall sing the 4 long notes syncopated in such a way that one always follows another by a quarter part of a beat on the downbeat <note>original: "ad thesin"</note>.

  *Fourth:* 16 Choirs shall sing the 4 long notes syncopated, so that one choir always follows the other by a half-rest with one "sigh" <note>a "suspirio" is a musical term for a crotchet or quarter-note rest</note> on the upbeat <note>original: "ad arsin"</note>.
  *Fifth:* 16 other choirs shall sing the 4 long notes in this manner: that one always follows the other in order by an eighth part of a beat on the downbeat.
  *Sixth:* 16 Choirs shall sing the 4 long notes syncopated in this order: that one always follows the other in order by a half-beat with one eighth-part on the upbeat.
  *Seventh:* 16 Choirs shall sing the 4 long notes syncopated, so that one always follows the other by one "sigh" and with a fourth part of the same on the downbeat.
  *Eighth:* 16 Choirs shall sing the 4 long notes syncopated in this manner: that one always follows the other after the middle of a beat, and simultaneously with a "sigh" and a half of the same on the upbeat.
  You see, therefore, how through a certain admirable power of combination, 8 different systems of Choirs—each of which is again divided into 16 other choirs—when multiplied by 8, produce 128 four-voice choirs; these, multiplied again by 4, produce 512 voices. But so that you may perceive the power of combination more clearly, we have decided to place the entire operation here before your eyes.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical demonstration of polyphonic expansion from page 413, where Kircher calculates the exponential growth of voices and choirs possible within his combinatorial system.</meta>

414               **Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance**

But if one looks into these statements with a somewhat more discerning eye, he will see that this canon can be arranged in such a way that there is neither a fixed number nor a limit to its polyphony. For if someone were to take the previously mentioned four long notes and make them into <term>maximas</term> <note>The longest note value in medieval and Renaissance music, typically equal to eight whole notes or "beats."</note> of 8 beats, to which all the remaining voices would respond in proportional order, the said canon would be sung by 1,024 voices. Just as the notes are doubled, so too the duration of the time-beats would be twice as long as the duration of the previously mentioned canon. Each of the 14 long notes of the four-part sets <note>original: "tetraphoniorum"</note> would be sung by 256 choirs, which, when multiplied by 4, produce the said 1,024 voices.

And so, by multiplying the value of the long notes, you can proceed into infinity. For example, if someone were to set 4 long notes to a value of 4,000 beats, and then arranged the canon by a proportional sequence of rests, he would immediately establish 32,000 choirs with which the canon could be sung; these, when multiplied by four, would produce 128,000 voices, and the canon would be singable by just as many voices. Likewise, 4 long notes multiplied to a measure of 8,000 beats will yield 64,000 choirs and 256,000 voices by which the canon will be sung. Finally, if you set 4 long notes to be 32,000 beats, or <term>tactus</term> <note>The steady pulse or beat of the music.</note>, you will have a canon singable by 1,024,000 voices. If, lastly, the 6 said long notes were 400,000 beats, there would arise from the said progression of notes 3,200,000 choirs; that is, 12,200,000 voices by which the canon is rendered singable. Thus, by increasing the value of the 4 said long notes to infinity, an infinite multitude of choirs and voices will also follow; from this, the greatest and most incomprehensible power of combination lying hidden beneath music may be made apparent.

*Corollary I.*

From these things it is clear that if a canon of 512 voices is sung in the space of a quarter of an hour, it will follow that a canon of 12,200,000 voices would not be completed in the space of 232 days, even if it were sung perpetually. And from this it is also gathered how great a canon of voices must be to last for a whole year, or even 10, 100, or 1,000 years! All of these can easily be deduced through the rules of proportions.

*Corollary II.*

From this it is clear that if all the people in the whole of Italy, or even Spain, or Germany, or France were musicians, they would by no means be sufficient to sing that last canon; but let these things suffice to demonstrate the wondrous power of musical combination.

*Corollary III.*

From this is clear that passage from the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, chapter 14: *And the voice which I heard was as of harpers harping on their harps, and they sang as it were a new song, etc. And no man could say the song, but those 144,000 who were purchased from the earth.* <note>original: "Et vocem quam audiui, sicuti Cytharædorum cytharizantium in cytharis suis, & cantabant quasi canticum nouum, &c. Et nemo poterat dicere canticum nisi illa 144000, qui empti sunt de Terra."</note> This is not only to be taken 

<margin>The one hundred and forty-four thousand singers of the Apocalypse.</margin>

allegorically, as it can and ought to be understood literally. For it is certain that if someone, a little while before, were to set those 4 long notes at 4,500 beats and then arrange the canon by a proportional sequence of rests, he would be about to establish 36,000 choirs, assigning 4 singers to each choir; these choirs, multiplied by 4, would produce 144,000 singers, such as the passage in the Apocalypse says sing a new song before the throne of the Lamb. May Divine Goodness grant that after the use of this corruptible life, we may deserve to rejoice in such admirable and unheard-of music in the blessedness of eternal life.

# PREFACE.

[Decorative initial O] All musical instruments are, for the most part, reduced to three categories. Those of the first category are called **stringed** <note>original Greek: ἔγχορδα (*enchorda*), or ἐντατὰ (*entata*), meaning "stretched"</note>, which consist of nerves or strings, and which are stirred into harmonic motions by plectrums <note>A small flat tool used to pluck strings, like a guitar pick.</note> or fingers. These include Lutes <note>original: *Testudines*, referring to the tortoise-shell shape of early lutes.</note>, Psalteries, Lyres, Sambucas, Pandoras, Barbitons, Nablums, Pectides, Harpsichords, and countless others of this kind. In the second category are **wind instruments** <note>original Greek: ἐμφυσώμενα (*emphysomena*), πνευμάτικα (*pneumatika*), or ἔμπνευστα (*empneusta*)</note>, which produce sound when inflated or stirred by the breath, such as Pipes, Flutes, Horns, Clarions, Trumpets, Buccinas <note>A curved brass instrument used by the Roman army.</note>, and Bugle-calls. In the third category are **percussion** <note>original Greek: κρουστὰ (*krousta*)</note>, such as Drums, Sistrums, Cymbals, and Bells. Each of these must be treated in order, so that the origin of sound in each may become more clearly known. Furthermore, just as the invention of strings was easily achieved, so too no one should doubt that it was most ancient and belonged to the earliest times; for since nothing is more common—indeed, more necessary—than the use of threads for various tasks, whether for binding or making things, it follows that any stretching of any kind of thread [creates sound]...

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Book VI, where Kircher introduces a tripartite classification of musical instruments into strings, winds, and percussion. He argues that stringed instruments are likely the oldest due to the ancient human necessity of using cords and threads.</summary>

416 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance.
...stirs a certain pleasing sound, and from the various tension of these same strings, various sounds are also born. As I said, nothing was easier for the **Masters of Music** <term>Musurgis: a term Kircher uses for those skilled in the making and theory of music</term>, having first been taught by this experience, than to eventually invent instruments of every kind. Regarding their antiquity, it is well established; for Sacred Scripture teaches us in Genesis 4 that the **many-stringed Cithara** <note>original: *Cytharam polycordam*</note> existed before the Flood. The Book of Kings and the Psalms also testify that David used the ten-stringed psaltery. But concerning the construction and properties of ancient musical instruments, see what we discussed in Book 2 of this work. Furthermore, although nothing is better known or more commonplace than the sound of strings, I would venture to say that nothing is more unknown than its cause and origin—so much so that, with few exceptions, it has hardly been correctly examined by anyone. This gave me a powerful incentive to apply myself with all possible diligence and no small expense to experiments with sound, until I finally arrived at the knowledge of such hidden causes. What I have achieved through this continuous study and practice, let the reader's fair judgment decide. Truly, in order to maintain a harmonic order in all things within our musical art, we have divided this book into four parts. In the first part, we will treat **String-wisdom** <term>Chordosophia: the theoretical science of string vibrations</term>; in the second, multi-stringed instruments; in the third, **wind instruments** <term>Pneumaticis</term>; and in the fourth, **percussion instruments** <term>pulsatilibus</term>.

->### PART ONE<-
->**String-wisdom**, or on the Nature, Property, and causes of sound produced by chords or strings.<-

This First Part will comprise three Chapters. The first two will contain matters that seemed to pertain to the theory of this doctrine; the third, however, will teach the practice itself regarding the art of **string-division** <term>chordotomicam: the mathematical measurement and cutting of strings to produce specific pitches</term>. Moreover, so that we may proceed with a more orderly method in this most orderly of sciences, we have placed several **Propositions** <term>Lemmata</term> after some Definitions and Axioms, so that what is to be said hereafter concerning the causes of sounds in strings may be better understood.

### Definitions.
A **pendulous string** is a string stretched vertically by a weight.
A **layered string** is a string stretched horizontally by a weight.
**Course-recourses**, or **vibrations** <note>original Greek: *diadromi*, referring to the path or "running through" of a vibration</note>, are the natural vibrations of pendulous strings: their back-and-forth motion.
**Vibrations** of strings <term>Diadromi</term> are the vibrations of layered strings produced by force.
**Equal vibrations** are those that cover an equal space in an equal time.
The **duration of a vibration** is the length or time in which the vibration of the string itself is completed.
**Equi-durable vibrations** of strings are those which occur in equal time, even if they move through unequal distances.
**Momentum** is the excess of moving power over the obstacles to motion.

### Hypotheses.
Vibrations of equal strings that cover equal distances have the same duration.
Vibrations of equal strings have the same duration, even if they are unequal in distance.

*Book VI. On Instrumental Music.* 417

The lengths of unequal strings are in a **squared ratio** <note>original: *duplicata ratione*; in 17th-century mathematics, a "duplicate ratio" refers to the ratio of the squares of two numbers</note> of the durations of their vibrations—that is, their back-and-forth courses, or **vibrations** <term>Diadromorum: a Greek-derived term Kircher uses for the oscillation or "running through" of a string's movement</term>.
In equal strings, the portions of equal vibrations, or oscillations, are related to one another in duration just as whole oscillations are; and as the physical space of the string is to another string, so sound is to sound, and thus one oscillation is to the next.

**Axioms** <note>original: *Pronunciata*; fundamental principles or "pronouncements" offered as self-evident truths</note>

1. Those things which are equal in duration to a third thing are equal in duration to each other.
2. The squares of given times are also the squares of other times equal to those given times.

**Lemma I.**

When three magnitudes are proportional, the first is said to have a **squared ratio** to the third compared to the ratio it has to the second. But when four magnitudes are proportional, the first is said to have a **tripled ratio** <note>original: *triplicatam rationem*; a cubed ratio ($x^3$)</note> to the fourth compared to the ratio it has to the second. And so on thereafter.

->81 &nbsp; 54 &nbsp; 36 &nbsp; 24 &nbsp; 16<-
->A &nbsp; B &nbsp; C &nbsp; D &nbsp; E<-
<note>The diagram shows five vertical lines of decreasing height, representing a geometric progression where each value is 2/3 of the previous one.</note>

Let the magnitudes A, B, C, D, and E be in continuous proportion, so that the ratio of A to B is the same as B to C, C to D, and D to E. The ratio of the first magnitude A to the third magnitude C is called the **squared ratio** of that ratio which the first magnitude A has to the second magnitude B. This is because between A and C, two ratios are placed which are equal to the ratio of A to B—namely, the ratio of A to B and B to C. Thus, the ratio of A to C "enfolds," so to speak, the ratio of A to B squared, which is to say, placed twice in order. Furthermore, the ratio of the first magnitude A to the fourth magnitude D is called the **tripled ratio** of that ratio which the first magnitude A has to the second magnitude B; for between A and D, three ratios are found which are equal to the ratio of A to B—namely, A to B, B to C, and C to D. Therefore, A to D includes the ratio of A to B tripled, or placed three times in order. In this same way, the ratio of A to E is called the **quadrupled ratio** of A to B, because four equal ratios are placed between A and E, and so on to infinity.

Since we will frequently mention these terms in the following pages, and there are few who correctly understand said terms, it seemed appropriate to interpret them a bit more at length here, so that nothing may hinder the reader in this work.

What we mean by a squared or tripled ratio, we declare by this example: Since it is established from Euclid’s *Elements*, Book 6, Proposition 20, that the ratio of a square to another square is the **squared ratio** of the ratio of the side of the first square to the side of the second, it follows that if the ratio of the sides is continued through three terms, the ratio of the square to the square is that which exists between the first term and the third. Thus, if the side of the first square is three **palms** <term>palmorum: a traditional unit of measure based on the width of the hand</term> and the side of the second is one palm, the first square

->1 &nbsp; 2 &nbsp; 3<-
<note>A diagram of a large square divided into a 3x3 grid of nine smaller squares. Numbers 1, 2, 3 are written along the side and bottom to show the dimensions.</note>
->1 &nbsp; 2 &nbsp; 3<-

will have a ratio to the second of 9 to 1, such that it contains the latter nine times. For the ratio of 9 to 1 (which is a nine-fold ratio) is called, according to this Lemma, the **squared ratio** of the triple ratio (such as 9 to 3 and 3 to 1), as is clear from these three terms: 9, 3, 1. For when I multiply 1 by 3, and 3 by itself, 9 is produced; and 9 to 1 is said to be a squared ratio because 9 was produced by the double multiplication of 1 by 3, and 3 by itself.

For since in one minute the heavy body descends from A into b, and in 1 minute it descends the distance bc from b into C, and in the minute cd the heavy body descends from C into D, and in one minute from D it falls into E, and so on for the rest; since these minutes are equal, yet the spaces through which the heavy body falls in equal minutes are unequal, the increments of velocity must necessarily hold the same ratio as the squares of the times. For a heavy body falling from A into B through one foot in one minute will, in two minutes, fall 4 feet from A into C; and in a space of 3 minutes it will fall 9 feet from A into d. In a space of 4 minutes it will fall 16 feet from A into e; in a space of 5 minutes it will fall 25 feet from A into f. Finally, in a space of six minutes it will fall 36 feet from A into G. These will be the squares A, I, L, M, N, while the differences between the squares will be the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Therefore, the increments of velocity have the same ratio as the squares of the times.

But truly, the two triangles IAC and HAB are the halves of two squares I and A, and accordingly are in the same ratio—namely the doubled ratio <note>The "doubled ratio" refers to the relationship between the squares of the sides (the square of 2:1 being 4:1)</note>—of that which the sides IC and HB have. Thus the motion of two minutes is to the motion of one minute, because the side CA has the same ratio to side BA as side CI has to side HB, and therefore their squares will also be in that same doubled ratio. ### Lemma IV.

Whenever motion occurs along a perpendicular line and an inclined line, which are joined by a straight line perpendicular to the inclined line, then those two motions are equal to one another <note>In this context, "equal" refers to the time duration of the motion, not the distance or speed.</note>.

[Diagram: A right-angled triangle ABC. Point A is at the top, B is at the bottom of the vertical side, and C is at the end of the horizontal base. A line BD is drawn from vertex B to meet the hypotenuse AC at a right angle at point D.]

Let the perpendicular line be AB, and the inclined line be AC. Let a normal <note>original: *normalis*; a line at a right angle</note> line BD be drawn from any point on line BA—namely from B—to the inclined line AC at point D. I say that a heavy body moving from A to B, and from A to D upon the inclined plane, reaches the end of its motion in the same time. That is, the motions which occur through AB and AD are equal, not in velocity (since it is better known than it needs to be said that an object runs through a perpendicular path faster than an inclined one) but in duration. For since as AC is to AB, so the square of AC is to the square of AB; and as AC is to AD, so the square of the time of AC is to the square of the time of AD. Therefore, as the square of AC is to the square of AB, so the square of the time of AC is to the square of the time of AD. Therefore, as AC is to AB, so the time of AC is to the time of AD, according to the 22nd proposition of the Sixth Book <note>original: *per 22 Sexti*; referring to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book VI, Proposition 22, concerning proportional areas and sides</note>. But as AC is to AB, so the time of AC is to the time of AB. Therefore, the time of AB is equal to the time of AD, which was to be demonstrated.

#### On the parabolic generation of the line in projectiles.

From this wonderful proportion of motion, it was noted by the distinguished mathematicians of this time <note>Likely a reference to Galileo Galilei, who published the parabolic trajectory of projectiles in 1638</note> that heavy bodies, tied by no bond, by the impulse of the thrower and from the force of this declared proportion, describe a line—I know not what—that resembles a parabola. But let us look into the matter a little more deeply. Since two motions can be considered in any projected heavy body—the natural and the violent—natural motion seeks a perpendicular path, while violent motion seeks a path toward that part toward which the heavy object was obliquely impelled. It happens that from this, in objects projected obliquely, a certain middle motion results, by which the heavy body [describes] a line...

[bracket symbol in right margin]

But because gravity drives it toward the center, let us suppose that in the time the ball moves through OH, gravity moves the ball away from the line OQ by the space of the line OB, which is part of the perpendicular line of motion OX. In like manner, let the line HV pass through point H parallel to OX; likewise, let the lines MR, Rπ, and QY be drawn through points M, R, and Q—each and every one parallel to one another and to OX.

And let the displacement of the ball from line OQ, as soon as it reaches line MR, be as great as the portion OL of the perpendicular line OX; and the displacement of the ball from line OQ as soon as it reaches line Rπ be as great as OP; and let the displacement of the ball from line OQ as soon as it reaches line QY be as great as the perpendicular line OX itself. In the same way, while the ball moves through HM, it will be displaced from OM at Kr, and through MR at C, and through RQ at Y. Since these spaces of the displaced ball are equal to the spaces OB, OL, OP, and OX—that is, while they increase according to the quantity of the lines OB, BL, LP, and PX—it necessarily follows that they increase according to the **series of odd numbers continued from unity**.

If we therefore set OB as 1, BL will be 3, LP will be 5, and PX will be 7. Or, OL will be 4, OP will be 9, and OX will be 16. But in this same way proceed the squares of OH, OM, OR, and OQ (or BF, LK, PC, and XY, which are equal to them as opposite sides of parallelograms). Since, therefore, the square BF is 1, the square LK will be 4, and the square PC 9, and the square XY 16. It follows that as OX is to OP, so is XY to the square PC; and as OP is to OL, so is the square PC to the square LK; and as LO is to OB, so is the square LK to the square BF.

If, therefore, a semi-parabola or a whole parabola AOY were described according to the points O and Y, passing through point O and through points A and Y, the squares intercepted within OX and the parabola AOY will also have the same proportion to one another as OX, OP, OL, and OB have among themselves—as we have shown at length in the *Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: *Arte lucis & umbræ*; referring to Kircher's 1646 work on optics</note> in the chapter on **Conic Sections**. Therefore, the sides of these squares will be congruent to the sides PC, LK, BL, and BF, and to the sides PZ, LE, and BS. The ball, therefore, at points O, F, K, C, and Y, will always be in the parabola AOY. The same can be demonstrated for any other projection of a heavy body; thus, a projected ball will, by its motion, *affect* <note>In this context, "affect" means to take on the qualities of or follow the path of.</note> a parabola, which was to be demonstrated.

I said it will *affect* a parabola, because I do not believe that a line of this sort caused by projectiles is a **perfect parabola**, as many mathematicians of this time, following **Galileo**, believe. Rather, it is something similar. The reason for my doubt is that it has nothing from which it may be generated; for every parabola has its origin from the section of a **Cone**. In projectiles, however, no section of a cone can be conceived, unlike in the business of sundials <note>original: *sciatherico negotio*; the science of dialing or measuring time by shadows</note>, where light and shadow, by their circuits, pour out true cones, which are then cut by the "cone-cutting" <note>original: *conotomo*</note> plane of the horizon to produce conic sections of every kind. Where the foundation of conic sections is missing, the true properties <note>original: *affectiones*</note> of the sections can by no means be conceived. So it is in a thicker and heavier string: if it were suspended from its two ends, it is accustomed to incline downwards somewhat in the middle because of its weight, and to create a curved figure...

# CHAPTER I.

### On the origin, causes, and properties of sound in strings.

**W**e shall briefly explain this doctrine—which is otherwise vast and wide—through the following Theorems, according to the plan of our instruction.

### Theorem I.

**A** *ny sound is composed of as many degrees of highness and lowness as the number of times the eardrum is struck by moved air in a given time.*

The harmonic number in this context is called nothing other than the number of motions, or percussions of the air, by which the sense of hearing can be affected and moved. Furthermore, since "low" or "high" <note>original: *graue, vel acutum*; literally "heavy" or "sharp," the standard Latin terms for bass and treble pitches.</note> is uniquely regarded by Musicians as that which derives its origin from the number of motions and percussions of the air, it is clearly evident that sounds, as well as all consonances and dissonances, are nothing other than the various numbers of air motions reaching the ears and being carried even to the soul by the help of the auditory nerves. Therefore, any sound, as the proposition holds, is composed of as many degrees of highness or lowness as the number of times the eardrum is struck by moved air in a given time. For example: if the eardrum is struck twelve times in some given time, the sound then heard will be composed of 12 degrees of highness, and the soul, through its auditory power, will feel itself to be affected by these 12 degrees much differently than by any other number of percussions. From this, it is clear why, according to Plato, the soul is called a "numbering number" <note>original: *numerus numerans*; a Platonic concept suggesting the soul has an innate mathematical structure that allows it to perceive order and harmony.</note>; for the number, by separating sounds from sounds, discerns highness from lowness, and places the laws of relaxation and tension in all things. Consequently, harmony, or the perception of consonant numbers, is nothing other than the comparison of two or more different motions which affect the eardrum at the same time. But let us show this matter by an example:

-> [A diagram consisting of two horizontal lines; the top line is labeled A on the left and B on the right, the bottom line is labeled C on the left and D on the right.] <-

Let there be two strings AB and CD. If AB should strike the air 12 times and CD 6 times by its vibration, and if they strike the ear at the same time and with the same duration, the soul will necessarily feel the consonance of an **octave** <note>original: *consonantiam octauam*</note>, considered under the double ratio of vibrations <note>The 2:1 ratio (12:6).</note>. For just as string relates to string, and 6 vibrations of air to 12, so the motions of the air inherent in the eardrum relate to one another. Now, since these two motions are in a double ratio...

### THEOREM I.

**S**ound in strings is nothing other than the very rapid percussion of air, caused by the trembling of the string.

For as often as a string is plucked from its state of rest and released, it immediately seeks its original straightness; however, due to the force of its motion, it is carried beyond the center and oscillates back and forth. In this back-and-forth movement, it strikes the surrounding air, which, being pushed and agitated, creates the sensation of sound in the ear.

### THEOREM II.

**T**he swifter the vibration <term>diadromos</term> <note>Greek: *diadromoi*; refers to the oscillations or "runs" of the string.</note>, the more acute the sound; the slower the vibration, the deeper the sound.

For example <note>original: *V. g.* for *verbi gratia*</note>, if one string completes its motion in a shorter time than another, the air is struck more frequently, and thus a higher pitch is perceived.

### THEOREM III.

**T**he lengths of strings are in inverse ratio to the number of their vibrations.

Reason <note>original: *R.*, likely *Ratio* (Reason/Proportion).</note>: If a string is divided in half, the resulting part, being shorter and stiffer, will vibrate twice as fast as the whole string. Thus, the ratio of the whole string to its half is 2:1, which produces the <term>diapason</term> <note>The Greek term for an Octave.</note>.

**I**f the ratio is 3:2, it produces the <term>diapente</term> <note>The Greek term for a Perfect Fifth.</note>.
**I**f the ratio is 4:1, it produces the <term>disdiapason</term> <note>The Greek term for a Double Octave.</note>.

...trembles six times in the same amount of time, and therefore a twelfth would be twice generated, just as an octave is generated three times. For a two-foot string <note>original: *bipedalis*</note> unites its vibrations more quickly with the vibrations of a one-foot string <note>original: *A pedalis*</note> than with the vibrations of a three-foot string <note>original: *C tripedalis*</note>; thus, string B will also reach consonance with string A sooner than with string C. You see, therefore, that the origin <note>original: *genesis*</note> of consonances consists in nothing other than **isochronous** <note>Greek: *isochronois*; meaning "equal-timed" or occurring at the same interval</note> beats—that is, simultaneous ones—such that the **coincidence** <note>Greek: *symptosis*; the mathematical "falling together" or meeting of points</note> of the aforementioned string C, the beats of string B, and the beats of string A are coincident, and are perfectly completed at the same moment of time; when the soul perceives this coincidence of beats, it then forms within itself the first appearance of consonance.

### Corollary <note>original: *Porisma*; a geometric or logical deduction</note>

From this it is evident that consonances are all the more pleasant and sweet—whether considered individually or together—the more frequently the percussions of the air are united at the same time; and one consonance surpasses another by as much as the movements of the air of which they consist meet more frequently. Moreover, they are sweeter the simpler they are, and they are simpler the more they [tend] toward unity <note>The text ends mid-sentence; "toward unity" refers to the mathematical ratio 1:1, or the unison.</note>

### Theorem IV.

**Whether a string tightened by a tuning peg <term>verticillus; a small whorl or peg used to adjust tension</term> or by a weight is equally stretched in all its parts?**

It is asked here first whether a stretched string is tense in all its parts equally—that is, does the force or power of the tension communicate its impression more to those parts close to the source of the tension than to those far away? The reasoning for this proposition [that tension might be unequal] is that those things seem more strongly stretched which are harder to move; but the parts closer to the source of the tension are harder to move. Furthermore, we almost always see strings break near the ends, rather than in the middle.

I respond briefly that the string is everywhere equally stretched. Let string AB be equally stretched according to all its parts; and let a weight G be suspended from the middle of string AB at point F. I say that this weight will pull the string to point G, and the tension will be the same in both GB and GA. Again, let part AF of string AB be divided at H; I say the same weight G will pull the string AF to point I, and the string AH (fixed at L) will be pulled by the weight to point K after the midpoint is passed. And proceeding thus unto infinity: because the weight attached to string AB at point F pulls points L and H of the string to proportional spaces KI, just as if it were attached at points L and H. This is clearly shown by strings AIF and AKH as they pass through points K and I. 

Therefore, a weight tied to a single part of the string moves it only as much from its place as it would move it if it were tied successively to each part taken separately. For although AB is moved twice as much by the attached weight G than AF is, AF resists twice as much by the weight attached at H, and AH resists four times as much by the weight attached at K than AB does by the weight attached at G. For the more remote parts of the strings have the same proportion to their lengths; and it is just as difficult to move a four-foot string by a weight as it is to stretch a one-foot string with the same weight. Therefore, just as AB relates to FG, so AF relates to HI, and AH to LK. It is clear, then, that a string stretched by the same weight produces equal resistance everywhere.

[A diagram illustrating the geometry of a stretched string: a horizontal line AB with points L, H, and F marked. Point G represents the weight pulling point F downward to form a triangle AGB. Lines AKI and ALK show the steeper angles and greater resistance created when the same weight is applied to shorter segments of the string.]

### Theorem V.

**The vibrations <term>diadromi; from the Greek for "running through," referring here to the back-and-forth oscillation of a string</term> in strings stretched in any manner are different both in magnitude and in velocity.**

It is certain that the first vibration <term>diadromus</term> in a string stretched in any way is the greatest of all those which occur while the string's tremor lasts. For if the next one following were equal to the first, it would cover the same space due to an equal impulse; and consequently, the third would also be equal to the first and second due to an equal impulse; and thus all the remaining ones would be equal, and consequently the motion of the string (according to the Lemma) would be perpetual. Since this is absurd, the remaining vibrations of the string until it reaches rest must necessarily be smaller and smaller. 

In this alone lies the greatest difficulty: where is the motion of the string faster—at the beginning or at the end? Whether this motion behaves like the flight of a projectile, or like the motion of a stone thrown upward, which is faster the closer it is to the source of the impulse, and slower the further it is from the same... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the final word "remotior" (further) is split by the catchword "Hhh" at the bottom of the page.</note>

### Book VI. On Instrumental Music. 427

...in horizontally stretched strings, in which the struck string eventually comes to rest. It is asked, therefore, why strings pulled by force outside the line of direction, or rest, are carried beyond and to this side of the said lines until they rest in the same? We respond that strings, however they are stretched, when struck, move in the same way as a stone toward the center <note>original: "versus centrum"; referring to the center of gravity</note>. If anyone were to allow a stone to fall toward the center of the earth, it is certain that, because of the violent impulse, it would by no means rest immediately upon reaching the center; rather, just as was demonstrated in Lemma I, it would move back and forth with frequent <term>diadromos; the back-and-forth paths or cycles of a vibrating string</term> until it finally rests in the center. Therefore, the natural impulse by which it seeks the center is the cause of the cycles repeated back and forth. 

Truly, since the stone is at its greatest force and most rapid motion when it is at the center, it necessarily overshoots into the opposite side until its impulse—somewhat broken by the resistance of the air—drives it back toward the center again. Borne toward the center with this new impulse, it will run back and forth for as long as it takes for the diminished impulse to finally rest in the natural center. Just as the hanging string AB <note>A pendulum used as an analogy for a horizontal string</note> beautifully teaches us; for this, being raised to point C and falling from there, completes its cycle at L—but not further <note>The original Latin text likely contains a typo here, "non verò in L", where it should refer to a point beyond L</note> because of the resistance of the air. From L, however, sliding through the center B with a new impulse, it completes its cycle not at N because of air resistance, but at S; from S indeed to V, and from V to R, until finally it rests in the center B as the cycles diminish. 

You see, therefore, how the force or impulse is gradually and proportionally diminished, and how it is impossible for two equal cycles to occur throughout the entire time of motion. For if we were to posit two equal cycles, they would necessarily be produced by an equal impulse. Therefore, if the string fell from C and finished at L, it would necessarily return from L to C, and from C to L again, and thus there would be perpetual motion, as was demonstrated in Lemma I. Lest this absurdity be admitted in nature, the force must necessarily be proportionally diminished so that it can finally reach the end of its motion. You see, then, that the natural impulse of the string, by which it seeks the center, is the cause of the travel back and forth across the center. But the reason it does not run out as far as it might <note>original: "ex L in M"</note> is the resistance of the compressed air.

### Theorem VIII.

The greatest cycle of a string completes its entire space in the same time as the smallest, or as each of the other intermediate cycles complete theirs.

I say, therefore, that just as in a vertically stretched string all cycles are <term>equidiurnal; of equal duration, regardless of the distance traveled</term>, so it is also in horizontally stretched and struck strings. The former was demonstrated in the first Lemma; the latter we shall explain here. Let FG, then, be a string laid out horizontally, which, when pulled to point A, makes the <term>epidromos; the segments of the string's path</term> AB, BC, CE, and ED. I say all these paths, however unequal they may be in length, are nevertheless of equal duration; that is, the path AB completes its space in the same time as the paths BC, CE, and ED.

For since the violence and impulse with which the string FG is pulled outside the line of rest to A is greater as the path is longer, hence it also traverses its space as much more swiftly as the space it completes is greater. Necessarily [it follows...]
