Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-making. 545

Again, they had another type of monody <note>A solo vocal or instrumental melody.</note> that was organic or instrumental, which was performed in the same way by some distinguished kithara player, lyre player, or flute player. Truly, "polyodic" music <note>Music performed by several voices or instruments.</note> was established for several performers, either with the same or different kinds of instruments playing alternately in public for a proposed prize, as has been said. Moreover, they frequently joined the voice to the kithara, lyre, or flute; sometimes they presented a "symphony" mixed with different instruments and voices, which they varied with a wonderful combination of voices and instruments. Reason dictates and authors confirm that the Ancients had no other music besides this, unless perhaps someone asserts they possessed some celestial music inaccessible to human wit—which would be ridiculous, not to say foolish, to claim.

With these things thus properly established, I say first: if we look at the variety of things discovered regarding music, or at the theory itself, we will find without controversy that modern music is much nobler, more perfect, and endowed with greater variety than the ancient. So much so, that to prove this, nothing else seems required but a demonstration of our assertion taken from experience and the induction of facts. While I do this, I promise to speak always with great respect and reverence for venerable antiquity, since it is from them that we have drawn whatever we possess that is perfect. However, I protest here <margin>The Author’s Disclaimer</margin> that I do not speak of just any music of the moderns—for I know that countless defects are committed in it everywhere, even by the most skilled musicians—but rather of music established with the highest perfection and according to the most ingenious inventions unearthed in this age, and especially of the polyodic or harmonic style <note>The multi-voiced or polyphonic style.</note>.

### §. I.
### Theoretical Music.

Almost all the monuments of the ancient Greek musicians that survive are those of Aristides Quintilianus, Bryennius, Plutarch, Aristotle, Callimachus, Aristoxenus, Alypius, Ptolemy, Euclid, Nicomachus, Boethius, Martianus Capella, Valla, and others flourishing in the last century. Most of these Greek manuscripts, bound together into one huge volume, are preserved in the Library of the Roman College <note>The Jesuit university where Kircher lived and worked.</note> like a vast treasury of things <margin>Greek Manuscript Authors on music in the Library of the Roman College</margin>. If you properly compare all these authors (just as I have compared them with the greatest study more than once, one with another), you will find nothing so different in one that is not found in all the others. For besides analogous, celestial, human, and divine music, they are all primarily concerned with the multiple composition, division, and mixing of <term>tetrachords</term> <note>A series of four notes, the fundamental building block of ancient Greek scales.</note> and the systems of the <term>diapason</term> <note>The octave.</note>. Then, each one applies himself with the greatest zeal to determining the different tones or modes. Thirdly, their whole industry is occupied with composing and determining the three genres—Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic—and subdividing them into the smallest intervals. <margin>Praise of Boethius</margin> In the exact and most ingenious description of these things, Boethius <note>The 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory text for a millennium.</note> seems to have deservedly snatched the palm from all others. For he treated the individual precepts of the ancient musicians so subtly, elucidates obscure points so clearly, and supplies defects so skillfully, conducting himself so perfectly in his most learned work, that while he demonstrates that nothing of ancient music was hidden from him, he seems not only to have described ancient music but to have restored it, by heaping his own countless discoveries upon the inventions of his predecessors. Thus, whatever is found scattered in all the others may be seen collected, increased, and digested with the most exquisite study in Boethius.

Let no one object to us that there were many other authors who treated a different kind of music than the one mentioned <margin>Objection</margin>; for since the said authors made no mention of them—though they undoubtedly would have, had they existed—the objection raised carries no weight, nor can it stand by any reason. For by this logic, one might say there were many in past centuries who discovered and demonstrated that true "squaring of the circle" <note>A famous mathematical problem: constructing a square with the same area as a circle using only a compass and straightedge.</note> so anxiously sought by mathematicians until now, but that the books do not survive due to the [iniquity] <margin>Its solution</margin> of the times...

...lost to the injuries of time. This is a truly ridiculous and utterly foolish objection; for in this way, one could claim that anything at all existed in past ages. It is certainly not the mark of a prudent philosopher to argue from those things of which no certain trace remains to us, toward those things which we certainly know and understand. We understand the music of the ancients, therefore, from the surviving monuments left to posterity which have been reviewed, and we also know our own present music. Let us therefore establish a comparison, so that we may finally understand what should be thought of the matter.

<margin>In what the musical theory of the ancients consisted.</margin>
The theory of the ancients consisted, as has been said, in three things: namely, in the composition of tetrachords <note>A scale of four notes</note> and systems; in the division of the modes; and in the distinction of the three genera <note>The Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic styles of tuning</note>. Who does not know that in this modern age, these things have been demonstrated much more subtly, easily, and exactly, not only by arithmetic but also by geometric precision? The ancients thought that a whole tone could by no means be divided into two equal parts; today, supported by algebraic industry and the science of irrational numbers, we divide not only the tone but the proportion of any consonance with almost no effort. As for the differences of the tones or modes, we arrange them more easily due to the invention of musical notation (unknown to the ancients) and its arrangement upon the staff <note>original: "pentegramma"</note>; thus we also determine them more perfectly. The same must be said of the threefold genus, as will be shown later; it adds to this that all these things are brought to light much more clearly by that innumerable variety of musical instruments which the ancients lacked.

### §. II.

*Ancient-Modern Vocal Music*

<margin>The vocal music of the ancients.</margin>
But I come to vocal or artificial music, which I cannot deny is in many ways more excellent and noble in modern times. For as was said in the second supposition, the artistic music of the ancients consisted in this: that some poet would sing a poem, most perfect in all its meters, to the sound of the lyre, the kithara, or the flute, with such variety of gesture, such energy, and such efficacy of action, that he easily carried the minds of the listeners wherever he wished. And this was not so much harmony as it was a certain poetic, metrical, or theatrical music, of the kind we perform today on stages and in theaters. As I said, I would not deny that this poetic music was admirable, acquired through the greatest study and tireless practice, and that it had the greatest and most effective power to incite the minds of the listeners to any emotion whatsoever; nevertheless, I assert it was of such a nature that posterity should by no means despair of reaching its excellence.

<margin>The theatrical or recitative music of the ancients.</margin>
For just as the Greeks, drawn by a natural impulse toward stages and theaters, were carried away with a prepared and most eager mind to listen to the poet and the Voice-Trainer <note>original: "Phonascum"</note>; so they were moved in a wonderful way by the actions, gestures, and emotions of the person appearing in public, according as the theme or subject of the poem required. However, this was such that the music achieved no effect unless the person was equipped with a perfect knowledge of poetry, distinguished skill in singing, and a certain admirable cleverness of action. And although moderns must concede something to the ancients regarding this remarkable musical talent, it must not be denied that today there are found musical authors endowed with such dexterity and skill that they yield nothing to the ancients. He who has seen the admirable theatrical exhibitions here in Rome at various times,

<margin>The wonderful effects of theatrical music exhibited in our times.</margin>
performed both by Cardinal Francesco Barberini and by others in other places, and who has heard the excellence of the harmonic compositions, will be forced to confess with me: that in human affairs, whether you look at the decorum and magnificence, or the unusual and extraordinary textures of the harmonic compositions, one could desire nothing more beautiful or pleasant. The actors exhibited the history of the things to be expressed with such efficacy, and with such vivid gestures and such variety of emotions, that the listeners, often unable to contain themselves, broke out into shouts, groans, sighs, and strange movements of the body, clearly expressing by outward signs the heat of the internal emotions by which they were incited. For there is nothing more agreeable to human nature...

### §. III.
### *The Ancient-Modern Harmony of Many Voices.*

I move now to polyody <note>Kircher uses this term to refer to multi-part vocal music, or polyphony</note>, or the harmony of many voices, which we properly call music or harmony. # §. IV.
### *Ancient-Modern Instrumental Music.*

<margin>The instruments of the Ancients are not to be compared with modern ones.</margin>

**B**ut I come now to modern instrumental music, which, when compared to the music of the ancients, undoubtedly carries away the palm of victory. The ancients transmitted to posterity hardly any other kind of instruments besides Lyres, Citharas, Pipes, and various Flutes. We have displayed their forms in the preceding pages, insofar as it was possible to find them here in Rome within the treasury <note original="gazophilacio">Kircher is likely referring to the extensive collections of antiquities in Rome, including his own famous museum, the Musaeum Kircherianum.</note> of all antiquity. These instruments, however, hold no dignity when compared with ours, since most of them consist of no more than four, or at most seven, strings, without a neck or any yoke <note original="iugo">referring to the crossbar or fingerboard</note>. They were accustomed to be struck with a plectrum <term>plectrum: a small tool, like a modern guitar pick, used to pluck strings</term> alone, as we showed in the previous propositions. I do not believe it possible by any means for such a technique to produce that grace of harmony which our Citharas <note original="Cytharæ">Here Kircher refers to instruments of the lute or guitar family.</note> achieve through the most subtle movement of the fingers. Since no interval can be assigned that is so small or minute that it cannot be produced by the pressure of the fingers, it follows that those trembling, compressed ornaments and "warblings" <note original="teretismisque">A Greek-derived term for melodic embellishments.</note>—which the Italians call *gruppi* and *trilli*—cannot be performed with a plectrum alone. These ornaments, which provide the highest grace to a symphony, along with passages of incredible speed and "biting" articulations <note original="pressuræ mordicantes">likely referring to *mordents* or sharp attacks</note>, can only be exhibited through the ingenious play of the fingers.

Furthermore, three types of instruments are in use today, just as among the ancients: namely, stringed, wind <note original="pneumatica">literally "pneumatic" or air-driven</note>, and percussion. Of each of these, there is such a great variety constructed with such exquisite genius, as you see described throughout this work; yet among the ancients, you will find no trace of them. The ancients entirely lacked keyboard instruments <note original="Polyplectris abacis">literally "many-plucked tables"</note>, which are called *tastaturas* <term>tastaturas: the early term for a musical keyboard (from the Italian 'tasto', meaning touch)</term>, even though nothing more beautiful or ingenious could be devised in this field.

But you will say that the very fact that hydraulic organs <term>hydraulic organ: an ancient pipe organ powered by water pressure</term> were constructed by Archimedes (as Tertullian witnesses) and cherished by Nero (as Vitruvius witnesses), is an irrefragable argument that the ancients had some use of organs. I respond that it is true that hydraulic organs were first invented by Heron of Alexandria and constructed by Archimedes. 

<margin>What the hydraulic organs were like.</margin>

Vitruvius correctly asserts that Nero was also accustomed to be greatly delighted by them. However, anyone who correctly weighs the construction of the Vitruvian organ (as described in our *Musical Mechanics*) will clearly find that the work was as imperfect compared to modern organs as the Lyres and Citharas of the ancients were imperfect compared to our Lutes <note original="Testudines">literally "tortoises," the standard Latin term for lutes due to their curved backs</note>, Theorbos, Pandoras, Harps, Harpsichords, and countless others, as we have shown elsewhere. For there was no proportion of wind to animate the pipes, nor any correct distribution of the order of Octaves in the pipes, as is evident from the manufacture of the instrument cited above. 

Today, however, organs and all keyboard instruments have ascended to such perfection that nature seems to have set a limit here for craftsmen, beyond which they cannot progress. Anyone who has seen the wonderful construction of organs in Germany, France, and Italy—the ranks of pipes most artificially distributed, the immense variety of "stops" <note original="iocorum">literally "jokes" or "toys," referring to the various sound effects and stops in an organ</note>, the vastness of the pipes rising up like columns, the remarkable craftsmanship of the foot-keyed keyboard which they call the *pedal*, the multitude of registers, the ingenious disposition of the wind-chests—will be forced to confess with me that nothing remains to be added to such perfection. This single harmonic mass can now mimic the sounds of little birds, now human voices, now Pipes, Shawms, Bagpipes, Trumpets, and every other imaginable instrument. 

What shall I say of the Automata <note original="Automatis">mechanical self-playing musical devices</note>, of which such a variety has emerged today? If anything similar had existed among the ancients, they would have undoubtedly sold them to posterity as miracles of nature and art, carved into stones and statues. For it was so ingrained in the Greek character to extol even small things to the very heavens; in order to show themselves to posterity as the achievers of discovered things, they were accustomed to boast of their own works beyond what can be said. Certainly, not everything written about Archimedes is of eternal truth. That "burning mirror" which miraculously burned ships at a vast distance is a matter repugnant to the truth and the principles of Catoptrics <term>Catoptrics: the branch of optics dealing with reflection</term> in my *Great Art...* <note>The text cuts off here; Kircher is referring to his own work *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* (The Great Art of Light and Shadow).</note>

<margin>The excellence of the musical instruments of our time.</margin>

He dismisses ancient hydraulic organs as primitive and suggests that Greek accounts of their own inventions were often exaggerated.</summary>

at great length, in our work on light and shadow, we have refuted these claims. Furthermore, the spheres of Archimedes <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) was said to have created a mechanical planetarium; the poet Claudian wrote a famous poem praising this "glass world."</note>, which Claudian describes as a miracle of art, can in no way be compared with modern inventions of clocks and admirable machines. However, these things are known only to those who, driven by a curiosity to understand the world, have inspected and considered the royal treasuries <note original="cimeliarchia">from the Greek 'keimeliarchion,' a repository for precious objects or a cabinet of curiosities.</note> and marvelous works in various regions. Just as things lose their value when they become too common, so too must these ancient things suffer a loss in our estimation. By the same logic, I say that not everything the Greeks narrated about their "miraculous music" is true, as will be discussed more broadly later. Since their musical style cannot be unknown to us from the works they left to posterity, there was nothing so hidden or ingenious among them that the highly trained minds of the moderns—equipped with the variety of resources that the invention of printing <note original="typographicum inuentum">Kircher highlights the printing press as a revolutionary tool for musical education and distribution.</note> has brought us—could not attain, provided they are willing to apply themselves consistently.

And from this discourse, which perhaps lasted longer than was proper, I have clearly demonstrated, unless I am mistaken, that modern music is in many ways superior to that of the Ancients and endowed with greater variety. I assert this against those who, loathing and despising the present, are accustomed to attribute some kind of "divine music" to the ancients—the likes of which they cannot demonstrate from any Author. Thus, the same thing seems to happen to them as to those who, while possessing precious things at home, admire straw and ferns abroad, looking up to them and valuing them as nothing compared to their own domestic treasures.

I do not doubt that the Ancient Greeks had a distinguished and judicious music, but it was suited to their own genius, inclination, and the customs of their country. <margin>Modern music is more excellent than that of the Ancients.</margin> If it were heard today, it would perhaps neither be held in such high esteem nor obtain the dignity it held among its own people. But you will say that the Chromatic and Enharmonic genera <term>genera: the three classifications of Greek melody (Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic) based on the tuning of the four-stringed lyre</term>, which stirred such great emotions in the souls of men, have perished and are utterly unknown to us, and therefore we can by no means reach their level of perfection. In truth, anyone who knows what the Chromatic and Enharmonic truly are will be forced to admit, from those same aforementioned monuments of the Ancients, that these genera were not even much approved of by the Ancients themselves; indeed, they were rather prohibited in many places. However, I will speak more fully of these three genera in the following sections, where I shall reveal my mind more clearly. And here I bring an end to my discourse.

### QUESTION VI.

### Whether, why, and how Music has the power to stir the minds of men, and whether those things written about the marvelous effects of Ancient Music are true.

If the stories told are true—of Alexander the Great being incited to fury by the power and efficacy of Timotheus’s music <note>Timotheus of活跃 Milesus was a famous musician; the legend says he could make Alexander reach for his sword or calm down just by changing the musical mode.</note>, and of the youth of Tauromenium <note>A city in Sicily (modern Taormina).</note> who was inflamed with anger but returned to gentleness by the work of Pythagoras, as soon as he changed the mode and sounded a spondaic melody—one might rightly ask here by what power this happens. Although we have dealt with these matters at length in Book 9, this place seems to demand that we explain more fully certain things that were perhaps touched upon too sparingly there.

It should be noted, therefore, that this vehement stirring in the minds of men can happen in various ways. First, by a certain supernatural power, or the power of a Demon. The Devil, as if using the sound of the Lute <note original="Cytharæ">Specifically the kithara or lute family instruments.</note> as a sign of a pact entered into, can so powerfully disturb the humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed in ancient medicine to control health and temperament</term> of the human body that he produces an infallible effect of fury, madness, or some other violent impulse. This was mentioned in the *Teratologia* <note>Referring to accounts of marvels or monsters.</note> regarding the lutenist of the King of Denmark <note>Reference to King Eric I "the Good" of Denmark, who allegedly killed four of his men after a musician played a specific "fury-inducing" mode.</note>, who incited the King to such madness that, seized by rage, he slew two of his own men; which certainly, as is clear from the circumstances, could not have happened without the work of a Demon.

Secondly, those troubled by a Demon, like Saul and others, could be liberated by the dispersing of the smoky vapor of black bile <term>black bile: or "melancholy," one of the four humors; Kircher suggests demons use this physical substance to influence the mind</term>, in which the Demons who disturb minds most enjoy residing...

# Book VII. On the Ancient-Modern Art of Music, etc. 551

...is stirred in a unison manner, whence arises a very great variation of emotion according to the nature of the tone and the theme.

Therefore, if our musicians wish to renew the miracles of the ancient musicians, they must look back, first to explore the inclination and natural disposition of a subject <note>In this context, the "subject" is the person listening to the music.</note>; then, according to that same disposition, they should adapt harmonic rhythms <note>original: "numeros"</note> and a verbal theme congruent with them. They should not doubt that they will cause the same effects as the ancients did. For the same thing happens in the diverse complexions <note>The "complexion" refers to a person's physical and psychological constitution based on their balance of bodily fluids or "humors."</note> of men as in that most beautiful experiment we showed in Book 9, where different liquids poured into glass cups are agitated according to the diverse disposition of rhythms and proportions. Likewise, a string does not move another unless they agree in perfect unison, or in an octave or fifth, but most perfectly in unison. For the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus animalis"; in the 17th century, these were believed to be extremely fine vapors that acted as the medium between the soul and the body, traveling through the nerves.</note> is like another multi-stringed instrument; if you tune your harmony to it, you will undoubtedly seize it wherever you wish and sweep it into whatever emotions you desire.

From this it also happens that while we watch those performing dances, we are animated into similar movements, namely from the similarity of harmonic proportions and rhythms affecting our spirit through similarity and <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "Sympathia"; the natural resonance or "feeling-with" between two things that share a common nature.</note>. Thirdly, it is well known how much power speech possesses over the minds of listeners. Who is ignorant of the movements which certain great preachers impress upon the minds of their listeners? I heard in Malta and in Sicily a great servant of God of our religion preaching with such ardor that, because of the tumult of sobbing and weeping and the noise of spontaneous scourging <note>Public displays of penance, such as self-flagellation, were common during powerful or emotional sermons in the Baroque period.</note>, it was sometimes necessary to interrupt the sermon violently; and he achieved this as often as he wished. <margin>Words have great power over the human soul</margin> For the preacher knew the inclination of his listeners; he knew the "string" he had to touch, so that it is no wonder he aroused such great movements. Thus harmony naturally affects man; rhythm and the proportion of the air's motion affect the spirit, the organ of the motive faculty; words present an object to the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasię"; the mental faculty that processes sensory images and presents them to the emotions.</note>, which, if it be pleasant, will stir up similar emotions and movements; if sad and mournful, it will elicit tears, groans, and sighs; if it breathes a martial fury, it will impel those of a martial disposition to the same, and so on for the rest.

You see, therefore, how music can move the passions of our mind; you see also how the ancients performed those miracles by the power of music upon the minds of men. Having explained these in order, nothing remains but for us to explain more fully the causes of such great changes by bringing them back to the anvil of physics.

### PHYSIOLOGICAL INQUIRY VII.

### How harmonic rhythm moves the emotions.

Since <note>original: "παθημάτα" (pathemata)</note> "sufferings" or "passions," which moral philosophers call "passions of the soul" <note>original: "ψυχῆς πάθη" (psyches pathe)</note>, whether the subject be the sensitive, bodily, and material appetite, necessarily the said passions will also be subject to material conditions, as will be discussed at length in *Musical Ethics*. For they consist in a certain combination of the primary elementary qualities and can be called vapors of the four humors, mixed in various ways according to the objects of the imaginative faculty. For when an object is full of indignation and zeal, the spirits, vapors, and the gall-bladder <note>Yellow bile, stored in the gall-bladder, was associated with anger and the "choleric" temperament.</note>, raised by the power of the imagination, will acquire a hot and dry temperament. <margin>Whence the emotions are born</margin> These, stirred and agitated by very subtle, tumultuous, and stinging movements, will drive the mind into anger, fury, and rage—passions most similar to themselves. And if the object be pleasant, delightful, and full of love, bloody vapors raised from the storehouse of the liver, acquiring a hot and humid temperament and agitated by sweet and temperate movements, will affect the mind kindly and sweetly, whence joy, hope, confidence, love, and gladness arise. But if the object be horrid, sad, dismal, and tragic, vapors raised from the receptacle of black bile <note>original: "atra bilis"; the humor associated with melancholy.</note>, endowed with a cold and dry temperament, will imbue the animal spirit with the same quality they possess; whence grief, sadness, pain, commiseration, lamentation, and similar emotions are born. Finally, if the object be soft,

...gentle, delicate, sweet, and moderate—a middle ground between sadness and joy—the vapors will acquire a cold and moist temperament. The <term>animal spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus animalis"; in the 17th century, these were believed to be extremely fine vapors that acted as the medium between the soul and the body.</note>, being imbued with this temperament, will stir the soul toward similar passions. Thus will be born moderate joy, rest, and tranquility, a certain confidence of soul, honest love, and the like. We have seen how the <gloss>emotions</gloss> <note>original: "affectiones"</note> are born; now let us see how these same things are aroused by the power of music.

Music therefore possesses something entirely similar to the origin of the affections. For harmonic sound is a certain motion that stirs the air in precisely the same proportion of which the sound itself consists. Because the air is continuous with the animal spirit (which is similarly in perpetual motion), it happens that the soul is stirred by harmony—for harmony is naturally implanted and conate <note>Innate or born within.</note> to the soul, as shall be discussed in our *Metaphysical Music*. When the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> is excited by the "object" <note>In this context, the "object" is the subject matter or theme of the music.</note> presented by the words, the air stirs a natural humor <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament.</note> that is entirely similar and proportionate to that object and the harmonic movements. 

The vapor rising from that humor is then mixed with the animal spirit, which has already been stirred to the <gloss>rhythms</gloss> <note>original: "numeros"</note> of the harmony and the continuous harmonic air. Finally, by its agitation, this mixture compels the soul toward affections proportioned to the rhythms and words. For there lie hidden in individual things certain proportions, through whose concurrence all the "exotic" <note>Extraordinary or supernatural-seeming.</note> operations of things are perfected. Just as these shine forth in the wonderful consensus and dissent of things—which the Greeks call <term>sympathy and antipathy</term>—so do they most greatly shine in the business of harmony. 

<margin>How harmonic rhythm stirs the spirits, and how these stir the affections.</margin>

Therefore, harmonic rhythm first stirs the internal air and impresses harmonic motions upon it; next, it impels the imagination; this, once impelled, stirs the humors; the vaporous humors, mixed with the spirit or internal air, finally incline the person toward that which they represent. In this way, and no other, harmony moves the passions. 

Just as there is an infinite variety of harmonic motions, so too is there an infinite variety of the resulting affections. If anyone were to perfectly understand the reasoning behind these, he could undoubtedly perform the greatest miracles of nature in arousing the passions of the soul through the power of music. Nothing else would be required but to perfectly tune the harmonic and metrical rhythms to a spirit "pregnant" with some affection; once this is done, it is impossible that the intended effect would not follow.

But you may ask why we so rarely experience similar stirrings of the affections today. I answer that this happens because the harmonic motion does not correspond to the animal spirit in every respect. For this reason, the spirit is either dissipated more than is proper by the harmonic motion, or it becomes too sluggish, or it becomes thin in an unequal and inconstant way. 

<margin>Why modern music does not perform the miracles of the ancients.</margin>

If someone were able to adapt harmony so that the spirit was moved by the exact same motion as the harmonic rhythms, he would undoubtedly produce the intended effect. He would achieve the same thing that happens with two <term>polychords</term> <note>original: "polychordis"; likely referring to multi-stringed instruments like lutes or harpsichords.</note> tuned exactly in unison: when one is stirred by harmonic melodies, it produces the same harmony in the other, even though it is untouched, as will be shown in our *Musical Magic*. I have chosen to demonstrate all these things more at length in this passage so that the <term>musurgus</term> <note>A "music-maker" or composer, from the Greek "musourgos."</note> might more fully understand the cause of the stirring of the affections, and have a means by which he might finally arrive at a perfect knowledge of the art. Those who desire more on this matter should consult the first part of Book 9, and other things inserted here and there on this argument throughout this work.

Furthermore, since the cause of all diversity in tones is the diverse placement of the **semitone** <note>The smallest interval in the musical system of this time; a half-step.</note>; therefore, placed at the beginning, it produces one form of song; in the middle, another; at the end, another; and so on in the remaining intervals it produces one and then another form. I respond that since the semitone differs most from the other tones, it is also necessary that by its motion in the <term>tetrachords</term> <note>A scale of four notes spanning a "perfect fourth."</note> or species of the fourth, fifth, and octave, it causes the greatest change. In the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>A perfect fourth interval.</note>, when it is placed in the lowest position, it always produces I know not what sadness or mourning in the human soul. The reason for this is nothing other than that the voice, softening at the extremity of both the ascending and descending fourth, imbues the following tones with its softness to some extent. These tones, imbued with the softness of the semitone, consequently provide soft affections of the soul: love, sadness, and confidence, as appears in the following notes. Here the semitone, placed at the beginning when ascending, and at the end when descending, possesses I know not what "softness," as I said. But placed in the middle, it presents I know not what boldness, magnanimity, and severity; because the softness of the semitone is so blunted by the surrounding tones that, while it cannot exercise its own power, it is consequently forced to be under the law of the others. Thus, it is no wonder that effects result that are suitable to those tones. But placed at the end of some tetrachord, it portends I know not what indignation because of the two preceding tones, which exasperate the semitone.

It is added that since the harmonic motion of the semitone is much faster than the motion of the whole tone—for just as the proportion <term>sesquivigesima quarta</term> <note>The ratio 25:24, which Kircher uses here for the semitone.</note> is to the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>The ratio 9:8, a whole tone.</note> or <term>sesquinonal</term> <note>The ratio 10:9, a minor whole tone.</note>, so is the motion of the semitone to the motion of the tone—it follows that wherever it is placed, it always produces a notable alteration. Placed in the highest position after two tones, just as it easily dies away due to the thinness of its motion, so it cannot exercise its power because of the tyranny of the preceding tones. But placed in the first position, as it is slower, so it also shows its power more vigorously and livelily against the weaker power of the following tones, while it forces them to be under its own law. Placed in the middle, it so conquers the tones surrounding it, as if by certain flatteries, that the tones, having laid aside their wildness, become somewhat tamed.

### COROLLARY I.

You see, therefore, how from the diverse placement of the semitone in the tetrachord, three diverse tones are constituted, each of which responds to a different affection. You also see how in the octave the semitone changes its position seven times, and how from this change seven species of octave arise, concerning which we treated extensively in the fourth book. And since in each species the semitone is found twice, how from this fourteen tones or modes are born, and how, after two dissonant ones are rejected as if they were bastards, twelve true and customary tones finally emerge. Furthermore, it must be noted that the semitone does not obtain the same power when placed everywhere, but a different power in individual steps because of the respect of its motion to the preceding...

Hence, if the melody runs through or exceeds the whole octave, the song is spirited; if only a fourth <term>diatessaron</term>, it is modest and pleasant; if a fifth <term>diapente</term>, it possesses a moderate quality; a minor third brings dejection and smallness of soul. Therefore, the **semitone** is not without merit, as we have said elsewhere, the **soul of all music**;

<margin>The semitone is the soul of all music</margin>

for indeed, by its placement, it distinguishes both the modes and the genera, and procures all the vigor and grace of harmony. It seems that nature has, in a certain way, established it for the satisfaction of hearing, since without it, nothing in music is pleasing. For when the notes *Re, mi* are heard, the hearing is not satisfied but waits for *Fa* to be added; and when *Sol, fa* is perceived, unless *mi* follows, the hearing does not rest. 

Hence, that tone which has the major third <gloss>ditone</gloss> placed at the bottom is rightly considered active and full of effort, the power of which is **rhythm and motion** <note>original Greek: ῥύθμος καὶ κίνησίς</note>, seeking its end, namely the fourth <term>diatessaron</term>, of which the semitone is like its **soul** <note>original Greek: ψυχή</note>, sought with every effort. Furthermore, this power of the semitone gains a great deal of increase from the proportion of time and the rhythm itself; the proportion of time consists in the rise and fall <gloss>arsis and thesis</gloss> of the beat, and rhythm in the slowness and speed of movement. If a triple or double proportion is added to this, it acquires the power to move and incite the emotions in every number.

### COROLLARY II.

It is clear, finally, from this discourse, how different tones emanating from the placement of the semitone produce different affections in the soul of the listeners.

**The First Mode, Dorian**, according to the ancients and Lucian, is **solemn** <note>original Greek: σεμνός</note>, religious, sacred, and grave; according to Apuleius, it is warlike and most fit for performing heroic songs; it maintains a wonderful gravity combined with alacrity.

**The Second Mode, Hypodorian**, possesses a gloomy gravity according to the ancients, and is not at all flattering.

**The Third Mode, Phrygian**, is called **divinely inspired** <note>original Greek: ἔνθεος</note> by Lucian, and religious by Apuleius; for it has a severe insulting quality of indignation, whence it is also called **crooked** <note>original Greek: σκόλιος, implying something convoluted or agitated</note>; it is impetuous and suited to warlike matters. Likewise, it is like the tragic iambic, distracting and seizing the soul, and as it were, placing it outside of itself; so says Aristotle in the 8th book of his *Politics*, chapter 5, and Plato in the 3rd book of *The Republic*.

**The Fourth Mode, Hypophrygian**, is humble and most fit for weeping, since it has a sad complaint, a certain supplication, and lamentation. Yet, since this tone is almost the same as the third and is frequently confused with it, I do not see why it should stir up such different affects from the former.

**The Fifth Mode, Lydian**, is harsh, threatening, and cheerful, proper to the Lydians. Hence Plato, in the 50th dialogue of *The Republic*, rejects the Lydian and Ionian harmony as being "drunken." 

<margin>The Nature of the Tones</margin>

According to Lucian, it is **Bacchic** <note>original Greek: βακχικός</note>, that is, frenzied or insane; it corresponds to our eleventh mode.

**The Sixth Mode, Hypolydian**, has a tearful restraint; it is called a pious and, as it were, "wailing" mode, since it moves one to tears; it responds to our twelfth mode.

**The Seventh Mode, Mixolydian** <note>original: "Myolydius"</note>, moves the affects and renders them flexible and contracted, as it is mixed from Dorian gravity.

**The Eighth Mode, Hypomixolydian**, has a natural pleasantness.

**The Ninth Mode, Aeolian**, is mild and of wonderful sweetness for performing lyric poetry; it is called "foreign" by the moderns.

**The Tenth Mode, Hypoaeolian**, also possesses a remarkable sweetness.

**The Eleventh Mode, Ionian**, which the moderns call the fifth, is called **pleasant** <note>original Greek: γλαφυρός</note> by Lucian and **lascivious** by Apuleius; it is most fit for iambic and trochaic poems, the most natural of all, and not the least in musical harmony.

**The Twelfth Mode, Hypoionian**, tempers the softness of the Ionian and responds to our sixth mode.

And these are the affects which the Ancients attribute to the twelve tones, in which, however, they are by no means consistent with themselves; and there is such confusion in determining these matters that one hardly knows whom to follow...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of musical history from Book 5, specifically focusing on the transition from ancient notation to the system developed by Guido of Arezzo and later refined by Johannes de Muris.</meta>

556 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Regarding what we said previously in Book 5, Chapter 2, where we provided a specimen of that ancient music with dots <note>original: "punctis"; referring to neumes or early punctum notation</note>, I noted that the earlier method was intolerably difficult. When Guido noticed this, he applied his mind seriously to how he might meet such great difficulty with a new and easy method. It finally happened that on the feast of St. John the Baptist, while he was more attentively revolving the Hymn *so that your servants may with loosened voices* <note>original: "ut queant laxis resonare fibris"</note> in his mind, he reasoned with himself—not so much by human as by divine instinct—in this way: "What if the first syllables of this hymn could be of some assistance to me in the effort I have conceived in my mind?" No sooner said than done. For from *Ut queant laxis*, while he wrote it separately, he took *Ut*; and from *resonare fibris*, *Re*; from the joining of these syllables, *Ut, Re*, he established a tone. Then from *mira gestorum*, he added *Mi* to the aforementioned *Ut, Re*; and he made *Ut, Re, Mi*, to which he added the first syllable from *Famuli tuorum*, *Fa*, and there came forth *Ut, Re, Mi, Fa*. Finally, from the first syllables of *Solve polluti* and *Labii reatum*, he produced *Sol, La*. Thus he produced six syllables: *Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La*. These he arranged step-by-step between four lines, using dots in place of notes, so that they might be easily grasped and sung by students, as you see here.

->[Musical staff with notes and text below: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, sol, fa, mi, re, ut.]<-

Proceeding from these happy beginnings to facilitate the new invention in every musical task, he arranged these same syllables on the left hand <note>The "Guidonian Hand," a mnemonic device where parts of the hand represent different notes</note> in such a way that the semitone *mi-fa* always had two tones below it and as many above it, just as is evident in the hand and the Guidonian scale in Book 5.

He added these seven letters—A, B, C, D, E, F, G—which they had used in place of notes up until his own time, to honor the custom of the ancients. And lest anyone should be so ungrateful toward the Greek musicians as to not know that this science came from them, he placed the letter Gamma ($\Gamma$) at the lowest seat of the hand, to which he willed the first syllable or voice, *ut*, to respond. Thus, following the natural order of the seven letters corresponding to the voices, he completed the entire scale <margin>Invention of the musical scale</margin>, upon which all the secrets of the whole of music not undeservedly depend. I would gladly explain it in this place, had we not already provided for it abundantly in Books 3 and 4. Guido was also the first to adapt the keyboard <term>Abacum claviarium: the layout of keys on an instrument</term>, which the Italians call *tastatura*, divided by its intervals, to the harpsichord <note>original: "clavicymbalo"</note>, as is evident in a certain letter cited in Book 5. From this, as if from a certain fountain, the logic of the whole of polyphony flowed forth. For from the consonance of strings struck by small wooden jacks <margin>Origin of the multi-stringed keyboard</margin>, he finally successfully discovered the method of polyphony, or the harmony of several voices, which he taught should be established not only on the multi-stringed instrument, but also with suitable voices. And these were the first elements of Guido’s figured music, which, like the beginnings of all things, still displayed something crude, unpolished, and undigested, since he used only dots in place of notes, without any certain measure or proportion of time. This continued until about two hundred years later, when Johannes de Muris, by bringing the Guidonian invention back to the anvil <note>A metaphor for refining or reworking a tool</note>, <margin>Johannes de Muris, inventor of musical notes</margin> completed the musical art in all its numbers. For from the symbols *b* <note>soft b</note> and $\natural$ <note>square or hard b</note>, with which signs Guido used to mark the pitch-lines or voices, he derived notes through continuous addition or subtraction, each of which is double the preceding one in terms of the duration of time.

And the notes signified by *b* he called "minims"; but the notes indicated by a black *b* [Musical symbols] he called "semiminims"; those same with a tail, "fusas"; and with two tails, "semifusas." Thus from a single *b*, four different species of notes emerged: minims, semiminims, fusas, and semifusas. The remaining notes of longer duration [Musical symbols: Breve, Semi-breve] he formed from the hard or square *b*. From a truncated *b*, with both tails cut off, he formed this note which he called the "breve." He derived the "semibreve" from a round *b* deprived of its tail. He formed the "long" from a perfectly square *b* with an elongated tail [Musical symbols]. Finally, he formed the "maxima" from an extended tail and the product of a square twice as large, as is evident to the side. <margin>Long, Maxima</margin> I wished to describe these here in detail so that it would be clear from what principles the invention of notes emerged. To these notes he gave a perfect measure of time for harmonic modulations, and with the greatest skill he measured out individual harmonic durations through them; in a word, he gave a soul to the whole of harmony.

### CHAPTER II.

#### On the Dignity and Excellence of Ecclesiastical Song

That Ecclesiastical song has been in use from the very beginnings of the nascent Church at all times is shown by Saint Paul in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 14: *When you come together, each of you has a psalm*; and to the Ephesians, chapter 5: *Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and songs.* <note>original: "p psalmis, hymnis & canticis"</note> Saint Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> in *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3, says: "The holy melody of the psalms, which is joined to almost all priestly mysteries <term>Sacerdotal mysteries; refers here to the sacraments, particularly the Eucharist</term> and adheres to the nature of their substance, ought not to have been missing from the most supreme and principal mystery of all." Tertullian, in book 2 of *To His Wife*, writes: "Psalms and hymns sound between the two <note>referring to a Christian husband and wife</note> and they mutually challenge one another to see who might sing better to their God; Christ, seeing and hearing such things, rejoices." Saint Athanasius also, in his *Apology for Flight*, indicates that psalmody was customarily celebrated in the Church; for in narrating how he escaped the hands of his enemies when Arian <note>Arianism was a major Christological heresy in the early Church that denied the full divinity of Christ.</note> soldiers raided the church to capture him, he says: "I remained in my chair, having sent the deacon to sing the psalm (*For his mercy endures forever*)." Regarding this history, see more extensively Socrates, Nicephorus, and other ecclesiastical writers. Philo, in his book *On the Contemplative Life*, narrating the beginnings of the ecclesiastical institution and speaking of the early Christians, says: "Not only do they understand the hymns of the ancients with more subtlety, but they themselves compose new ones to God, modulating them in all meters and sounds with a sufficiently honorable and sweet composition; for one, rising from the midst of all, intones a psalm in honorable melodies." Dionysius the Areopagite, in the place cited before, finally says: "The Bishop, returning again to the holy altar, <margin>Book 3, *On the Hierarchy*</margin> begins to sing the sacred psalms, and all the ecclesiastical orders sing with him." Saint Justin [writes]: "Simply singing is not [only] suitable for children, but singing with inanimate instruments, and with dancing and rattles [is not]; therefore the use of such instruments was removed from the Churches, and simple singing was left. <margin>Response to Orthodox Question 107</margin> For this excites us and the soul toward an ardent desire for that which is sung in the poems; it soothes the affections rising from the flesh, expels evil thoughts, and waters the soul." Saint Jerome [notes]: "In the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, in the evening, and at the middle of the night, <margin>In the epitaph of Paula, on Psalm 116</margin> they sang the psalter in order, nor was it permitted for any of the sisters to be ignorant of the psalms. And just as the martyrs praise the Lord in the Land of the Living, so the monks, who sing psalms to the Lord day and night, ought to have the same piety as the martyrs, for they themselves are martyrs. For what the Angels do in Heaven, the Monks do on earth." The recitation of psalms, according to the testimony of Basil, <margin>On the Psalms</margin> provides the most abundant and pleasant fruits: it is the tranquility of souls, the arbiter of entering into peace, by whose help overflowing and tumultuous thoughts draw back and find rest. The psalm is the counselor of friendship, the union of those who disagree, the mediator for establishing peace between enemies, a kind of amulet for routing and driving away demons, and a solicitor of angelic protection. The utility of singing psalms consoles sad hearts, makes minds more grateful, struggles against the weary, awakens the lazy, and invites sinners to lamentation. For however hard the hearts of carnal men may be, as soon as the sweetness of the psalm sounds, it bends the soul toward the affection of piety—so says Basil. Furthermore, Dionysius, in the place cited, indicates that psalmody was performed with alternating voices in these words: "They carry out the custom of singing hymns to one another as if in one concordant and harmonious dance of things." <margin>Letter 63</margin> Saint Basil also [describes] the singers divided into two parts, with alternating turns...

testifies that they were accustomed to sing; while they sang psalms, they used to stand, so that through the posture of the body they might demonstrate the internal disposition of the mind, and show that they were prepared either for taming the flesh or for physical exercise for the sake of themselves and their brothers. This custom was later confirmed by various Councils. How much sweetness Saint Augustine perceived from this kind of psalm recitation, he himself testifies sufficiently in his *Confessions*. He says: "How much I wept in your hymns and canticles, moved by the voices of your sweet-sounding Church: those voices flowed sharply into my ears, and your truth melted into my heart, and from it a fervor of piety glowed, and then tears ran down, and it was well with me with them; and yet then, when the scent of your ointments was so fragrant, we did not run after you." <note>Augustine is quoting the Song of Solomon here.</note> And: "Therefore I wept more during the songs of your hymns, formerly sighing for you; and finally breathing again, as much as the breeze allows in a house of straw." (And a little later:) "However, when I remember my tears, which I shed at the songs of your Church in the beginnings of the restored faith of my salvation, and then I am moved not by the singing, but by the things that are sung, I again acknowledge the great utility of this institution, etc."

From these examples brought forward, unless I am mistaken, it is clear enough that Ecclesiastical song has always flourished in the Church.

### CHAPTER III.

#### How Psalm, Canticle, and Hymn differ.

We properly call Psalmody the "Davidic Music," <note>Referring to the Psalms of King David from the Old Testament.</note> which has flourished in the Church at all times. Saint Chrysostom asks and wonders why, more than all other scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, all Christians have so loved the book of the Psalms of David, and have wished to have this alone on their lips. In the church, he says, for those keeping vigil through the night, David is first, middle, and last; at dawn, the musical modulations of hymns are sought, and David is first, middle, and last. In monasteries, in the flocks of virgins imitating Mary, and first and middle at the funerals of the dead, David is first, middle, and last. In the deserts, men crucified to the world speaking with God, David is first, middle, and last, <margin>The excellence of Davidic hymns.</margin> because nothing is more divine than them, nothing more sacred, nothing more suited to moving the soul than the symphony of sacred song; while in the Church, those of diverse ages and virtues sing together like an indistinct harmony <term>Indiscreta concordia; a harmony where individual voices blend into a single, unified sound</term> of various strings; they rejoice with the Angels, Christ takes pleasure in His own songs, and the whole heaven exults.

A psalm, therefore, is nothing other than a certain sacred poem composed by David, concerning whose nature we treated most extensively in Book 2. Hymns, however, according to the testimony of Saint Augustine, are songs containing the praises of God; if it is praise but not of God, it is not a hymn; and if it is both praise and God's praise, but is not sung, it is not a hymn. It is necessary, therefore, that if it is a hymn, it must have these three: praise, God's praise, and song. Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in iambic poem 15, says:

*Modulated praise is a hymn, as I think;*
*A psalm with singing is psalmody.*

Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a 1st-century Jewish philosopher whose descriptions of the "Therapeutae" were viewed by early Christians as a model for their own ascetic and musical practices.</note> recorded that those first Christians sang hymns; he says: "They not only contemplate, but also compose canticles and hymns to the praise of God in various types of meters and poems, arranging rhythms into a more august and religious form; then, rising, he first sings a hymn in praise of God, either recently composed by himself, or written by one of the ancient prophets, for ancient poems of that kind exist in trimeter verse and hymns with their accents among the sacred rites of singing before the altars." From this, the antiquity of hymns is clear enough. The Annals refer to the fact that in the Council of Antioch, 1300 years ago, Paul of Samosata was condemned because he rejected <note>original: "exploserit," literally "hissed off the stage" or exploded</note> the psalms and hymns composed in honor of Christ in that century as being too recent. Regarding the ecclesiastical hymns—

Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-making, etc. 561 [handwritten: 559]

Saint Jerome teaches that Saint Hilary published a book of <note>original: "sticorum librū"; likely referring to "hymnorum monasticorum" or "mysticorum," meaning monastic or mystical hymns.</note> hymns. Saint Augustine also teaches that Saint Ambrose was the author of many hymns. According to the Council of Toledo, it is known that some were composed with great zeal for the praise of God and the triumphs of the Apostles and martyrs, such as those published by the most blessed Doctors Hilary and Ambrose, which were later greatly expanded by Prudentius and others, about whom we shall speak elsewhere.

Saint Hilary, in the prologue to his exposition of the psalms, distinguishes a "canticle" from a "psalm." He says a **psalm** is when, the voice being silent, only the striking of the accompanying instrument <note>original: "Organi"; in this early context, "organ" refers generally to a musical instrument like a psalter or lyre, not necessarily the modern pipe organ.</note> is heard. A **canticle**, however, is when the choir of singers, using its freedom, is not bound to the harmonious obedience of the instrument, but exults solely in the melody of the sounding voice. <margin>What is a Canticle?</margin> A "canticle of the psalm" is when the voice of the singing choir follows and rivals a preceding instrument, imitating the manner of the psalter with the modulations of the voice. Conversely, a "psalm of the canticle" is when the art of the harmonizing instrument is adapted to a human hymn led by the choir. Saint Jerome assigns a slightly different distinction between the psalm, the hymn, and the canticle: **Hymns** are those which marvel at the strength and majesty of God, and always at His benefits or deeds; these are contained in all psalms to which "Alleluia" is either prefixed or added. **Psalms**, however, properly belong to the "Ethical" place <note>That is, the realm of moral conduct.</note>, so that through the instrument of the body, we may know what is to be done and what is to be avoided. But he who disputes concerning higher things, and as a subtle observer explains the harmony of the world and the order and concord of all creatures, he sings a **spiritual song** (or canticle). Or certainly (to speak more clearly for the sake of the simpler folk), the psalm refers to the body, while the canticle refers to the mind. Euthymius, in his preface to the psalms, says that a psalm is properly that song which is brought forth by a sweet voice simultaneously with the instrument of the psalter; but an **ode** or **canticle** is a certain musical voice with harmony brought forth by the mouth alone. Furthermore, regarding who was the author of the canticle, various people hold various opinions. Most make Moses the first creator of the canticle, whence this is far older than the psalm; for the use of the canticle endured until the times of David, who was the first of all to begin writing psalms. For although they used the instrument of the psalter before then, its use was without any art and quite common, for it was played only to soothe the flocks. David, therefore, beautifully adapted an instrument of this kind and transferred its use to God.

An **Antiphon** is a "reciprocal voice," namely, with two choirs singing psalms alternately in a changed order, or one by one. <margin>What is an Antiphon?</margin> Isidore makes Saint Ignatius the first creator of these in the Greek Church. Paulinus, in his *Life of Saint Ambrose*, attributes them to Ambrose in the Latin Church with these words: "At this time—namely 338 AD—antiphons, hymns, and vigils first began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan; the devotion of this celebration remains not only in that same Church, but through almost all the provinces of the West." Saint Augustine credits Saint Ambrose with this same thing: "It was well instituted," he says, "that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions, lest the people wither away with greater weariness; from that time it has been retained to the present day, with many and almost all your flocks imitating it throughout the rest of the world." Some ascribe this to Pope Saint Damasus, as is read in his acts.

### CHAPTER III.

### On the dignity of Gregorian Chant and its abuse, which has crept into Churches everywhere.

From Saint Ambrose and Damasus until the times of Gregory the Great, ecclesiastical song remained in that simplicity which the new institution and the condition of the times required, without any distinction of modes, signs of time, or measure. But as has been said, they sang either psalms or hymns with a clear voice <term>antiphonally <gloss>original Greek: ἀντιφώνως (antiphōnōs)</gloss></term>, that is, with alternating choirs.

560 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...they were [awaiting]. Therefore, to reconcile ecclesiastical chant with a greater dignity, Gregory the Great—having first assembled men most skilled in musical matters, of which he himself was most expert—set himself seriously to this task: to distinguish ecclesiastical chant with certain notes <note>original: "notis"</note>, which have been discussed elsewhere, and to arrange Masses, hymns, and psalms according to the artistry of the tones <term>tonorum artificium; the system of eight church modes</term> through the rules of song. He did this so that those singing the psalms, through a perfect measurement of voices, might instill a focused feeling of piety in the listeners. This he finally accomplished for the greatest good of the entire Christian Commonwealth. And this is that Gregorian chant, most celebrated throughout the whole Church. Following in his footsteps, subsequent Popes, through the work of men skilled in music, have at all times increased it with many distinguished additions, as is evident from the ancient Graduals and Antiphonaries. In these books, beyond the wonderful artistry and the admirable arrangement of the tones, a sense of piety shines forth; they are so well-suited to stirring whatever affections are in the soul of the listeners that they seem to have been instituted not by human, but by a certain divine instinct.

<margin>The excellence of ecclesiastical hymns</margin>

Two Germans in particular showed themselves to be such masters: Notker <note>OCR: "Notuerus"; referring to Notker the Stammerer</note>, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Gall, and Hermann the Lame <note>original: "Hermannus Contractus"</note>, Count of Veringen. Both were men of great genius who, in their songs composed according to the Gregorian rule <note>original: "amussim," meaning a level or ruler</note>, seem to have shown more musical talent than a huge flock of others with six hundred wagonloads of songs. What can ever be heard more suited to piety than those divine hymns? *Sing, my tongue, of the Savior's glory* <note>original: "Pange lingua gloriosi"</note>, etc., and: *From the sun's rising hinge* <note>original: "A solis ortu cardine"</note>; *Praises to the Paschal Victim* <note>original: "Victimæ paschali laudes"</note>; and countless others which the manuscript Graduals, Antiphonaries, and Hymnals of the ancient monks display. In these, they handled all the modes most successfully; and they did not merely handle them, but applied them to the subject matter according to the condition of the material. They expressed this with such artistry through the native character of the modes that it is known to those who judge these things—not by their own whim, as is now done, but by art and applied study—that nothing more perfect could have been made by man.

Ecclesiastical chant is, therefore, full of majesty, and possesses I know not what power for stirring souls toward God, especially if it is performed with the required decorum and care. I do not think anything more effective can be found for calming the soul than listening to monks or clerics singing the said hymns and canticles in that unison <note>original: "vnisona"</note> symphony of alternating equal voices, with a constant tenor <term>tenore; here meaning a steady, sustained duration</term> preserving the required proportion of time and measure. Consequently, for this reason alone, those in charge and the leaders of this business ought to insist upon the dignity of this ecclesiastical chant with the greatest zeal. However, we see with sorrow that this is not so studiously observed by

<margin>Abuses in ecclesiastical chant</margin>

everyone today. There are those who perform this angelic duty of singing psalms and praising God with no, or certainly very little, decency; by rushing too much, or by mutilating syllables, or by committing various other defects. They would do a worthwhile thing if they would listen to and hereafter obey the warnings which Saint Bonaventure religiously hands down concerning this matter in *The Mirror of Discipline*, Part 1, Chapter 16, in these words: *They ought to say the office distinctly, continuously, entirely, and orderly. Distinctly, lest they confuse the things to be said by "chewing" the words, or uttering them thinly, or by rushing too much. Continuously, so that interruptions do not occur by talking in between. Entirely, so that they omit nothing of what is to be said. Finally, they should strive to execute the office orderly in substance, time, manner, and all things.* Thus says Saint Bonaventure. But let these things suffice concerning ecclesiastical chant.

In this way, harmony may shine forth not only in the ensemble, but also in the voices and in the very gestures of the body with elegant proportion, just as singers endowed with judgment do.

### CHAPTER V.

#### On the defects and abuses of modern Composers, or those whom they commonly call "Componistas."

It is certainly impossible that, in such a great crowd of musicians, notable abuses and defects should not be committed. For while all are naturally affected by music, and everyone—out of that natural self-love <note>original: "philautia"; Greek for vanity or excessive self-love</note>—prefers to be heard rather than to hear, and each values only his own things and not others', it happens that even men of the lowest sort set their hand to the business of composition <note>original: "melotheticum negotium"</note>, which is the proper domain of skilled musicians who are powerful in judgment. From this, there are almost as many "music-makers" <note>original: "Musurgi"</note> as there are choir masters, and as many "polyphonists" <note>original: "symphonetæ"</note> as there are singers. Since these are for the most part ignorant and inexperienced in theory, and do not possess any judgment in discerning the dignified from the undignified, they think the whole craftsmanship of music—or the "melotactic" art <note>the art of arranging melodies</note>—consists in this alone: adding voices upon voices. They take no account of the Mode <note>original: "Toni"; the musical scales or church modes</note>, its nature and properties, and much less of the melody to be applied to the words, or other circumstances that constitute a perfect musician. Certainly, it is necessary that intolerable defects are born from this. How many composers are found today who, when beginning a composition, first judiciously look around to see: what is the theme? for which mode? which words? for what time and measure? which harmony or rhythm do they suit? How few musicians are found today who compose supported by their own 

<margin>
In composing, one must not trust the fallible judgment of the ears.
</margin>

skill, and by true, certain, and infallible science! Instead, they do whatever they do by sole and naked experience. To be more certain of a finished composition, they first flee to the harpsichord <note>original: "clavecymbalum"</note> as if to a "Lydian stone" <note>a touchstone used to test the purity of gold</note>. There, first studiously weighing individual parts, they learn the harmonies and the summaries of them and similar things from that instrument. This is an altogether dangerous business and exposed to innumerable errors and deceptions. For from this it happens that they foully mix consonants with dissonants; they repeatedly place semitones where nature flees from them, and omit them where nature requires them. Hence they arrange tritones and major sixths so clumsily that they turn the stomachs of the experts. If their compositions were recalled to the rules of arithmetic, you would find that nothing is able to stand. Nor is it enough to say that these things achieve their success on the harpsichord, since it is one thing to stand by the fallacious judgment of the ears, and another to stand by the scrutiny of irrefragable science. If they were skilled in music, they would judge otherwise; if they had expertise in intervals, they would have no need of all these [instruments]. Therefore, for a music-maker and composer to uphold his profession with dignity, it is necessary at the very least that he be skilled in the eminent science of harmonic intervals according to arithmetic precepts.

Another no less intolerable defect flourishes among modern musicians: they reject all imitation. I call "imitation" when one discusses in detail the various styles of the most illustrious composers, studiously examines individual parts, and converts the unique things occurring in them to his own use. But a most foul custom has grown up elsewhere and especially here in Rome, so that none of those who preside over the various church choirs as masters either values or deigns to sing any music except his own. Indeed, self-love...

Book VII. On Antique-modern Music-making. 563

...most foolish. Who, even if they were a born poet, will ever produce anything of dignity in a poetic style unless they have read and studied to imitate those eminent leaders of the poets—Virgil, Ovid, Horace, and others? What variety will our music-makers <term>musurgi; those who craft or "work" music</term> show us if, neglecting this practice of imitation, they insist only on their own inventions?

In every age, both in the present and in the preceding century, music has produced men greater than any exception: those who, joining theory to practice with such exquisite study and persistent labor, mastered all parts of music so thoroughly that they seem to have snatched away from others any hope of reaching further. Who today can match the genius and dexterity of Josquin des Prez <note>Latin: "Iodocus Pratensis"</note>, Jacob Obrecht, or Cipriano de Rore? Who among the moderns can achieve the ingenious weaving of harmonies found in Orlando di Lasso, Cristóbal de Morales, or Palestrina <note>Latin: "Praenestinus"; referring to Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina</note>? Furthermore, there were in Germany, France, and England many—and today there are still some—endowed with an admirable skill in music. If one were to weigh their melodic style <term>stylus melotheticus; the method of composing melody</term> and melodies in the balance, they would undoubtedly find beneath them such an exact form of music, and such ingenious and elaborate compositions, that they would assert nothing could be added or taken away. If modern musicians were to penetrate these works, and if they would excerpt the best parts, who does not see that from such a great variety of inventions they could always turn something new to their own use? But while they arrogantly despise whatever is "foreign"—whatever has come from outside the sphere of their own country—it is no wonder that such miserable compositions, subject to so many errors and vices, come forth daily even in the most prominent places. I wish, however, to except here the skilled musicians and those powerful in judgment, whom we shall mention in the following pages.

Furthermore, the greatest inconveniences follow this lack of imitation: for while each person values only his own work, while he adores only his own filth <note>original: "sordes"; suggesting unrefined or "dirty" drafts</note>, the result is that their entire art and craftsmanship is exhausted in ten or twenty cadences <term>clausula; a musical ending or cadence</term>. These they have nevertheless stealthily stolen from others and made their own with a few minor changes. Hence, such a meager variety of harmonic style is perceived everywhere in the churches. Hence, you may almost always perceive the same chirping <term>teretismus; a meaningless vocalization or warbling</term>, the same clucking <term>glocismus; a sound compared to a hen's cluck</term>, and the same cadences to the point of nausea and disgust. Indeed, if ever a certain cadence receives any applause from the listeners, it is impossible to say how much that same cadence is exhausted in almost all churches, and how heavy a yoke it is forced to undergo; for they stuff it indiscriminately not only into Masses, but also into psalms, hymns, motets—in short, into all compositions. This is certainly a clear proof of musical poverty and a lack of skill in inventing new modes of composition. This arises from nothing other than the contempt for imitation, as I said, and a lack of application and a weariness of labor, which causes them to abandon every effort to penetrate excellent things with a noble spirit.

<margin>Why few musicians compose well</margin>

Added to this is that most people complete their compositions not so much by the incentive of honor or their own reputation, as by a sordid greed for the profit and money for which they gape. Hence, nothing is truly elaborate, nothing is weighed exactly according to the laws of music; instead, whatever is hastily collected from here and there and poorly stuffed into the proposed theme—even in the space of a single night—is exposed to the ears of the simple. Let the song be whatever it may; as long as money is collected, it suffices. Oh, foul vileness of soul! Certainly, this is one of the greatest impediments to reaching remarkable perfection in music. For what else would you expect from a man intent on profit and greed than something hasty, inconsiderate, and distorted by the carelessness of a hurried pen? Those who, on the contrary, care for their own reputation weigh everything with persistent study and ponder with exquisite judgment, so that everything may hang together beautifully. They watch with singular care lest anything should be gaping, unseemly, or committed against harmonic laws; in this way, it is impossible for the intended beauty of the composition <term>melothesia; the art of composing melody</term> not to emerge.

Another defect which most modern musicians commit is this: they do not study how to adapt words to harmonic measures skillfully or according to the rules of prosody. But even this should not seem strange, since many are so ignorant of the Latin language that they grasp neither the meaning, nor the rhythm, nor the length of the syllables in the chosen theme. Hence those ridiculous pronunciations and foul errors; while they shorten long syllables and lengthen short ones, they tear the language apart so foully that nothing could be more discordant. Added to this is another much more intolerable defect: when they do not distinguish the emotion <note>original: "affectionem"; the specific mood or rhetorical intent of a text</note> of the theme. I shall explain this by an example.

Bbbb 2 I happened upon...
