564 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance.*

I recently came across a composition on this theme: *God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes, where there is no mourning, crying, or pain, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Absterget Deus omnem lacrymam ab oculis eorum, ubi nullus luctus, clamor aut dolor &c."</note> in which the author plays excessively with the words *tears, mourning, and pain*, striving in every way to make the musical phrase exceedingly sad. Who does not see in this "play" a most grave defect of judgment? For I cannot imagine what tears, pain, or mourning have in common with the excessive joys of the celestial fatherland and the dancing and exultation of blessed spirits <note>Kircher argues that because the text is about God *removing* sorrow, the music should be joyful, not sad.</note>. Not long ago, another composer, by contrast, in a different subject—*Death hastens mournfully* <note>original Latin: "Mors festinat luctuosa"</note>—plays with these words through each voice in the manner of a fugue, in which neither the song nor the mode responds to the emotion, nor does the tempo suit the action. For what does mournful death have to do with leaps or with a loose and most lively impulse of movement?

[A musical staff appears here with diamond-shaped notes in a C-clef. The lyrics below the notes read:]
Death hastens mournfully, it hastens, it hastens. [repeated parts]

Composers of Masses fall into this same error. While they ought to express the voice *Kyrie eleison* <note>Greek for "Lord have mercy"</note> before God through a humble affection of a suppliant and prostrate soul, they instead repeat it with ridiculous leaps and an incongruous increase of fast, diminished notes in musical phrases more fitting for dance-halls and theaters than for the Church. But perhaps they are to be forgiven for this, since they do not understand what the Greek words mean. I could bring forward countless compositions of this sort here; but because musicians can easily understand my mind from a few examples, I thought it superfluous to dwell on them any longer.

It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, what modern musicians should avoid and what they should imitate, so that, having avoided these "harmonic monsters," they may reach the intended perfection of music. Above all, let them consider this rule to be kept: that they should obtain for themselves all authors, whether written or printed, examine each one, and like a busy bee, convert the better juice of the flowers into honey, not easily despising any foreigner. 

<margin>What musicians should avoid and what they should imitate</margin>

For those who have traveled through Germany, France, and England, and have duly examined musical works published in every genre of harmonic style, will find those melodies <term>melissimata; literally "honeyed songs," referring to elaborate melodic passages</term> worked out with such diligence, labor, and tireless scrutiny of musical ornaments, and such variety of invention in properly adorning compositions, that they will be forced to confess they could do nothing similar themselves. For this study of imitation is the same as the study of wide reading among poets and orators. Who among Italian poets will ever hope to arrive at a distinguished skill in vernacular poetry unless he first grasps the most praised monuments of Petrarch, Dante, Tasso, Ariosto, Sannazaro, and countless others, holding them, as it were, in mind and memory? What painter will hope to reach any perfection of art unless he has studied to imitate with every effort the surviving monuments of the paintings of Albrecht Dürer, Raphael of Urbino, Michelangelo Buonarroti, Guido Reni, Peter Paul Rubens, and other princes in the art? I say the same must be performed by musicians, without which they should know for certain they will produce nothing worthy of themselves.

They will learn from the French the dance-like style <term>stylus hyporchematicus; music intended for dancing or active movement</term>, swelling with exotic triple rhythms; from the English, the symphonic style, flourishing with a wonderful variety of instruments; from the Germans, the harmonious and ingenious weaving of many voices. Thus the image of Helen <note>Kircher refers to the legendary beauty of Helen of Troy, often used as a metaphor for a "perfect" beauty created by combining the best features of many different people.</note>, fashioned from the most proportional members of all other images, will express a harmony most perfect in all its parts. How this is to be performed, and how it has been performed by ingenious authors at all times, we shall now attempt to manifest.

# PART II.
## CHAPTER I.
### *On Pathetic Musurgy and the method of establishing it well and properly.*

Since the sole end of pathetic music <term>musurgia pathetica; the art of composing music that moves the emotions (pathos)</term> is to move various affections according to the nature of the proposed and assumed theme: and since the first foundation of this variation and change of passions are the Tones or Modes, which the Greeks therefore not incongruously call *tropes* <note>original Greek: "tropos"; meaning a "turn" or "way" of expressing a mood</note>; we shall begin from them.

Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-making. 565

Before we proceed, I cannot wonder enough at the vain and useless labor of certain **music-pretenders** <note>original: "Musicastrorū," a derogatory term for amateurish or pseudo-musicians</note> in the correct assignment of tones. It seems to me that such people are perpetually occupied in filling the sieve-like jar of the **Danaids** <note>A Greek mythological reference to a task that can never be completed</note>; while they do nothing but try to demonstrate that they have revealed something great to the world, once everything is finished and the matter is well considered, they are found—just like all the others—to have been "fishing in the air," empty of both brains and purse. I too have struck against this rock not infrequently. For I have compared as many Greek and Latin manuscript monuments concerning musical matters as I could obtain; while weighing them and comparing one with another, I found such a confusion of opinions regarding tones and their limitations, and such diverse views, that among those who differ I have not found even one who completely agrees with another. First of all, you would greatly wonder that this musical dispute flourished most intensely even among the primary classical authors: **Aristoxenus, Cleomedes, Aristides**, and others whom I cited above. While **Ptolemy** stubbornly contradicts Aristoxenus, **Briennius** and **Alypius** contradict him, and others contradict **Nicomachus**. Ptolemy established the order of Tones and the logic of the systems much differently than those earlier authors who preceded him; **Boethius** did it differently again, although no one is more worthy of being followed than this most judicious author. Therefore, a dispute regarding the correct constitution of tones has flourished at all times, and no one has been found until now who has resolved it. 

<margin>Diverse opinions on the number of Tones</margin> **Glareanus** <note>Heinrich Glareanus (1488–1563), a famous Swiss music theorist</note> indeed, in his *Dodecachordon* <note>Kircher writes "decachordo," but refers to Glareanus's influential work *Dodecachordon*</note> after twenty years of labor, set himself up as the distributor of justice in this dispute; but even he is so inconsistent and varied in his views, and differs so much from the ancients, that it clearly appears he was by no means able to avoid this tide of confusion. **Franchinus** <note>Franchinus Gaffurius (1451–1522)</note>, somewhat older than him, differs entirely from everyone else while he too devises new machines and structures. **Galileo** <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei and a leading music theorist</note>, while he busies himself with restoring the tones, destroys them through excessive persecution of modern music. The **Moderns** who followed these, while they busy themselves trying to make the predecessors agree with the ancients, go off in different directions and disagree on the whole business. First, they are entirely caught up in names: where one establishes the **Dorian** as the first tone, another the **Phrygian**, and another the **Lydian**. Some establish only three tones, others eight, others 12, 13, 14, 15, 24; finally, there are those who establish 72. Given such inconsistency and variety, it is no wonder that such disparate judgments follow regarding the nature and property of the tones: some say the first is lascivious, soft, and petulant, while others call it grave, tempered, and chaste. When I saw this ridiculous altercation and noted that the entire dispute lay not in the nature of the thing (which is immutable) but only in terms, words, and names, I judged it should be rejected as useless and contributing little to the perfection of music. For what does it matter to the beauty of our music whether the ancients used this or that system? Whether they established the Dorian, Phrygian, or Lydian as first? Whether this one begins the tones from *Mi* or that one from *Re*? All these things contribute nothing to our purpose, seeing as they depend on the whim of men and have no other cause than the "good pleasure" of those who laid the first foundations of this faculty; for so it seemed fit to them.

Since, therefore, music is a perfect science and its seeds are implanted in humans by nature, it is certain that it has principles of eternal truth and immutable reasons for the **affects** <term>affects: the specific emotional states or "passions" that music is intended to evoke</term>, as was shown at length above in Book 2. Abstracting, therefore, from all such grammatical trifles and vain altercations—which, depending as they do on the inconsistent principle of human will, would never reach an end or limit—I have seriously kept watch so that I might intimately penetrate the nature of the seven species of the **diapason** <term>diapason: the Greek term for an octave</term>, in which the business of all music of the passions turns as if on a hinge. For from the nature of these intervals, I hoped that, by the wise guidance of nature, I would finally reach the nature of individual tones through the causes hidden beneath such diverse intervals. Thus, I would finally apply individual tones to their corresponding affects, which is the goal of all music. Furthermore, I would clearly show by these means that there was never anything in the music of the ancients that is not also contained in ours; for nature has never failed in anything, and the vigor of genius has not diminished in any way—indeed, in the present time, it is both more vigorous and better equipped with all the resources that past centuries have brought forth for us. And although we described the nature of harmonic intervals at length a little earlier in other parts of this work, it seemed right here to apply them to practical music-making as an **experienced definition** <note>original Greek: "ἔμπειρον ὅρως" (empeiron horos)</note>. In doing this, I shall compel no one to agree with me, but let each have their own judgment based on the fairness of the matter proposed; for neither...

He argues that instead of arguing over labels, musicians should focus on the immutable natural laws of the octave and how specific intervals scientifically trigger human emotions (affects).</summary>

# 566 [of the] Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

For I do not wish to be heard here as some Aristarchus, nor as a Pythagorean **"he himself said it,"** <note>original Greek: "αὐτὸς ἔφα" (autos epha). This refers to the 'Ipse dixit,' a plea to authority where a statement is accepted as true simply because a master said it.</note> but I only wished to stir musicians by this humble work of mine, so that they might leave behind useless disputes and consult nature; having thrown away the useless husk, they might embrace the kernel and the marrow.

Since, therefore, the science of music is the science of **sonorous number**; and because every sound—as has been stated elsewhere—involves a movement of the air, which indeed, if it be well-proportioned, affects the soul and the hearing in a good way; but if it be poorly proportioned, it affects them badly. From this come the first foundations of **consonance and dissonance**. Furthermore, since harmonic number essentially consists in the various rising of intervals, and since rising and falling <note>original: "ascensus" and "descensus"</note> wonderfully alter harmonic motion—as when the progression moves from low <note>original: "graui", meaning deep or low-pitched</note> to high <note>original: "acutum", meaning sharp or high-pitched</note> and from there back again to low—it necessarily follows that through different intervals the soul is affected in various ways by the <term>implanted spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritum implantatum." In early modern physiology, this "spirit" was a subtle substance that acted as a bridge, carrying sensory data like sound from the ears to the soul.</note>, which, as stated above, is the immediate subject of harmonic motion. Furthermore, since certain smaller intervals in motion differ wonderfully from other larger ones, such as the semitone from whole tones, it also happens that according to the diversity of this...

### Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music, etc. 567

...something severe; the following interval, G to A <note>original: "sol, la"</note>, is even more stirred, cheerful, happy, and joyful. The fourth indeed, D to E <note>original: "re, mi"</note>, being the most stirred, conveys I know not what choleric <note>In historical medicine, the "choleric" temperament was associated with fire, anger, and quick action.</note> and indignant motion. Thus, different intervals express different emotions <note>original: "affectus"</note>, because one always has a higher pitch <note>original: "constitutionem," referring to the physical setup or tension of the string</note> than the other. Hence, they increase in intensity as if by steps. Since the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>A subtle fluid thought by early scientists to carry sensory information through the nerves to the brain.</note> is agitated in a similar way—sometimes faster, sometimes slower—it is no wonder that the spirit expresses thoughts in one way or another, and likewise moves the <term>sensitive appetite</term> <note>The faculty of the soul that experiences desires or feelings based on sensory input.</note> in various ways.

But since the semitone <note>The smallest interval in traditional Western music, such as the distance between E and F.</note> has a notable and very perceptible difference from the whole tone, it is such that if it were placed in the position of a whole tone it would be **unutterable** <note>original Greek: "ἀνεκφώνητον" (anekphōnēton)</note> or unpronounceable. For no other reason can the <term>tritone</term> <note>An interval of three whole tones, famously difficult to sing and often avoided in early music for its "harsh" sound.</note> be performed without a sense of horror, except that it lacks a semitone. From this, the semitone acquires one kind of motion when placed at the beginning, another in the middle, another at the end, and another in other intervals. For when it is relaxed at the beginning, it will be more softly stirred; but in the middle, since it has a higher pitch—affected variously both by its position and by the whole tones pressing in on both sides—it will acquire another form of motion and sound. This must be understood for any other position as well.

But so that the curious reader may see the difference of sounds shining forth in a single octave, I shall place here the individual steps of the diatonic octave, together with the speed of motion which each step has compared to the preceding one, so that the curious reader may more clearly penetrate those things we have said previously. Let there be, therefore, eight strings equal in length and thickness, stretched according to the steps of the diatonic octave. And let the first string, when struck, make 48 vibrations. I say that the string D <note>original: "Re"</note> will make 54 vibrations, so that the velocity of vibration of two strings expressing a major tone, C to D <note>original: "ut, re"</note>, has a ratio of 48 to 54. The strings D and E <note>original: "Re, Mi"</note> have a velocity ratio of 54 to 60. E to F <note>original: "Mi, Fa"</note> is 60 to 64. F to G <note>original: "Fa, Sol"</note> is 64 to 72. G to A <note>original: "sol, la"</note> is 72 to 80. D to E <note>original: "re, mi"</note> <note>Kircher is here calculating a second tetrachord.</note> is 80 to 90. E to F finally is 90 to 96. Here you see that the higher the pitch of the note, the more sharply and intensely it sounds. Thus, even if a lower semitone has an equal proportion with others higher in position, it still differs from them in motion and force. For the semitones E-F and D-E possess a different speed as they are set higher and higher, and consequently affect the animal spirit in different ways.

| C to D | D to E | E to F | F to G | G to A | A to B | B to C |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 48 | 54 | 60 | 64 | 72 | 80 | 90 | 96 |
| (8 to 9) | (9 to 10) | (15 to 16) | (8 to 9) | (9 to 10) | (8 to 9) | (15 to 16) |

Indeed, since we have demonstrated all these things in *Instrumental Music* <note>original: "Musica organica"</note>, we refer the reader there. Sounds relate to the sense of hearing in the same way as colors relate to the power of sight. For it is so certain that objects imbued with different colors affect the sight differently according to their various positions, that anyone who denies it should be judged to be lacking eyes. Hence, the semitone corresponds quite fittingly to **white**, as if it were the form of all colors; and it is closest to light, but intensely...

To yellow, indeed, corresponds the minor third; to red, the major third; to flame-colored, the fourth; to golden, the fifth; and to purple, the sixth. The octave, however, we attribute to green—the most beautiful and pleasant of all colors, composed of gold and purple <note>In Kircher's color theory, green sits at the harmonic center of the spectrum.</note>. The remaining colors we apply, not without reason, to the dissonances leading toward black, the other extreme of colors. Thus, black refers to the major second or tone, dark brown to the tritone, ash-gray to the major sixth <note>There is a slight discrepancy here between Kircher’s table and his text regarding the "ash-gray" and "flame" assignments.</note>, and azure aptly refers to the seventh. From the mixture and skillful <term>syncopation</term> <note>The technique of shifting the rhythmic accent so that a normally weak beat is stressed.</note> of these, a most beautiful harmonic picture emerges.

### COROLLARY

<margin>Which intervals move the spirits more</margin>

From this discourse, it is clearly evident that the cause of the various stirrings of the emotions <note>original: "affectuum"</note> is none other than what we have said: the different ratio of the <term>animal spirit</term>, which is incited differently according to the various degrees of tension and relaxation of the harmonic motion impressed upon the air. Hence, <term>Cadences</term> and larger uncompounded intervals possess greater power over the soul, inasmuch as they incite the spirit with greater force. Thus, the fifth can do more than the fourth, the octave more than the fifth, and so on for the rest. For the higher the distance they have from the <term>unison</term> <note>When two notes are at the exact same pitch.</note>, the greater, more unusual, and more extraordinary an effect they will produce in the soul.

This is evident in preachers and orators who, to stir emotion in the minds of men, are accustomed to raise and strain their voices beyond the usual level. Nature itself has taught this to animals. A dog seething with rage forms a very sharp, vehement voice according to the arousal of his <term>bilious humor</term> <note>In the theory of the Four Humors, yellow bile was associated with fire and anger.</note>. For this reason, music especially prays for uncompounded intervals arranged with judgment.

It is also clear from this that the **diatonic genus** <note>The standard musical scale consisting of seven notes (like the white keys on a piano).</note> is natural and, as it were, innate to our soul; thus, it is most suitable for stirring the emotions, whatever others may say to the contrary. The <term>Enharmonic</term> and <term>Chromatic</term> genera, due to their tiny intervals, impress almost nothing but a certain "softness," being closer to the unison than is proper. I say the diatonic is natural above the others because I see that all the peoples of the whole world naturally produce this in their songs. This is clear from various examples which I have drawn from the mouths of the Fathers of our Society <note>The Jesuits, of which Kircher was a member.</note> who gathered here in Rome in the year 1645 from all over the world. I thought it would be worth the effort if, for the sake of the curious reader, I presented here several songs commonly used by different nations. From these it will be clear that nature teaches men the diatonic genus.

#### Turkish "Allah Allah"
[Musical notation with lyrics "Alla alla" underneath]

I hear that some Turkish priests, whenever they solemnly intone that "Allah Allah" of theirs, use this kind of phrase filled with strange, unusual, concise, and jarring intervals. Kepler also made mention of this in his *Harmonics* <note>Johannes Kepler's *Harmonice Mundi* (1619).</note>, yet nothing occurs in this—as some object—that is not diatonic.

The Chinese, as Father Semedo <note>Álvaro Semedo (1585–1658), a Jesuit missionary to China.</note> of our Society (who lived among them for many years) related to me, use this phrase while they worship Confucius.

#### The Chinese custom of singing before the idol called Confucius.

They perform it at their more celebrated festivals with such mental intensity and such unusual bodily movements that you would call them all frantic and out of their minds. We provide the notes from the Author with the same faithfulness with which he reported them.

Book VII. On the Music-making of the Ancients and Moderns, etc. 569

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning Tones or modes, and harmonic tropes, and their nature and properties in stirring the <term>affects</term>. <note>In the Baroque period, "affects" (Latin: *affectus*) referred to specific emotional states—such as joy, sorrow, or anger—that music was intended to trigger in the listener.</note>

At this point, I cannot wonder enough at those certain individuals who—in order to introduce novelty by any means and to boldly suppress the splendor of modern music—assert that our <term>modes</term> <note>The scales or melodic patterns used in composition; the ancestors of our modern major and minor keys.</note> are in no way the same as those of the ancients. They claim that the ancient modes were far different, and that they were more majestic and more suited for stirring the passions. 

But just as they assert this easily, so too can their claims be easily refuted. If what they say is true, let them show us some specimen of such great excellence, or let them produce an Author from whom that incomparable music can be gathered. Since they do not do this, they seem to be acting just like <term>mountebanks and quacks</term> <note>original: "Circumforanei & Agyrtæ." These were traveling medicine shows or street performers who sold dubious remedies.</note> who, in order to sell their rotten wares more easily to the simpler folk, boastfully claim—not without the laughter of more skilled physicians—that their goods have come from some unknown paradise in India, and that they possess utterly unheard-of powers for restoring youth and curing all diseases. Is it possible that of this sort...

How, furthermore, the twelve tones are born from these twelve "cardinal" strings of the tones must be briefly explained.

Since, therefore, every <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "diapason." The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note> is composed of a fourth and a fifth, and since six species of octaves can be considered in two ways—either according to the <term>harmonic</term> or the <term>arithmetic</term> disposition—the modes are formed as follows. According to the first (harmonic) disposition, when in each of the six species a <term>fourth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron."</note> is placed above and a <term>fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente."</note> is placed below, the six **Authentic** tones are born. According to the latter (arithmetic) disposition, when in each of the six species a fifth is placed above and a fourth is placed below, the six **Plagal** tones will emerge. Thus, six Authentic and six Plagal tones joined together constitute the twelve tones. Since all of these things were explained very fully in the fourth book, we did not wish to be repetitive here. Therefore, it should suffice to clarify our meaning with the examples provided here.

->**The harmonic disposition of the Authentics.**<- 
Authentic modes have the fifth below and the fourth above within the octave.

Plagal modes have the fourth below and the fifth above in the Octave, as is evident.

And upon this mutual combination of tones, the secret of the whole of music not undeservedly depends; for in this, the differences of all tones—not only the natural and regular ones, but also the <term>fictitious</term> <note>original: "fictorum." We have distinguished these intervals with black notes so they might be more easily perceived. # 572 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

"...which is expanded not toward cheerfulness, but toward gloom; it is vehement, neither varied nor versatile." <note>original Greek: "ἣ διακεχυμένον οὐκ ἐπ' ἱλαρὸν ἀλλὰ σκύθρωπον, καὶ σφοδρὸν οὔτε ποικίλον οὔτε πολύτροπον." Kircher is quoting ancient authorities on the character of the Dorian mode.</note> The Dorian harmony, he says, seems to possess something masculine and magnificent, majestic, and has more severity and vehemence than of softness or hilarity; for it is neither varied nor wandering, and such were the customs of the Dorians. As Aristides Quintilianus <note>A 3rd-century Greek music theorist.</note> also notes. The Aeolian was held to be cunning, proud, and inflated, yet sincere, amorous, and liberal, according to the testimony of Athenaeus; however, it was somewhat empty—that is, simple and dry—and such were the Thessalians, the inhabitants of Aeolia. The Ionian song, according to Quintilianus, was austere, dry, hard, bold, contentious, persistent, and severe, and such were the Ionians, the people of Asia. And these three peoples can be aptly compared in Italy to the Tuscans, the Romans, the Lombards, and the Bruttians or Calabrians. In Spain, to the Castilians, the Portuguese, and the Aragonese. In France, to the Parisians, the Aquitanians, and the Occitans. In Germany, to the Austrians, the Belgians, and the Saxons. But this is a <note>original: "παρέργως" — a side note or incidental remark.</note>. Whatever the case may be, the ancients usually called the Dorian *semnon*, that is, sacred <note>original: "σεμνόν"</note>; the Phrygian *entheon*, that is, furious or inspired <note>original: "ἔνθεον"</note>; and the Ionian *glaphuron*, that is, Bacchic or elegant <note>original: "γλαφυρόν"</note>. The Pythagoreans used the Dorian in the morning when they rose to shake off lethargy and make themselves fit for contemplation. But with the Hypodorian, according to Quintilianus, they prepared the mind for sleep in the evening once their cares and labors were settled.

<margin>
A comparison between the modern peoples of Europe and the ancient Greeks.
</margin>

And these are the things read in the monuments of the Ancients concerning the nature of the modes; however, in determining this nature, I find as many different opinions and whims as there are writers. Since I found this same inconstancy among modern authors, it seemed right to "bring the process of the modes back to the anvil" <note>An idiom meaning to re-examine or rework a concept from its foundations.</note> and to more accurately weigh the laws of their individual <term>repercussions</term> <note>The specific intervals or "reciting tones" that characterize a mode's melody.</note>, ascents, and descents, so that I might determine what truly resides in them according to nature. 

Hence, it seemed best to present certain examples of each mode in a four-voice harmony here. These have been composed according to every rigor, avoiding all <term>diminutions</term> <note>Breaking long notes into many fast, short notes.</note> and other <term>chromaticisms</term> <note>Notes outside the standard scale used for color.</note> which they call <term>coloraturas</term> <note>Elaborate melodic ornamentations.</note>. Our single intention is that the simple nature of the mode be shown through an always equal tenor <note>A steady, unornamented pace.</note> of notes; for I believed that the unique property of each would appear better this way than if I proposed it adorned with various flourishes. For, as I indicated above, it is most certain that one and the same mode can excite different affects not only in two subjects of different temperaments (as will be seen in the *Magic of Consonance and Dissonance*), but also in one and the same person—now sadness, if proceeding through notes and a measure of time that is languid and mournful; now joy and sadness mixed, if the laws and norms of the modes proceed through triple meter and excited leaps of notes. Therefore, so that the nature of each might be properly established, all modes must be expressed with the same tenor of notes and measure of time. This we have provided in the following paradigm of the modes. In this, we have also avoided the mixing of different modes as much as possible, lest through this troublesome mixture the mode lose its power and natural <term>pathos</term> <note>The emotional power or "suffering" evoked by the music.</note> along with its natural character. In doing this, we swear by the words of no single master <note>A reference to Horace: "nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri," meaning he is an independent thinker not bound by one school of thought.</note>; but following Nature as our guide, we have discovered this more probable nature of the modes, which we have described based on the natural position and progression of intervals. But if anyone finds something better, we promise we shall subscribe to it not unwillingly.

### The property of the twelve regular and natural Modes demonstrated by examples.

We have placed opposite each Mode its own <term>metathesis</term> <note>A Greek term for transposition or rearrangement.</note>, or transposition, which are commonly called "fictitious modes." From these it is clearly evident that the first and second, the third and fourth, the fifth and sixth, the seventh and eighth, the ninth and tenth, and the eleventh and twelfth are entirely similar and almost the same, as if nature itself teaches this order of modes. But having indicated these things in passing, let us now begin the matter itself.

### Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-making. 573

### Examples of Affective Music Displayed in the Twelve Tones.

The **First Tone** serves wonderfully for the feelings of religion, piety, and love for God; for it possesses a certain marvelous energy, by which it ravishes the soul with a most sweet confidence and fills it with the love of heavenly things. To demonstrate this matter, we have composed the following four-voice piece <note>original: "tetraphonium"—a composition for four parts</note>; in which you can see how the opening words correspond exactly to the emotions. For in the phrase "Hear us" <note>original: "exaudi nos"</note>, with which the soul anxiously seeks something from God, an emotion full of confidence shines forth, which a certain burning ascent of the mind toward God designates. Conversely, the descent through B-flat <note>original: "B molle"</note> into that same place shows a humble and pious feeling. The singer follows these emotions in the subsequent passages through the rise and fall of notes sweetly syncopating with one another.

## Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-making, etc. 575

<margin>Nature of the Fourth Tone.</margin>
The **Fourth Tone** is so similar to the third that even skilled music-makers <note>original: "Musurgi"</note>, deceived by the similarity of the cadences <note>The concluding sequence of notes or chords in a musical phrase.</note>, occasionally confuse one with the other. However, those who well understand the **repercussions** <term>repercussio: in modal theory, the specific intervals or "melodic heartbeat" that identify a tone</term> of the tones will easily observe the difference. Regarding these, see what we have treated extensively concerning the differences between tones in Books 3 and 4. Since it is so close to the third tone, it also serves to excite similar emotions. It loves gloom and grief, combined with a certain indignation and an "effervescence of the blood"—the kind of feeling common to those who are dissolved into tears and wailing by vehement pain. You can see that this composition possesses a quality of bitter grief.

<margin>Nature of the Fifth Tone.</margin>
The **Fifth Tone** is cheerful, full of majesty, and raises the soul to lofty heights; it possesses a certain power to incite the soul toward heroic virtues. It fills the spirit of those devoted to solemn and difficult tasks with the cheerfulness and fortitude needed to carry them out. It is of great dignity and majesty in church chants.

# CHAPTER III.

### *On the arrangement of the constitution of places and time for stirring the emotions.*

**S**ince we have already discussed which emotions music most effectively leans toward, both in the preceding sections and in various other places in this work, we have judged it unnecessary to deal with them more extensively here. Therefore, in this section, we shall only show what "pathetic music" <note>From the Greek *pathos* (passion/suffering). In this context, it refers to music designed to move the listener's emotions, not "pathetic" in the modern sense of being pitiable.</note> is, and how it ought to be applied in practice. But let us begin the matter without further wandering.
<margin>What Pathetic Music is.</margin>
Pathetic music is nothing other than a harmonic <term>melothesia</term> <note>The art of composing a melody or musical setting.</note>, or a composition established with such art and genius by a skilled <term>Musurge</term> <note>A composer or "music-worker."</note>, that it stirs the listener to any given emotion of the mind. Four conditions are required to establish it properly: first, that the composer skillfully selects a theme suited to stirring the emotion; second, that he adapts the chosen theme to a fitting Tone <note>The "Tones" refer to the musical modes discussed on previous pages.</note>. Third, that he exactly fits the rhythm, or the measure of the words, to the harmonic rhythm and measure. Fourth, that he presents the music—composed according to said conditions and to be delivered and sung by the most skilled <term>phonascis</term> <note>Vocal trainers or singers who specialize in the emotional delivery of a piece.</note>—at a fitting place and time. Let us declare these conditions a little more fully through individual paragraphs.

# §. I.

### *On the conditions proposed just above necessary for pathetic music.*

**S**uch is the power and efficacy of the soul toward artificial sound, that when sound is expressed with words suited to stirring some effect, it truly performs in the soul what it signifies. For, as we have said, external Sound acts upon the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>In early modern physiology, "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid that acted as the intermediary between the soul and the physical body.</note> as if upon a certain string of the soul. It possesses that secret power so that as soon as the spirit is incited, the soul is immediately moved to that emotion which the strings—or rather the animal spirits—are accustomed to bring about by their nature. If anyone perfectly understood this consensus, he would be able to seize a person into any emotion whatsoever by voice alone. The ancient Poets knew this; hence they accommodated their verses to the emotions in such a way that whoever read them more attentively understood the emotions of the characters even from the rhythm itself. Who, for example, in this verse of Virgil: *"Whom I—? But it is better to calm the troubled waves"* <note>original: "Quos ego? sed motos præstat componere fluctus." From the *Aeneid*, Book 1. Neptune begins an angry threat but cuts himself off, demonstrating emotional restraint.</note> does not see a remarkable cooling of the mind? Who, while reading that: *"The hoof shakes the crumbling field with a four-footed sound"* <note>original: "Quadrupedante putrem sonitu quatit ungula campum." From the *Aeneid*, Book 8. This line is famous for its onomatopoeia, where the rhythm of the words mimics the sound of a galloping horse.</note> does not seem to see not only the rush of the running horse, but even to hear the sound itself? The Orators knew this, as did the actors of Comedy and Tragedy. But since similar things have been treated elsewhere, we will not dwell on them. Yet if a naked voice obtains such great power in the poetic art, how much greater power will it obtain in harmonic motion? Musicians and composers have known this at all times, laboring with the greatest zeal so that when they wished to excite an emotion, they first selected a fitting theme as the base and foundation of the entire fabric to be constructed. Once this was done, just as poets chose a type of meter fit for stirring an emotion, so the composers chose a mode or Tone suitable for the business at hand, corresponding to both the chosen theme and the emotion. This they then accommodated to the harmonic measure and the right, fitting proportion of time, and other clauses according to the condition of the subject, so that they might finally achieve the intended effect and emotion.

**Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-Making. 579**

**Section II.**

**On the appropriate location for pathetic music.**

It can hardly be said how much importance the location holds in the performance of pathetic music <note>As noted previously, "pathetic" refers to the capacity to move the *pathos* or passions of the soul.</note>. For if the location is not suitable, the music must necessarily lose much of its vigor and efficacy.

First, therefore, a small and narrow place is unfit for this business, both because of the stronger reflections from the walls and because of the crowding of the singers <term>phoniscorum</term> <note>From the Greek *phonaskos*, referring to vocalists or singing teachers.</note> who are closer to one another than is proper, by which the confused voices lose their power.

Second, a place full of people, or decorated with tapestries, or furnished with various household goods, or filled with books and papers, is by no means convenient for our purpose. Indeed, by obstacles of this kind, the voices are variously broken and reflected in part, and in part stifled, losing their brilliance and energy. Experience teaches this: for in a church empty of people and devoid of tapestries and other impediments, music resonates better than in the same place when it is filled with a confused multitude of people. Likewise, a place filled with wool and straw absorbs voices so that they are perceived with difficulty, and only bluntly.

Third, a place that is too vast is also inconvenient because of the dissipation of the voices. Hence, in open fields, public crossroads, and vaster temples, music loses most of its grace. The location, therefore, ought to be a middle ground between vastness and narrowness; it should have flat walls delicately coated with a harder plaster <note>Kircher uses the term *gypsum*.</note>; and it should be equipped with a vault or a flat ceiling, for in this way the reflection of sound will be equal. <margin>Just as solitary places bring about sorrow, so do delightful gardens bring joy.</margin> But concerning the construction of places fit for music, see our *Echotectonica* <note>Kircher's term for "sound-architecture," a subject he studied extensively to understand how buildings amplify or echo sound.</note>. Deserted places also, such as in forests near great rocks or by tranquil rivers, are most suitable; for the silence of solitudes and the reflection of the rocks, as well as the very constitution of the place, wonderfully sharpen the power of the music—provided that a place luxuriating with too many herbs and shrubs is avoided, for in these the voices are marvelously dissipated and stifled. A place with a flat precipice, at the foot of which sits a tranquil lake, is the most suitable of all.

In a word, different places serve to arouse different passions. A place of solitude fits best for grief and for emotions of contempt for human affairs. In gardens filled with greenery and a variety of flowers, happy, cheerful, and pleasant music contributes wonderfully to the effects of joy, gladness, and melting love, with all things conspiring to achieve the intended effect—provided it lacks the aforementioned impediments. The same must be said of other places; for just as the eye takes in horror from the sight of a horrid place, or gladness and love from a pleasant one, so the hearing—having seen a place conducive to a certain emotion—is moved by music fit for a similar emotion. With the help of both eyes and ears, the mind is stirred toward the corresponding emotion with a doubled increase. The Ancient Musicians knew this, and they established their theaters in various ways to arouse various emotions in the listeners. <margin>The triple arrangement of the Theater.</margin> From this, a triple form of the Theater emerged: Comic, Tragic, and Satyric. The **Comic** was depicted with various palaces and a varied arrangement of homes and crossroads. The **Tragic**, through a display of black apparatus, incited listeners to sadness and mourning of the mind, while by its mournful face it easily recalled the historical event to the listeners through tragic gesture and story.

The **Satyric**, through forests, gardens, the pleasantness of trees, and the bubbling of fountains, easily inclined the mind toward those emotions which satyric poems represent—matters involving pleasures, loves, and other allurements of soft minds. If the music matched these, it can hardly be said how much energy they obtained to sweep the listeners away into any emotion whatsoever. But of these things we speak more diffusely elsewhere; therefore, let us return to our purpose.

<margin>What the arrangement of the musicians contributes.</margin> The placement of the singers should not be in a circle; for in this arrangement, the voices are not perceived equally by the listeners. Instead, it should be in a position facing the listeners, forming a straight line or something of an arc; for thus the voices fall better and more equally upon the ears of the listeners. The singers, truly, should preserve the equality of the voices as much as possible, lest one [overpower] the other...

They should maintain a decent posture and the best physical bearing, so that nothing is present that might be dissonant or offend the eyes and ears of the listeners; we leave the remaining circumstances to the consideration of the prudent Choir Master <term>Symphoniarchæ</term> <note>A leader of a musical ensemble or choir; here, Kircher implies a director who manages the "staging" of the performance.</note>. Indeed, this distance depends on the intensity of the Musicians’ voices. For in this way, through a prior disposition, the softened soul will receive a more ready impression from the music that follows. Let these remarks suffice regarding the place and the positioning.

### Section III.
*On the time when Music must be presented to achieve its effect.*

There are four primary differences of time that contribute greatly to the perfect discernment of music: morning, evening, midday, and nighttime. The Morning, swelling with vapors and thicker air, as well as Midday, due to the more vehement agitation of the air, are less suitable. The Evening—since the vapors have been dispelled by the daytime Sun and the air has been purified—as well as the Nighttime, on account of the untimely silence and the steady state of the air, are exceedingly recommended. Regarding these matters, if you please, consult our *Phonocamptica* <note>Kircher refers here to his own scientific studies on the "bending" of sound, or acoustics, often found in his work *Phonurgia Nova*.</note>, in which we have treated this subject more extensively. Furthermore, the four seasons of the year must be considered, and in each, the conditions of the blowing winds peculiar to every nation.

<margin>Which months are more suitable for Music.</margin>
The months of May, June, July, August, September, and October, on account of the dry and thin constitution of the air, are much more suitable for music than the months of November, December, January, February, March, and April, which are condemned to perpetual vapors and rains. In these latter months, the air is thick and foul <note>original: *fæculentus*</note>, and does not yield such clear voices. Finally, the North winds <note>original: *Aquilonares*</note> here in Rome, which dry the air and make it clear, are most suitable for voices. The South winds <note>original: *Australes*</note>, on the contrary, are exceedingly hostile to voices due to their humidity and vaporous breath. I have said "here in Rome," because winds that are dry and hot for us are humid and cold in other regions; thus, each person should guide himself according to the nature of the winds peculiar to each nation.

<margin>Which winds.</margin>
Let this be a universal rule: a cold, dry wind or a hot, dry wind is always more suitable for performing music than a hot, humid wind or a cold, humid one. However, when I speak of wind, I do not mean the gust itself (for this, as it utterly scatters voices, is entirely unfit for this business), but rather such-and-such a constitution of the air caused by such-and-such a wind.

From what has been said, unless I am mistaken, it appears clearly enough how many things must be considered so that pathetic music may exert its power over the souls of men. Nothing remains, therefore, but for us to gird ourselves to explain the secrets of pathetic music a little more clearly.

## CHAPTER IV.
*On the practical application of pathetic composition.*

Since there are various affections of mortals, and individual objects do not excite everyone to the same affections, so that I might investigate this discrepancy more deeply, I have selected certain themes from Holy Scripture suitable for individual affections, which contain the primary emotions of love, grief, joy, indignation...

...of indignation and anger, of mourning and lamentation, of vehement sadness, of presumption, arrogance, despair, and finally, of wonder. Having done this, I decided that eight or more of the most excellent <term>musurgos</term> <note>musical masters or composers</note> in the whole world—men distinguished in judgment and genius, and especially renowned for their knowledge of harmony—should be chosen. I sent letters to various parts of the world, urgently requesting that each of them compose certain paradigms of sympathetic music <note>music that "resonates" with the human soul</note> based on these same themes, suited to the aforementioned emotions.

Through this established exchange with musicians, I hoped I might arrive at an absolute understanding of <term>pathetic music</term> <note>From the Greek *pathos*; music designed to evoke deep emotional states, not "pathetic" in the modern sense of being pitiable.</note>. Since the chosen composers were the most learned in all music, and the most prominent among various nations—Italy, Germany, England, and France—and since each was asked to complete their compositions on the same eight themes expressing those primary emotions of the soul, I believed I would immediately recognize toward which emotions each man's genius inclined; first the composers themselves, and then the listeners. I wished to see whether different nations agreed or disagreed in their expression of the passions <note>original: *pathematum*</note>, and in what that discrepancy consisted. Indeed, I was confident that I would obtain from this single effort magnificent aids for the restoration of pathetic music. And this plan of mine, as it was wonderfully approved by all, was immediately put into execution. However, while this work was being hurried through the press and making great strides in the meantime, the aforementioned song-composers <term>melothetæ</term> were slower in the task imposed upon them than the haste of the work could sustain. Lest this delay cause notable harm to the work, we have omitted those pieces, as necessity urged. Nevertheless, I shall see to it that as soon as I have obtained a wealth of the said melodies, I shall make them public in a special book, God willing. Yet, so that this book does not conclude without a specimen of pathetic music, we have decided to treat the various styles of music-making <term>musurgia</term>; so that through ingenious <term>melothesias</term> <note>the art of musical composition</note>, it may be discerned which emotions can be more aptly stirred by each style.

### CHAPTER V.
### On the various artistry of harmonic styles.

Musical style can be considered in two ways in this place: either as "impressed" or "expressed."
An impressed harmonic style is nothing other than a certain habit of the mind depending on a person's natural temperament, by which a musician is inclined to follow this rather than that method of composition. This variety matches the diversity of temperaments shining forth in men. An expressed style is nothing other than a certain ratio and method that shines forth in various compositions. We reduce the classification of these styles to eight primary types. Thus, the first is the **Ecclesiastical** style <margin>What the various musical styles are</margin>, which is of the sort used in the compositions of Masses, Hymns, Graduals, and Antiphons. This is again twofold: **Bound** and **Free**. The **Bound** style is that which is executed precisely according to the <term>Cantus Firmus</term> <note>The "fixed song," a pre-existing plainchant melody used as the basis for a polyphonic composition.</note> or choral melody which it takes as its subject. The **Free** style is that which resides in the liberty of the composer, restricted by no subject of a plainchant. Most fitting examples of all these are supplied to you by the ecclesiastical works of Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina <note>original: *Petri Aloysij Prænestini*</note>, Cristóbal de Morales, and from the older masters, Josquin des Prez <note>original: *Iudoci Pratensis*</note>, Jacob Obrecht, Cipriano de Rore, Orlande de Lassus, and countless others; and in this time, the most celebrated papal musician, Gregorio Allegri. But so that you may see an absolute specimen of Church Music, we shall place here the "Crucifixus" <note>The Crucifixion</note> composed by Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, which is deservedly admired by all musicians as a work of the most exquisite genius.

->**The Canonic Style**<-

The **Canonic style** is a harmonic process in which several voices are folded into one. Since this was discussed at length in Book 5, we refer the reader there. This style finds its most appropriate place in the compositions or counterpoints of Church song, and at all times it has been held in high esteem by all musicians. For it demonstrates great dexterity of musical genius; yet among modern musicians, such a noble style has almost faded away: since there are scarcely any who apply their mind or genius to such a laudable style. Whether this is for the sake of avoiding labor, or due to ignorance, or for other reasons, I leave to the fair reader to judge.

Nevertheless, lest such an ingenious kind of music perish with time, two most noble Roman musicians applied their minds to its restoration. The first of these was **Romano Micheli** <note>Romano Micheli (c. 1575–1659) was an Italian composer and polemicist who specialized in extremely complex canons, often challenging other musicians to solve his musical "riddles."</note>, a Roman, who, through various published works, has attempted to restore <term>canonic music</term> <note>A "canon" is a piece of music where a single melody is performed by multiple voices starting at different times, creating complex overlapping harmonies from a single written line.</note> adorned with various new inventions. An example of this is his Canon which is distributed into 9 choirs and can be sung by 36 voices...

**Explanation of the aforementioned Canon.**
The **Bass** begins as it is written.
The **Tenor** sings together with the Bass at the interval of a twelfth, but through **contrary motions** <note>A technique where one voice moves up in pitch while the other moves down by the same interval.</note>.
The **Alto**, however, enters after one beat <note>original: "tempus", a unit of musical measurement in 17th-century notation.</note> at the <term>diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave.</note>.
The **Soprano** <note>original: "Cantus"</note> sings together with the Alto at the interval of a nineteenth, but through those contrary motions.
And thus the first Choir is established.
The four parts of the **Second Choir**—namely the Bass, Tenor, Alto, and Soprano—sing in the same manner as above, but enter after two beats.

The second musician is **Pietro Francesco Valentini** <note>Pietro Francesco Valentini (c. 1570–1654) was an Italian composer and music theorist famous for his extraordinarily complex "riddle" canons.</note>, a Roman; a man born to advance the art of music. The following canon of a single line, which is *A la, mi, re* <note>These are solmization syllables—the "do-re-mi" of the 17th century—indicating the pitch A.</note>, can be sung by two, three, or four voices, even in contrary motions <note>A technique where one voice moves up in pitch while another moves down by the same interval.</note>. Several ways (many others being omitted) are demonstrated by the numbers placed above and below each note for the consonances. The parts enter at the points indicated by dots (to clearly suggest the entry of the aforementioned parts) after four <term>semiminim</term> <note>A note value in early music roughly equivalent to a modern quarter note.</note> beats of equal measure.

[Musical staff with notes and numbers. Above the staff are numbers: 12, 10, 3. 5., 3. 3., 3., 3. 5., 6. 6., 12, 10, 3. 5., 3. 3., 3., 3. 5., 6. 6. Below the staff are numbers: 4 6 8 8, 6 6, 5, 6 6, 5 5, 4 6, 8 8, 6 6, 5, 6 6, 5 5. Text below notes: Blessed are you, Virgin Mary <note>original: "Beata es Virgo Maria"</note>]

A canon of a single line based on the vowels, to be sung by four voices, in which two parts proceed against another two, or three against one, in contrary motions.

[Musical staff. Above the staff is inverted text: O Christ, hope of a truly loving soul. Living flame of fire of a loving soul. <note>original: "Christe spes animæ vere diligentis. Viua ignis flamma animæ amantis."</note> Below the staff is the same text.] <margin>Linear Canon.</margin>

Furthermore, several clever devices, which are omitted for the sake of brevity, should be noted. If this leaf is turned over so that the upper part is changed into the lower, the present Canon (which can also be sung by two, three, or four voices in various ways) can be sung from the end to the beginning, in both words and notes, just as if the page had not been turned; as is understood from the same words and notes drawn from the opposite side of each part of the Canon.

And these are the things I thought should be said regarding the canonic style. However, he who desires more concerning our musical invention in composing Canons should consult Book VIII, where he will find some wonderful and rare things regarding this matter.

The **Motet style** <margin>Motet Style.</margin> is a harmonic process that is serious, full of majesty, flourishing with the greatest variety, and bound by no specific subject. It is called "Motetish" because the mode or tone assumed is covered by the mixing of other sounds with such artifice that, being entangled in ingenious variety, the underlying logic is scarcely discerned except at the end. Ingenious examples which will leave you in awe are found in the works of the authors cited previously, and above in Book V, page 322, *Lord, I suffer violence* <note>original: "Domine vim patior"</note>, and the hymn *Hail Star of the Sea* <note>original: "Ave maris stella"</note>, page 316.

The **Fantastic style** <margin>Fantastic Style.</margin> is suited to instruments; it is the most free and unrestrained method of composing, bound by neither words nor a harmonic subject. It is established to show off genius and the hidden logic of harmony, and to teach the ingenious arrangement of harmonic passages and <term>fugues</term> <note>A compositional technique where a short melody is introduced by one part and then taken up by others and developed.</note>. It is divided into those types commonly called **Fantasias**, **Ricercatas**, **Toccatas**, and **Sonatas**. Look for compositions of this kind in Book V, pages 243 and 311; consider the three-voice piece <note>original: "triphonia"</note> composed by us on pages 466, 480, and 487; and in Book VI, see those adapted for various instruments.

### 586 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance <note>original: "Artis Magnæ Consoni, & Dissoni"</note>

<margin>The Madrigal Style.</margin>
The **Madrigal style** is a certain harmonic process most suitable for expressing the virtues of moral actions, passions of love, and other clever allusions to myths and histories. Regarding these, see the distinguished works of Luca Marenzio, Agostino Agazzari, the Prince of Venosa <note>Carlo Gesualdo (1566–1613), a composer famous for his intense, experimental, and highly chromatic madrigals.</note>, and countless others. Some believe they take their name from their first inventor, *Madrigallo* <note>While Kircher notes this theory, modern scholars generally believe the term "madrigal" derives from the Latin "matricalis," meaning a song in the mother tongue (vernacular) rather than Latin.</note>. Examples of these may be seen in the following pages.

<margin>The Melismatic Style.</margin>
The **Melismatic style**, so named from the "sweetness of melody" <note>original: "à dulcedine melodiæ"</note>, is a harmonic style most suited to poetic verses and meters. It consists of two, sometimes three, or most often four sections, according to the requirements of the meter. Individual sections are distinguished by certain signs <note>Musical symbols such as repeat marks.</note> which indicate the repetition of a phrase or harmonic section. To this style belong all those songs commonly called **Ariettas** and **Villanellas** <note>Lighthearted, often rustic or folk-like vocal forms popular in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note>, because they are taken up at home or in the country for private recreation or for the practice of singers. See examples of this style in the works of Giovanni Battista Ferrini, and in Book 5, pages 314 and 321, and various examples of "musarithmic composition" <note>Kircher's term for his mathematical system of composing music using combinations of pre-set rhythms and melodies.</note> in Book 8.

<margin>The Dance and Theatrical Style.</margin>
The **Hyporchematic style** <note>From the Greek "hyporchema," a song meant to be accompanied by dancing.</note> is most suitable for playful and festive celebrations and is of two kinds: **Theatrical** and **Dance-like**. The **Theatrical** style serves for the staging of theatrical choruses and is established according to the laws of poetic meter. The **Dance-like** style, however, serves for dances <note>original: "Choreis"</note>, established by the distinguished law of rhythm, corresponding in every way to the proportions of the movements, gestures, and steps of the dancers. There are as many species of these as there are types of movement in choral dances. They are commonly called **Galliards**, **Courantes**, **Passamezzos**, **Allemandes**, and **Sarabandes** <note>These were the standard social and courtly dances of the late Renaissance and early Baroque eras, each with a distinct character and rhythmic feel.</note>. The noble musician **Girolamo Kapsberger** <note>Hieronymus Kapsperger (c. 1580–1651), a German-Italian virtuoso performer and composer for the lute and theorbo.</note>, a German, has provided us with examples of these. He is most famous for his publication of almost innumerable musical volumes, both in manuscript and in print. Possessing the greatest talent and aided by other sciences in which he is skilled, he has successfully penetrated the secrets of music. It is to him that posterity owes all those harmonic elegances commonly called <term>strascinos</term> <note>Slurs or slides between notes.</note>, <term>mordentias</term> <note>Mordents; a rapid alternation between a principal note and the note below it.</note>, and <term>grupos</term> <note>Trills or turns.</note>, which are usually employed by string players on the theorbo and the lute. He introduced the true method of both playing and <term>intabulating</term> <note>The process of arranging vocal or ensemble music for a single instrument like the lute or keyboard, or the specific notation (tablature) used for those instruments.</note> (to use a common term). He has treated almost all kinds of harmonic styles with the highest excellence.

In the choral dance, the harmonic time and the movements and gestures of the dancers must correspond perfectly. These two things seem to be naturally implanted in humans; as soon as we hear a harmonious and rhythmic melody, we are incited by a certain hidden stimulus to movements similar to the proportions of the harmonic rhythms. Indeed, the more the proportions of musical time have intervals suited to dance movements, the easier the effect produced in those dancing. But since all these things have been demonstrated partly in Book 6 and are to be demonstrated in Book 9, we refer the reader there.

**Paradigm I. Of a Dance Melody. By Girolamo Kapsberger.**

<margin>The Symphonic Style</margin>

The symphonic style is a specific method of composing those *Symphonias* <note>In the 17th century, a "symphony" referred to any harmonious ensemble of instruments rather than the specific multi-movement orchestral form we recognize today.</note> in which a harmonious consonance of various instruments is employed; this style varies according to the diversity of the instruments used. 

For there is one symphonic style for the harmony of stringed instruments <note>original: *Chelyum*, referring to the lyre or violin family</note>, another for the blending of lutes <note>original: *testudinum*, literally "tortoises," a classical poetic term for lutes</note>, another for the concord of pipes and flutes, and finally another for performing a symphony of trumpets and drums. However, you may see examples of all these in Book 6, *On Instrumental Music* <note>original: *Musica organica*, referring to music played on instruments rather than sung</note>. There are also those works which they simply call "Symphonias," a specimen of which—taken from the author cited just before <note>Girolamo Kapsberger, whose work was featured on the preceding pages</note>—we have provided for you here.

<margin>The dramatic or recitative style.</margin>

Finally, the Dramatic or <term>Recitative Style</term> <note>a style of singing that imitates the rhythms and inflections of speech, used to move the plot forward in operas and oratorios</note>—familiar to comedies, tragedies, and dramas—is bound by the laws of poetic meter. For this reason, it generally shuns formal harmonic cadences and the exuberant "dancing" of polyphonic voices; instead, it focuses primarily on expressing the emotions <note>original: *affectibus*, referring to the "Doctrine of the Affections," where music was intended to provoke specific emotional states in the listener</note> signified by the underlying subject matter.

Claudio Monteverdi was once especially famous for this kind of style, as his *Arianna* <note>original: *Ariadna*; Monteverdi's 1608 opera, of which only the famous "Lament" survives</note> demonstrates. Following him, Girolamo Kapsberger published various works in the recitative style; these are composed with the highest judgment and skill, and are certainly most worthy for musicians to imitate. The following example is one such instance, in which he introduces a dialogue between children and parents condemned to the punishment of hellfire. It is presented with such ingenuity, judgment, and artifice of harmonic rhythm that it expresses the complaints and laments of the wretched almost as if they were real.

[Musical notation with lyrics in English:]
Life of my soul, I honor you in heaven <note>original Italian: "Vita de l'Alma mia t'o noro in cie lo"</note>
Beautiful soul, whom I loved so much, you died, yes, but the flame will never die <note>original Italian: "Anima bella, che cotanto amai moristi si, ma nō morrà gia mai la"</note>

It should be noted that each of these musical styles we have reviewed is suited to exciting different <term>affectus</term> <note>The "affections" or specific emotional states that Baroque music aimed to trigger in the listener.</note> in the listener. In this way, the **Ecclesiastical style**, full of majesty, wonderfully draws the mind toward grave and serious divine matters, impressing upon the soul the very same emotional movement that the music itself conveys. The **Motet style**, being flowery with remarkable variety, likewise contributes to exciting various emotions. The **Madrigal style** is most suitable for sweeping the mind toward love, compassion, and other softer affections. <margin>To which emotions each style incites the soul.</margin> The **Hyporchematic style** <note>A style of music associated with dancing and rhythmic movement.</note>—if it is more agitated—is useful in a singular way for exciting joys, dances, wantonness, and abandon in the soul. Finally, the **Recitative style**, by insisting closely on the subject matter of the text, incites the listeners toward whatever specific emotions it reports.

### What kind of singers are required who are suitable for presenting pathetic music.

Even if a <term>Pathetic Melothesia</term> <note>From the Greek *melothesia* (composition); here referring to a composition designed to move the passions.</note> were composed according to the full rigor of every rule, if it does not find <term>phonascos</term> <note>Singing masters or vocalists trained in the expressive delivery of text.</note> who are truly distinguished in this art, it will move nothing, nor will it achieve its intended goal. But if the music obtains singers who are skilled, dexterous, gifted with pleasing voices, and, so to speak, perfectly suited for this task, then without a doubt the "pathetic" harmony—as if awakened from a stupor and having gained new vigor—will begin to powerfully stir the soul. This harmony then achieves an even greater and more excellent increase of its power...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher categorizes various musical styles—such as Ecclesiastical, Madrigal, and Recitative—by the specific emotions they are meant to provoke in the listener, while emphasizing that even the best composition fails without skilled, expressive singers.</summary>

598 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

[Music] will then achieve its full power when it finds its material in a theater, adorned with appropriate stage equipment, and is presented by musical actors dressed in theatrical costume. These performers must know how to bring grace to the harmony and decorum to the entire action through the expression of their face and eyes, the movement of their hands and feet, and the appropriate gestures of their whole body.

Furthermore, there are very few <term>Phonaskoi</term> <note>From the Greek 'phōnos' (voice) and 'askein' (to train); here referring to master vocalists who specialize in the emotional and dramatic delivery of music.</note> found today who are equipped with all the qualities required to move an audience, as these particular "Graces" <note>A reference to the Three Graces of mythology, implying the rare combination of beauty, charm, and joy in performance.</note> rarely combine in a single person. Nevertheless, Rome at this time (to say nothing of other places) certainly does not lack most excellent musicians. <margin>Praise for the Roman musicians or singers.</margin> Among these, Domenico Colombo <note>original: "Dominicus Columbus"</note> rightly deserves praise. Born in San Severino, and formerly an Imperial musician, he is now a most delicate Papal musician. Beyond his skill in music and the excellence of his voice, he is also distinguished by his knowledge of other subjects, as well as the liveliness of his wit...

<summary>Kircher argues that music reaches its full emotional potential only when combined with theatrical elements like acting and costume, though he laments the rarity of performers who possess both vocal and dramatic talent, ultimately praising the Roman singer Domenico Colombo.</summary>

§. II.
*On the Emotion of Sorrow.*

The emotion of sorrow is a <term>passion of the soul</term> <note>In the 17th century, "passions" were considered physical and psychological movements caused by external stimuli.</note> by which we are touched by an intrinsic pain of compassion—either because of significant adversity (for example, the death of parents, children, or friends) or similar disastrous events. Therefore, so that such emotions of sorrow may be expressed in harmonic melodies, you must first have a grasp of the energy of sorrow and the movements of the soul that manifest during grief. If you adapt similar harmonic movements to these, you will undoubtedly achieve what you intend. By what industry of genius you may follow this, the following examples teach; these were arranged with the highest genius by the aforementioned authors, showing how much the emotion...

<margin>Praise of Giacomo Carissimi.</margin>

Giacobus Carissimus <note>Giacomo Carissimi (1605–1674), one of the most celebrated Italian composers of the early Baroque, famous for developing the oratorio.</note>, a most excellent and widely renowned composer, served for many years as the most worthy Music Director of the Church of Saint Apollinaris at the German College. He stands out above others for his genius and the grace of his compositions, having a particular power to transform the souls of his listeners into whatever emotions he chooses. Indeed, his compositions are full of vigor and a living spirit.

Among countless other works of great value, he composed the dialogue *Jephte* <note>The story of Jephthah from the Book of Judges, who vowed to sacrifice the first thing he saw upon returning from victory—which turned out to be his only daughter.</note>, using words taken from Sacred Scripture. In this work—using the musical style they call **recitative** <note>A style of singing that imitates the rhythms and cadences of speech, allowing the story to be told clearly.</note>—he first expressed with singular genius and a sharp pen the victories, triumphs, and the celebrations of the Daughter, who comes out to meet her father with every kind of instrument and dancing, congratulating him on the hard-won victory. Then, he suddenly and beautifully portrays the father Jephte, stunned by the sight of his only-begotten daughter, as he is snatched from joy into sorrow and lamentation. This is due to the irrevocable sentence of the vow he made concerning his daughter and her hopeless fate. Carissimi exhibits this shift by changing the musical tone to express opposite emotions.

To this, he afterwards joins a 6-voice **lament** <note>original: "planctum".</note> of the virgin companions, who wail and mourn the wretched fate of the daughter. It is composed with such skill that you would swear you could hear the actual sobs and groans of the mourners. For although he began the dialogue in a festive and dancing Tone <note>The "Tones" refer to the Church Modes, the predecessor to our modern scales. Carissimi starts in the 8th Mode, which was traditionally associated with cheerfulness.</note>, such as the Eighth, he established this lament in a very different Tone—namely, a mixture of the Fourth and Third. As one presenting a tragic story in which intense sorrow and anguish of the soul follow joy, he very appropriately adopted a lament in a Tone that was, as they say, "poles apart" <note>original: "toto caelo dissideret"; literally "differed by the whole sky," a Latin idiom for being completely opposite.</note> from the Eighth. In this way, he could better express the difference in emotions through their opposite natures. 

Indeed, nothing can be more suitable for presenting similar sad events and tragic stories, which are always followed by such differing emotions. However, because the full text of the dialogue is too long to be inserted here, I have decided to omit it on purpose and wished to include only the 6-voice lament here, so that ingenious composers might have a model to imitate—namely, a singular specimen of the craft of **pathetic music** <note>In the 17th century, "pathetic" (from the Greek *pathos*) did not mean "pitiful," but rather music capable of stirring deep, powerful emotions in the listener.</note>.

Avan- <note>This is a catchword, a printer's tool where the first syllable of the next page is printed at the bottom of the current one.</note>

<summary>A tribute to the composer Giacomo Carissimi, focusing on his oratorio Jephte as a masterpiece of emotional contrast. The text highlights how Carissimi uses specific musical modes and the recitative style to transition from celebratory joy to the profound grief of a father’s tragic vow.</summary>

### Section III.
**Examples of the Joyful Affect, or Happiness and Exultation.**

Happiness or joy is a passion <note>In the 17th century, "passions" were understood as physical and psychological states where the soul is moved by external forces.</note> by which the soul rejoices in the possession or enjoyment of a desired good. Physically, it is caused by the dilation <note>original: "dilatione cordis." Kircher follows the medical theory of his time, which held that joy physically expanded the heart, while sorrow contracted it.</note> of the heart through the thinning of the implanted spirits <note>Referring to the "vital spirits," believed to be subtle vapors that circulated through the body to mediate between the soul and the physical organs.</note> produced by the force of a harmonious air that is similar to those spirits.

Whoever, therefore, wishes to excite this passion in a human being through musical rhythms <note>original: "harmonicis modulis."</note> must necessarily use harmonic movements that are similar and proportionate to the movements of those spirits. This was excellently achieved by the **Prince of Venosa** <note>Carlo Gesualdo (c. 1566–1613), the Prince of Venosa, was an Italian nobleman and composer renowned for his highly emotional and experimental madrigals.</note> in a certain madrigal which begins *Already he wept* <note>original: "Gia pianse," referring to the madrigal *Già piansi nel dolore* (I once wept in grief). This piece is famous for its "madrigalisms," where the music mimics the meaning of the words—shifting from slow, dark tones for "weeping" to fast, bright ones for "joy."</note>; in which the reader will find everything that could be desired.

### I. Paradigm of the Prince of Venosa’s Joyful Affect.
