§. V.

->On other affects: indignation, wonder, dancing, despair, and presumption.<-

[Marginal note:]
<margin>Names of the Musicians who today preside over Music in the principal Churches of Rome</margin> Besides these principal ones, there are other affects that Music can exhibit, which are displayed throughout the most noble compositions of the most excellent choir masters <note>original: "Symphoniarchæ"</note> of the Roman Basilicas: Orazio Benevoli, Bonifacio Gratiani, Francesco Foggia, Stefano Fabri, and Domenico Cecchielli. The first of these presides at St. Peter's; the second at the Church of the Professed House of the Society of Jesus; the third at St. John Lateran; the fourth at St. Louis of the French National Church; and the fifth at St. Mary Major. They lead the music with the highest praise. To these may be added the masters of the remaining churches, whose names I intentionally omit as they do not occur to me at this moment.

First is the affect of fury and indignation; an example of which is that clause of the Psalm: *The sinner shall see, and shall be angry, he shall gnash with his teeth, and pine away* <note>original: "Peccator videbit, & irascetur, dentibus suis fremet, & tabescet." This is Psalm 112:10 (Vulgate numbering).</note>. These words argue for a certain kind of fury. The illustrious Knight Gino Angelo Capponi <note>Gino Angelo Capponi (1605–1688) was an Italian nobleman and amateur composer who worked with Kircher.</note> beautifully teaches how such words should express the affect they signify in a certain verse cited above: *The sinner shall see, and shall be angry, he shall gnash with his teeth, and pine away.*

In this, you see that the intervals of the musical phrases express a certain choleric quality. For since the choleric affect <note>In the theory of the four humors, the "choleric" temperament was associated with fire, anger, and quick movement.</note> stirs up vehement and swift motions in the soul, these are beautifully seen expressed by the speed of the notes. In this same manner, you may easily express the affects of wonder, presumption, pride, and other passions <note>original: "pathemata"</note>.

->On the Melismatic Style.<-

The Melismatic style, as I said above, is a succinct, brief, and harmonic style, suited to meters and verses for 3 or 4 voices. In this style—through a sweet and affectionate concord of voices without any vehement stirring, and with all longer flourishes <note>term: "diminutionibus" refers to the practice of breaking long notes into many fast, decorative notes</note> omitted—the affects are stirred by artistic ligatures <note>term: "ligaturas," a method of connecting notes that often created expressive dissonances</note> and a beautiful progression of harmonic feet. It is most suitable for matters of devotion.

However, this style is twofold: one is *Hyporchematic* <note>original: "Hyporchematicus," a Greek-derived term for music accompanied by dance</note>, or dance-like; the other is *Ecclesiastical*. To the first are referred all those vain songs which are commonly called *Ariettas* and *Villanellas* <note>These were light, often secular song forms popular in Italy.</note>, of which we have given some examples in the preceding pages. The second belongs properly to the Church. To this are referred all the ecclesiastical hymns—though not in the style used by Palestrina <note>original: "Prænestinus," referring to Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, the master of Renaissance polyphony</note>—and moral subjects adhering to the *cantus firmus* <note>The "fixed song" or pre-existing plainchant melody used as the basis for a polyphonic composition.</note>, but those which proceed in an even concord of 4 voices. Therefore, we call all songs of this kind by the fitting name "melismas," that is, brief and sweet harmonies. Examples of these are Christmas songs <note>original: "Natalitiæ"</note> and those which are usually sung in churches before the Sepulcher during Holy Week. The Germans and the French excel in these. They primarily possess the affects of joy and sorrow. But so that the matter may be made more clear, we have decided to subjoin the following paradigms. The first two are by Kapsberger <note>original: "Capspergeri." Giovanni Girolamo Kapsberger (c. 1580–1651) was a famous lutenist and composer in Rome.</note>; the third is composed with new musical art <note>original: "arte noua musurgica"</note> by one of my students. The fourth and fifth show the method by which two diverse and contrary affects—namely, of Religion and of vain worldly joy—can and should be expressed under one and the same Tone, specifically Tone IV. The Melismatic species is most suitable for theaters.

### CHAPTER VII.

#### On musical licenses, or the use of certain dissonances.

**On exotic compositions, or the extraordinary use of dissonances, and musical phrases involving various emotions.** <note>original: "clausulisque." In Baroque theory, a *clausula* is a formal musical cadence or phrase that concludes a section.</note>

There is a great controversy among musicians regarding the arrangement of dissonances—specifically how they may be made effective within a harmonic ensemble. In order to resolve this, we must treat them in this section. These "licenses" <note>A "license" is a permission to break a formal rule of counterpoint for a specific expressive purpose.</note> include the placement of two <term>fifths</term> <note>Parallel fifths—two voices moving in the same direction while staying five notes apart—were strictly forbidden in classical composition because they were thought to destroy the independence of the voices.</note>. Also the use of <term>fourths</term>, <term>sevenths</term>, and <term>seconds</term> without a <term>ligature</term> <note>A "ligature" or tie connects a dissonant note to a previous stable note to "prepare" the ear; Kircher is discussing using these harsh sounds suddenly, without preparation.</note>, as well as the arrangement and use of the <term>tritone</term> and the <term>semidiapente</term> <note>The tritone is an interval of three whole tones, famously nicknamed "the Devil in music" for its instability; the semidiapente is a diminished fifth.</note>, each of which must be addressed.

#### §. I.

#### On the license of two fifths, and of other dissonances.

The common laws dictate that two perfect consonances should not be continued immediately by a leap. These rules are so widely accepted among all musicians that if anyone were to contravene them, they might seem, if not unskilled, then at least reckless. Nevertheless, there could occasionally be an occasion, especially in <term>tetraphonies</term> <note>Four-part vocal or instrumental compositions.</note>, where the sequence of two fifths might be so absorbed by the fitting arrangement of the remaining harmonies that it would produce an effect not only far from discordant, but even highly agreeable.

Such...

Such is the most judicious following composition by Girolamo Kapsperger <note>original: "Hieronymi Kapspergeri." Kapsperger (c. 1580–1651) was a famous German-Italian virtuoso of the lute and a pioneer in early Baroque music.</note>, in which the author has judiciously used two <term>fifths</term> <note>Parallel fifths occur when two musical parts move in the same direction while remaining an interval of a fifth apart; this was usually forbidden in strict counterpoint.</note> for his specific purpose and to move the emotions. He has placed them with such grace, however, that even the most skilled musician must have a very sharp ear to notice or judge them while they are being performed together. He will likewise find certain intervals that sound discordant to the judgment of the unskilled, which nevertheless win a wonderful grace in the minds of the listeners when performed correctly. We have clearly marked the fifths with their respective numbers [5 5 5 5], and the specific intervals with this sign *; I would wish the keen <term>music-maker</term> <note>original: "Musurgum." Kircher uses this term to describe a composer or one who understands the deep science of music.</note> to take note of these.

624 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

Therefore, I say it is permissible for a Musician who has already perfected his art to use them <note>Referring to parallel perfect intervals, which were generally forbidden in strict counterpoint.</note>, as long as he absorbs them with such skill that they do not display their full force; and also if the words, the subject matter, or a play of wit requires it. For example, if someone were to set that verse of Prudentius <note>Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a 4th-century Roman Christian poet.</note>, "They offer twice five loaves" <note>original: "Bis quinque panes offerunt."</note>, he could skillfully play upon the arrangement of "two fifths" in the stated ratio. You will find similar examples among the ancient authors, such as Obrecht, Josquin des Prez <note>original: "Pratensem," referring to Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), a master of Renaissance polyphony.</note>, and Cristóbal de Morales in the following example, which this celebrated author undoubtedly placed there intentionally, as is clear from the composition itself.

->Cristóbal de Morales, Glory to the Father.<-

[Four staves of musical notation for four voices, with the word "Gloria" printed beneath each staff. Small numbers "55" appear above the third and fourth staves to indicate the intentional use of parallel fifths.]

For since the reason why the sequence of two perfect Consonances is prohibited is because in continuous octaves and fifths, the voices (which are in unison with each other) have no variety; once that "unison-ness" is removed through the mixing of several voices, I do not see why two fifths should not be permitted to a skillful <term>Musurgo</term> <note>Kircher's term for a "musical craftsman" or composer.</note>. There is, however, a first Unison, when two or more voices hold the same notes in a skip. The second Unison is two octaves, which is a "replicated unison." The third Unison is two fifths, called a "remote unison." Since the origin and nature of these were explained at length in the preceding book, we refer the reader there. As for the 2nd, 7th, 9th, the <term>ditone</term> <note>A major third.</note>, and the <term>semidiapente</term> <note>A diminished fifth.</note>—since we have treated their use at length in the fifth book in its own section—I have judged it unnecessary to treat them more extensively here; especially since we are not speaking here of the Second, Seventh, Ninth, and similar dissonances that are made effective through <term>syncopation</term> <note>A rhythmic technique where a note is held across a beat, often creating a temporary dissonance that resolves.</note> or resolution, but rather those that are stable by themselves without any binding. These, we say, can occasionally be put into use and rendered consonant solely by the help of the <term>arsis</term> <note>The "lifting" or upbeat of the hand in conducting or keeping time.</note>—that is, when they fall on the rise of the beat or measure—or by a particular measure of time, which will be discussed in what follows.

§. II.
Concerning the license of the Fourth, or Diatessaron.

The common opinion of Musicians has struck the Fourth from the number of consonances, understanding this always when it undergoes an arithmetic disposition <note>In music theory, the "arithmetic" division of an octave results in a fourth positioned below a fifth, which was traditionally considered unstable or dissonant in two-part writing.</note>. However, calling this dispute back before the judge, we find that it is not as dissonant as the common crowd of Musicians depicts it. For it is certain that the Fourth, standing by itself without a tie or syncopation, and being loose and free from all violence of bonds, sounds freely as a consonance...

<summary>This page discusses "musical licenses," arguing that forbidden intervals like parallel fifths can be used for poetic or clever effect, citing masters like Morales and Obrecht. Kircher also begins a defense of the musical Fourth, challenging the common contemporary view that it is purely dissonant.</summary>
<keywords>parallel fifths, counterpoint, Cristóbal de Morales, Josquin des Prez, diatessaron, musical license, consonance, dissonance, arsis, Musurgia Universalis</keywords>

--- Page 677 ---
<meta>This page continues Kircher’s technical defense of the musical interval of the fourth. He argues that while many theorists consider the fourth a dissonance, it can function as a consonance when properly "shadowed" or supported by other intervals like the third or sixth.</meta>

Book VII. On Antique-modern Music-making, etc. 625

...as long as it is surrounded by such consonances that absorb its harshness. But let us confirm what has been said with examples.

— The Fourth sounds as a consonance, first, when a transition is made from an imperfect to a perfect consonance and the Fourth falls on the <term>arsis</term> <note>The "lifting" or weak part of a musical measure.</note> of the beat; then it will sound consonant despite the fact that <margin>Use of the Fourth.</margin> it has an arithmetic arrangement <note>The mathematical ratio of a Fourth (4:3). In the Pythagorean tradition, the placement of the smaller number at the bottom of a stack of intervals was often considered less stable or "arithmetic."</note>, as seen in the following example. Second, when the Soprano <note>original: "Cantus"</note> and Tenor proceed by one or more sixths, then the middle voice, compared to the high voice, will always have a Fourth in the arithmetic arrangement; as in the second example, it will produce an excellent consonance. For when it is placed between two consonances—namely, the Third and the Sixth, even though they are imperfect—it will be overshadowed by them, just as a lesser thing is by greater things. This is also known to be derived from nature itself and from art. For since higher sounds are generated by faster motions, while lower sounds are from slower motions, the lower sounds are for the most part weaker than the higher ones. Thus, a dissonance—which a lower motion would otherwise make discordant—is made into a pleasing consonance by the higher motion, supported by a lower third.

— Hence, simple <term>imperfect consonances</term> <note>Intervals like thirds and sixths which, unlike octaves and fifths, were considered to have a "sweet" but less stable sound.</note>, namely Thirds or Sixths, are not as pleasing in the lower registers as they are when repeated in the higher voices. For it happens (as will be discussed in the ninth book) that the union of the "strokes of vibration" <note>Kircher is describing what we now call frequency; higher pitches vibrate faster, and he believes these rapid vibrations "blend" more easily to the human ear.</note> occurs more frequently in higher voices than in lower ones; consequently, the discordance that lies hidden beneath the Fourth is more easily absorbed through this union. But these things have been treated more extensively elsewhere.

I. Example. II. Example.

Book VII. Of Ancient-Modern Musurgy, etc. 627

Secondly, the Fourth can be justified at the beginning, middle, and end of a piece solely through the measure of **perfect time** <note>In early music theory, "perfect time" refers to triple meter (three beats per measure), which was historically associated with the Holy Trinity and considered "complete" or "perfect."</note>; as Jean Cousin the Frenchman demonstrated in a most learned composition which he wrote in favor of the Fourth, and which we shall set down below. For the rhythmic delivery of perfect time possesses something similar to **ligatures** <note>A "ligature" is a grouping of notes written as a single symbol, often indicating they should be sung to one syllable or played with a specific rhythmic connection.</note>, because while it is divided unequally through **arsis** and **thesis** <note>Terms derived from Greek meaning the "lift" (weak beat) and the "fall" (strong beat) of a musical measure.</note>, it seems to bind notes that would otherwise be dissonant, and constrains them as if they were conspiring together into a dissonance.

But so that the Musician may have something to practice, let us here present a **Fantasia**, in which everything pertaining to musical "licenses" <note>Artistic permissions to break standard rules for a specific effect.</note> and the use of legitimately applied dissonances—especially the use of the Fourth at the beginning, middle, and end without a ligature—seems to be demonstrated with the greatest study and diligence. In this work, the Musician will also find the perfect rule of **double counterpoint** <note>A sophisticated technique where two musical lines are written so they can be swapped (the top becomes the bottom) and still sound harmonious.</note> and the exotic **syncopations** of the notes in perfect time; so much so that this composition can, not without merit, be called the **steward and distributor** <note>original: "promus condus," a Latin idiom for a household manager who stores and gives out supplies; here, Kircher means the piece contains all the "supplies" of musical knowledge.</note> of the whole of musical science.

In this work, the most skilled Musician will find innumerable things most worthy of observation. The Singer, or **Phonascus** <note>A term for a singing teacher or choirmaster.</note>, will have something with which to exercise his skills. Certainly, among so many musicians in the City of Rome, I found no one who could sing it perfectly; until finally, after long practice and various trials, they acquired some familiarity with it. Many musicians, too, who are ignorant of the more secret laws of harmony, have rejected many things without reason. I have decided to deliberately ignore their sayings, as they have hardly any knowledge of **speculative music** <note>Theoretical music studied as a mathematical and philosophical science, rather than just practical performance.</note> or the science of proportions.

Therefore, having set aside these unskilled judges of things, I call upon the most skilled Musicians of all Europe to explore the secrets of this composition; and if indeed they are lovers of truth and weigh each detail in the scale of right reason and judgment, they will confess that whatever has been said up to now is most true and rests on an unshakeable foundation of reason. And since the measure of time is rendered most difficult for those unaccustomed to it due to the frequent syncopations of the occurring phrases; for this reason, I would wish that singers, as an exercise, would learn to pronounce each phrase exactly in order. For in this way, both the harmony of the composition and the perfect arrangement of the **fugues** <note>Musical themes that "chase" each other through different voices.</note> following each other with beautiful artifice will be more clearly revealed. So that the composer might also more easily perceive the connection of individual notes, we have presented the whole composition exactly transposed; lest we should seem to have omitted anything that might be profitable to one eager to learn.

->**Fantasia in favor of the Fourth**<-

### *Book VII. Concerning Ancient-Modern Music-making, etc.* 635

CHAPTER VII.

*Concerning Chromatic and Enharmonic Compositions.*

**T**here is a great controversy among modern authors regarding compositions of the three-fold genre <note>The three "genera" of ancient Greek music: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic, which differ by the intervals used in their scales.</note>. Some believe that modern music is purely Diatonic; several others say it is mixed or "participated" (as they call it); some assert that Chromatic and Enharmonic compositions were the most used in antiquity and were suited, if anything was, for stirring the passions <note>original: "affectibus concitandis"</note>; others have asserted the opposite. On these matters, consult Nicola Vicentino <note>An Italian Renaissance theorist (1511–1576) famous for building an "archicembalo" to play ancient Greek intervals.</note> at the end of his fourth book. We have decided to indicate in this place what we think amidst such confusion and what we have observed in authors, so that we may perform this task most excellently.

<margin>What are Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic monody and polyody? And how do they proceed?</margin>
First, it must be noted that Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic monody <term>monody: music consisting of a single melodic line</term> is one thing; polyody <term>polyody: music for multiple voices, or polyphony</term> is another. Diatonic monody is when a single voice always proceeds through two whole tones and a semitone (half-step), according to the testimony of Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose writings on music were the standard for medieval and Renaissance education.</note>. Chromatic monody is when the voice alone, according to the cited Boethius, always proceeds by two semitones and an "incomposite semiditone" <note>original: "semiditonum incompositum" — a minor third treated as a single interval rather than a scale step.</note>. Enharmonic monody, however, is when a single voice always proceeds by two quarter-tones <note>original: "dieses"</note> and an "incomposite ditone" <note>original: "ditonum incompositum" — a major third treated as a single interval.</note>. There is no doubt that monody of this kind was in use among the ancients; and today no one should doubt that such things can be both composed and sung, as will be seen in what follows.

The only question is whether these genres can be adapted to several voices, or whether polyphonic compositions can be made Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic? Therefore, I answer briefly: if the rule prescribed by Boethius regarding the progression of the three genres is to be strictly held, it can by no means be fulfilled in a harmony of several voices. Since a progression from tone to whole tone and to a semitone—while maintaining harmony across different voices—is incongruous due to the different cadences of the other voices, unless we wish to assign the same intervals to every individual voice. But then it should not be called polyphonic (many-voiced), but "isophonic" <note>meaning "same-sounding," where everyone sings the exact same intervals</note> or a monody singable by multiple voices. However, a four-part piece <note>original: "tetraphonium"</note> can be made simply Diatonic, so that the Diatonic progression in each individual voice always follows the progression of another voice in the manner of a fugue <term>fugue: a compositional technique where a melodic theme is introduced by one part and successively taken up by others</term>, while the remaining voices meanwhile maintain other intervals, both composite <note>intervals made of multiple steps</note> and incomposite <note>simple steps</note>. But so that the matter may be plain to the eye, it seemed fitting to show here a simple Diatonic example, without any mixing of genres as far as possible, so that from this harmonic model <note>original: "paradigmate"</note> the reader may judge what is to be thought of the Diatonic style of the Ancients.

Model of Pure and Simple Diatonic music according to the mind of Boethius.

**Book VII. On Antique-modern Music-making, etc. 637**

the ears can scarcely endure them, nor can they be avoided. It is clear from these things fourthly, that modern music— <margin>Modern Music is not purely diatonic, but a mixture of the remaining genres.</margin> as Vicentino <note>Nicola Vicentino (1511–1576) was an influential music theorist who tried to adapt ancient Greek musical systems for use in Renaissance polyphony.</note> correctly shows in this paradigm—is by no means simply diatonic, but mixed or "participatory," since without this mixture and participation of intervals borrowed from other genres, no variety nor grace of harmony can be attained, whatever others may say to the contrary. It is clear fifthly, that the music of the Ancients, if it followed the process prescribed by Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose mathematical definitions of music dominated medieval and Renaissance thought.</note>, was most simple and devoid of variety, indeed harsh and unrefined; therefore, a mixture of genres and a promiscuous <note>original: "promiscuus" — here meaning a flexible or blended approach rather than a rigid, singular scale.</note> progression of intervals was necessary to defend the dignity of ancient music. I am not unaware that others feel differently, but whoever correctly weighs Boethius’s Chapter 23 will be forced to admit, even unwillingly, that the matter stands so. We have spoken of purely diatonic composition; now let us turn our pen to Chromatic and Enharmonic compositions.

### On Chromatic and Enharmonic Compositions.

**T**he first man, so far as I know, who devised anything regarding compositions of the three genres was Nicola Vicentino. When he saw that the division of tetrachords <term>tetrachord: a series of four notes spanning a perfect fourth, the basic building block of ancient Greek scales</term> according to the three genres described by Boethius could not suit polyphonic composition <term>melothesia: the art of composing a melody or musical setting</term> and our method of composing, he engineered another method, which he treats at length in an entire book. Meanwhile, there were some admirers and fierce defenders of ancient music who, for that reason, wrongly and undeservedly mocked the said Vicentino, claiming he had changed the genres wisely established by the ancients and substituted I know not what counterfeit genres. But anyone who examines the matter a little more deeply will be forced to admit that Vicentino performed this led by the highest reason, and that a chromatic-enharmonic polyphony <term>polyphonia: music with multiple simultaneous voice parts</term> could not have been achieved except through the method of composition he passed down. But so that the matter may be deeply understood, it seemed appropriate here to demonstrate from the first principles the difference of the modes according to both Boethius and Vicentino.

### On the Genres.

<margin>The system which Nicola Vicentino applied in composing chromatic-enharmonic music.</margin>
**T**he Diatonic, therefore, which Vicentino uses, is not the same as the ancient one; for Boethius forms the Diatonic tetrachord from a minor semitone and two major tones having the <term>sesquioctava: the 9:8 ratio, the standard mathematical definition of a "whole tone"</term> proportion. But the Diatonic tetrachord that Vicentino uses consists of a major semitone and two tones, one minor <term>sesquinona: the 10:9 ratio, a slightly smaller "minor tone" used in just intonation</term> and the other minor <term>sesquioctava: the 9:8 ratio</term>. Therefore, the fourths and fifths in Boethius’s system in this genre are perfect, yet they do not admit any ditone <note>a "major third" made of two 9:8 tones, which sounds out of tune in harmony</note>, semiditone, or hexachord; or, what is the same thing, neither Thirds nor Sixths can be associated in the said genre by any means. <margin>In what Vicentino differs from Boethius.</margin> In our Diatonic, however, there is the greatest use of Thirds and Sixths; they emerge from the division of the fourth into a major semitone and two tones, of which one is minor and the other is major. For from this, a slightly lengthened fourth and a shortened fifth will assign harmonies most pleasing to the ear; <margin>The Ancients did not use thirds and sixths.</margin> let it be clear even from this that there is much greater variety in music in this age than formerly, since at that time there was no use of thirds and sixths, nor could there be while retaining the tetrachord of the said diatonic genre. Whence modern music may not undeservedly be called "participatory" and a mixture of the parts and intervals of the three genres, and certain chromatic species.

The Boethian Chromatic genre similarly differs from that of Vicentino and the method of certain moderns. Boethius, for the tetrachord of the Chromatic genre, requires a minor and major semitone along with a semiditone, that is, a <term>trihemitone: an interval consisting of three semitones, equivalent to a minor third</term>. Vicentino’s Chromatic, on the contrary, requires a major and minor semitone and then a semiditone or an uncomposed minor third, as follows.

<margin>With what intervals the Enharmonic tetrachord sounds.</margin> Finally, the tetrachord <term>tetrachord: a series of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth</term> of the Enharmonic genus, as described by Boethius <note>original: "Boetio descripti"</note>, consists of two dieses and an uncomposite ditone <term>ditone: an interval of two whole tones, essentially a major third</term>, as has been stated elsewhere. In this context, a diesis <term>diesis: a microtonal interval smaller than a semitone</term> is nothing other than half of a minor semitone; indeed, the name "diesis" was born from the division of a semitone into two equal parts. Vicentino’s tetrachord, however, consists sometimes of two dieses, and sometimes of two dieses with a comma <term>comma: a very small interval resulting from the difference between two other intervals</term> and a ditone—that is, two tones, one of which is major and the other minor—and he uses these as the requirements of the composition <note>original: "melothesias" — the art of melodic construction</note> dictate. <margin>Enharmonic species of the Fifth</margin>

### The Four Species of the Enharmonic Fifth

| First Species | Second Species | Third Species | Fourth Species |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [Notation: Tone - Diesis - Diesis - Ditone] | [Notation: Diesis - Tone - Diesis - Ditone] | [Notation: Diesis - Diesis - Tone - Ditone] | [Notation: Ditone - Tone - Diesis - Diesis] |

| <note>A Fifth starting with a whole step.</note> | <note>The whole step is shifted to the second position.</note> | <note>The whole step is shifted to the third position.</note> | <note>The whole step is placed between the major third and the quarter-tones.</note> |

<column-break/>

As we have demonstrated with the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>the interval of a perfect fourth</note>, the variety of musical "species" or patterns is created by moving the smallest intervals—the <term>dieses</term> <note>original: "diesis"; in ancient Greek theory, this refers to a quarter-tone or a microtonal interval</term>—to different positions within the scale. 

In this <term>enharmonic genus</term> <note>the most complex of the three ancient Greek musical styles, characterized by the use of microtones</term>, the melody is built upon the <term>ditone</term> <note>a major third</note>. Just as the semitone provides the "flavor" of the diatonic scale, these tiny quarter-tones and wide leaps of the major third provide the unique, piercing character of the enharmonic style.

The student should observe that in the <term>diapente</term> <note>the interval of a perfect fifth</note>, there are four possible species because there are four possible placements for the additional whole tone that distinguishes the Fifth from the Fourth.

**Diatonic Species.**
[Musical staff showing the standard steps of a scale using diamond-shaped notes, labeled 6 and 7 above]

**Chromatic Species.**
[Musical staff showing the scale with sharps and flats used to create smaller steps]

**Enharmonic Species.**

You see, therefore, in each of the diatonic species the movement of a semitone <note>a half-step</note>; in the chromatic, the movement of a <term>semiditone</term> <note>a minor third</note>; and finally in the enharmonic, the progression of a <term>ditone</term> <note>a major third</note>. Just as the movement of the semitone establishes different diatonic tones in various species, so the movement of the minor third establishes various chromatic tones in the chromatic genus, and the movement of the major third establishes the various enharmonic tones in the enharmonic genus. We have expressed these leaps in each species using black notes. The reason the enharmonic species contain more notes is that more <term>dieses</term> <note>quarter-tones</note> are required to complete the fourth, fifth, and octave, as is evident from the examples.

Having thus determined the species of the Octave in this triple genus, anyone can easily form the <term>clausulae</term> <note>musical cadences or ending formulas</note> of the twelve tones proper to each genus. With these tasks completed, nothing remains but for me to now reveal the method by which anyone can compose melodies of every kind according to this triple genus. Therefore, proceed in this manner:

<margin>
How chromatic composition is to be restored according to the rules
</margin>

Since the chromatic genus consists of semitones and "incomposite" <note>unbroken or leap-like</note> minor thirds, if someone wishes to compose in that genus, they can do so according to all the chromatic modes proposed previously, even if a whole tone never occurs in them—except for the diatonic steps from *ut* to *re*, from *re* to *mi*, from *fa* to *sol*, and from *sol* to *la* <note>the standard syllables of the hexachord system, similar to modern do-re-mi</note>. If, however, a whole tone should occasionally occur, it must be divided into two semitones, major and minor, and then one must proceed according to the rules we handed down previously. But lest we seem to have treated the matter only in theory, it seemed fitting to provide the harmonic cadences here for the better instruction of the curious <term>musurgus</term> <note>original: "musurgus"; a term for a skilled composer or "music-maker"</note>.

A composer can, however, write chromatic cadences in all the diversity of the eight Tones, avoiding only this: that a whole tone be introduced anywhere (for example, from *ut* to *re*, or *re* to *mi*, or *fa* to *sol*, or *sol* to *la*). If a whole tone does occur in this genus, the remedy will be to divide the tone into two parts—that is, two semitones, one major and one minor. Which of these two semitones should take the first or second place is left to the judgment of the composer, who will arrange them as the occasion, the words, the emotions, or similar circumstances require. To ensure he does not err in the chromatic tone, we wanted to include here first the progression of the first chromatic tone, according to which the following <term>melothesia</term> <note>the art of composing melody</note> is arranged.

**Chromatic Cadences.**

[Four staves of musical notation follow, illustrating various chromatic melodic patterns. The notation includes frequent accidentals such as sharps, flats, and double-sharps—represented by crosses—showing the "clausulae" or melodic formulas used to end musical phrases in the chromatic style.]

Furthermore, just as the <term>diatonic genus</term> <note>the standard musical scale of whole steps and half steps</note> proceeds by its own proportioned steps and leaps, and in the <term>chromatic</term> the diatonic order is interrupted so that two <term>semitones</term> <note>half-steps</note> are created from a single whole tone, followed immediately by an uncomposite <term>trihemitone</term> <note>a minor third, literally "three half-tones"</note>; so too the **Enharmonic genus** breaks the order of both the diatonic and chromatic by a certain <term>irrational</term> <note>original: *aloga*, referring to proportions that do not fit into simple whole-number ratios</note> proportion, dividing a semitone into two <term>dieses</term> <note>quarter-tones or micro-intervals</note>, which a <term>ditone</term> <note>a major third</note> immediately follows.

If anyone, therefore, wishes to form enharmonic cadences, let him observe only this: that he never places a whole tone or a major semitone in any part, but proceeds through the middle parts of the minor semitone—that is, the **dieses**—which should be followed by a ditone or major third, while proceeding with leaps of Fourths and Fifths. <margin>How enharmonic composition is to be established</margin> However, so that the matter may be better understood, it seemed appropriate to provide this paradigm of enharmonic cadences, from which the reader will perceive my intention better than through many winding paths of words.

Note, however, that **syncopations** <note>rhythms that shift the accent to the "off-beat"</note> should be avoided as much as possible in this genus, lest the softness and enharmonic sweetness be disturbed by the harshness of the syncopation. The notes should not be "diminished" <note>broken into very fast, short values</note>, nor should the tempo be fast; for since these intervals are the smallest possible, they would escape the ears if played with such speed. Nor should the tempo be too slow, otherwise the same loss of clarity would occur. 

But before we proceed to the paradigm of pure "Vicentinian" enharmonic composition <note>referring to Nicola Vicentino, a 16th-century theorist who attempted to revive ancient Greek microtonal music</note>, I thought I should first display the **repercussions** <note>the characteristic melodic intervals that define a specific musical mode</note> of the 8th Enharmonic Tone, upon which the following song is composed.

**Paradigm of Enharmonic cadences.**

[Four systems of musical notation on five-line staves follow, featuring various notes and accidentals. Small 'x' marks <note>these 'x' marks represent the enharmonic diesis or quarter-tone, a hallmark of Vicentino’s system</note> are placed below or beside specific notes to indicate microtonal shifts. Truly, nothing remains but for us to set down here some examples of composition in both the **chromatic** and **enharmonic** styles, so that from them, as if from a model, the method of proceeding in similar cases might become clear. Let no one persuade themselves, however, that we are giving here the chromatic and enharmonic compositions of the ancients described by **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory text for a millennium</note> and others; for it is scarcely possible to perform these with multiple voices. Furthermore, if they were composed according to the decrees of the ancients, they could neither be sung, nor—even if they could be sung—would they find any favor with the ears because of the disordered leaps and horrid cadences; for you would hear the <term>tritone</term> <note>an interval of three whole tones, historically called the "devil in music" for its dissonance</note> almost everywhere, along with other dissonant intervals by which the ears are marvelously tormented.

All these things, whatever others may babble against him, **Nicola Vicentino** <note>A 16th-century theorist and composer famous for inventing the archicembalo and advocating for the revival of ancient Greek microtonal genera</note> judiciously foresaw. Hence he judged that the chromatic genus must necessarily be divided in such a way that he avoided both whole tones in the chromatic and major semitones in the enharmonic. For the use of musical practice <note>original: *praxeos melotheticæ*</note>, if these intervals should ever occur, he first divides them, and then uses the divided parts. Nor can any other more convenient method be supplied to us, as is evident in the following chromatic composition. 

Whenever, truly, we make mention of "pure chromatic," it is to be understood as the pure Boethian chromatic, not indeed that which Vicentino taught; since we have described that above, I have thought it superfluous to repeat it here. Neither, however, ought that genus which Vicentino prescribes be properly called "mixed," nor is it entirely pure chromatic and enharmonic. This is because music may only be called "pure diatonic," "chromatic," or "enharmonic" when it is composed strictly according to the rigor of the rules prescribed by Boethius. It is not properly "mixed" because, while he insists on the course of the rules for pure chromatic and enharmonic, he is necessarily forced to divide the Boethian intervals to achieve his aim. By doing so, the "purity" is destroyed, yet the intended mixture of the <term>diatonic</term> <note>the standard scale of tones and semitones</note> is not obtained. What sort of thing is properly "mixed," therefore, will be indicated below. But all these things will be more clearly revealed from the following examples.

This <term>composition</term> <note>original: "Melothesia," referring to the art of setting a melody</note> is almost entirely chromatic, and uses enharmonic steps in only two places; if it were filled entirely with chromatisms, besides lacking variety, it would remarkably irritate the ears. Therefore, it is necessary for it to be mixed and shared with the <term>diatonic</term> <note>the standard scale system of whole and half steps used in Western music</note> style. Furthermore, the rules that teach how to recognize major and minor semitones were handed down above; but as for the notes marked by some sign, those alone shall be sung according to that sign. Notes without a sign, however, will be expressed by the sign of the ordinary clef, whether by a "harsh b" <note>original: "b incitatum," referring to a natural or sharp sign</note> or by a "soft b" <note>original: "b molle," the origin of our modern flat sign</note>.

Therefore, those people are to be laughed at who, persuaded by a certain false imagination, think that pure chromatic and enharmonic compositions can not only be conveniently made for several voices, but that nothing more effective than these can be given for stirring the emotions. This is so far from being true that nothing is more repugnant, as we showed a little while ago; but now that the chromatic composition has been provided, let us also provide the Enharmonic one, so that we do not seem to have hidden anything from the curious musician. 

Truly, how the "pure Enharmonic" is to be understood was stated above; and although that could easily be done according to the rules explained earlier and the mind of **Boethius** <note>The 6th-century philosopher whose works transmitted Greek music theory to the Middle Ages</note>; since, however, as I said, it can only be continued for a long time with great difficulty without <term>tritones</term> and <term>false fourths</term> <note>dissonant intervals that were traditionally avoided in polyphonic singing</note>; therefore, I would not advise musicians to spend their effort on continuing in pure chromatic or enharmonic styles for many measures. Because of the occurrence of these "exotic" intervals, they can neither be easily performed by singers, nor, if they were performed, would they achieve that grace which some people imagine they would. Note that this sign **x**, wherever it is placed, always denotes the <term>enharmonic diesis</term> <note>a microtonal interval, often a quarter-tone, used to bridge the smallest gaps in the enharmonic scale</note>.

### COROLLARY I.

From this <term>composition</term> <note>original: "Melothesia," the art of melody-making</note> it is clear that many steps and leaps occur which are irrational and <term>illogical</term> <note>original: "alogos," referring to mathematical ratios that do not fit the standard Greek musical proportions</note>, which could by no means be admitted in the <term>diatonic</term> <note>the standard scale system of whole and half steps</note> style. Such intervals include the minor and major tone, the smallest and largest major third, the fourth and fifth; and I truly do not know what natural repugnance the aforementioned diatonic genus has with these chromatic-enharmonic styles. Scarcely—indeed, not even scarcely—can many voices be so arranged in this style that illicit intervals are avoided. For just as shadow follows light, so "false fourths," diminished fifths, and "false octaves" follow this style. Or, if you wish to avoid these faults, you would find yourself establishing a diatonic composition instead, contrary to your intended goal.

<margin>The difficulty of composing in pure chromatic and enharmonic styles</margin>

I have certainly left no stone unturned in my effort to find, through the diligence of combination and the rules of arithmetic harmonic consonance, a way to make this business work—but in vain. For legitimate harmony always possessed a certain <term>diatonic</term> character, while that which was "spurious" and faulty smacked of a chromatic-enharmonic nature. Consequently, I have almost despaired of harmonizing the "pure" chromatic or enharmonic styles in a concert of several voices.

Added to this was the fact that <term>enharmonic</term> <note>the most complex of the three ancient Greek musical scales, using intervals smaller than a semitone, often called "quarter-tones"</note> composition finds singers with great difficulty who can perform it exactly. This is because the steps are too minute to be reached by the human voice, which is far too slippery and flexible. Therefore, so that the unity of the harmony might be perceived exactly, it would have to be expressed with the help of a "triharmonic pipe organ" <note>original: "organi physaulij triharmonici," a specialized organ Kircher designed to play in all three Greek genera</note>. Yet even that would not be a secure undertaking, due to the organist's lack of skill; because of the unusual <term>keyboards</term> <note>original: "tastaturas"</note>, he would easily strike one note instead of another, unless through long use and experience he finally acquired some mastery of the practice. 

However, if these kinds of compositions were transferred to the "compositional drum" <note>original: "tympanũ melotacticũ," a pinned cylinder used in automatic musical instruments</note> of an Automatic Triharmonic Organ by mathematical mastery, they could be perfectly exhibited in this way without any danger of error—just like any diatonic composition. In this manner, the differences between each style could be exactly perceived.

Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-Making. 647

### COROLLARY II.

It is also evident that this music of the Ancients, composed of the triple <term>genus</term> <note>The three types of scales: Diatonic (whole/half steps), Chromatic (half steps/minor thirds), and Enharmonic (quarter-tones/major thirds)</note>, was more a matter of theoretical speculation than something widely practiced. This is because it is simply impossible for a melody consisting of purely continued diatonic, chromatic, or enharmonic intervals to sound pleasing to the ears. If we were to stand by the rules of <term>Boethius</term> <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works were the primary source for Greek music theory in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note>, and in the <term>diatonic</term> style always progressed by whole tones and major semitones, words can hardly describe how much the ears would be displeased by this same "warmed-over cabbage" <note>original: *crambe repetita*, a Latin idiom for a tiresome, boring repetition</note> of repeated intervals; indeed, this was clear from the example provided above.

If, however, we were to progress in the <term>chromatic</term> style always by semitones and minor thirds <note>original: *trihemitonia*, literally "three half-tones"</note>, the fabric of the melody would become utterly tedious. We would be unable to use a whole tone, a major third, a fourth, or a fifth—without which all the vigor of music perishes. Finally, if we should progress by <term>dieses</term> <note>quarter-tones or microtones</note> and major thirds in the enharmonic style, a great difficulty arises for two reasons. First, one would have to abstain from all <term>syncopation</term> <note>the suspension of notes across beats</note>, without which all the grace and beauty of music fails. Second, all <term>diminutions</term> <note>fast, decorative notes that break down longer note values</note> would have to be avoided with the greatest care. For if one proceeds by the tiny intervals of the quarter-tones, these would vanish entirely if the voices were moved too quickly; the same would happen if the tempo were too slow. Thus, a certain moderate "middle ground" would have to be held in practice, which is nearly impossible <note>original: *ἀδύνατος* (adynatos)</note>.

If these species are occasionally inserted into the diatonic style and expressed in short phrases in proportion to the piece, there is no doubt that, due to the unusual nature of the intervals, they can do much to stir the emotions of the soul, as will be seen shortly. From this, it is clear enough that the Ancients never exhibited these types of scales in <term>polyphony</term> <note>music with many simultaneous voice parts</note>, but only in <term>monody</term> <note>a single melodic line</note> through a highly flexible voice. Nor in our own chromatic and enharmonic examples are all the voices of this type; rather, one voice is occasionally chromatic or enharmonic, while the rest maintain the diatonic style. Whence I infer that our entire method of composing and singing is not purely diatonic, but is <margin>Our method of singing is not purely diatonic but mixed.</margin> "mixed" or "participated," and is forged from all three genera, as was proven at length above. Therefore, having properly examined these things, let us see what should be thought concerning the ancient music of the Greeks.

## CHAPTER VIII.

## On the mixed Diatonic-Chromatic-Enharmonic style.

We have shown in the preceding sections that <term>composition</term> <note>original: *melothesia*</note> according to the pure, continuous triple genus of the ancients—diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic—can hardly be achieved without a clash of prohibited intervals. If, perhaps, such a thing could be produced with great labor, it would nevertheless be so forced, harsh, and brittle due to the unrefined leaps that the ears could scarcely endure it, as was clear from the examples placed just before.

Lest the famous triple genus of music, celebrated for so many centuries, should seem to have been established in vain, a great desire came upon my mind to restore the perhaps lost chromatic-enharmonic method, as far as the powers of my intellect would permit. That is, to find some way by which chromatic and enharmonic compositions could be arranged so that, with all harshness removed, they might be not only pleasing to the ears, but also wonderfully capable of arousing the emotions. Whether I have achieved this, let the judgment of skilled and fair-minded musicians decide.

While I was working on these things, I happened by some chance or fortune upon the acquaintance and friendship of **Galeazzo Sabbatini of Pesaro** <note>A prominent Italian composer and music theorist (c. 1597–1662)</note>. From my interactions with him, I immediately gathered that the man was highly skilled not only in theoretical music, but also in practical application, and moreover was an outstanding...

...and a composer perfect in every respect; as will be clear from his compositions to be presented shortly. Before we return to our main purpose, however, we will first set forth certain principles according to the mind of Sabbatini <note>Galeazzo Sabbatini (1597–1662) was an Italian composer and theorist whom Kircher admired for his ability to integrate complex theory into practical music.</note>. To these, our own inventions will be added so that a restoration of the three <term>genera</term> <note>The three types of scales: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note> may finally be brought to light. Let no one think, however, that we are going to produce purely chromatic or enharmonic compositions here; rather, we shall mix them with diatonic elements in such a way that they finally achieve the desired effect. We write this not for purely practical musicians, who would have difficulty understanding our intention, but for those who possess theory joined with practice. And since we are about to construct an exotic musical structure, we have thought it necessary to lay foundations proportioned to it.

There are, therefore, three genera of music already mentioned quite often: the diatonic, the chromatic, and the enharmonic. The **Diatonic** is that which proceeds from Tone to Tone and to the major semitone, and vice versa; but just as this is "pure," so it does not allow for <term>accidents</term> <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to sharps or flats that move a note outside the natural scale.</note>; hence, whenever it moves from Tone to Tone, or from a major semitone to another of its kind, it loses its natural state. The **Chromatic**, however, does not proceed only through the intervals of the diatonic genus, but also proceeds through the major to the minor <term>diesis</term> <note>A very small musical interval, often smaller than a semitone.</note>, and from this to others of this kind; it possesses different consonances and strings which it can use, both purely and mixed with diatonic strings, and consequently it has "looser reins" than the diatonic. The **Enharmonic** possesses the greatest breadth; for it contains within itself not only all the intervals of the diatonic and chromatic genera, but also has other particular intervals, both pure and mixed, as well as different consonances and progressions, as will be seen later in the <term>tetrachords</term> <note>A series of four notes bound by the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> of each. From this, it can undoubtedly be brought into effect in both pure and mixed forms, though not without special study and the most exquisite industry, which we intend to provide here.

And since, for the reasons stated above, we studiously avoid the "pure" genera, we proceed by another method in our diatonic system: namely, alternating from a **minor Tone** (in the proportion of 10 to 9) to a **major Tone** (consisting in the proportion of 9 to 8). Although the major Tone exceeds the minor by one <term>comma</term> <note>The "Syntonic Comma," a tiny mathematical difference in pitch (81:80) resulting from different ways of tuning intervals.</note> (in the proportion of 81 to 80), it is necessary that the intervals by which they are divided be different. The minor Tone is divided first by a semitone (which consists in the proportion of 16 to 15) and then by a diesis (consisting in the proportion of 25 to 24)—that is, it is resolved into the parts of which it consists. The major Tone is divided in two ways: either by a major semitone in the proportion of 27 to 25 and then a diesis in the proportion of 25 to 24; or by a semitone of 16 to 15 and a major diesis in the proportion of 135 to 128, from which it is composed, as will be clear to anyone multiplying the intervals and comparing one with the other.

But now let us inquire into the ratios of each in their appropriate tetrachords, so that the variety of each genus, their intervals, progressions, consonances, and "accidents" (whether pure or mixed) may become known, and finally, what use all of these may have in composition. We shall place here three tetrachords, of which the first two are conjunct and the third is disjunct, as is clear in the following diagram. A **conjunct tetrachord** is so called when the second begins where the first ends; thus you see the first tetrachord ends in E, where the second begins equally. A **disjunct tetrachord** is so called when the last note of the preceding and the first of the following differ by a whole interval; as is clear in the second and third tetrachords, where the last note of the second tetrachord ends in A, but the first note of the following tetrachord begins in G. However, since all these things were handed down by us most extensively in Book 4, I have thought it superfluous to dwell on them longer in this place.

In this diagram, each set of four notes represents a <term>tetrachord</term> <note>A scale of four notes used as the building block of Ancient Greek music theory.</note>; the letters signify the keys <note>Pitch names: B (represented by the natural sign), C, D, E, etc.</note>, and the numbers placed between them represent the mathematical proportions of the intervals, which the names written below explain.

You see, therefore, that in the **first tetrachord** the progression is by a **major semitone**, then by a **minor tone** and a **major tone**. In the **second**, however, the progression is by a **major semitone**, then by a **major tone** and a **minor tone**. Finally, in the **third**—which is twice as high in pitch—the progression follows the same intervals as in the first.

From this it is clear that the progression does not always occur through the same intervals, but through diverse ones; but let us look more closely at the matter in the continuous order of the three tetrachords, which we have reduced to a common proportion of smaller terms.

### On the Tetrachords of the Chromatic Genus.

We can arrive at a knowledge of the Chromatic genus <term>Chromatic genus: a scale that uses smaller intervals, like semitones, more frequently than the Diatonic</term> by the same path through which we reached our understanding of the Diatonic. It must therefore be known that in the Chromatic genus, established according to our rules, one must proceed by the minor semitone, the major diesis <note>a very small interval, often the difference between a sharp and a flat</note>, and the semiditone <note>a minor third</note>. 

In order that you may more clearly perceive the rationale of the whole Chromatic genus in the movement of harmonies, we will here arrange three tetrachords <note>four-note scales</note> of the Chromatic genus; from these, you will discover which intervals and consonances <note>harmonious sounds</note> are permitted and which are forbidden to be used in the chromatic style.

Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-making, etc. 653

The intervals reviewed belong to the chromatic genus. It should also be known that the **Accidentals** <note>In this context, accidentals refer to signs that modify the pitch of a note, such as flats and sharps.</note> which alter the notes or intervals are of two types: some signify the semitone $\flat$, others signify the **diesis** <term>Diesis: a very small interval, often used here to refer to a sharp (♯) that raises a note by a chromatic semitone</term>, whether chromatic or enharmonic. 

The semitone signified by the $\flat$ <note>original: "b"</note> properly belongs to the **diatonic genus** and lowers a note to a deeper pitch; it is the smallest interval of the diatonic genus and can be extended downward infinitely. It always possesses a determined **root number** which defines it, as was clear from the preceding harmonic discussion. Its root is a number derived from the number 15. Every $\flat$ can easily be stretched downward toward a major third, such that it will produce a harmony that is sweeter the lower the $\flat$ is tuned. This is because it will then have more divisors and common terms; the more common terms it has in agreement with others, the sweeter the harmony it produces. The same must be said of other intervals to which it proceeds. 

Conversely, the accidental sign $\sharp$ produces the opposite effect; for that sign, properly and artificially used in notes that it increases toward the acute <note>"Acute" refers to higher pitch/treble; "grave" refers to lower pitch/bass.</note>, cannot be explained through its own [simple] numbers. For example, the number 2 and the $\sharp$ cannot be formed together, because the $\sharp$ exists in the ratio of $\frac{25}{24}$. But the number 2, however many times it is multiplied by itself, cannot generate the number 25 or 24; therefore, it cannot "hold" a $\sharp$. For a number to constitute an interval or consonance, it must at least be able to serve as the greater or lesser term of such an interval; this does not happen with the number 2, which cannot produce 25 or 24, no matter how many times it is doubled, to establish the $\sharp$ represented by $\frac{25}{24}$.

The **Diesis** increases every interval or note to which it is joined toward the acute in the ratio of $\frac{25}{24}$, making it harsher and more "languid." This is partly because it is artificial, partly because it turns a natural note into an accidental one, and partly because it lacks its own significant numbers, as well as common and "friendly" numbers by which it could be measured with a common scale. Musicians should know this: a proportion or consonance is sweeter the more common terms it possesses. Conversely, when it has no common term, the harmony turns out unsuitable.

Therefore, so that anyone may perfectly understand the logic of the **chromatic genus**, they must especially note its progression: moving from the semitone to the $\sharp$; passing to a whole tone; and moving toward intervals and consonances augmented or diminished by the $\sharp$. Just as in the **diatonic genus** we do not use intervals and consonances absolutely or without a rule, this same principle must be extended to the chromatic, which allows for "looser reins" than the diatonic, as has been said.

Furthermore, the accidental note $\Delta$, which we call the **enharmonic diesis**, exists in the ratio of $\frac{128}{125}$. It is the smallest singable interval, and can only be expressed by the most skilled singers <note>original: "phonascis peritissimis"</note>; it is the proper accidental of the **enharmonic genus**. We have seen the logic of the chromatic genus shining forth in the three tetrachords; nothing further remains but to show how they are used in the business of harmony, and how a composer <note>original: "musurgus"</note> may adopt these same intervals to complete the true chromatic compositions intended thus far. This is the ultimate end and goal of this entire narrative. 

Therefore, a master composer, skilled and cautious in the chromatic style, is required for the start of a composition. He should diligently foresee the intervals proper to the chromatic genus and accommodate them to the bass with such industry that he finally achieves his intended goal. However, lest we be more of a hindrance than a help to the reader with a multitude of rules, we will here subjoin several **paradigms** <note>Models or examples.</note> composed with all rigor. From these prototypes, the curious reader will easily understand my meaning, for they will be guided by the hand, as it were, to create similar works with similar artistry. In these compositions, I would have you note that we will present works of the chromatic genus that possess a certain mixed logic of all three genera, and thus may be easily translated through various transpositions into the usual method of modern compositions.

658 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance.
->On the Enharmonic Genus,<-
->as discovered by the Author<-

Many of the Ancients have handed down various accounts concerning the <term>enharmonic genus</term><note>One of the three classifications of tetrachords in ancient Greek music, known for using very small intervals called quarter-tones.</note>, and while they certainly agree on some points, they differ on others. They all agree that it is so difficult to sing that it has been almost entirely abandoned, and that it was only ever sung by those most highly skilled in the art. Furthermore, they agree that in any given <term>tetrachord</term><note>original: "tetrachordo." A scale of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> it proceeds by way of a <term>diesis</term><note>original: "diesin." A microtonal interval smaller than a semitone.</note> and a <term>ditone</term><note>original: "ditonum." An interval of two whole tones, equivalent to a major third.</note>; and that it could only be performed in <term>monodies</term><note>original: "monodijs." Music consisting of a single melodic line.</note>, and not at all in <term>polyodies</term><note>original: "polyodijs." Music for multiple voices or parts; polyphony.</note>. They also agree that it possessed several tetrachords, both conjunct and disjunct, and that it cannot be sung in its "pure" or unmixed form. 

However, they disagree because some assigned several different species to this genus. For some assigned its intervals by means of harmonic numbers, others by means of dissonant and enharmonic ones; others, leaving everything to the judgment of the ears, confused the individual details indiscriminately, as has been proven extensively elsewhere. But they differ most significantly in defining the nature of the enharmonic diesis; for Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and theorist of the 4th century BCE who emphasized the role of the human ear in music over mathematical ratios.</note> thought that it was...

### Book VII. On Ancient-modern Music-making. 659

...this is not to be understood as being made of equal quarter-tones <note>original: *dieses*</note>, but through differing quarter-tones, namely by the ratios of **128 to 125** and **25 to 24**.

Having established these as the indisputable principles of mathematical investigation, we shall arrange the **enharmonic tetrachord** <note>A tetrachord is a series of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth; it was the building block of ancient Greek scales.</note> in this manner. Therefore, to understand by which numbers, notes, and intervals the Enharmonic genus proceeds, we will set out three tetrachords here: two joined together and one separated, as follows. In the first tetrachord, the 1st step between $\natural$ and $\natural$ <note>Kircher uses a modified natural sign to indicate an enharmonic note raised by a quarter-tone.</note> is an **enharmonic quarter-tone**, and its proportion is indicated by the numbers **128 to 125**. Between $\natural$ and **C**, however, is the place of the **major or chromatic quarter-tone** in the proportion of **25 to 24**. Finally, between **C** and **E**, a **major third** <note>original: *ditonus*</note> is placed, as the proportion of **5 to 4** teaches; the same is to be observed in the remaining tetrachords.

| Tetrachord I | Tetrachord II | Tetrachord III |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 128 / 125 | 128 / 125 | 128 / 125 |
| 25 / 24 | 25 / 24 | 25 / 24 |
| 5 / 4 | 5 / 4 | 5 / 4 |

[Musical notation on a five-line staff with three sections corresponding to the tetrachords. Below the notes are the letters: $\natural$. $\natural$. C. E. E. E. F. A. $\natural$. $\natural$. C. E.]

When these intervals are reduced to a common mathematical term <note>This process allows different ratios to be compared on a single numerical scale, much like finding a common denominator in fractions.</note>, they relate to each other as follows:

1. First, an **enharmonic quarter-tone** <note>original: *diesis*</note> will be held, as between $\natural$ $\natural$ $\Lambda$ <note>The symbol $\Lambda$ represents a specific enharmonic pitch.</note> and **E E $\Lambda$**.

664		The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...so much so that the steps are divided according to the Author's mind, as the following paradigm reports:

->**B-flat (*fa*) | B-natural (*mi*) | Chromatic diesis | Enharmonic diesis**<-
->**Minor semitone | Major semitone | Minor semitone | Smallest semitone**<-

And in this, if you consider the Theory, he differs from me, as was clear from the previous discourse; if you consider the Practice, it can be tolerated in any case. Whatever the case may be, the Author has shown that he is not unskilled in Theory, having applied speculation to practice in such a way that he produced a not unpleasant effect.

Whoever, therefore, is going to compose in this genre of style, it is necessary that he knows to a hair <note>original: *ad unguem*; a Latin idiom meaning "to perfection" or "to the fingernail"</note> the reasons and proportions of the enharmonics declared a little earlier in the triple tetrachord. Second, he must not continue the enharmonic cadences <note>original: *clausulas enarmonicas*</note> through the entire context of the composition, but should artfully mix chromatic steps with enharmonic ones, and these with diatonic ones, according to the appropriate degrees. For otherwise it would become pure enharmonic, which we showed above is not without disgust and boredom. Therefore, we should by no means use them in an absolute way, but with great circumspection, caution, and judgment; for just as in the Diatonic style, which many people sing, it is not permitted to use just any intervals and progressions, but only those with discretion and the prescription of rules; so it is in the chromatic and enharmonic styles.

I have thought the rules should be omitted, lest the work be burdened by too great a multitude of things; it is enough for us to have shown some light in this place, by which the sagacious **music-maker** <term>Musurgus: a term used by Kircher for a skilled composer or "architect of music"</term> may be able to reach further knowledge of said things by means of study. And lest we seem to have prescribed things that are too difficult, we will place here for the sake of the curious reader a **three-voice piece** <term>triphonium: a composition for three voices</term> exactly composed according to the triple genus; from which, as if from a certain prototype, the reader can learn the manner of proceeding in compositions of this kind. This will, however, be sung with difficulty except by only the most skilled singers <note>original: *phonasci*</note>. Whatever it may be, practice will make all things easy. I do not doubt that the distinguished **Galeazzo** <note>Galeazzo Sabbatini (1597–1662), a composer and music theorist who collaborated with Kircher on experimental tuning systems</note> will apply his mind before others to composing things similar to this, according to the perspicacity of talent in which he excels.

**CHAPTER IX.**

*Concerning the Change of Mode, or Tone, or the Metabolic Style.*

The common crowd of musicians thinks that all those songs which they see marked with various signs like sharps (#), flats (b), and naturals (♮) are chromatic or enharmonic. This is truly a notable error, and one to be noted from this very chapter, because it has even seized those who wish to be held as consummate masters in Music. The cause of the error is that they do not understand in what the three harmonic <term>genera</term> <note>The three classifications of scales in ancient music: Diatonic (whole and half steps), Chromatic (half steps and minor thirds), and Enharmonic (quarter tones and major thirds)</note> properly consist; and therefore they confuse every change of one tone into another with either the chromatic or the enharmonic style. In truth, the chromatic and enharmonic styles are not established by the aforementioned signs, but by the intervals prescribed a little earlier. 

For if you find a <term>clausula</term> <note>original: "clausulam"; a melodic cadence or musical phrase</note> anywhere which proceeds by a semitone, another semitone, and an uncomposite <term>semiditone</term> <note>a minor third</note>, you will then call this phrase chromatic; if it proceeds by a <term>diesis</term> <note>a microtonal interval smaller than a semitone</note>, another diesis, and an uncomposite <term>ditone</term> <note>a major third</note>, you will then call it enharmonic. If indeed any phrase proceeds from a natural tone to an accidental or "feigned" tone <note>original: "fictum"; referring to <term>Musica Ficta</term>, the practice of adding accidentals not written in the basic hexachord system</note> through semitones or a diesis, or a semiditone or ditone, you will then call it a chromatic or enharmonic species, for it touches the strings <note>the specific pitches or "chords"</note> of these genera. 

But if it falls from a natural tone into any other through any interval whatsoever, then it shall be called a change of tone. In this place, some make a distinction between "mode" and "tone." They say it is a "change of tone" when the <term>system</term> <note>the overall scale structure or key center</note> of the tone is entirely changed; it is called a "change of mode" when a progression is made from a natural string of the tone to one that is not natural—as when a progression that ought to be made from whole tone to whole tone is instead made into a semitone or diesis, as was said a little before.

<margin>The metabolic style is the same as the transpositive.</margin>

Furthermore, both types of change have great emphasis and effect notable alterations in the listeners; they can be varied infinitely and are most fit for expressing any "affections" <note>the 17th-century theory that specific musical devices could trigger specific emotional states, or "passions," in the soul</note>. But this secret is known only to the more skilled masters, which we not incongruously call the **metabolic style** <note>from the Greek "metabole," meaning change or transformation; here referring to what we now call modulation</note>. Truly, I shall perform a worthwhile task if I insert here some examples of this metabolic style, so that the reader may more easily understand what I intend.

## Examples of the **Metabolic Style**

Giacomo Carissimi <note>Original: "Iacobus Charissimus." Carissimi (1605–1674) was one of the most celebrated masters of the early Baroque oratorio.</note>, the most famous Prefect of the musical choir in the German College, used this style with the highest judgment when he beautifully and ingeniously expressed Heraclitus and Democritus <note>Two Greek philosophers famously contrasted in art: Heraclitus "the weeping philosopher" and Democritus "the laughing philosopher."</note>—the latter weeping, the former laughing—in the following metabolic melody. Here, the frequent flats <note>Original: "b mollia."</note> contain nothing chromatic or enharmonic, as the unskilled convince themselves; rather, they only change the tone. The dialogue is composed with remarkable skill, in which these musical phrases of laughter and mourning are expressed with truly incredible variety. But since the composition was longer than is fitting for this space, we decided to omit it, being content with only a single phrase, so that in it, as if in a certain example, the logic of the metabolic style might be more clearly revealed.

### Example I of the Metabolic Style.

[Musical notation: Three staves of music for two voices and a continuo bass.]
**Top Voice:** ...and yet to weep <note>Original Italian: ".e. pur da piangere"</note>
**Middle Voice:** ...yet to laugh <note>Original Italian: "pur da ridere"</note>
**Bass Voice:** [Figured bass numbers: 6, 4/3, flat, 8/7]

You see, therefore, in this example, how the second voice, while it brings forth these Italian words *and yet to laugh*, appropriately expresses laughter through the notes themselves. The first voice, however, while it brings forth the words *and yet to weep*, expresses mourning and tears through a reversed style, contrary to the first.

[Musical notation: Three staves of music for two voices and a continuo bass.]
**Top Voice:** ...weep [musical trills], and yet to weep <note>Original Italian: "gere, tr. tr. tr. è pur da piangere"</note>
**Middle Voice:** ...and yet to laugh, <note>Original Italian: "è pur da ridere"</note>
**Bass Voice:** [Figured bass numbers: flat, 4/3, 4/3, flat, 8/7]

Since this diversity proceeds from the change of one tone into another and strikes the ears as something unusual, it will certainly stir the emotions <note>Original: "affectus." In Baroque theory, "Affects" were specific emotional states that music was designed to trigger in the listener.</note> remarkably, provided that the singers are those who know how to express it beautifully.

## CHAPTER X.
### Concerning Musical Time, and the Signs and Numbers by which both the Ancients and Moderns express it.

Although the entire secret of music lies in the precise and varied delivery <term>prolatione: in early music theory, this refers to the relationship between the values of different notes, specifically the semibreve and the minim</term> of time, I must confess that I have found nothing in all of music treated more confusedly or more imperfectly. I read entire works written on these matters by **Franchinus**, **Zarlino**, **Glareanus**, <note>Franchinus Gaffurius (1451–1522), Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), and Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563) were the most influential music theorists of the Renaissance; Kircher suggests their explanations of rhythm were unnecessarily complex.</note> and almost countless others; yet their writings are so disorganized and dissonant that even after you have spent much time reading them, you can scarcely discern what you have read once you are finished. Furthermore, the opinions of musicians on this subject are so divergent that you can hardly see which one you should follow. Therefore, so that some light might arise for the eager reader in such a dark matter, we have brought this subject back to the anvil <note>original: "ad incudem reuocantes"; a Latin idiom meaning to revise or refine a piece of work through careful labor</note> and have seen fit to explain it in this place in a few words, according to the true reckoning of harmonic time. And although we have also dealt with Time in the preceding books, we did so rather sparingly; here we shall be a little more detailed.

Musical time, therefore—or harmonic time—is nothing other than that space of time in which musical notes...
