[A musical staff with the 3/2 mensuration sign and notes]

Thus you see from these things why the Ancients added these numbers to the signs: namely, so that through them they might know what the value of a note was when produced under one measure of time in signs *without* numbers, and what the value of that same note is under one measure of time in signs *affected* by numbers.

Furthermore, at this point it seems appropriate to uncover another error that has crept into the sesquialtera proportion of time. Many call this "triple" <note>original: "tripla," a 3:1 ratio</note>, perhaps deceived by the error that three semibreves are sung to one breve, or three <term>minims</term><note>A shorter note value, half the length of a semibreve.</note> are sung to one semibreve. But since this proportion concerns only the notes, and this triple progression is hindered by various notes, it cannot rightly be called "triple" unless we refer it back to a **multiple proportion**, which we are not dealing with here, but rather with the **particular sesquialtera**.

In order to correct this error, others propose the ratio of the sesquialtera proportion as shown below; but again, they do so incorrectly. Indeed, songs in sesquialtera proportion, which are commonly in use,

[Two musical staves. The top one has a 'C' sign; the bottom one has '3' over '2']

cannot properly be called sesquialtera, but rather **proportions of equality**. This occurs when three semibreves are sung either against three semibreves, or against one breve and one semibreve (which are equivalent to three semibreves), as is evident in the example on the side. In that second example, although the final notes of the Bass relate to the notes of the Tenor in a sesquialtera proportion (that is, they relate as 2 to 3), nevertheless this should by no means be called a sesquialtera proportion for that reason. This is because the two notes of the Bass occupy exactly the same amount of time; indeed, the two are exactly equivalent to the three. Instead, they are to be referred to the "time of the proportion of equality" and to the "multiple proportion"—namely, to the **triple proportion**, as was said a little while ago.

Therefore, when mention is made of sesquialtera proportion, there is a transition from <term>imperfect time</term><note>Duple meter, where notes are grouped in twos.</note> to <term>perfect time</term><note>Triple meter, where notes are grouped in threes.</note>, or from a multiple proportion to a particular proportion. Proportions of different times are mixed so that one voice holds the measure of perfect time and another the measure of imperfect time. Or, what is the same thing, while two or more voices sing two semibreves, another voice sings three semibreves; thus, two are sounded against three. In other words, the <term>tactus</term><note>The basic pulse or beat directed by the hand.</note> or measure of one voice relates to the others as 2 to 3, while each voice produces two different proportions of performance at one and the same time. This is what the more technical musicians <note>original: "Musicidensationes" – likely meaning those who study the "density" or complexity of musical theory.</note> call "singing sign against sign." I shall clarify the matter with an example.

<meta>This page continues Father Athanasius Kircher’s critique of musical notation and terminology. Having just established that "hemiola" and "sesquialtera" are essentially the same 3:2 ratio, he now explains why they were historically distinguished by the color of the notes and argues for a simpler, more mathematical approach to rhythm.</meta>

682 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance.

<margin>What the hemiola proportion is.</margin>

...it happened suddenly <note>original: "repente"</note> that musicians ignorant of the Greek language established some difference between the **hemiola** and the **sesquialtera**.

There are, however, two types of hemiola: the major and the minor. If you look at the time, they are exactly equal; if you look at the notes, they differ, as is clear in the examples. As for why the **Hemiola** is for the most part represented by black notes, the reason is this: since in those times the sesquialtera proportion did not yet have the signs by which it could be distinguished from <term>imperfect time</term><note>Also known as "common time" or duple meter, indicated in early notation by a broken circle.</note>, they displayed all the notes of the sesquialtera proportion in a black color without any preceding sign or number, so that the distinction of the time would be indicated by the color. 

But later, as music became more illustrious through a variety of signs, they distinguished the difference in time for the sesquialtera proportion using notes without the black color, prefixing them with the number $\frac{3}{2}$ <note>The mathematical symbol for the sesquialtera ratio, where 3 notes are played in the space of 2.</note> proper to that proportion; and posterity then applied this to the hemiola as well. Others imagine I know not what "mysteries" or what indications of "affects" in those black notes of the hemiola. But let us leave everyone to their own fantasies. Our task is to show the errors creeping in through the passage of time, so that musicians may discern from this discourse of ours what should truly be established. 

Just as the sesquialtera proportion is familiar to music, so too would the <term>sesquitertia</term><note>A ratio of 4:3.</note>, <term>sesquiquarta</term><note>A ratio of 5:4.</note>, and <term>sesquisexta</term><note>A ratio of 7:6.</note> have some use in music, were it not for the difficulty of performing such proportions. For the further removed the proportions are from the sesquialtera, the more difficult they become to perform; wherefore modern musicians have prudently rejected all other proportions and retained only the sesquialtera along with the multiples. Indeed, if the sesquialtera is properly instituted, it acquires great grace in music, as is clear in the following little diagram, in which you see that 6 <term>semiminims</term><note>A note value in early music roughly equivalent to a modern quarter or eighth note, depending on the context.</note> are always sung in place of 4 of the same in an equal beat of imperfect time. Thus, the speed of the delivery relative to the beat is sesquialtera, a style that is both charming and elegant. But the example will explain our meaning more fully; see also the many examples of this kind arranged under the <term>sesquioctava</term><note>A 9:8 ratio.</note> and sesquialtera in Book 6, pages 482 and 483. For this time of the sesquialtera proportion demonstrates a certain energy and emphasis, and exhibits a physical motion exactly proportioned.

### Example of the sesquialtera proportion.

[Three musical staves displaying mensural notation. The first staff includes the time signatures 3/2 and 6/4, and the following staves are marked 6/4.]

When I considered this most confusing matter more deeply, I was greatly amazed that the Ancients wasted so much effort and time on a thing entirely useless—indeed, even futile—and wished to entangle minds in such a confusion of things, when this entire jumble <note>original: "farrago"</note> could have been resolved in a much more efficient way (which posterity later sensed), that is, through the mere placement of a "3" or a "2." For since all musical deliveries can be reduced to only two species of time—that is, to the binary and the ternary—as we have demonstrated from mathematical foundations in Book IV, it is in vain to do through many things what can be done through...

<meta>This page continues Kircher’s argument for simplifying musical notation. He previously discussed how different colors were used to represent rhythmic proportions; here, he argues that many ancient signs for tempo are now redundant thanks to the invention of modern note values like eighth and sixteenth notes.</meta>

Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-making. 683

Whatever can be done with fewer means is better. I shall demonstrate this through the following introduction. First, regarding <term>imperfect time</term><note>Also known as duple or binary meter.</note> or binary number, the ancients denoted an equal and unchangeable time with the sign **C**; this remains in use today. However, when they intended to indicate a changeable time, they placed certain signs before the voices, as seen in <margin>No. 8. [musical symbol]</margin> number 8. By this, they indicated that the voices must be performed twice as fast, as has been said. Since they did not yet possess **minims**, **semiminims**, **fusae**, or **semifusae** <note>These correspond to modern half, quarter, eighth, and sixteenth notes. In Kircher's time, these "shorter" notes were relatively recent inventions.</note>, nor did they know how they might multiply the value of the **maxima**, **long**, **breve**, and **semibreve** notes, they chose this sign (as in no. 8) to make the stated notes twice as fast. If they wanted them <margin>No. 9. 10. [two musical symbols]</margin> four times faster, they used the sign in no. 9; if eight times faster, they used the sign in the margin, as in numbers 9 and 10. However, since in our time there is a great variety of notes, and **fusae**, **semifusae**, and **chromae** have been added—by which the speed of time is displayed beautifully and most exactly—I do not see why the method of the ancients should be clung to any longer. This is especially true since these ancient signs hinder the <term>phonascus</term><note>original: "phonascos"; refers to a singing master, composer, or conductor.</note> to no small degree, requiring the utmost diligence and attention from him to pronounce the very same notes with such diverse deliveries. They might be excused, however, for using this method, as no other was available before the invention of the minim, semiminim, fusa, and semifusa notes. But in the delivery of <term>perfect time</term><note>Triple or ternary meter.</note>, or the ternary and <term>sesquialtera</term> proportions, no less confusion is seen. For by placing a number 3, or a 3 over a 2, before all the mentioned signs, they distinguished one delivery from another beautifully indeed; yet they assigned no difference in the actual duration of the time.

But I shall place the whole matter before your eyes with musical examples; here are the following clauses, which are indeed marked by different signs and numbers, but which alter nothing at all in the duration of time.

Example I. II. III. IV.
[Musical notation for examples I, II, III, and IV]

V. VI.
[Musical notation for examples V and VI] <margin>The reader should know that the breve notes designated in this last example, no. 2 and 3, ought to be long notes.</margin>

All these clauses are assigned through different signs, as was shown at length in the preceding pages; but if we examine the duration of time exactly, we shall see that they admit no difference at all regarding time. For the same duration of time is fulfilled in all of them, as is known to <term>musical philosophers</term><note>original: "philosophis musicis"; refers to music theorists who study the mathematical and physical laws of sound.</note>, and all can be reduced to Example IV, V, or II.

### On the various Rests by which perfect time was formerly noted.

Among all the musical figures, only the **maxima** <note>The longest note value in medieval and Renaissance music.</note> does not have its own specific rest. Therefore, when we called it a rest above on page 472, you should know that this was done improperly. Although the **maxima** does not have its own rest, its value is nevertheless measured by the rests of the **longa**, as the most skilled Pietro Francesco Valentini learnedly showed in a certain work written on this subject. The **longa** has two types of rests: that is, the rest of the **imperfect long**, which occupies two spaces within the <term>pentagram</term><note>The five-line musical staff.</note> as seen above in no. 1; this is used when the song is not in <term>lesser perfect mode</term>—that is, meanwhile, while the **longa** is imperfect...

[Musical notation with numbers 1 through 8 below various segments]

...having the value of two <term>breves</term><note>A "breve" was a standard note value, originally meaning "short," though in modern notation it is a double whole note.</note>, which are indicated by the two spaces that the rest occupies, just as if they were two breve rest notes. If, however, the other rest is a <term>perfect long</term><note>In this system, "perfect" means the note is divided into three parts (triple meter), whereas "imperfect" means it is divided into two (duple meter).</note> rest, it will occupy three spaces as you see in number 2. This is used when the song is in the <term>minor perfect mode</term>, and also when the song is in both the <term>major perfect mode</term> and minor perfect mode. This occurs when a <term>long</term> is perfect, with the value of three breves, indicated by the three spaces that the rest occupies on the staff. 

Thus, if the song is in the <term>imperfect</term> major and minor modes—specifically under the sign **C**, where the figures are without perfection—one <term>maxima</term> is equivalent to two longs. Then, the value of the maxima is measured by two rests of an imperfect long, as you see above in number 3. If, however, the imperfect long is under the major perfect and minor imperfect mode—that is, if the value of one perfect maxima is equivalent to three imperfect longs—then the maxima will be measured by three rests of an imperfect long, as appears in number 4. 

If the composition is under the major perfect and minor perfect mode—that is, the value of one perfect maxima is equivalent to three perfect longs—then the maxima will be measured by three perfect longs, as appears in number 5. Finally, if the composition is under the major imperfect and minor perfect mode—that is, when one imperfect maxima is equivalent to two perfect longs—then the maxima will be measured by two rests of a perfect long, as appears in number 6. Under this sign [slashed C] as in number 7, or in <term>perfect time</term>, three breves will equal one maxima. If it is in <term>imperfect time</term>, as in number 8, the rest will be equivalent to two <term>semibreves</term>. It seemed appropriate to specify all these things in this place, lest we should seem to have omitted anything in the business of music that might cause doubt.

And having treated these matters perhaps more extensively than was necessary, nothing remains except to put forward our opinion on this musical <term>prolation</term><note>original: "prolatione"; this refers to the rhythmic relationship between different levels of note values.</note>. Although we cannot deny that the ancients—at a time when they had no knowledge of musical signs and notes—were forced by necessity to devise such a jumbled heap of signs (not without ingenuity) so that they might help themselves in any way possible with rhythmic delivery. But since in this time music has made the greatest progress toward perfection, I do not see why the signs and notes of the ancients must be so stubbornly insisted upon, since they produce the greatest confusion and contribute nothing of great importance to the matter.

<margin>* 8 [musical notation symbol]</margin>
Whence certain distinguished musicians of this time reduce all types of rhythmic delivery to ternary <note>triple meter</note> and binary <note>duple meter</note>, retaining only the signs **C** and **[slashed C]**; see number 8 in the margin. Although these signs differ among the ancients, as has been said—because it was stated above that the latter sign [slashed C] should be performed twice as fast as notes marked by the **C**—in our time, this velocity is compensated for by the speed of our notes, such as <term>minims</term>, <term>semiminims</term>, <term>fusae</term>, and <term>semifusae</term><note>These correspond to our modern half, quarter, eighth, and sixteenth notes. Kircher argues that instead of changing the time signature to go faster, we should just use shorter note values.</note>. Hence, we judge it superfluous to use those ancient signs. Indeed, I have found that many of the most excellent musicians and those most skilled in theory have deliberately omitted them at this time, and have accepted a single sign everywhere.

We do not say these things to disparage the praiseworthy invention of the ancients or to call musicians away from studying them; rather, for all those whose intention it is to acquire a greater knowledge of this profession, we judge this doctrine of rhythmic delivery and time to be necessary, lest by putting one for another they be accused of ignorance by others. Therefore, so that the Republic of Music might be liberated from such great confusion, it would be the task of musicians to enter upon a new method and find new signs, by which all those things that were said so extensively and confusedly by the ancients might be reduced to a concise form. Thus, music might be restored to its perfection through small notes. I have provided this in a special treatise; if I find that this new institution does not displease musicians, I promise I will perhaps commit it to the light <note>i.e., publish it</note> on another occasion. And these are the things which I thought should be said concerning musical time.

Book VII. On Ancient-Modern Music-making, etc. 685

### Epilogue on Royal Music.

Before we conclude this book, it seemed appropriate to insert "Royal Music" here. I call it Royal Music because it was composed by Kings; so that the world may know that for Kings, whenever they are free from public cares, there is no study more powerful for relaxing the mind than music. I shall place in the first position that most beautiful Imperial <term>melothesia</term><note>From the Greek, meaning the art of musical composition or the setting of words to melody.</note> regarding the vanity of the world, composed by the Most August Emperor Ferdinand III<note>Ferdinand III (1608–1657) was the Holy Roman Emperor and a noted patron of the arts and a competent composer himself. Kircher frequently dedicated works to him.</note>. Just as he holds primacy in the political world by right, so too he appears to have no equal among those of his rank, whether you consider his variety of sciences, his skill in languages, or his knowledge of more profound music. Indeed, the wondrous emphasis of the hidden harmony will more truly proclaim the admirable character and incredible talents of a truly Imperial soul than I could describe with many words.

I understand also that the **Catholic King** <note>original: "Catholicum Regem." This title refers to the King of Spain, at this time Philip IV.</note> with truly great genius composed certain Litanies; because I have not yet been able to obtain them due to the pressing urgency of completing this work, I have been forced to omit them, even against my will.

**Louis XIII, Most Christian King** <note>The traditional title for the Kings of France.</note> of France; how much he valued this royal study of music, he demonstrated sufficiently with the following song; which it pleased me to insert opportunely in this place; so that this greatest King might both adorn this musical work with this notable song—a melody <term>melisma: a decorative musical phrase or song</term> most worthy of his Royal genius—and also place upon it the final finishing touch <note>original: "colophonem." ->**The Melody of Louis XIII, Most Christian King.**<-

[Musical score for four voices with diamond-shaped notes. The lyrics read: "You believe, oh beautiful sun"] <note>original French: "Tu crois ô beau soleil." This is an "air de cour" (courtly song) titled "Amante injuste et cruelle," traditionally attributed to the King himself.</note>

And these are the things which we thought should be said concerning the differences between ancient and modern music, and concerning the method of correctly establishing **pathetic music** <term>musica pathetica: music designed specifically to move the "passions" or emotions of the listener</term>.

In this work, whatever is perfect, I would wish you, Reader, to ascribe to God, the giver of all good things; whatever is defective, I would wish you to ascribe to me. Nothing therefore remains, except that, having finished the first volume of the *Universal Work on Music* <note>original: "Musurgiæ vniuersalis"</note>, we turn our pen to treating the curious matters of the second volume.
